name: Aileen Wuornos
victimProfile: Middle-aged men aged 40 to 65 who picked her up while she hitchhiked or solicited along Florida highways
captureMethod: Witnesses to a July 1990 crash in a victim's car described two women; pawned victims' property and a fingerprint tied to one alias led police to arrest her on an outstanding weapons warrant at a Volusia County bar.
sentence: Six death sentences (one jury verdict, 1992; five guilty or no-contest pleas, 1992 to 1993), plus 10-, 40-, 40- and 17-year terms for armed robbery
fateDetail: Lethal injection, Florida State Prison near Starke, October 9, 2002
summary: Executed by Florida in 2002. Aileen Wuornos shot seven men along Florida highways in 1989 and 1990; a jury convicted her of the Richard Mallory murder and she pleaded guilty or no contest to five more, receiving six death sentences.
narrative: Aileen Carol Wuornos shot and killed seven men along the highways of central and north Florida between November 1989 and November 1990. According to the Florida Commission on Capital Cases, a Volusia County jury convicted her of the first-degree murder of Richard Mallory in January 1992, and she then pleaded no contest or guilty to five further murders in Marion, Citrus, Dixie and Pasco counties, for six death sentences in all. She also confessed to killing a seventh man, Peter Siems, whose body was never found; no charge was brought in that case. Wuornos said she shot the men in self-defence after they attacked her. The courts rejected that account, and Florida executed her on October 9, 2002.

Mallory, 51, a Clearwater electronics store owner, was last seen on November 30, 1989; his body was found in Volusia County on December 13, shot with a .22-caliber pistol. Over the following year the bodies of David Spears (Citrus County, June 1, 1990), Charles Carskaddon (Pasco County, June 6), Troy Burress (Marion County, August 4), Charles "Dick" Humphreys (Marion County, September 12) and Walter Gino Antonio (Dixie County, November 19) were found near roads, each shot several times, their wallets and vehicles missing. Siems' car was found wrecked near Orange Springs on July 4, 1990.

Witnesses to the crash described two women leaving the car. According to Wikipedia's summary of the investigation, victims' belongings surfaced in pawnshops and a fingerprint on a receipt signed under an alias was matched to prints on file for Wuornos. On January 9, 1991, officers arrested her at The Last Resort bar in Volusia County on an outstanding concealed-weapon warrant under the name Lori Grody. Her companion, Tyria Moore, agreed to cooperate, and on January 16 Wuornos confessed, saying each man had tried to rape or assault her.

A Volusia County grand jury indicted Wuornos on January 28, 1991, according to her later postconviction brief. At trial from January 13 to 27, 1992, the state was allowed under Florida's Williams rule to present evidence of the other killings. The jury found her guilty and recommended death 12 to 0; on January 31, 1992, she was sentenced to death plus 10 years for armed robbery. The Florida Supreme Court affirmed on September 22, 1994, and the U.S. Supreme Court denied review in April 1995.

On March 31, 1992, Wuornos pleaded no contest to the murders of Humphreys, Burress and Spears. In Wuornos v. State, 644 So. 2d 1012 (Fla. 1994), the Florida Supreme Court recorded that she continued to assert self-defence at the plea colloquy and that her confessions "differed in substantial ways"; it upheld the pleas and the three death sentences imposed on May 15, 1992. She pleaded guilty in Dixie County to the Antonio murder and was sentenced to death on February 4, 1993; the Pasco County court imposed a sixth death sentence for Carskaddon the next day after she waived a penalty hearing.

Her postconviction lawyers argued that trial counsel should have uncovered Mallory's Maryland record, which the brief says included a 1958 plea to assault with intent to rape. The circuit court denied relief in 2000. In April 2001 Wuornos asked the Florida Supreme Court to dismiss her lawyers and end her appeals; a judge found her competent on July 20, 2001, and the court dismissed the appeals on April 1, 2002. ABC News reported that in a 2001 interview she said she needed to die for the killings, and Knight Ridder noted she had withdrawn the self-defence claim.

Governor Jeb Bush signed a death warrant on September 5, 2002. According to Capital Punishment in Context, he granted a brief stay on September 30 for a psychiatric examination, and three state-appointed psychiatrists found her competent. Wuornos was pronounced dead by lethal injection at 9:47 a.m. on October 9, 2002, at Florida State Prison near Starke, the second woman executed by Florida since 1976.

Wuornos was born Aileen Carol Pittman on February 29, 1956, in Rochester, Michigan, and was raised by her grandparents. According to Wikipedia and witnesses at her postconviction hearing, she described an abusive childhood and gave birth at 15. Her record before 1989 included a 1982 armed robbery sentence.

name: Alan Wade Wilmer Sr.
victimProfile: Young adults and one 14-year-old, mostly couples, killed or abducted near the Colonial Parkway and the James and York rivers, plus a 29-year-old woman in Hampton
captureMethod: Never arrested; named by state police and the FBI after his death, when DNA obtained posthumously matched crime-scene evidence
fateDetail: Died in December 2017 at his home in Lancaster County, Virginia, aged 63, years before he was publicly named
summary: Suspected, never charged. Fisherman Alan Wade Wilmer Sr., who died in 2017, has been named by the FBI and Virginia State Police as responsible for six of the eight Colonial Parkway victims of 1986 to 1989, plus a 1989 Hampton killing. One couple's case remains unsolved.
narrative: The Colonial Parkway murders are a series of killings and disappearances of young people in eastern Virginia between 1986 and 1989, centred on the Colonial Parkway between Jamestown and Yorktown and nearby stretches of the James and York rivers. Four couples, eight people in all, were killed or went missing. Since 2024, investigators have publicly named Alan Wade Wilmer Sr., a Lancaster County fisherman who died in 2017 at age 63, as the person responsible for most of these cases. He was never charged with any of them and his guilt was never tested in court; prosecutors and federal officials have said only that charges would have been brought had he lived. The killings of one couple, Annamaria Phelps and Daniel Lauer, remain officially unsolved.

The first case began on October 9, 1986, when Cathleen Thomas, 27, and Rebecca Dowski, 21, were last seen together at a computer lab at the College of William and Mary in Williamsburg. Their bodies were later found in their car along the Colonial Parkway. Fox News reported that both women had been stabbed and strangled. Almost a year later, in September 1987, David Knobling, 20, and Robin Edwards, 14, were found shot along the James River shoreline in Isle of Wight County; officials have said Edwards was sexually assaulted.

In April 1988, Keith Call, 20, and Cassandra Hailey, 18, both students at Christopher Newport University, left a party in Newport News and were never seen again. Call's car was found abandoned later that day near the York River Overlook on the parkway, and the couple's remains have never been found. The last case began on the night of September 4, 1989, when Phelps, 18, and Lauer, 21, left Amelia County for Virginia Beach. According to the Virginia State Police case file, Lauer's car was found the next afternoon at a westbound Interstate 64 rest area in New Kent County, and hunters found the couple's remains in woods about three miles east of the rest area on October 19, 1989.

For decades the cases were grouped together on the strength of their similarities: couples, isolated roadside locations and abandoned vehicles. Investigators were careful, however, not to treat them as a proven single series. As recently as January 2024, Virginia State Police said the similarities could not be ignored but that there was no forensic or physical evidence tying the Isle of Wight killings to the other double murders.

The first public break came on January 8, 2024, when state police and the FBI's Norfolk office named Wilmer as the suspect in the Knobling and Edwards killings and in the July 1989 death of Teresa Lynn Spaw Howell, 29, in Hampton, a case that is not one of the four couples. NBC News reported that Wilmer had no felony record, so his DNA was not in the national offender database; after he emerged in a review of the cold cases, investigators legally obtained his genetic material after his death, and it matched evidence from the crime scenes in June 2023. Prosecutors in Isle of Wight County and Hampton said charges would have been filed if he were alive. NBC News described him as a clam and oyster farmer who ran a tree service, kept a wooden fishing boat named the Denni Wade and died at his Lancaster County home in December 2017.

In January 2026 the FBI's Norfolk Field Office said advances in forensic science and DNA analysis had linked Wilmer to the deaths of Thomas and Dowski, and that it considered him responsible for at least six of the killings and disappearances between 1986 and 1989. The U.S. Attorney's Office for the Eastern District of Virginia said the evidence would have supported a federal prosecution had he lived. On September 18, 2026, WTVR reported, the FBI also attributed the disappearances of Call and Hailey to Wilmer. That finding rests on circumstantial evidence and similarities in timing, location and the way the couple vanished; the FBI acknowledged that direct forensic evidence from the scene is unavailable, and Call's brother publicly questioned it.

With those announcements, authorities attribute six of the eight Colonial Parkway victims, plus Howell, to Wilmer, a total of seven. None of these attributions has been tested at trial. Relatives of the victims have pressed for changes in the law so that the DNA of people who were never convicted, such as Wilmer, can be compared against other unsolved cases. Thomas's brother has said he believes the true number of victims is higher than eight. The Wikipedia article on the case also discusses other killings that some investigators have suggested may be connected, but the authorities have not tied them to Wilmer. The Phelps and Lauer case remains open with the Virginia State Police.

name: Albert DeSalvo

victims.suspected: 1 to 13

victimProfile: Women aged 19 to 85, most living alone, sexually assaulted and strangled in their own apartments in Boston and nearby cities
captureMethod: Identified by police in late 1964 from a sexual assault victim's description in an East Cambridge case; he later confessed to the stranglings while held at Bridgewater State Hospital
sentence: Life imprisonment (January 18, 1967) for unrelated armed robbery and sexual assault offenses; never charged with any of the stranglings
fateDetail: Stabbed to death by a fellow inmate at Walpole State Prison, Massachusetts, in November 1973; no one was ever convicted of his killing
summary: Killed. Albert DeSalvo confessed to the 13 Boston Strangler murders of 1962 to 1964 but was never tried for them. Serving life for unrelated assaults and robberies, he was stabbed to death at Walpole prison in 1973. 2013 DNA tied him to one victim, Mary Sullivan.
narrative: Albert DeSalvo was a Massachusetts laborer and Army veteran who confessed to the 13 killings attributed to the Boston Strangler, a series of sexual assaults and strangulations of women in Boston, Cambridge, Lynn, Lawrence and Salem between June 1962 and January 1964. He was never charged with or tried for any of the murders. Instead, he was convicted on January 18, 1967, of unrelated armed robbery and sexual assault offenses and sentenced to life in prison. In November 1973 he was stabbed to death at Walpole State Prison. In 2013, DNA evidence linked him to the last of the killings, the murder of 19-year-old Mary Sullivan, but whether he committed the other 12 remains disputed.

The murders began on June 14, 1962, and ended on January 4, 1964, when Sullivan was found raped and murdered in her apartment on Charles Street in Boston. According to CBS Boston, the women were aged 19 to 85. Authorities at the time attributed 11 of the deaths to the Strangler, CBS Boston reported in 2013; DeSalvo's confession covered those 11 and two more. According to Associated Press reporting in 2017, investigators compiled lists of more than 300 suspects, and DeSalvo was never on them.

DeSalvo came to the attention of police through a different series of crimes. In late 1964, Boston-area police were investigating sexual assaults by an intruder known as the Green Man or the Measuring Man. According to the Wikipedia article, an East Cambridge woman assaulted on October 27, 1964, by a man posing as a detective gave a description that led police to DeSalvo, and after his photograph was published many women identified him as their attacker. He was sent to Bridgewater State Hospital, the state facility for the criminally insane, for evaluation.

At Bridgewater in 1965, DeSalvo described the Strangler killings to a fellow patient, George Nassar, whose attorney, F. Lee Bailey, then took on DeSalvo's case. According to the Wikipedia article, DeSalvo then gave detailed confessions to Assistant Attorney General John Bottomly. CBS News reported in 2001 that because the confession was made while he was a mental patient it could not be used against him, and CBS Boston reported in 2013 that it had been ruled inadmissible. With no hard evidence connecting him to the murders, prosecutors tried him only on the Green Man assaults and robberies. After a January 1967 trial he was convicted and sentenced to life. According to the Wikipedia article, in February 1967 he escaped from Bridgewater with two other inmates and surrendered through his lawyer three days later, after which he was moved to the maximum-security prison at Walpole.

At Walpole, DeSalvo recanted his confession. He was found stabbed to death in the prison in November 1973; the Wikipedia article gives the date as November 25 and says a trial of an inmate for the killing ended in a hung jury. CBS Boston reported in 2018 that no one was ever convicted of his death.

Doubts about the confession are a substantial part of the record. The author Susan Kelly, who believes DeSalvo fabricated his account, and the former FBI profiler Robert Ressler both doubted that one person committed all the murders, CBS News reported in 2001; Kelly believes several killers were involved. Sullivan's family, including her nephew Casey Sherman, argued in 2003 that DeSalvo's account did not fit her death: he said he strangled her with his hands, while she was strangled with ligatures, and DNA found on her body after a 2001 exhumation did not match him, CBS News reported. Associated Press reporting in 2017 added that he did not match witness descriptions. Nassar has also been named as a possible suspect, which he denies; in a 2018 interview with CBS Boston he said he had no doubt DeSalvo was the Strangler.

In July 2013, the Boston Police Department and Suffolk County District Attorney Daniel Conley announced that a Y-chromosome profile from a water bottle used by a DeSalvo nephew was a familial match to semen preserved from the Sullivan scene. DeSalvo's remains were exhumed, and according to the National Institute of Justice, DNA from his femur and teeth matched, leaving no doubt that he raped and murdered Sullivan. Officials stressed that no DNA was known to exist for the other killings, so his responsibility for the remaining 12 deaths rests on his recanted confession.

name: Albert Fish

victims.suspected: 5 to 15 (contemporary police and psychiatric estimates); he claimed about 100, unverified

victimProfile: Children aged 4 to 10 in the New York City area
captureMethod: The association emblem on the envelope of an anonymous letter he mailed to the Budd family in November 1934 was traced to a Manhattan rooming house, where Detective William F. King arrested him.
sentence: Death (first-degree murder, Westchester County, March 1935); appeal and clemency plea failed
fateDetail: Electric chair, Sing Sing Prison, Ossining, New York, January 16, 1936
summary: Executed at Sing Sing in 1936. Albert Fish was convicted in 1935 of the 1928 murder of 10-year-old Grace Budd in New York after a letter he sent her family was traced to him; he also confessed to two earlier child killings.
narrative: Albert Fish, born Hamilton Howard Fish, was a New York house painter convicted by a Westchester County jury in March 1935 of the first-degree murder of 10-year-old Grace Budd in 1928 and executed at Sing Sing Prison on January 16, 1936. Courts convicted him of one murder. According to the Wikipedia article and the EBSCO Research Starters entry, he confessed to three child killings in New York that police could trace: Francis McDonnell on Staten Island in 1924, Billy Gaffney in Brooklyn in 1927 and Grace Budd in 1928. Contemporary police and psychiatric estimates attributed roughly five to fifteen deaths to him, and he made far larger, unverified claims.

The first traced killing took place in July 1924, when 8-year-old Francis McDonnell disappeared from Port Richmond on Staten Island and was found strangled in nearby woods. Witnesses described an older grey-haired man seen in the area that day, and according to Wikipedia Fish admitted the killing in March 1935, after his conviction in the Budd case. On February 11, 1927, 4-year-old Billy Gaffney disappeared from a Brooklyn apartment building; his body was never found. A trolley motorman later identified Fish from a newspaper photograph as the man seen with a crying boy that day, and Fish described the killing in a letter to his attorney.

On May 28, 1928, Fish answered a classified advertisement placed by 18-year-old Edward Budd of Manhattan, who was seeking farm work. Calling himself Frank Howard and posing as a farmer, he visited the family twice, and on June 3, 1928, according to the Great American Trials account on Encyclopedia.com, he obtained the parents' permission to take Grace to a children's party. She never returned. In 1930 a building superintendent, Charles Edward Pope, was arrested in the case and spent 108 days in jail before being acquitted.

The case went unsolved for six years. On November 11, 1934, the Budd family received an anonymous letter describing Grace's killing. Detective William F. King of the New York Police Department noticed that the envelope carried the emblem of the New York Private Chauffeur's Benevolent Association. A member said he had left some of its stationery at a rooming house on East 52nd Street in Manhattan, and the landlady there matched the handwriting to a recently departed lodger named Albert Fish. King waited at the rooming house and arrested Fish on December 13, 1934. Fish confessed to the Budd murder and led officers to Wisteria Cottage, an empty house in Irvington in Westchester County, where remains were recovered.

Fish was tried in White Plains before Judge Frederick P. Close from March 11 to March 22, 1935, with Elbert F. Gallagher prosecuting and James Dempsey defending. He did not deny the killing; the defense argued that he was insane. Psychiatrist Fredric Wertham testified for the defense that Fish was mentally irresponsible, while the prosecution's experts said he was abnormal but legally sane. On March 22, 1935, after about four hours of deliberation, the jury found him sane and guilty of first-degree murder, and he was sentenced to death. According to the EBSCO entry, an appeal and a plea to the governor both failed.

Fish was electrocuted at Sing Sing in Ossining, New York, on the evening of January 16, 1936, at the age of 65. His claims of victims in many states and of about 100 children harmed were never substantiated; Wikipedia notes it is unclear what he was counting. Police also considered him a suspect in several other unsolved child deaths in the New York area between 1926 and 1932, none of which resulted in charges.

Fish was born in Washington, D.C., on May 19, 1870. His father died in 1875, and he was placed in St. John's Orphanage, where he was frequently beaten; his family had a history of mental illness. He moved to New York City around 1890, married Anna Mary Hoffman in 1898 and had six children; she left him in 1917. By the time of his arrest he had served a prison term for embezzlement and had twice been held in mental hospitals, mainly over obscene letters sent to women.

name: Alfredo Prieto
victimProfile: Young couples and women in Northern Virginia and Southern California, among them two George Washington University students and a 15-year-old girl kidnapped in a robbery
captureMethod: Arrested at his residence in California after the September 1990 Ontario kidnapping and murder; a 2005 DNA database match later tied him to the 1988 Reston killings
sentence: Death in California (1992) for the murder of Yvette Woodruff; two death sentences in Virginia for the capital murders of Rachael Raver and Warren Fulton III, finally imposed on December 16, 2010
fateDetail: Lethal injection (pentobarbital) at Greensville Correctional Center, Jarratt, Virginia; pronounced dead at 9:17 p.m. on October 1, 2015
summary: Executed. Alfredo Prieto was sentenced to death in California for the 1990 murder of a 15-year-old girl and in Virginia for the 1988 killings of two George Washington University students in Reston. Virginia executed him in October 2015.
narrative: Alfredo Rolando Prieto was a Salvadoran-born man convicted of three murders: the December 1988 shooting deaths of Rachael Raver and Warren Fulton III, both 22, near Reston, Virginia, and the September 1990 killing of 15-year-old Yvette Woodruff in Ontario, California. He was sentenced to death in both states. After 14 years on California's death row he was extradited to Fairfax County, Virginia, where he was tried for the Reston killings, and he was executed by lethal injection at Greensville Correctional Center on October 1, 2015. DNA evidence linked him to further killings for which he was never tried, and the Wikipedia article puts the total number of victims at nine.

Prieto was born on November 18, 1965, in El Salvador, and according to the Wikipedia article his family moved to Pomona, California, in 1981. The article says he served a prison term for a 1984 shooting in Ontario in which the victims survived, and the California Supreme Court opinion in his case also refers to that shooting. After his release he lived for a time in Arlington, Virginia, before returning to California in 1990.

Raver, a 1988 George Washington University graduate and former Division I soccer player, and Fulton, a GW senior and baseball captain, were last seen on December 3, 1988, after leaving a bar in Washington, D.C., after midnight, The GW Hatchet reported. Their bodies were found on December 6 in a vacant lot off Hunter Mill Road near Reston. Both had been shot, and Raver had been raped. The case remained unsolved for 17 years.

On September 2, 1990, in Ontario, California, Prieto and several accomplices robbed and kidnapped a group that included a woman, her 17-year-old daughter and the daughter's 15-year-old friend, Yvette Woodruff, according to the California Supreme Court and the California Department of Corrections and Rehabilitation. The three were raped; the mother and daughter were stabbed and survived, and Woodruff was shot in the head at close range. Prieto was arrested at his residence on September 6, 1990. A San Bernardino County jury convicted him of first-degree murder with special circumstances on January 21, 1992, and returned a death verdict that March. The California Supreme Court affirmed the death judgment on April 21, 2003.

After California began requiring DNA samples from convicted inmates, Prieto's profile entered the national database, and in 2005 DNA evidence from the Reston case was matched to him. A Fairfax County grand jury indicted him that year and he was extradited to Virginia on April 28, 2006. A jury convicted him of capital murder in June 2007, but the penalty phase ended in a mistrial. A 2008 retrial produced convictions and two death sentences, which the Supreme Court of Virginia set aside because of an unclear verdict form. A new sentencing jury recommended death on November 5, 2010, after rejecting his claim of intellectual disability, and Judge Randy Bellows imposed the sentences on December 16, 2010. The Supreme Court of Virginia affirmed them in January 2012.

DNA also linked Prieto to the 1988 rape and murder of Veronica Jefferson, 24, in Arlington. He was indicted in that case, but prosecutors later dismissed the charge, saying a further death sentence was not worth the expense, NBC Washington reported. He was also linked to the 1989 shooting death of Manuel Sermeno, 27, in Prince William County. The Wikipedia article further attributes to him the May 1990 killings of Stacey Siegrist and Anthony Gianuzzi in Rubidoux, California, and the June 1990 killings of Lula Mae and Herbert Farley; he was never prosecuted for any of these deaths.

Virginia scheduled his execution for October 1, 2015. His lawyers challenged the state's use of pentobarbital obtained from the Texas prison system after its supply of midazolam expired, and a federal judge briefly blocked the execution before the order was lifted, Reston Now reported. Gov. Terry McAuliffe declined to intervene and the U.S. Supreme Court refused a stay. Prieto, 49, was pronounced dead at 9:17 p.m. It was Virginia's first execution in three years.

name: Amy Archer-Gilligan

victims.suspected: 5 to 24

victimProfile: Elderly residents of the Archer Home for aged people in Windsor, Connecticut, and her second husband, Michael Gilligan
captureMethod: A resident's sister took her suspicions to the Hartford Courant, whose 1916 reporting on the home was followed by a police investigation, exhumations and evidence of arsenic purchases
sentence: Death by hanging for the first-degree murder of Franklin R. Andrews (1917), set aside by the Connecticut Supreme Court of Errors in 1918; life imprisonment for second-degree murder at the 1919 retrial
fateDetail: Transferred from the state prison at Wethersfield to the Connecticut State Hospital (now Connecticut Valley Hospital), Middletown, in 1924 after being declared insane; died there in 1962 while still committed
summary: Died (other). Amy Archer-Gilligan, who ran a home for elderly people in Windsor, Connecticut, was convicted of poisoning resident Franklin Andrews with arsenic in 1914. Sentenced to life in 1919, she was moved to a state psychiatric hospital and died there in 1962.
narrative: Amy Archer-Gilligan was the operator of a home for elderly and infirm people in Windsor, Connecticut, who was convicted of murdering one of its residents, Franklin R. Andrews, by arsenic poisoning in 1914. She was indicted on five counts of murder by poison, but was tried only on the Andrews count. A Hartford jury convicted her of first-degree murder in 1917 and she was sentenced to hang; after the Connecticut Supreme Court of Errors ordered a new trial, she was convicted of second-degree murder in 1919 and sentenced to life imprisonment. She was later moved from prison to the state psychiatric hospital in Middletown, where she died in 1962.

Born Amy Duggan in Milton, Connecticut, on October 31, 1873, according to the Wikipedia article, she married James Archer in the late 1890s. Around 1901 the couple became live-in caretakers for John Seymour, a Newington widower, and after his death in 1904 they continued taking in elderly boarders at the house. In 1907 they moved to Windsor and opened the Archer Home, which took paying residents. James Archer died in 1910; Connecticut History, a project of CT Humanities, records the cause as kidney failure. In 1913 Amy married Michael Gilligan, a widower, who died about three months later, in February 1914.

Deaths at the home were unusually frequent. Connecticut History reports that 60 residents died there between 1907 and 1916, 48 of them in the last five years. Andrews, a resident who appeared healthy and had been working outdoors, died after falling ill at the end of May 1914. His sister, Nellie Pierce, found papers showing he had given Archer-Gilligan money, including a 500 dollar loan. When the district attorney showed little interest, she went to the Hartford Courant, which on May 9, 1916, published the first of several articles calling the home a murder factory. A police investigation followed. According to the Wikipedia article, bodies were exhumed and local merchants testified that she had bought large quantities of arsenic, saying it was for rats.

The indictment charged five counts of first-degree murder by poison, four by arsenic and one by strychnine, according to the 1918 Connecticut Supreme Court opinion in State v. Gilligan. Prosecutors elected to proceed on the Andrews count alone. At trial in the Hartford County Superior Court in June 1917, the State introduced evidence that three other people connected with the home had died of arsenic poisoning in 1914: Michael Gilligan in February, a resident named Smith in April and a Mrs. Gowdy in December. The jury convicted her and she was sentenced to death. On April 30, 1918, the Supreme Court of Errors found that this evidence of other deaths had been wrongly admitted, because the State's other proof had already largely excluded accident or mistake, and ordered a new trial.

The second trial took place in 1919. Accounts of how it ended differ. Connecticut History says that in June 1919 she pleaded guilty to a reduced charge of second-degree murder; the Wikipedia article says she raised an insanity defense, that her daughter Mary testified about her morphine use, and that the jury again found her guilty. The Connecticut Supreme Court, in a 2015 opinion, describes the outcome as a conviction for second-degree murder. She received a life sentence and was held at the state prison in Wethersfield.

In 1924 she was reported to the governor as insane and transferred to the Connecticut State Hospital in Middletown, now Connecticut Valley Hospital, where she remained for about 38 years until her death on April 23, 1962. She never testified at either trial, Connecticut Public Radio reported in 2015. The number of people she killed has never been established. She was charged in five deaths and convicted in one; Connecticut History says arsenic was found in more than two dozen former residents, and author Ron Robillard told Connecticut Public Radio that the prosecutor of the day believed she had probably killed up to two dozen people.

The case is widely cited as an inspiration for the 1939 play Arsenic and Old Lace and the 1944 film adaptation. Her records remained in dispute decades after her death: when Robillard sought her hospital files, the Connecticut Supreme Court ruled on September 22, 2015, that her medical and dental records from the psychiatric hospital were exempt from disclosure under the state's psychiatrist-patient privilege.

Resident Franklin R. Andrews dies after falling ill following supper on May 29.

Tried in Hartford County Superior Court on the Andrews count; convicted of first-degree murder and sentenced to death.
Connecticut Supreme Court of Errors orders a new trial, ruling that evidence of other poisoning deaths was wrongly admitted.
At the retrial she is convicted of second-degree murder and sentenced to life imprisonment.
Declared insane and transferred from Wethersfield state prison to the state hospital in Middletown.
Dies at the Middletown state hospital, aged 88.
Connecticut Supreme Court rules her psychiatric hospital medical and dental records exempt from public disclosure.

name: Angel Maturino Resendiz
victimProfile: Men and women of all ages, most attacked in homes beside railroad tracks; several women were also sexually assaulted
captureMethod: Fingerprints at the Benton scene and DNA linking the Benton and Sirnic murders identified him; after an FBI Ten Most Wanted listing, his sister negotiated his surrender to a Texas Ranger at the El Paso border crossing.
sentence: Death (Harris County, Texas, May 2000) for the capital murder of Claudia Benton; affirmed by the Texas Court of Criminal Appeals in 2003
fateDetail: Lethal injection, Huntsville Unit, Texas, June 27, 2006
summary: Executed in Texas in 2006. Angel Maturino Resendiz, the Railroad Killer, was convicted of the 1998 murder of Dr. Claudia Benton near Houston, admitted 11 killings along rail lines in Texas, Florida, Kentucky and Illinois, and was linked by the FBI to at least 15.
narrative: Angel Maturino Resendiz, the Railroad Killer, long sought under the alias Rafael Resendez-Ramirez, was a Mexican national who rode freight trains and killed people in homes and along tracks in Texas, Florida, Kentucky and Illinois between 1997 and 1999; later confessions reached back to 1986. A Harris County, Texas jury convicted him of capital murder on May 18, 2000 for the killing of Dr. Claudia Benton, and he was sentenced to death. The Associated Press reported in July 2000 that he had told Florida detectives he killed 11 people in Florida, Texas, Illinois and Kentucky; the FBI linked him to at least 15 murders. Texas executed him on June 27, 2006.

The earliest documented killings were in Florida on March 23, 1997: Jesse Howell, 19, was beaten with a railroad air brake coupling near Belleview and Wendy Von Huben, 16, was strangled; her remains were found in July 2000 after Resendiz directed investigators to them, according to the Associated Press. In August 1997 Christopher Maier was killed beside tracks in Lexington, Kentucky, and his companion Holly Dunn survived a rape and beating. In October 1998 Leafie Mason, 87, was beaten to death in Hughes Springs, Texas. According to the Department of Justice Inspector General, Dr. Benton, a pediatric neurologist, was killed in her home in West University Place near Houston in December 1998; fingerprints at the scene and in her stolen Jeep matched Resendiz, and a warrant followed in January 1999.

In spring 1999 pastor Norman Sirnic and his wife Karen were beaten to death with a sledgehammer in Weimar, Texas; the Inspector General reported that DNA linked those murders to the Benton case, and the FBI formed a task force in Houston on June 8, 1999. The same review found that Border Patrol agents apprehended Resendiz near Santa Teresa, New Mexico on June 1, 1999 and returned him to Mexico the same day because no lookout appeared in the INS fingerprint system. He soon re-entered; the Texas Court of Criminal Appeals opinion records the June 1999 killings of Noemi Dominguez in Houston, Josephine Konvicka near Schulenburg, Texas, and George Morber and his daughter Carolyn Frederick in Gorham, Illinois.

The FBI placed him on its Ten Most Wanted list in June 1999. His sister contacted authorities, and on July 13, 1999 he crossed from Ciudad Juarez and surrendered to Texas Ranger Drew Carter and federal officers at the El Paso port of entry, according to the Inspector General and NBC News.

At trial the defense argued insanity; United Press International reported that a defense expert called him a paranoid schizophrenic, while FBI profiler Alan Brantley testified that he was an organized sexual serial killer, not a psychotic. The jury rejected the defense after about 11 hours and convicted him on May 18, 2000; the judge imposed death on the jury's answers to the special issues, and he reached death row on May 24, 2000. In May 2003 the Court of Criminal Appeals affirmed the conviction and sentence over two dissents.

He was never tried for any other killing. Wikipedia records that in September 2001 he admitted three earlier killings in the San Antonio area, two of them in 1986, and that he was suspected but not charged in deaths in Carl, Georgia (1998) and Colton, California (1997). His lawyers argued he was not competent to be executed because he believed he was half-man, half-angel and could not die, but a Houston judge found him competent on June 21, 2006, and Mexico's request for clemency was not granted. NBC News reported that the U.S. Supreme Court rejected final appeals and he was executed by lethal injection on June 27, 2006; in his last statement he said he deserved his punishment and asked the victims' families for forgiveness.

Resendiz was born August 1, 1959 in Izucar de Matamoros, Puebla, Mexico, per the birth certificate cited by the Inspector General (Texas prison records give 1960). Texas prison records list prior convictions in Florida for burglary, vehicle theft and aggravated assault, federal immigration and fraud offenses, and a New Mexico burglary. He was deported or returned to Mexico repeatedly and re-entered each time.

Noemi Dominguez killed in Houston and Josephine Konvicka killed in Fayette County, Texas.

name: Anthony Sowell
victimProfile: Black women aged 25 to 53 from Cleveland's Mount Pleasant neighborhood, many struggling with drug addiction
captureMethod: Police serving warrants on a rape complaint found bodies in his Imperial Avenue home; a passerby recognized him from news coverage two days later
sentence: Death on each of 11 aggravated murder counts (August 12, 2011); affirmed by the Ohio Supreme Court December 8, 2016
fateDetail: Franklin Medical Center, Columbus, Ohio, of a terminal illness while on death row
summary: Convicted by a Cuyahoga County jury in 2011 of 11 aggravated murders after the remains of 11 women were found at his Cleveland home in October 2009; sentenced to death, affirmed on appeal, died in state custody in February 2021.
narrative: Anthony Sowell, called the Cleveland Strangler in news coverage, was convicted by a Cuyahoga County, Ohio jury on July 22, 2011 of 11 counts of aggravated murder for the killings of 11 women whose remains were found at his home at 12205 Imperial Avenue in Cleveland in late 2009. The Ohio Supreme Court's 2016 opinion in State v. Sowell puts the killings in the two and a half years before October 2009. He was sentenced to death on August 12, 2011, the Ohio Supreme Court affirmed on December 8, 2016, and he died in state custody on February 8, 2021 without being executed.

The Ohio Supreme Court identified the victims as Crystal Dozier, Tishana Culver, Leshanda Long, Michelle Mason, Tonia Carmichael, Kim Yvette Smith, Amelda Hunter, Nancy Cobbs, Telacia Fortson, Janice Webb and Diane Turner. Wikipedia, citing Cleveland press reports, lists Dozier, 38, as the first to disappear in May 2007 and Turner, 48, as the last in September 2009. The court recorded that seven women died of ligature strangulation, that Culver's injuries were consistent with manual strangulation, and that the cause of death for Long, Smith and Turner was undetermined homicidal violence. Five survivors testified to a pattern of being lured with drugs, then assaulted and choked.

In December 2008, Gladys Wade reported that Sowell dragged her into his house and strangled her until she lost consciousness; she escaped and flagged down a cruiser. Sowell was arrested but released because the officer mislabeled the offense on the report. Newsweek reported that families of six victims later sued the City of Cleveland and shared a $1 million settlement with no admission of wrongdoing.

The case broke after Latundra Billups told police in September 2009 that Sowell had choked and raped her at his home. According to the Ohio Supreme Court, officers executed a search warrant on October 29, 2009; Sowell was not home, and two decomposed bodies were found on the third floor. Over the following days searchers found eight more bodies inside the house and in the backyard, and a skull in a bucket in the basement was identified as Long's. In all, police recovered ten bodies and one skull. Sowell was arrested on October 31, 2009 after a member of the public recognized him from news broadcasts on Mount Auburn Avenue. In recorded interrogations he did not admit the killings and said he had no memory of them.

Sowell was indicted on 11 counts of aggravated murder with death-penalty specifications plus dozens of counts of rape, kidnapping, tampering with evidence and abuse of a corpse. He first pleaded not guilty by reason of insanity, then not guilty. Trial began June 6, 2011 before Judge Dick Ambrose. The jury convicted him of all 11 murders and nearly every other count, acquitting him only of an aggravated robbery charge involving Wade; the court had earlier dismissed three counts relating to Long. The jury recommended death on August 10, and the judge imposed 11 death sentences on August 12, 2011.

The Ohio Supreme Court affirmed 5-2 in an opinion by Justice Terrence O'Donnell. It agreed the trial judge had closed a suppression hearing without the required findings, an issue on which the ACLU of Ohio filed an amicus brief, but held the error did not require a new hearing or trial. Justice William O'Neill dissented, joined in part by Chief Justice Maureen O'Connor. Wikipedia reports the U.S. Supreme Court denied certiorari in October 2017; News 5 Cleveland reported that in May 2020 the Eighth District Court of Appeals upheld the dismissal of his post-conviction petition.

Sowell was moved to the Franklin Medical Center in Columbus on January 21, 2021 for end-of-life care and died there on February 8, 2021, aged 61; the Ohio Department of Rehabilitation and Correction said the illness was not COVID-related. He was born August 19, 1959 in East Cleveland and served in the U.S. Marine Corps from 1978 to 1985. According to the Ohio Supreme Court, he was convicted of attempted rape in 1990, served 15 years and was released in 2005.

timeline.text: Anthony Sowell born in East Cleveland, Ohio.

Convicted of attempted rape in Cuyahoga County; serves 15 years.
Released from prison; moves to 12205 Imperial Avenue, Cleveland.
Crystal Dozier, 38, the first known victim, last seen.
Gladys Wade reports being strangled at the house; Sowell is arrested but released after the offense is mislabeled on the report.
Diane Turner, 48, the last known victim, disappears.
Latundra Billups reports to police that Sowell choked and raped her.
Police executing a search warrant find two bodies on the third floor of the house.
Sowell arrested on Mount Auburn Avenue after a passerby recognizes him from news coverage.
Search ends with ten bodies and one skull recovered from the house and yard.
Trial begins in Cuyahoga County Common Pleas Court.
Jury convicts Sowell of 11 counts of aggravated murder and most other charges.
Judge Dick Ambrose imposes 11 death sentences after the jury's recommendation.
Ohio Supreme Court affirms the convictions and death sentences, 5-2.
U.S. Supreme Court denies certiorari.
Dies of a terminal illness at Franklin Medical Center, Columbus, aged 61.

name: Arthur Gary Bishop
victimProfile: Five boys aged 4 to 13 from the Salt Lake City area, several of whom lived near him or knew him, lured with offers of money, candy or toys
captureMethod: Questioned by Salt Lake police over the disappearance of Graeme Cunningham, whom he had planned to take on a trip, he confessed to all five killings and led officers to the remains
sentence: Death on five counts of first-degree murder (jury verdict, March 23, 1984), plus consecutive terms of five years to life on five aggravated kidnapping counts and five years to life on one count of aggravated sexual abuse of a child
fateDetail: Lethal injection at the Utah State Prison, Draper, Utah; pronounced dead at 12:15 a.m. on June 10, 1988, after he abandoned his appeals
summary: Executed. Arthur Gary Bishop was convicted in 1984 of abducting and murdering five boys, aged 4 to 13, in the Salt Lake City area between 1979 and 1983. He dropped his appeals and was executed by lethal injection at the Utah State Prison on June 10, 1988.
narrative: Arthur Gary Bishop was a Utah man convicted of abducting and murdering five boys, aged 4 to 13, in the Salt Lake City area between 1979 and 1983. A Salt Lake jury found him guilty in March 1984 of five counts of first-degree murder, five counts of aggravated kidnapping and one count of aggravated sexual abuse of a child, and returned five death sentences. After the Utah Supreme Court upheld the convictions and he abandoned further appeals, he was executed by lethal injection at the Utah State Prison in Draper in the early hours of June 10, 1988.

The five victims named in court records and contemporary reporting were Alonzo Daniels, Claude (Kim) Peterson, Danny Davis, Troy Ward and Graeme Cunningham. According to UPI, Alonzo Daniels, 4, disappeared on October 16, 1979; Kim Peterson, 11, vanished on November 8, 1980; Danny Davis, 4, was taken from a South Salt Lake supermarket on October 20, 1981; Troy Ward, 6, disappeared on June 22, 1983; and Graeme Cunningham, 13, went missing on July 14, 1983. The Deseret News later reported that Daniels was last seen in the courtyard of his family's apartment complex and that Ward was taken from a park where he was to meet a friend. The Utah Supreme Court opinion lists Daniels as aged 14, but UPI, the Deseret News and the Wikipedia article all give his age as 4.

The investigation that ended the series centered on Cunningham. According to the Utah Supreme Court, the boy had been planning a California trip with a friend and with the defendant, who was then using the name Roger Downs and had been described to police as the friend's father. Detectives learned that Downs had telephoned Cunningham shortly before he disappeared, and that he might also be using the names Lynn Jones and Arthur Bishop; Lynn Jones was wanted for forgery or theft and Arthur Bishop for a probation violation. On July 24, 1983, Bishop arrived at the Cunningham home while police were there and was taken in for questioning.

The court opinion records that after about an hour of unhelpful answers Bishop briefly asked for a lawyer, then said he wished to continue and took officers to his residence, where he produced a revolver and several hundred photographs of boys. Back at the station he confessed to abducting and killing all five boys, and he directed officers to sites in Big Cottonwood Canyon and near Cedar Fort, Utah, where their remains were recovered. UPI reported on August 1, 1983, that he had been charged with capital homicide and kidnapping in the five deaths. Police later said, according to UPI, that three of the boys had been beaten, one strangled and one possibly shot, and prosecutors said four had been sexually abused.

Bishop's trial in Salt Lake City lasted about a month. Jurors convicted him on Monday, March 19, 1984. During the penalty phase they heard his taped confession, in which, according to UPI, he said he had lured the boys to his home with treats, toys and money and could not stop; his mother and older brother testified in an effort to spare his life, and he did not testify. On March 23, 1984, the same jury returned death verdicts on all five murder counts. The trial judge, identified in the Deseret News as Judge Jay Banks, also imposed consecutive prison terms on the kidnapping and sexual abuse counts.

Utah law required the death sentences to be reviewed by the state Supreme Court. Bishop's appeal raised more than forty issues, including a challenge to the admission of his confession; the court affirmed the convictions and sentences on February 3, 1988. That month, UPI reported, he described life on death row as tedious and worthless, dismissed his anti-death-penalty attorneys and asked that the sentence be carried out, and the Deseret News reported he wanted the victims' families to find peace. After the court lifted his stay on May 2, Third District Judge Frank G. Noel signed an execution warrant. Bishop declined a last meal and was pronounced dead at 12:15 a.m. on June 10, 1988, the 99th execution in the United States since the Supreme Court lifted its moratorium on capital punishment. In a written statement he apologized to the families; Graeme Cunningham's mother called the execution his last self-serving act.

Bishop was born in 1952 in Hinckley, Utah, a small town about 130 miles south of Salt Lake City, and UPI reported that residents remembered him as an honor student, Eagle Scout and Mormon missionary. Investigators in Box Elder County and in California examined whether he was linked to other child deaths, including that of 9-year-old Thomas Walling, according to UPI and the Deseret News, but he denied further killings and was never charged in any other case.

Troy Ward, 6, disappears from a Salt Lake park.

UPI reports Bishop has been charged with capital homicide and kidnapping in the five deaths; funerals for the boys are held.
Jury convicts him of five counts of first-degree murder, five of aggravated kidnapping and one of aggravated sexual abuse of a child.

name: Arthur Shawcross

victims.suspected: 11 murders plus 2 child deaths resolved by a 1972 manslaughter plea; police initially reviewed up to 17 deaths or disappearances

victimProfile: Women aged 20 to 59 in Rochester, most of them sex workers; two children aged 8 and 10 in Watertown in 1972
captureMethod: A State Police helicopter searching for a missing woman found June Cicero's body near Northampton Park and spotted Shawcross's car leaving the area; he admitted the killings under questioning.
sentence: 10 consecutive terms of 25 years to life, 250 years minimum (Monroe County, February 1991); additional term after a 1991 guilty plea to one murder in Wayne County
fateDetail: Died of cardiac arrest at Albany Medical Center after falling ill at Sullivan Correctional Facility, Fallsburg, New York
summary: Convicted by a Monroe County jury in December 1990 of 10 murders of Rochester-area women and sentenced to 250 years to life; pleaded guilty to an 11th in Wayne County. Paroled in 1987 after a 1972 manslaughter plea for two children's deaths. Died in custody in 2008.
narrative: Arthur John Shawcross was a New York serial killer convicted of murdering 11 women in the Rochester area between March 1988 and December 1989. In December 1990 a Monroe County jury found him guilty of 10 counts of second-degree murder, and in February 1991 Judge Donald Wisner imposed 25 years to life on each count, a 250-year minimum that the district attorney called the longest sentence in state history, UPI reported. The Associated Press reported that three months later he pleaded guilty to strangling an 11th woman found in neighboring Wayne County. Separately, in 1972 he had pleaded guilty to first-degree manslaughter in the deaths of two children in Watertown, New York, and was paroled in 1987.

The Rochester murders began in March 1988 with Dorothy Blackburn, 27. According to UPI, nine of the ten women in the Monroe County indictment were sex workers, and most were strangled or suffocated. Victims named in the Wikipedia article and wire reports include Anna Marie Steffen, Dorothy Keeler, Patricia Ives, June Stott, Marie Welch, Frances Brown, Kimberly Logan, Darlene Trippi, June Cicero and Felicia Stephens. At trial a police witness testified that Shawcross said he killed Keeler, 59, in the Genesee River gorge in spring 1989 after an argument, striking her with a log. Elizabeth Gibson, 29, found on November 27, 1989, was killed in Wayne County and charged separately.

UPI reported that on January 3, 1990, a State Police helicopter searching for June Cicero found her body in a culvert near Northampton Park west of Rochester and minutes later saw a car speeding away. Troopers followed it to Shawcross's home. He was questioned on January 4 and, according to police accounts reported by UPI, admitted the killings and gave information that led investigators to the bodies of Marie Welch and Felicia Stephens. He was arraigned on January 5, 1990, pleading not guilty to eight murders; a 23-member grand jury returned a 10-count second-degree murder indictment on January 23.

Wire reports in January 1990 recounted that after his 1987 parole Shawcross was placed in the village of Delhi, where residents learned of his record and his landlord evicted him; he was then quietly relocated to Rochester, where he worked nights stocking shelves. The placements drew public criticism of parole supervision.

The televised Monroe County trial opened in the autumn of 1990 before Judge Wisner, with First Assistant District Attorney Charles Siragusa prosecuting. Shawcross pleaded not responsible by reason of mental disease or defect. The Associated Press reported that defense psychiatrist Dorothy Lewis attributed his conduct to brain damage, childhood abuse and Vietnam service, while prosecution psychiatrist Park Dietz testified that he was feigning illness. The jury deliberated about six and a half hours before convicting him on all 10 counts in December 1990.

In People v. Shawcross, 192 A.D.2d 1128 (April 14, 1993), the Appellate Division, Fourth Department, unanimously affirmed the Monroe County judgment. The court rejected claims that the trial judge should have inquired into a defense expert's complaint about defense counsel and that the jury should not have been told the consequences of an insanity verdict, and it upheld the denial of his suppression motion, finding that he had voluntarily accompanied police and was not in custody when questioned.

Shawcross served his sentence at Sullivan Correctional Facility in Fallsburg. In 2001 sales of his artwork at a state inmate art show drew protests from victims' families and led New York to end the show, the Associated Press reported. On November 10, 2008, he was taken from the prison to Albany Medical Center and died there that night at 63; the Wikipedia article gives the cause as cardiac arrest. A 2024 WHEC report noted that police had initially considered 17 women as possible victims.

Shawcross was born June 6, 1945, in Kittery, Maine, and grew up near Watertown, New York. On parole for burglary in 1972, he was arrested that September for the death of Karen Ann Hill, 8, and later admitted killing Jack Owen Blake, 10, who had disappeared in May. On October 17, 1972, he pleaded guilty to first-degree manslaughter and received an indeterminate sentence with a 25-year maximum, serving about 14 years before his 1987 parole.

name: Axeman of New Orleans

victims.suspected: At least 6 killed and 6 injured in the attacks attributed to the series in 1918 and 1919; historians dispute which attacks belong to it, and totals of up to 17 killed have been cited

victimProfile: Italian-American grocers and their families, attacked in their beds above or beside their stores at night; victims ranged from a 2-year-old child to a grocer in his sixties
summary: Unidentified. An unknown attacker killed at least six people and injured six more in night-time axe attacks on homes in New Orleans and Gretna, Louisiana, between May 1918 and October 1919, most of them Italian-American grocers. Never solved.
narrative: The Axeman of New Orleans is the name the press gave to an unidentified attacker held responsible for night-time assaults on households in New Orleans and neighboring Gretna, Louisiana, between May 1918 and October 1919. According to the Wikipedia article, at least six people were killed and six injured in the attacks attributed to the series, and some tallies run higher. Most victims were Italian-American grocers and their families. No one was ever convicted of the series, the case was never solved, and the offender is presumed dead.

The first attack came on May 23, 1918, when grocer Joseph Maggio and his wife Catherine were found with their heads struck by an axe and their throats cut; both died. On June 27, 1918, grocer Louis Besumer and Harriet Lowe were attacked; Lowe died in August after surgery. Anna Schneider survived an attack on August 5, 1918, and Joseph Romano died two days after being struck on August 10, 1918. Wikipedia reports that the intruder usually chiseled out a rear door panel, used the household's own axe and stole nothing.

According to the Louisiana Supreme Court opinion in State v. Guagliardo, Charles and Rosie Cortimiglia were found in their bed in Gretna on the morning of Sunday, March 9, 1919, with their skulls fractured and their daughter, aged about 21 months, dead beside them; both parents recovered after emergency surgery at Charity Hospital. Back in New Orleans, grocer Steve Boca was injured on August 10, 1919, Sarah Laumann, 19, on September 3, 1919, and grocer Mike Pepitone was killed on October 27, 1919, the last attack attributed to the series.

The case is remembered for a letter dated "Hell, March 13, 1919" and signed by the Axeman, which the Times-Picayune published on March 16, 1919, according to Country Roads Magazine and Crime and Investigation. The writer said he would pass through the city at 12:15 a.m. the following Tuesday night and spare any home where a jazz band was playing. On the night of March 18 to 19, bands played across the city and no attack was reported. Historian Miriam C. Davis has argued that the letter's style suggests it was not written by the killer and that a local composer used the scare to promote a song, "The Axman's Jazz".

The investigation produced arrests but no lasting conviction. Wikipedia reports that police briefly held Joseph Maggio's brother Andrew and released him, and that other men arrested in 1918 were freed for lack of evidence. Louis Besumer, accused by Harriet Lowe before her death, was charged with her murder and acquitted by a jury on May 1, 1919. In Gretna, authorities arrested the Cortimiglias' neighbors and business rivals, Iorlando Jordano, about 66, and his son Frank, 17, whose family name was Guagliardo. Indicted on May 5, 1919, both were convicted by a jury; Frank was sentenced to death and his father to life at hard labor. Rosie Cortimiglia, the only witness connecting them to the crime, later retracted her identification. On April 5, 1920, the Louisiana Supreme Court annulled both convictions because the prosecution had withheld her written statement and announced impeachment evidence it never produced, and ordered a new trial. Smithsonian magazine reports that the two men were freed in December 1920.

The Mafia and the Black Hand extortion practice were widely blamed at the time, but according to Smithsonian the New Orleans police superintendent, Frank Mooney, and detective John Dantonio rejected that theory because a vendetta would not have left so many survivors. Later writers have proposed names for the killer, but no person was ever named by the police or a court as the Axeman.

Historians disagree about the series' boundaries. Newspapers in 1918 linked the attacks to axe and cleaver assaults on Italian grocers in 1910 to 1912, including the fatal attack on Joseph Davi in June 1911, and Davis argues the same offender was responsible. She excludes the Besumer, Schneider and Pepitone cases as unrelated and attributes axe attacks on Italian grocers elsewhere in Louisiana in 1920 and 1921 to the same man. None of these conclusions has been confirmed by any official finding.

Joseph Romano struck in his home; he dies two days later.

Iorlando and Frank Jordano (Guagliardo) indicted in Jefferson Parish for the murder of the Cortimiglia child; both are later convicted, Frank sentenced to death and his father to life.

name: Belle Gunness

victims.suspected: 14 to more than 40 (remains of at least 11 people dug up on the farm, plus three children and a headless woman in the fire ruins)

victimProfile: Middle-aged men, mostly Norwegian-born farmers and labourers, who answered her matrimonial advertisements and brought cash; also her husbands, several of her children and her foster daughter
captureMethod: Never arrested; after the April 28, 1908 farmhouse fire, the brother of a missing suitor and the La Porte County sheriff dug up human remains in the farm's hog pen, exposing the burials.
fateDetail: A headless woman's body in the fire ruins was ruled hers by the coroner in 1908 on the strength of dental bridgework; the identification has been disputed since, and a 2008 DNA comparison was inconclusive
summary: Suspected, never charged. Norwegian-born widow whose La Porte, Indiana farm yielded the remains of at least 11 people after an April 1908 fire; the headless body ruled hers in 1908 is disputed and 2008 DNA tests were inconclusive.
narrative: Belle Gunness is a Norwegian-born woman suspected of killing suitors, husbands and children at her farm outside La Porte, Indiana, and earlier in Chicago, Illinois, between about 1900 and 1908. She was never arrested, charged or tried. After her farmhouse burned on April 28, 1908, investigators unearthed the remains of at least 11 people on the property in addition to the three children and the headless adult woman found in the ruins. The Library of Congress research guide on the case summarises the press coverage of 1908 as reporting "over a dozen bodies" dug up between May 8 and May 29. Estimates of her total victims range from about 14 to more than 40; no court ever fixed a number.

According to the Wikipedia article and a Detroit Legal News case history, Gunness married Mads Sorenson in Chicago in 1884. Two of their four children, Caroline and Axel, died after showing symptoms the Legal News describes as consistent with poisoning; both were insured. Sorenson died on July 30, 1900, on the one day that two of his life insurance policies overlapped, and his doctor recorded natural causes. Gunness used the payout to buy a farm near La Porte in 1901. She married Peter Gunness there in April 1902; his infant daughter died within a week of the wedding, and he died about eight months later from a skull injury that Belle attributed to a falling sausage-grinder part. A coroner looked into the death, and she was not charged.

From about 1905 she placed matrimonial advertisements in Scandinavian-language newspapers describing herself as a comely widow with a large farm, Mental Floss and the Legal News report. Middle-aged men arrived with cash, and neighbours later recalled that they were not seen leaving. Among those named in later reporting were Wisconsin farmhand Henry Gurholt, Minnesota man John Moe and her foster daughter Jennie Olson, who disappeared in 1906 and whom Gunness said had gone to California. In January 1908 Andrew Helgelien, a South Dakota farmer who had exchanged dozens of letters with her, came to La Porte and withdrew $2,839 from a bank within days; he was never seen again.

At dawn on April 28, 1908, farmhand Joe Maxson woke to find the house on fire. Firefighters found four bodies in the basement: Gunness's children Myrtle, Lucy and Philip, and an adult woman without a head. Andrew Helgelien's brother Asle, who had grown suspicious after reading her letters, went to the sheriff on May 4 and then to the farm, where digging in the hog pen produced his brother's remains wrapped in burlap. Further digging turned up more burlap-wrapped remains in shallow graves; the count rose from five on the first day to 11 the next, after which, Mental Floss reports, police stopped counting. Traces of strychnine were found in some remains.

The county coroner concluded that the headless woman was Gunness. A La Porte dentist identified dental bridgework recovered from the ruins on May 19 as hers, while a physician who examined the body on May 9 said its height, weight and hands did not match the tall, heavy widow, according to the Wikipedia article. No explanation was ever established for the missing head, and reported sightings of Gunness continued for years.

Her former farmhand Ray Lamphere, whom she had dismissed after a quarrel, was arrested and charged with arson and four counts of murder. His trial began on November 9, 1908. On November 26, 1908, the jury found him guilty of arson and acquitted him of murder; the Morning Oregonian of November 27 reported that he was sentenced to the state prison on an indeterminate term and that two jurors had refused to convict on murder. He died of tuberculosis in prison about a year later. A confession he made to a clergyman before his death, published in January 1910, claimed that Gunness had killed another woman and planted the body before leaving.

In 1931 a Los Angeles County sheriff believed that Esther Carlson, a woman charged with strychnine poisoning, was Gunness; Carlson died of tuberculosis before trial and the identification was never confirmed. In 2007 and 2008 a University of Indianapolis team led by graduate student Andrea Simmons and anthropologist Stephen Nawrocki exhumed the body buried in Chicago as Gunness and sought a comparison sample from envelopes she had mailed; the material was too degraded, and the results were inconclusive.

Gunness was born Brynhild Paulsdatter Størseth on November 11, 1859, in Selbu, Norway, and emigrated to Chicago in 1881 to join her sister. Her farm site in La Porte remains a subject of local history, and the Library of Congress maintains a guide to the 1908 newspaper coverage.

name: Bobby Joe Long
victimProfile: Women aged 18 to 28 in the Tampa Bay area, several of them dancers or sex workers from the North Nebraska Avenue nightclub strip
captureMethod: Abduction survivor Lisa McVey gave police details of his home and car after he released her, and carpet fibers from his vehicle matched fibers found on the victims.
sentence: Death for the murder of Michelle Simms (1986; reimposed 1989) plus life sentences on eight other first-degree murder and related counts under a 1985 Hillsborough County plea; 99 years and a further life term for 1984 rapes in Pasco and Pinellas counties
fateDetail: Lethal injection, Florida State Prison, Raiford; pronounced dead at 6:55 p.m. on May 23, 2019
summary: Executed in 2019. Bobby Joe Long pleaded guilty to eight 1984 murders of women in the Tampa Bay area and was sentenced to death for one; a survivor's account of her abduction led police to him.
narrative: Bobby Joe Long, recorded by Florida prison officials as Robert J. Long, was convicted of eight first-degree murders of women in the Tampa Bay area of Florida between May and November 1984. He pleaded guilty in Hillsborough County in September 1985 and was sentenced to death for one killing, that of 22-year-old Michelle Denise Simms. According to the Florida Supreme Court's 2013 opinion, he confessed to eight Hillsborough County murders and one in Pasco County; Bay News 9 reported that authorities attributed at least ten killings to him, including that of Artiss Ann Wick in March 1984. Florida executed him by lethal injection on May 23, 2019.

The Department of Corrections record lists offense dates for the eight murders: May 10, May 27, June 7, September 6, September 30, October 4, October 14 and November 10, 1984. A UPI report from November 1984 said the first identified victim, Ngeun Thi Long, was a dancer at a Nebraska Avenue lounge whose body was found on May 13, and that the victims appeared to have been chosen from the strip's dancers and women with prostitution arrests. WTVT (Fox 13) reported that most were strangled, some had their throats cut and others were bludgeoned. The same record shows separate 1984 convictions for rapes in Pasco and Pinellas counties; Fox 13 reported that survivor Linda Nuttall was attacked after Long answered a classified advertisement she had placed; the press called him the 'Classified Ad Rapist'.

The investigation turned on a survivor. On November 3, 1984, Long abducted 17-year-old Lisa McVey as she rode her bicycle home from work, held her about 26 hours and sexually assaulted her before releasing her. She left fingerprints in his apartment and gave detectives details about the apartment, the car and an ATM withdrawal she had overheard. Long was arrested on November 16, 1984, and charged with her kidnapping and sexual battery. UPI reported that carpet-fiber analysis linked him to the murders and that after his arrest he told police where to find one victim's body.

According to the Florida Supreme Court, Long waived his Miranda rights in the McVey case and, when questioning turned to the unsolved homicides, confessed to nine murders even though no attorney was provided after he suggested he might need one. A Pasco County jury first convicted him of murdering 18-year-old Virginia Johnson, and he was sentenced to death on May 3, 1985. On September 23, 1985, he pleaded guilty in Hillsborough County to eight counts of first-degree murder, nine of kidnapping, eight of sexual battery and a probation violation, according to the Eleventh Circuit; the state agreed not to seek death except for Simms. A jury recommended death for Simms by an 11-1 vote, and the sentence was imposed on July 25, 1986.

The Florida Supreme Court vacated that death sentence on June 30, 1988. A second jury unanimously recommended death, the sentence was reimposed on July 21, 1989, and the court affirmed it on October 15, 1992. The Pasco County case went differently: the Florida Supreme Court vacated the Johnson conviction in 1987 and 1992, holding the confession had been obtained in violation of his right to counsel, and on March 6, 1997 reversed it a third time and directed an acquittal.

Courts rejected later postconviction claims, including Florida Supreme Court rulings in 2013, 2016 and 2018 and a federal habeas petition. Governor Ron DeSantis signed his death warrant on April 23, 2019. Final motions argued that the sedative etomidate in Florida's lethal injection protocol was dangerous given his epilepsy and brain injury; the Florida Supreme Court denied relief on May 17, and the Eleventh Circuit affirmed denial of a stay on May 22, finding the claims barred by delay and res judicata. Long was pronounced dead at 6:55 p.m. on May 23, 2019, at Florida State Prison. Lisa McVey, by then a Hillsborough County sheriff's deputy named Lisa Noland, witnessed the execution.

Long was born on October 14, 1953, in Kenova, West Virginia. According to the Wikipedia article, he suffered childhood head injuries, married in 1974, divorced in 1980 and moved to the Tampa Bay area in 1983. The 1984 UPI report described him as a 31-year-old out-of-work radiology technician.

Arrested in Tampa and charged with kidnapping and sexual battery of Lisa McVey; confesses to nine murders in questioning.

Sentenced to death in Pasco County after a jury convicts him of murdering Virginia Johnson, 18.

name: Carl Panzram

victims.suspected: 5 corroborated by investigators; Panzram also claimed killings in Portuguese Angola

victimProfile: Boys and young men, including sailors, hitchhikers and a 14-year-old newsboy; the one proven victim was a 47-year-old prison laundry foreman
captureMethod: Arrested in Baltimore on a Washington, D.C., burglary charge; he volunteered his murder confessions while held in the District jail and later in a written autobiography.
sentence: Death by hanging (1930) for the 1929 murder of Robert Warnke; earlier 25-year federal sentence (1928) for burglary in Washington, D.C.
fateDetail: Hanged at the United States Penitentiary, Leavenworth, Kansas, on September 5, 1930
summary: Executed 1930. Carl Panzram, a career burglar, confessed in 1928 to 21 murders in several states and abroad; he was convicted of only one, the 1929 killing of a Leavenworth prison foreman, and was hanged in Kansas.
narrative: Carl Panzram was a career burglar and prison escapee who, after his arrest in 1928, confessed in writing to 21 murders committed between about 1920 and 1928 in New York, Massachusetts, Connecticut, Pennsylvania and Portuguese Angola. He was convicted of one murder: the June 20, 1929 killing of Robert G. Warnke, a civilian laundry foreman at the United States Penitentiary at Leavenworth, Kansas. According to the Federal Bureau of Prisons, he was convicted of that murder, sentenced to hang and executed at Leavenworth on September 5, 1930. The San Diego State University finding aid for his papers notes that his prison records show convictions only for burglary and larceny apart from the Leavenworth murder.

Panzram's own account, as summarized in the Wikipedia article drawn from his autobiography, begins in 1920, when he said he lured sailors from New York port bars aboard a stolen yacht and shot them, dumping the bodies in Long Island Sound. He said that in 1921 and 1922, in Portuguese Angola, he killed a boy and six men. In July 1922 he said he beat a boy to death in Salem, Massachusetts; the article identifies the victim as Henry McMahon. He also described strangling a boy near New Haven, Connecticut, in 1922 and shooting a man near Kingston, New York, in 1923. Investigators corroborated only five of the confessed killings.

The last confessed murder was that of Alexander Uszacke, a 14-year-old newsboy, in Philadelphia in the summer of 1928. On August 30, 1928, Panzram was arrested in Baltimore on a Washington, D.C., burglary charge. Held at the Washington Asylum and Jail, he volunteered confessions to the boys' killings. Philadelphia authorities indicted him for the Uszacke murder, but he was never tried on it. In Washington he was convicted of burglary and, according to the finding aid, sentenced to 25 years, to be served at Leavenworth; Wikipedia gives the sentence as 25 years to life.

In the District jail a young guard, Henry Lesser, befriended him. The finding aid records that Lesser encouraged Panzram to write his life story and smuggled the pages out. In that manuscript Panzram stated that he had murdered 21 people, committed more than a thousand sexual assaults on males and thousands of burglaries and arsons, and felt no remorse. The finding aid notes that elsewhere he boasted of 23 killings.

Within a year of his transfer to Leavenworth, Panzram killed again. The Bureau of Prisons reports that on the morning of June 20, 1929, Warnke, a 47-year-old Army veteran from Cleveland, Ohio, employed at the prison since 1921, was struck on the head with a heavy flat iron shortly after reporting to the laundry. The first responding officer subdued Panzram, who was placed in isolation and refused to make a statement. The Bureau says there was no known conflict between the two men.

Panzram was tried in federal court in 1930 for Warnke's murder, convicted and sentenced to death. The finding aid states that the psychiatrist Karl Menninger examined him and found him of sound mind at the time of the killing. Panzram refused to let anyone appeal on his behalf and, according to Wikipedia, rejected efforts by opponents of capital punishment to seek clemency for him. He was hanged at Leavenworth on September 5, 1930.

Lesser kept the manuscript for four decades. Parts of it appeared in 1970 in Killer: A Journal of Murder by Thomas E. Gaddis and James O. Long, later adapted into a 1995 film. In 1980 Lesser donated the papers to San Diego State University.

Panzram was born Charles Panzram on a farm near East Grand Forks, Minnesota, to immigrants from East Prussia; Wikipedia gives his birth date as June 28, 1891, the finding aid June 28, 1892. According to the Grand Forks Herald, his father left when he was eight and he was first arrested at eleven for burglary. He was sent to the state training school at Red Wing, where he said staff beat and sexually assaulted him, claims not independently verified. From his teens he passed through the Fort Leavenworth military barracks, the Montana State Prison, the Oregon State Penitentiary, Sing Sing and Clinton Prison, escaping several times.

Sentenced to seven years in the Oregon State Penitentiary for burglary under the alias Jefferson Baldwin; escapes in 1918.

Convicted of burglary in Washington, D.C., and sentenced to 25 years, to be served at the federal penitentiary at Leavenworth, Kansas.
Kills laundry foreman Robert G. Warnke, 47, with a flat iron at Leavenworth.
