name: Carlton Gary

victims.suspected: 7 to 9

victimProfile: Elderly women aged 59 to 89 who lived alone in the Wynnton neighborhood of Columbus, Georgia
captureMethod: A pistol stolen in a 1977 burglary in the victims' neighborhood surfaced in Michigan and was traced through relatives to Gary, who was arrested for burglary; his fingerprints then matched those from four murder scenes
sentence: Death, imposed August 27, 1986, on each of three counts of malice murder, with convictions on three counts each of rape and burglary
fateDetail: Lethal injection at the Georgia Diagnostic and Classification Prison, Jackson, Georgia; pronounced dead at 10:33 p.m. on March 15, 2018
summary: Executed. Carlton Gary, the Columbus, Georgia "Stocking Strangler," was convicted in 1986 of the 1977 murders of three elderly women, Florence Scheible, Martha Thurmond and Kathleen Woodruff, and executed by lethal injection in March 2018.
narrative: Carlton Gary was convicted in 1986 by a Muscogee County jury of murdering three elderly women in Columbus, Georgia, in 1977: Florence Scheible, 89, Martha Thurmond, 69, and Kathleen Woodruff, 74. Known in the press as the "Stocking Strangler," he was found guilty on three counts each of malice murder, rape and burglary and sentenced to death on August 27, 1986. Prosecutors said he was responsible for a total of nine attacks on elderly women in Columbus in 1977 and 1978, seven of them fatal. After more than three decades of appeals, Georgia executed him by lethal injection at the state prison in Jackson on March 15, 2018.

Gary was born in Columbus on September 24, 1950, and, according to The Atlanta Journal-Constitution, moved to Florida as a young child. Between September 1977 and April 1978 a series of attacks struck women who lived alone in Columbus's Wynnton neighborhood. According to the 2012 opinion of the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Eleventh Circuit, the uncharged deaths introduced at trial as similar crimes were those of Fern Jackson on September 16, 1977, Jean Dimenstein on September 24, 1977, Mildred Borom on February 12, 1978, and Janet Cofer on April 19, 1978. Two women survived: Gertrude Miller, who was raped and beaten on September 11, 1977, and Ruth Schwob, who was attacked on February 11, 1978. The AJC reported that Schwob, 74, survived by pressing a panic button. CBS News reported that most of the victims were choked, often with their own stockings.

The case went unsolved for six years. The Eleventh Circuit opinion says police had no viable suspect until 1984, when a gun stolen in a 1977 burglary in the area was found in Michigan in the possession of Gary's cousin, a discovery made through Michigan's gun registration laws. Gary was arrested for burglary on May 3, 1984, and was indicted the next day, according to an Associated Press chronology published by WTVC. His fingerprints matched latent prints from four of the crime scenes. In statements to officers, according to the court, Gary said he had been present at seven of the scenes as a burglar but blamed the rapes and murders on a boyhood friend, Malvin Crittenden; the AP reported that investigators found nothing to corroborate that claim.

Before Columbus, Gary had a record in several states. The AJC reported that his fingerprints were found in 1970 at the Albany, New York, home of Nellie Farmer, 85, who was raped and strangled, but that he was convicted only of robbery. In 1975 Marion Fisher, 40, was raped and strangled near Syracuse, New York, and evidence from her case was later linked to Gary's DNA; according to the Wikipedia article, the Onondaga County district attorney declined to charge him because he was already on Georgia's death row. He was never tried for either death. The AJC reported that Gary escaped from a New York county jail in 1977 and was later imprisoned in South Carolina for a string of restaurant armed robberies.

The Georgia Supreme Court sent the case back in 1987 for a hearing on whether Gary had effective counsel, then affirmed the convictions and death sentences on March 6, 1990. State habeas relief was denied between 1995 and 1997, and federal habeas relief was denied by the district court in 2004 and by the Eleventh Circuit in February 2009. After the U.S. Supreme Court declined review in November 2009, the state set an execution date of December 16, 2009. The Board of Pardons and Paroles denied clemency, but the Georgia Supreme Court stayed the execution hours before it was due so that DNA evidence could be tested.

The DNA testing gave mixed results. The AP reported that testing showed a match between Gary and Jean Dimenstein, one of the uncharged deaths. His lawyers pointed to semen on clothing worn by Gertrude Miller, who had identified him at trial, that did not match him, and argued that other samples from the convicted cases were contaminated at the state crime lab. They also cited a shoeprint from a size 10 shoe, disclosed years after trial, although Gary wore a 13 and a half, and a bite-mark exemplar that defense experts said did not match his teeth. The state disputed these claims. A Muscogee County judge denied his extraordinary motion for a new trial on September 1, 2017, finding the evidence unlikely to have changed the verdict, and the Georgia Supreme Court declined to hear an appeal in December 2017.
Gary, 67, was put to death on the night of March 15, 2018, the first execution in Georgia that year. He declined to make a final statement and was pronounced dead at 10:33 p.m.

name: Charles Cullen

victims.suspected: Up to 40 by Cullen's own estimate

victimProfile: Hospital and nursing-home patients, mostly elderly but as young as 21, under his care as a nurse
captureMethod: Somerset Medical Center reported unexplained digoxin overdoses; detectives traced his drug-dispensing records and a nurse colleague wore a wire, after which he confessed
sentence: 11 consecutive life terms in New Jersey (March 2, 2006); six life terms in Lehigh County and life without parole in Northampton County, Pennsylvania (March 10, 2006); 18 life terms in all
fateDetail: New Jersey State Prison, Trenton
summary: Imprisoned. Former nurse who pleaded guilty to murdering 29 patients with drug overdoses at New Jersey and Pennsylvania hospitals from 1988 to 2003; sentenced in 2006 to 18 life terms. He has estimated his own toll at up to 40.
narrative: Charles Cullen is a former nurse who pleaded guilty to murdering 29 patients at hospitals and a nursing home in New Jersey and Pennsylvania between 1988 and 2003. The Associated Press reported that he pleaded guilty to 22 murders and three attempted murders in New Jersey and seven murders and three attempted murders in Pennsylvania, and that prosecutors in seven counties agreed not to seek the death penalty in return for his help identifying victims. In March 2006 he received 11 consecutive life terms in New Jersey and seven more in Pennsylvania, 18 in all, and is held at New Jersey State Prison in Trenton. Cullen has said he may have killed up to 40 patients; that is his own estimate, not a court finding.

According to the AP, the earliest known killing was that of John W. Yengo, a 72-year-old Jersey City municipal judge treated at Saint Barnabas Medical Center in Livingston, New Jersey, in 1988; Cullen admitted putting lidocaine into his intravenous line. The Philadelphia Inquirer reported that he injected lethal doses of drugs, chiefly the heart medication digoxin but also insulin and lidocaine, into patients' IV lines or fluid bags at about ten facilities over 16 years. The Superior Court of Pennsylvania, in a 2010 opinion in civil suits against St. Luke's Hospital in Bethlehem, recorded that he worked in its coronary care unit from June 2000 until June 2002, when the hospital accepted his resignation after confronting him about diverted medications, and that he later confessed to killing five named St. Luke's patients, Irene Krapf, Samuel Spangler, Paul Galgon, William Park and Daniel George.

Cullen joined Somerset Medical Center in Somerville, New Jersey, in September 2002. According to CBS News's 60 Minutes, the 2003 death of the Rev. Florian Gall with very high digoxin levels was the second unexplained overdose in two weeks, prompting a pharmacist to alert the state poison control center. The Pennsylvania opinion records that Somerset attributed abnormal lab results to Cullen and fired him in October 2003. Somerset County detectives then built a case with the help of Amy Loughren, a nurse and friend of Cullen's, who reviewed drug-dispensing records, recorded calls and wore a wire at a restaurant meeting with him, CBS reported. He was arrested in December 2003 and confessed that month to New Jersey State Police to killing patients in both states.

The pleas came in stages. In April 2004 Cullen pleaded guilty in Somerset County to 13 murders and two attempted murders at Somerset. In December 2004, the AP reported, he pleaded guilty in Newark to the Yengo murder, bringing his admitted total to 24 murders. In June 2005 he admitted five more digoxin killings, reaching 29. On March 2, 2006, Superior Court Judge Paul Armstrong in Somerville imposed 11 consecutive life terms as victims' relatives addressed him; Cullen said he had nothing to say. On March 10, 2006, Lehigh County President Judge William Platt imposed six life sentences after Cullen repeatedly demanded the judge step down and was gagged, and a Northampton County judge sentenced him in absentia to life without parole for the 1998 death of Ottomar Schramm at Easton Hospital.

In August 2006, with the sentencing judge's permission, Cullen donated a kidney to a New York man, the Inquirer reported. The case produced New Jersey's Cullen Law requiring health care employers to report misconduct, and in 2010 the Pennsylvania Superior Court held that St. Luke's had a duty to tell next of kin when it should have known an employee had killed a patient. In a 2013 interview with 60 Minutes, Cullen said he had thought he was ending suffering but did not know whether he would have stopped. The 2022 Netflix film The Good Nurse dramatized the case.

Cullen was born in West Orange, New Jersey, on February 22, 1960, the youngest of eight children. According to the Wikipedia article, he served in the United States Navy before a 1984 discharge that followed psychiatric admissions, graduated from nursing school in Montclair and started at Saint Barnabas in 1987; he had a history of depression and suicide attempts. Detectives told the AP that Cullen said he acted out of depression; prosecutors rejected his mercy-killing explanation.

name: Charles Ng
victimProfile: Men, women and two infants from the San Francisco Bay Area and Calaveras County, including two families, a co-worker and people answering sale advertisements, abducted with Leonard Lake and taken to a rural property in Wilseyville
captureMethod: After fleeing to Canada, he was stopped by security guards on suspicion of shoplifting at a Hudson's Bay Co. store in Calgary, Alberta, shot one guard in the hand and was held until police arrived
sentence: Death, on 11 counts of first-degree murder with a multiple-murder special circumstance (jury verdict April 30, 1999; affirmed by the California Supreme Court on July 28, 2022)
fateDetail: Under sentence of death in California; the Wikipedia article lists him at the California Medical Facility as of 2025. California has carried out no executions since 2006.
summary: Under sentence of death. Charles Ng was convicted in 1999 of 11 murders committed with Leonard Lake in 1984 and 1985, centred on a rural property in Wilseyville, California. Extradited from Canada in 1991, he remains on California's death row.
narrative: Charles Chitat Ng is a former U.S. Marine who was convicted in Orange County, California, on February 24, 1999, of 11 counts of first-degree murder for killings committed with Leonard Lake between July 1984 and April 1985. The victims were abducted in the San Francisco Bay Area and Calaveras County, and the case centred on Lake's property in Wilseyville, in the Sierra Nevada foothills. A jury returned a death verdict on April 30, 1999, and the California Supreme Court affirmed the judgment on July 28, 2022. Lake died by suicide in police custody in June 1985. Ng remains under sentence of death in California, which has not carried out an execution since 2006.

Ng was born in British Hong Kong on December 24, 1960, according to the Wikipedia article. He joined the U.S. Marine Corps, where, the article says, he was implicated in the theft of weapons from the Kaneohe Bay armory in Hawaii and served about 18 months at Fort Leavenworth. The California Supreme Court opinion records that a man he met in Hawaii gave him Lake's address in the summer of 1981, and that in 1982 Ng lived with Lake and Lake's wife, Claralyn, in Philo, Mendocino County.

According to the court's summary of the trial evidence, 12 people went missing between July 1984 and April 1985. Harvey and Deborah Dubs and their 16-month-old son Sean disappeared from their San Francisco apartment on July 25, 1984; Paul Cosner vanished in November 1984 after leaving to deliver a car he was selling; Clifford Peranteau, who worked with Ng at a San Francisco moving company, disappeared in January 1985, and Jeffrey Gerald in February. In April 1985 Kathleen Allen and her boyfriend Michael Carroll disappeared, followed later that month by Lonnie Bond Sr., his fiancee Brenda O'Connor, their infant son Lonnie Bond Jr., and their friend Robin Scott Stapley, all connected to a house in Wilseyville.

The disappearances were linked only after June 2, 1985, when a reserve officer saw Ng leave South City Lumber in South San Francisco with an unpaid vise. Ng walked away; Lake was found with a pistol and silencer registered to Stapley, identified himself as Stapley, and was arrested. At the station he swallowed cyanide and died days later. The car proved to be Cosner's, and a utility bill inside led investigators to Wilseyville, where they found property from the Dubs home. A five-week search uncovered a bunker with a concealed cell and thousands of burned bone and tooth fragments that forensic anthropologists attributed to at least four adults, one child and one infant. On July 8, 1985, the bodies of Bond and Stapley were found buried nearby. Investigators also recovered buried videotapes; UPI reported in 1992 that one played at a closed preliminary hearing showed Ng and Lake threatening two handcuffed women.

Ng fled to Canada. On July 6, 1985, security guards at a Hudson's Bay Co. store in Calgary stopped him on suspicion of shoplifting; UPI reported that he fired a .22-caliber pistol and wounded a guard in the hand before being subdued. Investigators then told UPI of 25 missing people with some link to the pair. The Wikipedia article says he was convicted in Canada in December 1985 and sentenced to four and a half years. He fought extradition on the ground that he faced the death penalty; according to the Wikipedia article the Supreme Court of Canada ruled against him by four votes to three on September 26, 1991, and he was handed over the same day. He was arraigned in Calaveras County on September 27, 1991.

Pretrial proceedings took seven years. The case was moved to Orange County, and the Supreme Court opinion notes that Ng filed 37 motions to replace his lawyers and for a period represented himself. Trial began in September 1998. Ng testified and blamed Lake for the killings. The jury convicted him of the 11 murders and found the multiple-murder special circumstance true; on the Cosner count the jury failed to reach a verdict, according to the Supreme Court opinion, although the Wikipedia article describes it as an acquittal. The Wikipedia article puts the cost of the prosecution at about 20 million dollars.

In its 2022 opinion the California Supreme Court rejected Ng's claims, including challenges to the handling of his self-representation, and affirmed the convictions and death sentence. Identification work has continued: in January 2025 Intermountain Forensics, working with the Calaveras Cold Case Task Force, announced that remains recovered in June 1985 had been identified as Reginald Frisby, born in 1956, who had never been reported missing. The total number of victims is unknown; a Calaveras County sheriff's lieutenant told CBS News in 2022 that he did not think anybody would ever know.

name: Christopher Wilder

victims.suspected: At least 8 killed; 11 or more abducted

victimProfile: Young women and teenage girls aged 16 to 33, approached at shopping malls and a racetrack with offers of modeling or photography work
captureMethod: Two New Hampshire state troopers, alerted by the FBI, recognized the gold Pontiac of a New York murder victim at a Colebrook gas station on April 13, 1984, and Wilder was shot twice with his own revolver in the struggle that followed.
fateDetail: Shot twice with his own .357 Magnum during a struggle with New Hampshire State Police Detective Leo Jellison at a gas station in Colebrook, New Hampshire; cremated in Florida
summary: Died before trial. Christopher Wilder, an Australian-born Florida businessman, is linked by the FBI to at least eight murders and eleven or more abductions across the United States between February 26 and April 13, 1984, when he died in a struggle with New Hampshire troopers.
narrative: Christopher Bernard Wilder was an Australian-born Florida contractor and amateur race-car driver whom the FBI linked to a cross-country series of abductions and killings between February 26 and April 13, 1984. He was never arrested or tried: he died on April 13, 1984, at a gas station in Colebrook, New Hampshire, after two state troopers confronted him. United Press International reported at the time that he was sought in the deaths, rapes and disappearances of 11 young women in eight states; the FBI has since put the deaths at eight or more, according to Fox News. No court ever ruled on the allegations; every attribution here comes from investigators and reporting.

The series began in Florida. Rosario Gonzalez, 20, disappeared from the Miami Grand Prix on February 26, 1984, where Wilder was competing; Elizabeth Kenyon, 23, of Coral Gables, vanished in early March. Both knew Wilder, and neither has been found. Time reported that police first sought Wilder for questioning about them. According to Time and Wikipedia, Theresa Ferguson, 21, was led away from a Merritt Island mall on March 18 and found strangled days later, and a Florida State University student abducted in Tallahassee on March 20 escaped from him in Bainbridge, Georgia.

Wilder then moved west. Time reported that Terry Walden, 23, went missing in Beaumont, Texas, on March 23 and was found bound and stabbed three days later; that Suzanne Logan, abducted in Oklahoma City on March 25, was found stabbed to death near Junction City, Kansas, where Wilder was formally charged with her murder; that Sheryl Bonaventura, 18, disappeared from a Grand Junction, Colorado, mall on March 29; and that Michelle Korfman, 17, vanished from a Las Vegas mall on April 1. Wikipedia records that Bonaventura's body was found in Utah and Korfman's in Southern California in May.

On April 4, Tina Marie Risico, 16, was abducted from a Torrance, California, mall with an offer of $100 for a photo session, UPI reported. Wilder kept her for nine days and drove east. The FBI said he used Risico to lure Dawnette Wilt, 16, into his car at a Merrillville, Indiana, mall on April 10; Wilt was stabbed and left near Penn Yan, New York, where she was found alive on April 12. Beth Dodge, 33, was then forced from her gold Pontiac at a mall in Victor, New York, and shot once in the back; Wilder took her car. He put Risico on a flight from Boston, and she reached Torrance police on April 13; the FBI regarded her as a victim.

Wilder had been added to the FBI's Ten Most Wanted list in the second week of April. On April 13, 1984, New Hampshire State Police Detective Leo Jellison and Trooper Wayne Fortier, alerted by the FBI, recognized the gold car at a Colebrook gas station near the Canadian border. Jellison grabbed Wilder as he reached for a .357 Magnum revolver; two shots were fired, the first passing through Wilder's chest and wounding Jellison, the second striking Wilder's heart. According to UPI, pathologist Dr. Robert Christie concluded that Wilder was not attempting suicide but was killed in the struggle while trying to shoot Jellison. Jellison recovered, and in June 1984 both officers received the state police Medal of Valor.

With Wilder dead, no charge was ever tried. Victims' families filed claims against his estate, which an arbitrator divided among them in 1986, according to Wikipedia. Florida and New York investigators have since examined Wilder as a possible suspect in earlier unsolved deaths, including those of Tammy Jo Alexander and Shari Lynne Ball, but as Fox News reported in 2024, none of those links has been confirmed.

Wilder was born in Sydney on March 13, 1945. Wikipedia records a 1963 probation sentence in Australia for a gang rape before he emigrated about 1970 and settled in Boynton Beach, Florida, where he prospered in construction and real estate. Time reported that he was convicted of attempted sexual battery in Palm Beach County in 1980, and that in 1982 he was charged in Sydney with sexual offenses against two 15-year-old girls; he was out on bail awaiting that trial when the 1984 series began.

name: Cleveland Torso Murderer
aliases: The Mad Butcher of Kingsbury Run

victims.suspected: 12 officially counted (7 men, 5 women); some researchers suggest 20 or more

victimProfile: Men and women living on the margins of Cleveland, many of them transients from the shantytowns of Kingsbury Run; only three were ever identified
summary: Unidentified. An unknown offender decapitated and dismembered 12 officially counted victims in Cleveland, Ohio, between 1935 and 1938, most found in or near Kingsbury Run. Investigated under safety director Eliot Ness; no one was ever tried.
narrative: The Cleveland Torso Murderer, also called the Mad Butcher of Kingsbury Run, is the unidentified offender held responsible for a series of killings in Cleveland, Ohio, between September 1935 and August 1938. According to the Encyclopedia of Cleveland History, published by Case Western Reserve University, the remains were believed to be those of 12 victims, seven men and five women, all of whom had been decapitated and most of whom had been dismembered. Only three were ever identified. No one was ever tried for any of the murders, and the case remains open.

The first two bodies were found together in Kingsbury Run, a creek bed that runs from East 90th Street and Kinsman Road to the Cuyahoga River, on September 23, 1935. One was identified by fingerprints as Edward Andrassy, 29, a former hospital orderly; the other was never identified. On January 26, 1936, the remains of Florence Polillo were found near Orange Avenue and identified by fingerprints; her head was never recovered. According to the Wikipedia article, the later victims included an unidentified man with six tattoos found in June 1936, whose death mask was displayed to the public in the hope of identifying him, and a woman found under the Lorain-Carnegie Bridge in June 1937 who was tentatively, but never conclusively, identified as Rose Wallace. Nine more bodies were discovered between June 1936 and August 1938, most of them in or near Kingsbury Run, the Cuyahoga River in the Flats, and the lakefront. Most victims appeared to be transients or derelicts living in shantytowns; several were found long after death, and the heads of several were never found.

The investigation was conducted by the Cleveland Police Department, with Detective Peter Merylo working the case for six years, according to the Encyclopedia of Cleveland History. Eliot Ness, the former federal agent, was Cleveland's director of public safety during the official murder period and took a direct role. Wikipedia reports that on August 22, 1938, six days after the last two bodies were found at the East Ninth Street dump within sight of City Hall, Ness dispatched search teams across the shantytown districts; the shantytowns in Kingsbury Run were then raided and burned, officially to clear unsafe housing and to fingerprint and move on potential victims. No further bodies attributed to the series were found in Cleveland after that date. Thousands of people were interviewed over the course of the investigation.

In July 1939 the Cuyahoga County sheriff's office arrested Frank Dolezal, a bricklayer who had known Florence Polillo, and announced that he had confessed to killing her. According to the Wikipedia article, Dolezal recanted and said the confession had been beaten out of him. He was found hanged in his cell in the county jail on August 24, 1939, before he could be tried; the death was officially recorded as a suicide. The Encyclopedia of Cleveland History notes that despite intensive police work there was never sufficient evidence to make a case against any other suspect. Various other names have been put forward by authors and researchers since, but no person was ever named in a charging document in connection with the series.

Investigators and later writers have also considered whether the Cleveland killings were connected to dismembered bodies found in western Pennsylvania. The Pittsburgh Post-Gazette reported that in May 1940 three headless bodies were found in boxcars in the Pittsburgh and Lake Erie Railroad yards at McKees Rocks, and that officials suspected the Kingsbury Run killer, but that an official link was never made. Some researchers argue that the Cleveland total is much higher than 12, with figures of 20 or more cited; Wikipedia also records a 1997 theory that more than one killer was responsible. None of these extensions is part of the official count.

The case has seen a new investigative effort in recent years. Cleveland 19 News reported in August 2024 that the Cuyahoga County Medical Examiner's Office had begun exhuming unidentified victims from unmarked graves at Memorial Park Cemetery in Highland Hills, working with the DNA Doe Project, a nonprofit that uses investigative genetic genealogy to identify unknown remains. Chief Medical Examiner Dr. Thomas Gilson said the work would be difficult given the age of the remains, and the DNA Doe Project said its aim was to return names to the victims. As of 2026 the offender has not been identified and, given the passage of nearly ninety years, is presumed dead.

timeline.text: Two decapitated bodies found together in Kingsbury Run; one identified by fingerprints as Edward Andrassy, 29.
Remains of Florence Polillo found near Orange Avenue and identified by fingerprints; her head was never recovered.

Remains of a woman found beneath the Lorain-Carnegie Bridge; tentatively identified as Rose Wallace, never confirmed.
Last two victims counted in the series found at the East Ninth Street lakefront dump, within sight of City Hall.
Safety director Eliot Ness orders a sweep of the shantytown districts; the Kingsbury Run shantytowns are raided and burned.
Frank Dolezal arrested by the Cuyahoga County sheriff's office and reported to have confessed to the Polillo killing; he later recanted.
Dolezal found hanged in his cell in the Cuyahoga County jail before trial; officially ruled a suicide.
Three headless bodies found in boxcars at McKees Rocks, Pennsylvania; suspected but never officially linked to the Cleveland series.
Cuyahoga County Medical Examiner's Office and the DNA Doe Project begin exhuming unidentified victims for genetic genealogy identification.

name: Connecticut River Valley Killer

victims.suspected: At least 7 women killed; 1 woman attacked and survived

victimProfile: Women aged 17 to 39, several of them hitchhiking, driving alone or outdoors in the Claremont and Newport area of New Hampshire and across the river in Vermont
summary: Unidentified. At least seven women were stabbed to death in the Connecticut River Valley of New Hampshire and Vermont between 1978 and 1987, and a pregnant woman survived a 1988 attack. The case remains open with the New Hampshire cold case unit.
narrative: The Connecticut River Valley Killer is the name given to the unidentified person believed responsible for the stabbing deaths of at least seven women on both sides of the Connecticut River in New Hampshire and Vermont between 1978 and 1987, and for a 1988 attack on a pregnant woman who survived. Most victims were found in woods near Claremont, Newport and Unity, New Hampshire; two were found in Vermont. No one has been charged, and the New Hampshire Attorney General's Office, which has never officially linked all of the killings, treats them as open cold cases.

The first death usually included is that of Catherine Millican, 27, last seen on October 24, 1978, when she went birdwatching in New London, New Hampshire. According to the New Hampshire Union Leader, her body was found the next night off Route 11 with multiple stab wounds. Mary Elizabeth Critchley, 37, was last seen hitchhiking in July 1981 and found in Unity that August; Wikipedia records her cause of death as undetermined. Bernice Courtemanche, 17, disappeared from Claremont on May 30, 1984, and Ellen Fried, 26, a nurse, was last seen at a Claremont payphone that July. Fried's skeletal remains were found near the Sugar River in the Kellyville section of Newport in September 1985; Courtemanche's were found in Newport on April 19, 1986, and WMUR reported she had been stabbed. Eva Morse, 27, last seen hitchhiking near Charlestown in July 1985, was found fatally stabbed in West Unity six days later.

The killings also crossed into Vermont. Lynda Moore, 36, was found dead in her home in the Saxtons River area of Westminster, Vermont, on April 15, 1986; the Vermont State Police list the case as an unsolved homicide, and WMUR reported more than 20 stab wounds. Barbara Agnew, a 39-year-old nurse, went missing on January 10, 1987, after her car was found at the northbound Interstate 91 rest area in White River Junction. According to the Vermont State Police, her body was found in woods in Hartland, Vermont, and an autopsy determined homicide; Wikipedia gives the discovery date as March 28, 1987.

The last attack attributed to the series was survived. On August 6, 1988, Jane Boroski, 22 and seven months pregnant, stopped at a store in Swanzey, New Hampshire, on her way home from the Cheshire County Fair. According to WMUR, a man parked beside her, tried to pull her from her car and stabbed her 27 times before driving off. She drove to a friend's house; she and her baby survived. She gave police a description and a partial license plate. The attacks appear to have stopped afterward. Boroski has spoken publicly for decades; authorities have not publicly confirmed the link to the killings.

According to Wikipedia, investigators noted that dump sites, wound patterns and circumstances were similar enough to suggest one perpetrator; because two victims were nurses found near the Sugar River in Kellyville, the unknown man is sometimes called the Kellyville Killer. Private investigators and journalists have proposed candidates, including a man who died in a 2005 murder-suicide, but police have never publicly named a suspect, and Boroski has said she does not believe that man was her attacker.

The investigation has shown renewed activity in the 2020s. On May 21, 2024, the New Hampshire Cold Case Unit, State Police Major Crime Unit and Claremont and Newport police executed court-authorized search warrants at a residence on Ayers Road in Kellyville, Newport. The Valley News reported that the homeowner, questioned years earlier about the Fried case, said investigators took antique swords and knives that had belonged to his father; he denied any involvement and has not been charged. Attorney General's Office spokesman Michael Garrity said the search followed several years of investigation and cautioned against drawing conclusions.

On October 29, 2025, the 47th anniversary of Millican's death, the Cold Case Unit and New Hampshire Fish and Game began searching the Esther Currier Wildlife Management Area in New London for physical evidence and released previously unpublished photographs of her. The Cold Case Unit asks anyone with information to call 603-271-2663, and the Vermont State Police continue to carry the Moore and Agnew cases as unsolved homicides.

name: Coral Eugene Watts

victims.suspected: roughly 90 unsolved cases (Michigan task force estimate, 2004); some estimates exceed 80

victimProfile: Young women, mostly strangers in their late teens to thirties, attacked alone at or near their apartments
captureMethod: Arrested by Houston police on May 23, 1982, after one of two women he attacked in an apartment escaped from a balcony and he was caught fleeing the scene.
sentence: 60 years for burglary with intent to commit murder (Texas, 1982, with immunity for the confessed murders); life without parole for the murder of Helen Dutcher (Michigan, 2004); life without parole for the murder of Gloria Steele (Michigan, 2007)
fateDetail: Died of prostate cancer on the prison ward of a hospital in Jackson, Michigan, while serving Michigan life sentences
summary: Died in prison in 2007. Confessed in 1982 to 12 murders under a Texas plea deal that granted immunity and a 60-year burglary sentence, then convicted by Michigan juries in 2004 and 2007 of two earlier stabbings.
narrative: Coral Eugene Watts was a serial killer active in Michigan and Texas from 1974 to 1982. In 1982 he confessed to 12 murders under a Texas plea agreement that gave him immunity from prosecution for those killings in exchange for a guilty plea to burglary with intent to commit murder and a 60-year sentence. He was never convicted of any murder he confessed to. His only murder convictions came two decades later in Michigan, where juries found him guilty of the 1979 killing of Helen Dutcher and the 1974 killing of Gloria Steele, neither covered by the immunity deal. He died in custody in September 2007; a Michigan task force told CBS in 2004 he remained a suspect in roughly 90 unsolved cases.

According to the Michigan Court of Appeals opinion in People v. Watts (2006), Gloria Steele, a 19-year-old Western Michigan University student, was found stabbed to death in her Kalamazoo apartment on October 30, 1974. Watts, then a student there, was arrested the next month for non-fatal choking attacks on two other young women at their apartment doors. He admitted being at Steele's complex the day before the murder but denied killing her. Wikipedia reports that he pleaded no contest to assault and battery and served a year in jail.

The same opinion recites that Rebecca Huff and Glenda Richmond were stabbed to death in the Ann Arbor area in 1980, that Watts became the chief suspect after police stopped him on November 15, 1980, while he was following a woman, and that he then moved to Texas, where more homicides and assaults quickly began. He never directly confessed to the Ann Arbor murders, which were not part of the Texas deal.

The Associated Press reported that nearly all the killings Watts confessed to occurred in 1981 and 1982 in the Houston area. He was arrested on May 23, 1982, after attacking two women in a Houston apartment; CBS News reported that one, Melinda Aguilar, escaped from a balcony and a roommate was pulled from a bathtub. On the day he was due to stand trial, Harris County prosecutors agreed to a deal: Watts pleaded guilty to burglary with intent to commit murder, received 60 years, and confessed to the unsolved killings with immunity from murder charges. AP reports in November 2004 put the count at either 12 or 13 killings, all but one in Texas.

According to AP, a Texas appeals court ruling and mandatory release laws cut more than 35 years from the term, making Watts due for release in April 2006. Wikipedia and CBS News report that the appellate court found he had not been properly advised that the bathtub counted as a deadly weapon, leaving him classified as a non-violent offender eligible for good-time credit.

Facing that release, Michigan Attorney General Mike Cox made a televised appeal in January 2004. AP reported that a witness, Joseph Foy, then came forward to say he had seen the December 1979 stabbing of Helen Dutcher, 36, in a Ferndale alley from his back porch. Watts was tried in Oakland County, where Circuit Judge Richard Kuhn admitted his Texas confessions as evidence of a pattern; the defense challenged Foy's identification from 85 feet away, 25 years earlier. A jury convicted Watts on November 17, 2004, and he received the mandatory sentence of life without parole on December 7, 2004.

On the day of that verdict, Kalamazoo prosecutors charged Watts with Steele's murder. On April 25, 2006, the Michigan Court of Appeals allowed evidence of the two 1974 Kalamazoo assaults and the Huff, Richmond, Susan Wolf and Yolanda Garcia murders to show identity and motive, while barring 11 other murders and six assaults as unfairly prejudicial. A Kalamazoo jury convicted him in July 2007, and he was sentenced to life without parole on September 13, 2007, according to Wikipedia and the Detroit Free Press. He died of prostate cancer eight days later, on September 21, 2007, aged 53.

Watts was born in Killeen, Texas, on November 7, 1953, and grew up in Inkster, Michigan. According to Wikipedia, he was treated at a Detroit psychiatric clinic after assaulting a woman in 1969 and enrolled at Western Michigan University in 1974.

name: Danny Rolling
victimProfile: College students aged 17 to 23 in Gainesville apartments; a Shreveport family of three (ages 8 to 55)
captureMethod: Already jailed for a September 1990 supermarket robbery in Marion County, he was tied to the Gainesville murders after a Shreveport Crime Stoppers tip, matching type B blood evidence, and a screwdriver and tape recordings recovered from his woodland campsite.
sentence: Death on five counts of first-degree murder, plus life terms on three sexual battery and three armed burglary counts (April 20, 1994)
fateDetail: Lethal injection, Florida State Prison, October 25, 2006
summary: Executed in Florida in 2006. Danny Rolling pleaded guilty in 1994 to murdering five college students in Gainesville in August 1990 and, days before his execution, confessed in writing to the 1989 killing of three members of the Grissom family in Shreveport, Louisiana.
narrative: Danny Harold Rolling, known as the Gainesville Ripper, murdered five college students in Gainesville, Florida, over four days in August 1990 and later confessed to killing three members of a family in Shreveport, Louisiana, in November 1989. He pleaded guilty in February 1994 to five counts of first-degree murder, was sentenced to death that April, and was executed by the State of Florida on October 25, 2006. Courts convicted him of five murders. He confessed to eight. Louisiana authorities attributed the three Shreveport deaths to him but never charged him.

The earliest killings attributed to Rolling took place in his hometown. ABC News reported that William Grissom, his daughter Julie and his grandson Sean were killed in Shreveport on November 4, 1989; the Wikipedia article gives their ages as 55, 24 and 8. Investigators later noted that the posing of the bodies and tape residue at that scene resembled what was found in Gainesville a year later.

According to the Florida Commission on Capital Cases record, Rolling broke into three student apartments in Gainesville while armed with a pistol and a knife. On August 24, 1990, he killed Sonja Larson, 18, and Christina Powell, 17, in the apartment they shared. On August 25 he killed Christa Hoyt, 18, a Santa Fe College student, after watching her apartment the previous day. On August 27 he entered an apartment shared by Manuel Taboada and Tracy Paules, both 23, killed Taboada in his bedroom and then killed Paules. The victims were stabbed; the court record describes sexual battery in each incident and the posing of bodies.

The investigation first focused on Edward Humphrey, an 18-year-old student arrested days after the murders on an unrelated charge, but ABC News reported that his type A blood did not match the type B semen found at all three scenes, and he was cleared. Rolling had been booked into the Marion County Jail on September 7, 1990, for a supermarket robbery; police did not know the killer was already in custody. In November 1990, Cindy Juracich, who knew Rolling from a Shreveport church, called Crime Stoppers to name him, and investigator Don Maines found the Grissom scene strikingly similar. Rolling's blood was type B, a screwdriver from his abandoned campsite matched pry marks at the Gainesville doors, and the AP reported that DNA taken after the robbery arrest linked him to the murders. A grand jury indicted him on five counts of first-degree murder on November 15, 1991.

According to the Florida Supreme Court's 2006 opinion, Rolling initially pleaded not guilty but on February 15, 1994, the day his trial was to begin, pleaded guilty to five counts of first-degree murder, three counts of sexual battery and three counts of armed burglary with battery. On March 24, 1994, the penalty-phase jury recommended death for each murder by a 12-0 vote, and on April 20, 1994, Circuit Judge Stanley R. Morris sentenced him to death on the murder counts and to life terms on the remaining charges.

The Florida Supreme Court affirmed the convictions and death sentences on March 20, 1997, and the U.S. Supreme Court denied review that November. State postconviction relief was denied and the denial affirmed in June 2002; the Eleventh Circuit affirmed denial of federal habeas relief in February 2006. Governor Jeb Bush signed a death warrant on September 22, 2006, and the Florida Supreme Court rejected a final lethal-injection challenge on October 18, 2006.

Rolling was executed by lethal injection at Florida State Prison and pronounced dead at 6:13 p.m. on October 25, 2006. The AP reported that he made no final statement and instead sang a hymn. Shortly before the execution he handed his spiritual adviser a handwritten confession stating that he alone had killed Julie, Tom and Sean Grissom in Shreveport and that Julie Grissom's former fiance was innocent; the AP published the note two days later.

Rolling was born in Shreveport on May 26, 1954. According to the Wikipedia article, his father was a Shreveport police officer who abused his wife and sons. The AP reported that he served about eight years in prison in Alabama, Georgia and Mississippi for robberies before the Gainesville killings.

name: David Berkowitz

victims.suspected: 6 killed and 7 wounded in the eight charged shootings; in 2024 the NYPD also attributed an April 1976 Bronx shooting that wounded a woman

victimProfile: Young women and couples, mostly aged 17 to 26, shot while sitting in parked cars or walking near their homes in the Bronx, Queens and Brooklyn
captureMethod: A parking ticket issued near the scene of the final shooting placed his car in Brooklyn that night and led police to his Yonkers apartment
sentence: Six terms of 25 years to life (June 1978), one for each murder, reported as consecutive; first eligible for parole in 2002
fateDetail: Shawangunk Correctional Facility, Wallkill, New York; parole denied at his twelfth board appearance in May 2024
summary: Imprisoned. David Berkowitz, the 'Son of Sam', pleaded guilty in 1978 to six murders in New York City's 1976-77 .44-caliber shootings, which killed six and wounded seven. Sentenced to six terms of 25 years to life; parole denied twelve times.
narrative: David Berkowitz, known as the "Son of Sam" and the ".44 Caliber Killer", shot thirteen people in eight attacks in New York City between July 1976 and July 1977, killing six and wounding seven. According to the Associated Press, he pleaded guilty in 1978 and was sentenced to the maximum term of 25 years to life for each of the six killings. He has been imprisoned ever since and has been denied parole at every board appearance, most recently in May 2024.

A CBS News timeline of the case lists the attacks in order. On July 29, 1976, Donna Lauria, 18, was killed and Jody Valenti wounded as they sat in a parked car in the Bronx. On October 23, 1976, Carl Denaro and Rosemary Keenan were wounded in a parked car in Queens, and on November 27, 1976, Donna DeMasi and Joanne Lomino were shot near Lomino's Queens home; Lomino was left paralyzed. Christine Freund, 26, was killed in a parked car in Queens on January 30, 1977, and Virginia Voskerichian was shot dead outside her Queens home on March 8, 1977. On April 17, 1977, Valentina Suriani, 18, and Alexander Esau, 20, were both killed in the Bronx. Judy Placido and Sal Lupo were wounded leaving a Queens discotheque on June 26, 1977. The final attack, on July 31, 1977, in Bath Beach, Brooklyn, killed Stacy Moskowitz and cost Robert Violante the sight of one eye. ABC reported that police linked the shootings to a single gun only after the Freund killing.

A note left at the Esau-Suriani scene in April 1977 called the writer a monster and used the name "Son of Sam", ABC reported, and CBS News recorded that a letter signed the same way was mailed to Daily News columnist Jimmy Breslin on May 30, 1977 and published on June 6. The break came from the Brooklyn scene: according to the Associated Press and CBS News, a parking ticket found at the site of the last shooting led detectives to Berkowitz's car. According to Wikipedia, a Yonkers dispatcher had separately connected the "Sam" of the letters to the dog of his neighbors, the Carr family. CBS News reported that days after an August 6 incident in which a bucket of gunpowder and bullets was set alight outside the door of his neighbor Craig Glassman, detectives arrived at the building. Berkowitz was arrested at the wheel of his car outside his Yonkers apartment on August 10, 1977; police displayed the .44-caliber revolver the next day and found handwritten messages on the apartment walls.

After a court-ordered evaluation he was found competent to stand trial, CBS News reported. He pleaded guilty on May 8, 1978; according to Wikipedia the convictions were six counts of second-degree murder and seven counts of attempted murder. On June 12, 1978, he received 25 years to life for each murder, the maximum term, as the Associated Press summarized it. ABC and CBS News both described the result as six consecutive life sentences. He became eligible for parole in 2002.

According to Wikipedia, his neck was slashed by another inmate at Attica in 1979, and he was later held at Sullivan Correctional Facility before being moved to Shawangunk, where he announced an evangelical Christian conversion and asked to be called the "Son of Hope". He has often declined to seek release. At his third hearing in July 2006, ABC reported, he did not attend; the board commended his prison conduct but cited his "cold disregard" for life and the premeditated, unprovoked nature of the crimes. The Associated Press reported that the board rejected him again after a May 14, 2024 interview, his twelfth appearance.

In a 1993 television interview, according to Wikipedia, Berkowitz said he had fired the fatal shots in only three of the killings and attributed the rest to a satanic cult that included the Carr brothers, John and Michael, both of whom died within two years of his arrest. Yonkers police reopened the matter in 1996 and suspended it without charges. The case also produced New York's "Son of Sam" law, which diverted a criminal's earnings from accounts of the crime to victims. The U.S. Supreme Court struck it down on First Amendment grounds in Simon & Schuster v. Members of the New York State Crime Victims Board on December 10, 1991, and the state passed a revised statute in 1992.

Berkowitz was born Richard David Falco in Brooklyn on June 1, 1953 and adopted as an infant by Pearl and Nathan Berkowitz of the Bronx, according to Wikipedia. He graduated from Christopher Columbus High School in 1971, served in the Army, including in South Korea, and was honorably discharged in June 1974. CBS News noted that he began work as a part-time mail sorter for the Postal Service in the Bronx in March 1976, four months before the first killing, while living in an apartment on Pine Street in Yonkers.

name: Dean Corll

victims.suspected: 28 attributed by Houston police; 27 bodies recovered in 1973; a 2025 forensic review points to at least 30

victimProfile: Teenage boys and young men aged 13 to 20, most from the Houston Heights neighborhood
captureMethod: Never arrested; accomplice Elmer Wayne Henley shot him dead on August 8, 1973 and then led police to the burial sites.
fateDetail: Shot by accomplice Elmer Wayne Henley at 2020 Lamar Drive, Pasadena, Texas; the shooting was ruled self-defense
summary: Killed by his accomplice in 1973 and never charged. Dean Corll, Houston's 'Candy Man', is linked by police to 28 murders of boys and young men from 1970 to 1973; accomplices Elmer Wayne Henley and David Brooks were convicted.
narrative: Dean Arnold Corll was a Houston, Texas, electrician who, with two teenage accomplices, abducted and killed teenage boys and young men between 1970 and 1973. He was never arrested or charged. On August 8, 1973, his accomplice Elmer Wayne Henley, then 17, shot him dead at Corll's house in Pasadena, Texas, a killing authorities ruled self-defense. Houston police attributed 28 victims to Corll, and 27 bodies were recovered in August 1973. Henley and the second accomplice, David Owen Brooks, were both convicted of murder and sentenced to life terms.

According to the Wikipedia article, which draws on contemporary reporting and later investigations, the first known victim was Jeffrey Alan Konen, killed on September 25, 1970, and the last was James Stanton Dreymala, 13, killed on August 3, 1973. Victims were aged 13 to 20, and most were taken from the Houston Heights, a working-class neighborhood northwest of downtown. They were lured with the offer of a party or a ride, restrained, sexually assaulted and killed by strangulation or with a .22-caliber pistol. The bodies were buried in a rented boat shed in southwest Houston, on the beach at High Island on the Bolivar Peninsula and in woods near Lake Sam Rayburn.

The crimes came to light on the morning of August 8, 1973, when Henley telephoned Pasadena police to say he had shot Corll. ABC13 reported that Henley told officers Corll had tortured and murdered teenagers and that he and Brooks then led investigators to the graves. Police recovered 17 bodies from the boat shed on Silver Bell Street, four near Lake Sam Rayburn and six at High Island, for a total of 27. Brooks turned himself in the day after Henley's arrest. Police halted the search on August 13, 1973, after the 27th body was found, although Henley maintained that more victims were buried at the beach and in the shed.

A Harris County grand jury returned indictments on August 14, 1973: Henley on six murders and Brooks on four. Henley was tried in San Antonio in July 1974, convicted by a jury of six murders and sentenced to six consecutive 99-year terms. The Texas Court of Criminal Appeals reversed that conviction in 1978 (Henley v. State, 576 S.W.2d 66), and he was retried in Corpus Christi in June 1979, where a jury again convicted him of six murders on June 27, 1979. The Associated Press reported in 2020 that he was serving six life sentences. Brooks was tried in February 1975 for the June 1973 murder of William Ray Lawrence, 15, was convicted on March 4, 1975, and was sentenced to life imprisonment.

Identification of the victims continued for decades. Forensic work led by Harris County medical examiner's office anthropologist Sharon Derrick identified Randell Lee Harvey in October 2008, Michael Baulch in 2010, Steven Sickman and Roy Bunton in 2011 and Donald Falcon in 2014. ABC13 reported in May 2025 that Derrick's research points to at least 30 victims and that at least one set of remains is still unidentified. The Associated Press reported that Brooks died on May 28, 2020, aged 65, at Hospital Galveston after contracting COVID-19 while held at the Polunsky Unit. The house at 2020 Lamar Drive where Corll was killed was demolished on February 24, 2023, according to ABC13. KPRC reported that the Texas Board of Pardons and Paroles denied Henley parole on November 7, 2025, his 25th review, and set his next review roughly ten years away.

Corll was born on December 24, 1939, in Fort Wayne, Indiana, and his family later moved to Houston. He worked in his family's candy businesses in the Houston Heights, including the Corll Candy Company, which closed in June 1968; the free candy he handed out to local children earned him the nicknames 'Candy Man' and 'Pied Piper'. Drafted in August 1964, he served stateside and received an honorable discharge in June 1965. He then worked as an electrician and later a supervisor at Houston Lighting and Power, and in the spring of 1973 he moved into his father's former house on Lamar Drive in Pasadena, where he died.

The 27th body is found at High Island beach and the search is ended.

Brooks is convicted of the murder of William Ray Lawrence and sentenced to life.

name: Dennis Rader
victimProfile: Women, men and children in Wichita and Park City, Kansas, including a family of four, mostly killed in their own homes
captureMethod: A floppy disk he mailed to a Wichita television station was traced to Christ Lutheran Church and a user named Dennis, and familial DNA from his daughter's medical sample linked him to crime-scene evidence
sentence: Ten consecutive life sentences on ten counts of first-degree murder (August 18, 2005); a minimum of 175 years before parole consideration, according to KWCH
fateDetail: El Dorado Correctional Facility, Butler County, Kansas
summary: Serving life. Dennis Rader, the BTK killer, pleaded guilty in 2005 to ten murders in Wichita and Park City, Kansas, from 1974 to 1991 and received ten consecutive life terms. Oklahoma investigators named him a suspect in a 1976 disappearance; he is uncharged there.
narrative: Dennis Rader is an American serial killer, known by the self-chosen name BTK, who pleaded guilty in June 2005 to ten murders committed in Wichita and neighboring Park City, Kansas, between January 1974 and January 1991. He was arrested on February 25, 2005, more than 30 years after the first killings, and on August 18, 2005, a Sedgwick County judge sentenced him to ten consecutive life terms, one for each victim. He is held at the El Dorado Correctional Facility in Butler County, Kansas. In 2023 the Osage County Sheriff's Office in Oklahoma named him a prime suspect in the 1976 disappearance of a 16-year-old girl; he has not been charged in that case and denies involvement.

According to the Wikipedia article, the first four victims were members of the Otero family, Joseph and Julie Otero and two of their children, Josephine, 11, and Joseph Jr., 9, killed in their Wichita home on January 15, 1974. Kathryn Bright, 21, was killed on April 4, 1974; her brother Kevin was shot but survived. Shirley Vian Relford was killed on March 17, 1977, and Nancy Fox, 25, on December 8, 1977. After a gap of several years Rader killed Marine Hedge, 53, his Park City neighbor, on April 27, 1985; Vicki Wegerle, 28, on September 16, 1986; and Dolores Davis, 62, on January 19, 1991. Most of the victims were strangled. The killings went unsolved for decades, during which the killer sent letters to police and media that gave him his nickname, short for bind, torture, kill.

Through these years Rader lived an outwardly ordinary life in Park City. The Wikipedia article records that he served in the U.S. Air Force, worked as an installer for ADT Security Services in Wichita from 1974 to 1988, and from 1991 was a compliance officer and dogcatcher for Park City. He was a Scout leader and, the article says, was elected president of the congregation council at Christ Lutheran Church in Wichita in January 2005, weeks before his arrest. At sentencing he was 60, and USA Today reporting carried by The Spokesman-Review described him as a church president, Scout leader and suburban dogcatcher.

The case revived after BTK resumed contact with the media in the early 2000s. According to the ABA Journal, Rader sent 19 messages in all, ten of them in the 11 months before his arrest. He asked police whether he could communicate by floppy disk without being traced, and police replied through a newspaper advertisement that it would be safe. The disk he then sent to a Wichita television station showed it had last been saved by a user named Dennis and had been used at Christ Lutheran Church. Investigators also obtained, under subpoena, a medical tissue sample from his daughter, Kerri, and DNA testing showed a familial link to the killer, the ABA Journal reported; the Wikipedia article says the comparison was to DNA from under Vicki Wegerle's fingernails. Rader was arrested near his home on February 25, 2005, and charged three days later with ten counts of first-degree murder.

Rader changed his plea to guilty in June 2005, on the day his trial was to begin. At the sentencing hearing on August 18, 2005, he received ten consecutive life sentences. KWCH, the Wichita television station, reported that he must serve a minimum of 175 years before he can be considered for parole, and the Associated Press, via KMUW, listed his earliest possible release date as 2180. His wife divorced him in 2005, The Spokesman-Review reported. He was transferred to the El Dorado Correctional Facility, where he remains.

In 2023 the Osage County Sheriff's Office in Oklahoma, led by Sheriff Eddie Virden, named Rader a prime suspect in the disappearance of Cynthia Dawn Kinney, 16, who was last seen at a laundromat in Pawhuska on June 23, 1976, and has never been found. On August 22, 2023, investigators working with the Park City Police Department and assisted by the Kansas Bureau of Investigation searched the lot where Rader's former home had stood and recovered what they called items of interest, though no body or bones, KWCH reported. Undersheriff Gary Upton said the office was certain of Rader's involvement. The sheriff's office pointed to journal writings by Rader about laundromats and to his work at the time as a regional alarm installer, though the AP reported the sheriff could not confirm Rader installed alarms at the bank across the street. Rader told reporters he had been questioned but denied any role.

The district attorney did not share the sheriff's view. On September 11, 2023, Osage County District Attorney Mike Fisher said the information shared with him was insufficient to file charges and asked the Oklahoma State Bureau of Investigation to open a formal investigation, NBC News reported. Investigators also examined whether Rader was linked to the 1990 death of Shawna Beth Garber in McDonald County, Missouri; the Wikipedia article says cold-case investigators later concluded a different person was responsible. As of the sources reviewed, Rader has not been charged in either case.

name: Derrick Todd Lee
victimProfile: Women aged 21 to 44 in south Louisiana, most of them attacked in or taken from their own homes in and around Baton Rouge
captureMethod: A cheek swab collected by Zachary police and the attorney general's office on May 5, 2003, matched the DNA profile from the serial cases; Lee had left Louisiana and was arrested by police in Atlanta, Georgia
sentence: Life without parole for the second-degree murder of Geralyn Barr DeSoto (August 2004); death for the first-degree murder of Charlotte Murray Pace (imposed December 10, 2004), affirmed by the Louisiana Supreme Court in 2008
fateDetail: Held on death row at the Louisiana State Penitentiary, Angola; taken to an outside hospital on January 16, 2016, and died there on January 21, aged 47; the coroner later attributed the death to heart disease. Reports differ on whether the hospital was in Baton Rouge or Zachary
summary: Died in prison. Derrick Todd Lee was convicted of murdering two women in south Louisiana in 2002 and sentenced to death; DNA linked him to five more killings between 1998 and 2003. He died on death row in January 2016, aged 47, before any execution.
narrative: Derrick Todd Lee was a Louisiana man convicted in 2004 of murdering two women in the Baton Rouge area and linked by DNA to the deaths of five more women in south Louisiana between 1998 and 2003. A West Baton Rouge Parish jury convicted him of second-degree murder in the January 2002 killing of Geralyn Barr DeSoto, and he received life in prison; a second jury convicted him of first-degree murder in the May 2002 killing of Charlotte Murray Pace and sentenced him to death. He was never tried for the other killings. Lee died on January 21, 2016, aged 47, while still on death row at the Louisiana State Penitentiary at Angola.

According to the Wikipedia article, Lee was born on November 5, 1968, in St. Francisville, Louisiana, and before the murders had been convicted of entering an inhabited dwelling, of burglary and, in 1995 in Lake Charles, of a peeping offense. The killings attributed to him began, by the DNA count, with the 1998 disappearance of Randi Mebruer, 28, from her home in Zachary; her body has never been found. On September 24, 2001, Gina Wilson Green was found dead in her home near Louisiana State University, and on January 14, 2002, Geralyn DeSoto, 21, an LSU student, was found dead in her home, according to a WBRZ timeline.

Charlotte Murray Pace, 22, a recent LSU MBA graduate, was killed in her townhouse on Sharlo Avenue in Baton Rouge on May 31, 2002, according to the Louisiana Supreme Court. On July 9, 2002, the state police crime lab found the same DNA profile at the Green and Pace scenes, and the Baton Rouge police chief announced that the city appeared to have a single killer, WAFB reported. That same day a man forced his way into the Breaux Bridge home of Diane Alexander and attacked her until her son arrived; she survived and gave police the description used for a composite sketch. Three days later Pam Kinamore, 44, was taken from her Baton Rouge home, and her body was found near the Whiskey Bay exit of Interstate 10. Trineisha Dene Colomb, 23, of Lafayette, disappeared on November 21, 2002, and was found in woods near Scott, and Carrie Lynn Yoder, 26, was taken from her home near LSU on March 3, 2003, and found in Whiskey Bay ten days later. WBRZ reported that DNA tied each of these cases to the same unknown man.

The break came from a separate investigation. According to the Louisiana Supreme Court, Zachary police and the state attorney general's office, looking into other disappearances and murders, collected cheek swabs from Lee at his home on May 5, 2003, under a subpoena. The crime lab matched them to the serial killer's profile on May 25, an arrest warrant followed on May 26, and Atlanta police arrested Lee on May 27, 2003. CBS News reported that before the arrest authorities had traced him to an Atlanta motel through a call he made from the manager's phone. Lee waived extradition and was returned to Baton Rouge.

An East Baton Rouge Parish grand jury indicted Lee on June 25, 2003, for Pace's murder. He was first tried in West Baton Rouge Parish for DeSoto's killing and convicted of second-degree murder on August 10, 2004. The Pace trial began in Baton Rouge in September 2004. Prosecutors put on evidence of the Green, Kinamore, Colomb and Yoder killings and the Alexander attack, and Alexander testified against him. The jury convicted Lee in October 2004 and unanimously voted for death, finding that he had committed aggravated rape, and the court imposed the sentence on December 10, 2004.

On January 16, 2008, the Louisiana Supreme Court affirmed the Pace conviction and death sentence. It held that the cheek swabs were a search taken without probable cause or proven consent, but admitted the DNA because tips naming Lee after the sketch was published would have led to it lawfully. A state district judge denied post-conviction relief in August 2014, and in September 2015 the state supreme court rejected his further appeal, ABC13 in Houston reported. Lee was taken from Angola to an outside hospital on January 16, 2016, and died there on January 21; the coroner later attributed his death to heart disease.

Lee was suspected but never charged in other cases. Zachary police long suspected a connection to the August 1992 death of Connie Warner, 41, who lived in the same subdivision as Mebruer; her daughter told KPLC that her mother had reported a peeping Tom shortly before she disappeared. That case remains unsolved. The investigation also drew attention because profilers had initially said the killer was probably white, a view that DNA ancestry testing later contradicted, according to the Wikipedia article.

name: Donald Henry Gaskins
victimProfile: Acquaintances, relatives, hitchhikers and associates in the Florence and Sumter areas, among them teenagers and a two-year-old child, plus a fellow prison inmate killed for hire
captureMethod: Associate Walter Neeley told police Gaskins had killed Dennis Bellamy and John Henry Knight and later led investigators to buried bodies near Prospect
sentence: Ten life sentences (nine for murder, one for burglary) on guilty pleas after a 1976 death sentence was set aside; death sentence in 1983 for the murder of Rudolph Tyner
fateDetail: Electric chair, South Carolina, September 6, 1991, 1:10 a.m., hours after cutting his wrists
summary: Executed. Donald "Pee Wee" Gaskins was serving life sentences for nine South Carolina murders from 1970 to 1975 when he killed death-row inmate Rudolph Tyner with a bomb in 1982. Sentenced to death, he was electrocuted in 1991.
narrative: Donald Henry "Pee Wee" Gaskins was a South Carolina serial killer who was convicted of ten murders: nine killings committed between 1970 and 1975, for which he was serving life sentences, and the 1982 bombing death of fellow inmate Rudolph Tyner at the Central Correctional Institution in Columbia. A Richland County jury sentenced him to death for the Tyner killing in 1983, and he was executed in South Carolina's electric chair on September 6, 1991, aged 58. Gaskins later claimed to have killed around 100 people, but the Wikipedia article notes that law enforcement and journalists have discredited most of those claims.

Gaskins was born on March 31, 1933, in Florence County, and grew up near the rural community of Prospect. According to the South Carolina Encyclopedia, he stood barely five feet tall, which earned him his nickname, and he spent several years in a Florence reform school as a youth. The Wikipedia article says he served prison terms in the 1950s and 1960s for assault, the killing of a fellow inmate that was classed as manslaughter, and the rape of a 12-year-old girl, and that he was paroled for the last time in November 1968.

The Wikipedia article lists the killings attributed to him between 1970 and 1975, most of them in the Sumter and Florence areas. They include his 15-year-old niece Janice Kirby and Patricia Ann Alsbrook, 17, in November 1970; Martha Ann Dicks; Doreen Hope Dempsey, 22, and her two-year-old daughter Robin Michelle in 1973; Johnny Sellers and Jessie Ruth Judy in 1974; Silas Barnwell Yates in a 1975 murder for hire; Dianne Bellamy Neeley and Avery Leroy Howard in April 1975; 13-year-old Kim Gehlken; and Dennis Bellamy, 28, and John Henry Knight, 15, who were shot near Prospect in October 1975. WIS reported in June 2025 that Gaskins had admitted in court to poisoning Dicks, and that her remains, long lost after being sent to a college for study, had been found in a box on the College of Charleston campus.

Gaskins was arrested on November 14, 1975, after his associate Walter Neeley told police that Gaskins had killed Bellamy and Knight and had described other killings and burial sites, according to the Wikipedia article. On December 4, 1975, Neeley led investigators to land near Prospect where eight bodies were recovered. The South Carolina Encyclopedia says he was charged in Florence County with five murders and was sentenced to death on May 28, 1976, after a jury convicted him of killing Dennis Bellamy. That death sentence did not stand. The Fourth Circuit later recorded that Gaskins pleaded guilty under a plea bargain to several murders and was serving ten life sentences, nine for murder and one for burglary. In the sworn confession tied to that plea, he admitted killing 13 people between 1970 and 1975, according to the Wikipedia article; the Deseret News described him in 1991 as the confessed killer of 13.

While serving those sentences at the Central Correctional Institution, Gaskins worked on death row. There he was hired by Tony Cimo, the son of Myrtle Moon, to kill Rudolph Tyner, who had been sentenced to death for the 1978 robbery killings of Bill and Myrtle Moon at their grocery store in Murrells Inlet. The State newspaper reported that a first attempt with poison only made Tyner sick. According to the Fourth Circuit, Gaskins then had another inmate pass Tyner a cup-shaped speaker rigged with a wire, telling him it would let the two men talk between cells; when Tyner held it to his ear, the device exploded and killed him on September 12, 1982. Recorded collect calls between Gaskins and Cimo became key evidence. Cimo pleaded guilty to conspiracy, received eight years and was paroled after less than three, The State reported.

Gaskins was tried in the Richland County Court of General Sessions, prosecuted by Dick Harpootlian, and on March 24, 1983, was convicted of Tyner's murder and sentenced to death, with prior murder convictions and murder for hire found as aggravating factors. The South Carolina Supreme Court affirmed in State v. Gaskins (1985), state post-conviction relief was denied in 1987, and the Fourth Circuit rejected habeas petitions in 1990 and again on September 5, 1991, when it also refused a stay of execution.

Hours before his execution, Gaskins cut his wrists and arms with a razor blade, and he went to the electric chair with about 20 stitches, the Deseret News reported. He was pronounced dead at 1:10 a.m. on September 6, 1991. The Wikipedia article notes that his was the first execution in South Carolina in more than a century of a white defendant for killing a Black victim. The State reported in 2022 that he was convicted of ten murders, including Tyner's, confessed to 15 and led authorities to the remains of at least 13 people.

name: Donald Harvey

victims.suspected: No official attribution beyond the 37 he pleaded guilty to; Harvey's own claims ranged from about 50 to 87

victimProfile: Hospital patients, many of them elderly or chronically ill, at Marymount Hospital in London, Kentucky, and at Drake Memorial Hospital and the Veterans Administration Medical Center in Cincinnati; a small number of victims outside hospitals
captureMethod: A pathologist smelled cyanide during the March 1987 autopsy of Drake Memorial Hospital patient John Powell, and police traced the poisoning to Harvey, a nurse's aide on the ward.
sentence: Ohio (Hamilton County, 1987 and 1988): consecutive 20-years-to-life terms on 28 counts of aggravated murder, plus terms for attempted aggravated murder and felonious assault, recorded by the Ohio Department of Rehabilitation and Correction as 80 years to life; Kentucky (Laurel County, 1987): eight life terms plus 20 years, concurrent with the Ohio sentence
fateDetail: Beaten by another inmate at Toledo Correctional Institution on March 28, 2017; died two days later at a Toledo hospital
summary: Pleaded guilty in 1987 and 1988 to 37 murders of hospital patients and others in Ohio and Kentucky between 1970 and 1987; claimed as many as 87. Served multiple life sentences until he was beaten to death by another inmate in 2017.
narrative: Donald Harvey was a hospital orderly and nurse's aide who pleaded guilty in 1987 and 1988 to 37 murders in Ohio and Kentucky, most of them patients at hospitals where he worked between 1970 and 1987. Press coverage of his guilty pleas labeled him the "Angel of Death." The 37 count is the figure courts accepted; Harvey himself later claimed far more, with figures reported as high as 87, and the Associated Press reported that he claimed 18 additional deaths at the Cincinnati Veterans Administration Medical Center for which he was never charged. He received multiple life sentences and died in March 2017 after being beaten in his cell at Toledo Correctional Institution.

According to the Kentucky Historic Institutions account of the Marymount case, Harvey was hired as an orderly at Marymount Hospital in London, Kentucky, in May 1970, at 18, and left shortly after his last known killing there in January 1971; he later pleaded guilty to killing nine patients there by methods that included empty oxygen supplies and smothering. In March 1971 he was arrested in London for breaking into a neighbor's apartment and pleaded guilty to petty theft. He later worked at the Veterans Administration Medical Center in Cincinnati and then as a nurse's aide at Drake Memorial Hospital; the AP reported that 21 of the victims he pleaded guilty to killing were Drake patients.

The case broke open in March 1987. As WCPO-TV and the AP reported, a doctor performing an autopsy on 44-year-old Drake patient John Powell smelled cyanide, and police traced the poisoning to Harvey. WCPO anchor Pat Minarcin, following anonymous tips from Drake nurses, spent months matching Harvey's shifts against unexplained deaths on his ward, and the charges grew to two dozen. Harvey told detectives he preferred cyanide because it was hard to detect; the AP reported he also used arsenic, usually mixed into patients' food, and let some patients' oxygen run out.

On August 18, 1987, Harvey pleaded guilty in Hamilton County, Ohio, to 24 counts of aggravated murder, together with attempted aggravated murder and felonious assault counts, under a plea agreement that removed the death penalty in exchange for a full confession. The Ohio Department of Rehabilitation and Correction record for inmate A199449 lists 25 aggravated murder counts, four attempted aggravated murder counts and one felonious assault count on the 1987 Hamilton County dockets, with consecutive 20-years-to-life terms; he entered the Ohio prison system on October 26, 1987. On November 2, 1987, he pleaded guilty in Laurel County Circuit Court, Kentucky, to eight counts of murder and one of manslaughter for the Marymount patients, and Judge Lewis Hopper sentenced him to eight life terms plus 20 years, concurrent with Ohio. A further Hamilton County docket effective February 19, 1988, added three aggravated murder and three attempted aggravated murder counts; according to the Wikipedia article these non-hospital victims included a lover's father and two neighbors. The ODRC record gives a net sentence of 80 years to life and a first parole eligibility date of March 16, 2043.

Former Hamilton County Prosecutor Arthur Ney Jr. rejected Harvey's claim that he was a mercy killer, telling the AP: "He killed because he liked to kill." WCPO reported that at least 18 civil suits were filed by victims' families and that Harvey, held at Toledo Correctional Institution from 2008, began selling items to collectors online in 2011.

On the afternoon of March 28, 2017, guards found Harvey severely beaten in his cell in a protective custody unit at Toledo Correctional Institution. He died on March 30, 2017, at Mercy Health St. Vincent Medical Center in Toledo, aged 64, as NPR and the AP reported. In May 2019 a Lucas County grand jury indicted fellow inmate James D. Elliott on charges including aggravated murder; according to the Wikipedia article, citing the Toledo Blade, Elliott pleaded guilty and was sentenced in September 2019 to 25 years to life, later made concurrent with his existing sentence.

Harvey was born on April 15, 1952, in Hamilton, Ohio, and grew up in Booneville, Kentucky, according to the Wikipedia article and the ODRC record. He began working in hospitals at 18 with no formal medical training.
