name: Dorothea Puente

victims.suspected: 9 (charged); seven bodies recovered from her yard, one from the Sacramento River, one earlier death reclassified

victimProfile: Elderly, disabled or alcohol-dependent boarders, most of them Social Security or SSI recipients placed in her Sacramento boarding house
captureMethod: A social worker reported a missing tenant, police dug in the yard of 1426 F Street and found remains, and Puente, who had left Sacramento during the dig, was recognized at a Los Angeles motel bar and arrested five days later.
sentence: Two concurrent terms of life without parole for the first-degree murders of Benjamin Fink and Dorothy Miller, plus a concurrent 15 years to life for the second-degree murder of Leona Carpenter (December 10, 1993)
fateDetail: Central California Women's Facility, Chowchilla, California; natural causes, aged 82
summary: Died in prison 2011. Sacramento boarding-house operator charged with nine murders after seven bodies were dug from her yard in 1988; a Monterey County jury convicted her of three in 1993 and deadlocked on six. Two life terms without parole.
narrative: Dorothea Puente ran a boarding house at 1426 F Street in downtown Sacramento, California, where seven bodies were dug out of the yard in November 1988. Prosecutors charged her with nine murders committed between 1982 and 1988. According to the federal habeas order in Puente v. Mitchell (N.D. Cal., 2006), which recites the facts found by the California Court of Appeal, a Monterey County jury convicted her on August 26, 1993 of two first-degree and one second-degree murder with a multiple-murder special circumstance and deadlocked on six counts. She received two concurrent life terms without parole and died at the Central California Women's Facility in Chowchilla on March 27, 2011.

The earliest charged death was that of Ruth Munroe, 61, a friend who moved into Puente's flat in April 1982 and died there on April 28, 1982; the court record says toxicology showed a massive codeine overdose and the coroner listed the cause as undetermined. In August 1982 Puente was convicted of administering a controlled substance, grand theft and forgery, and was released from a five-year term on September 9, 1985. Everson Gillmouth, 77, who had moved in with her, was last heard from that September. On January 1, 1986 a body was found in a nailed wooden box beside the Sacramento River in Sutter County; a handyman testified that Puente had him build the box and dump it there. It was later identified as Gillmouth.

From 1986 Puente took in boarders, many referred by a county social worker. The court record lists the tenants named in the charges: Betty Palmer, 78; Leona Carpenter, 78; James Gallop, 62; Vera Faye Martin, 61; Dorothy Miller, 65; Benjamin Fink, 55; and Alvaro "Bert" Montoya, 51. Each disappeared within weeks or months of arriving, Puente gave explanations for their absence, and their benefit checks kept coming to 1426 F Street, where she forged the endorsements. She filled 35 prescriptions for the sedative flurazepam (Dalmane) between 1985 and 1988, and sedatives were detected in some of the remains.

The case broke after Montoya, last seen on August 24, 1988, missed appointments and his social worker, Judy Moise, filed a missing persons report; the Associated Press reported that police reopened the matter on her complaint. On November 11, 1988, detectives and Puente's parole officer visited the house, she gave permission to dig, and officers found bones and a shoe containing a foot that morning. Digging on November 12, 13 and 14 uncovered seven bodies. On November 12 Puente left for a nearby hotel and did not return. She was recognized at a Los Angeles motel bar and arrested on November 16, 1988.

An information filed July 3, 1990 charged nine counts of first-degree murder. A change of venue was granted in February 1992 because of local publicity, and the trial ran about eight months in Monterey County in 1993. The defense argued that the boarders had died naturally, or by suicide in Munroe's case, and that Puente had hidden the bodies to keep collecting their checks. The jury found her guilty of the first-degree murders of Fink and Miller and the second-degree murder of Carpenter; it deadlocked on the other six counts, 11 to 1 on four of them, and those counts were dismissed. The penalty jury also deadlocked, so no death sentence was imposed. On December 10, 1993 she was sentenced to two concurrent terms of life without parole and a concurrent 15 years to life.

The California Court of Appeal, Sixth District, affirmed the convictions on August 28, 1997 but ordered a hearing on juror misconduct claims, which the Monterey County Superior Court rejected on September 25, 1998; the California Supreme Court denied review. On March 10, 2006 the U.S. District Court for the Northern District of California denied her federal habeas petition, rejecting the argument that the evidence failed to prove the deaths were homicides. The Associated Press reported that she died of natural causes on March 27, 2011, aged 82.

Puente was born Dorothea Helen Gray in Redlands, California, on January 9, 1929, according to Wikipedia, which also records convictions for forgery in 1948, for running a brothel in 1960, and in 1978 for cashing tenants' government checks.

name: Eastbound Strangler
victimProfile: Four women aged 20 to 42 who worked in the sex trade in Atlantic City, found together in a roadside drainage ditch in November 2006
summary: Unidentified. The bodies of four women, two of them confirmed strangled or asphyxiated, were found facing east in a drainage ditch behind a Black Horse Pike motel in Egg Harbor Township, New Jersey, on November 20, 2006. No one has been charged.
narrative: The Eastbound Strangler is the name given to an unidentified killer, or killers, believed responsible for the deaths of four women whose bodies were found on November 20, 2006, in a drainage ditch behind the Golden Key Motel on the Black Horse Pike (Route 40) in Egg Harbor Township, New Jersey, just outside Atlantic City. The victims were Kim Raffo, 35, Tracy Ann Roberts, 23, Barbara V. Breidor, 42, and Molly Jean Dilts, 20. No one has been charged. The Atlantic County Prosecutor's Office described the case in 2023 as an open joint investigation with the Egg Harbor Township Police Department, and no arrest had been reported as of October 2026.

According to ABC News reporting in November 2006, the women were found within a few hundred feet of each other, face down in several inches of water with their heads turned east, toward the casinos. They were clothed but had no shoes or socks, and CBS News later reported that none of their purses, phones or other belongings were recovered. The orientation of the bodies gave the case its popular name. Decomposition indicated that the women had died on different days, ranging from about two days to roughly a month before discovery, ABC reported.

Autopsies established homicide in two of the four deaths. The Associated Press reported in November 2007 that Raffo, the most recently deceased, had been strangled with a rope or cord and had lain in the ditch for a couple of days; CBS News reported that Roberts died in a similar way, and ABC News described one death as asphyxia by unspecified means. The causes of death for Breidor and Dilts could not be determined because of the condition of their remains, according to the AP. CBS reported that toxicology found large amounts of cocaine in Raffo and Roberts, alcohol in Dilts and a potentially lethal dose of heroin in Breidor, and that investigators considered whether the victims had been sedated. Authorities have not said publicly whether one person killed all four women.

All four women were described in contemporary reporting as working in the sex trade in Atlantic City. Raffo was from Brooklyn, New York, and had lived in Florida before moving to Atlantic City; she was last seen early on November 19, 2006. Roberts was a former exotic dancer whom the AP described as being from Philadelphia and CBS as being from Delaware. Breidor, of Ventnor, was identified through dental records about a week after the discovery; CBS reported she had been missing since October 17. Dilts, from western Pennsylvania, was identified by a tattoo and had last contacted her family on October 7, 2006, according to CBS.

Then-Atlantic County Prosecutor Jeffrey S. Blitz formed a task force. CBS News reported criticism from a retired Egg Harbor Township police captain and an unnamed FBI source about how the scene was handled, which the prosecutor's office disputed, saying important evidence had been recovered from the victims' clothing and bodies. Several men were questioned over the following months. The most publicized was a former handyman at the Golden Key Motel, Terry Oleson, whose home in Alloway Township, Salem County, was searched in April 2007. He was arrested that month on an unrelated charge of secretly videotaping a teenage girl, to which he later pleaded guilty, and in June 2007 he provided DNA samples. Authorities never named him a suspect in the killings, he denied any involvement, and he was never charged in connection with the deaths.

The case slowed in later years. In July 2013, Acting Prosecutor Jim McClain told NBC10 Philadelphia that there was more than one person of interest but that the investigation had stalled, with little new information in recent years. The Wikipedia article states that a 25,000 dollar reward has gone unclaimed. In 2010, after the discovery of remains along Ocean Parkway on Long Island, investigators examined a possible connection to the Gilgo Beach killings, and the idea resurfaced in July 2023 when Suffolk County police said the Atlantic City deaths were among cases under review following the arrest of Rex Heuermann. On August 1, 2023, an Atlantic County Prosecutor's Office spokesman said that after comparing timelines and methods with Suffolk County investigators, there did not seem to be a connection between Heuermann and the 2006 homicides.

The Golden Key and neighboring motels were bought by the township with grant money and demolished in 2015, according to Casino.org. The prosecutor's office has continued to say it will follow all leads, and the four deaths remain unsolved.

Investigators search the Alloway Township home of a former Golden Key Motel handyman; he is not charged in the killings.
The former handyman, Terry Oleson, provides DNA samples; results are not disclosed and he is never named a suspect.
Prosecutor Theodore Housel describes the investigation as open and active one year after the discovery.
Investigators examine a possible link to the newly discovered Gilgo Beach killings on Long Island; no link is established.
Acting Prosecutor Jim McClain says there is more than one person of interest but the case has stalled.

Suffolk County police say the Atlantic City deaths are among cases under review after Rex Heuermann's arrest in the Gilgo Beach killings.

name: Edmund Kemper

victims.suspected: 10, including his grandparents, killed in 1964 when he was 15

victimProfile: Young women aged 15 to 23, mostly hitchhiking college students, plus his mother (52) and her friend (59)
captureMethod: Telephoned Santa Cruz police from Pueblo, Colorado, after killing his mother and her friend, confessed, and waited to be taken into custody
sentence: Eight concurrent life sentences (seven years to life per count), November 1973; death penalty unavailable under California's moratorium at the time
fateDetail: California Medical Facility, Vacaville; parole denied in July 2024, next eligible 2031
summary: Imprisoned. Edmund Kemper was convicted by a Santa Cruz County jury in 1973 of eight counts of first-degree murder for killing six young women, his mother and her friend in 1972 and 1973. He killed his grandparents in 1964 at age 15. Held at Vacaville.
narrative: Edmund Emil Kemper III is a California serial killer convicted by a Santa Cruz County jury in November 1973 of eight counts of first-degree murder. Between May 1972 and April 1973, while living with his mother in Aptos, he killed six young women, most of them hitchhiking college students, then his mother and her closest friend. According to Lookout Santa Cruz and the Wikipedia article, the jury rejected his insanity plea and found him guilty on all eight counts; he received eight concurrent life sentences and has been held since at the California Medical Facility in Vacaville. He had earlier killed his paternal grandparents in 1964, at age 15, a case handled through the juvenile and state hospital system rather than by criminal conviction.

The adult killings began on May 7, 1972, when Kemper picked up two 18-year-old Fresno State students, Mary Ann Pesce and Anita Luchessa, hitchhiking in Berkeley, and killed them, according to the Wikipedia article and Biography.com. On September 14, 1972, he killed 15-year-old Aiko Koo after picking her up on her way to a dance class. On January 7, 1973, he shot 18-year-old Cabrillo College student Cynthia Schall. On February 5, 1973, he picked up Rosalind Thorpe, 23, and Alice Liu, 20, on the University of California, Santa Cruz campus and shot them. The bodies were dismembered and left in the Santa Cruz mountains and on beaches, UPI reported in 1985, and the unsolved killings earned him the press nickname "the Co-ed Killer."

On the weekend of April 20 to 21, 1973, Kemper killed his mother, Clarnell Strandberg, 52, at their home with a hammer and a knife, according to UPI, then invited her friend Sara "Sally" Hallett, 59, to the house and strangled her. He drove east and, from Pueblo, Colorado, telephoned Santa Cruz police to confess. According to the Wikipedia article, officers did not at first take the call seriously; he called again, spoke to an officer he knew, and waited at the phone booth to be arrested. Investigators seized his car on April 27, 1973, according to a photo caption published by KRON4, and his statements led police to evidence.

Kemper was indicted on eight counts of first-degree murder on May 7, 1973, and pleaded not guilty by reason of insanity. Trial began on October 23, 1973, and he testified on November 1. Three court-appointed psychiatrists found him sane, Newsweek and UPI reported. On November 8, 1973, after about five hours of deliberation, the jury found him sane and guilty on all eight counts. He asked for the death penalty, but California then had a moratorium on capital punishment, so the court imposed concurrent terms of seven years to life on each count, according to the Wikipedia article.

Kemper first became eligible for parole in 1979. According to UPI and Newsweek, the Board of Parole Hearings denied release in 1979, 1980, 1981 and 1982, and again in 1988, 1991, 1994, 2007 and 2017; he waived hearings in 1985, 1997, 2002 and 2012. In July 2024 a three-member panel denied parole for seven more years at a hearing Kemper declined to attend. Lookout Santa Cruz reported that District Attorney Jeff Rosell told the panel Kemper "is still dangerous" and untreated, and that an April 2024 psychiatric evaluation rated him a high risk to reoffend; the board also cited a 2022 incident in which he groped a prison staff member. Kemper, then 75, used a wheelchair and had diabetes, heart disease and a prior stroke. He is next eligible in 2031.

Prison officials described his record as spotless, UPI reported in 1985. Newsweek reported that he scheduled appointments for other inmates, made ceramics and narrated audiobooks for the visually impaired until retiring from those roles after a stroke in 2015.

Kemper was born on December 18, 1948, in Burbank, California. On August 27, 1964, at 15, he shot and killed his grandmother, Maude Kemper, and grandfather, Edmund Kemper Sr., at their ranch near North Fork, according to the Wikipedia article and Biography.com. Court psychiatrists diagnosed paranoid schizophrenia and he was committed to Atascadero State Hospital. He was released to his mother's care on December 18, 1969, his 21st birthday, and moved to Santa Cruz County.

name: Edward Wayne Edwards
victimProfile: Two young couples aged 18 to 21 in Ohio and Wisconsin, and a man in his mid-20s whom he regarded as a foster son
captureMethod: Wisconsin investigators re-testing evidence from the 1980 Hack and Drew killings found an unknown DNA profile, matched it to a sample taken from Edwards in Louisville, Kentucky, and arrested him at his mobile home there
sentence: Two life terms in Jefferson County, Wisconsin, for the murders of Tim Hack and Kelly Drew (2010); two consecutive life terms in Summit County, Ohio, for the murders of William Lavaco and Judith Straub (June 2010); death, plus 10 to 25 years for aggravated robbery, in Geauga County, Ohio, for the murder of Dannie Boy Edwards (March 2011)
fateDetail: Died of natural causes on Ohio death row on April 7, 2011, at the Corrections Medical Center in Columbus, Ohio, about a month after his death sentence
summary: Died in prison. Edward Wayne Edwards pleaded guilty in 2010 and 2011 to five murders in Ohio and Wisconsin committed between 1977 and 1996. Sentenced to death in Geauga County, Ohio, for killing his foster son, he died of natural causes in April 2011.
narrative: Edward Wayne Edwards was an American con man and convicted serial killer who pleaded guilty to five murders committed in Ohio and Wisconsin between 1977 and 1996. He was arrested in Louisville, Kentucky, in July 2009 after DNA linked him to a 1980 double killing in Jefferson County, Wisconsin. In 2010 he received life terms in Wisconsin and in Summit County, Ohio, and in March 2011 a three-judge panel in Geauga County, Ohio, sentenced him to death for killing a young man he regarded as his foster son. He died of natural causes on Ohio death row in April 2011, aged 77, before any execution date arrived.

Edwards was born on June 14, 1933, in Akron, Ohio, according to the Ohio Department of Rehabilitation and Correction, under the name Charles Wayne Murray, according to the Wikipedia article. He spent the 1950s and early 1960s committing car thefts, robberies and other crimes, which he later described in a 1972 autobiography, Metamorphosis of a Criminal. He was placed on the FBI's Ten Most Wanted list in 1961 and was captured in Atlanta in 1962, the Associated Press reported. After federal prison and parole in 1967 he toured the country speaking to young people about avoiding crime. In a 2010 interview with the AP, he said the publisher had embellished most of the book.

The first killings for which he was convicted took place in Summit County, Ohio. William Lavaco, 21, of Doylestown, and Judith Straub, 18, of Sterling, were found dead on August 8, 1977, in Metropolitan Silver Creek Park in Norton, near Akron. Both had been shot at close range. Three years later, on August 9, 1980, Tim Hack and Kelly Drew, both 19, disappeared after a wedding reception at a dance hall in Jefferson County, Wisconsin. Their remains were found more than two months later several miles away, Drew's in woods and Hack's in a nearby cornfield. ABC News reported that investigators believed the pair had been stabbed and strangled. Edwards lived and worked near the dance hall and was interviewed by Wisconsin investigators at the time, but was not charged.

The Wisconsin case was reopened decades later. Investigators re-examining the evidence found DNA from an unknown donor, and a sample obtained from Edwards in Louisville produced what Jefferson County Sheriff Paul Milbrath called a confirmed hit, WAVE 3 News reported. Edwards was arrested at his mobile home in Louisville on the night of July 30, 2009, and returned to Wisconsin. The Wikipedia article says the investigation was prompted by a tip from his daughter, April Balascio. In May 2010 a Norton detective and a Summit County prosecutor's investigator interviewed Edwards in a Wisconsin jail, where he confessed to the 1977 killings.

Under a deal with prosecutors in both states, Edwards pleaded guilty on June 9, 2010, in Wisconsin to the murders of Hack and Drew, and on June 11, 2010, in Summit County Common Pleas Court before Judge Thomas Teodosio to two counts of aggravated murder for Lavaco and Straub. Teodosio imposed consecutive life terms, the maximum then available, because Ohio's death penalty statutes had been invalidated for crimes committed between 1974 and 1978. Wisconsin, which has no death penalty, imposed mandatory life terms for the Hack and Drew murders.

In a June 2010 jailhouse interview with the AP, Edwards confessed to a fifth killing: Dannie Boy Edwards, born Dannie Law Gloeckner, a man in his mid-20s whom the family had taken into their home in Burton, Ohio, in the mid-1990s. Edwards said he lured him to a secluded cemetery near the house in 1996, shot him twice with a 20-gauge shotgun and buried him in a shallow grave; the body had been found in 1997. Edwards gave his motive as life insurance money, though reported amounts differ, and he said he was confessing because he wanted to be sentenced to death. He told the AP he had killed only five people. Geauga County prosecutors indicted him on aggravated murder charges, and on March 8, 2011, he pleaded guilty in Geauga County Common Pleas Court. A three-judge panel imposed the death sentence he had asked for, the AP reported. The victim's sister told The Plain Dealer that life in prison would have been harsher.

Edwards was found dead in his cell at the Corrections Medical Center in Columbus on April 7, 2011, of what were believed to be natural causes, according to the Wikipedia article; Ohio prison records list him as released due to death. Some writers, notably a retired detective in a 2014 book, have since tied him to the Zodiac killings and other notorious crimes. The Wikipedia article says those claims were met with almost universal disdain, especially from law enforcement, and no court or investigating agency has attributed any killing beyond the five to him.

Pleads guilty in Wisconsin to the murders of Tim Hack and Kelly Drew; later receives mandatory life terms.

name: Freeway Phantom
victimProfile: Black girls and young women aged 10 to 18, abducted on errands or on their way home in Southeast Washington, D.C.
summary: Unidentified. The Freeway Phantom abducted and strangled six Black girls and young women, aged 10 to 18, in Washington, D.C., between April 1971 and September 1972, leaving their bodies beside roads in D.C. and Prince George's County, Maryland. No one has been charged; the cases remain open.
narrative: The Freeway Phantom is the press's name for the unidentified killer of six Black girls and young women, aged 10 to 18, abducted in Washington, D.C., between April 1971 and September 1972. Their bodies were left beside roads in the District and in Prince George's County, Maryland, several along Interstate 295. No one has ever been charged. The Metropolitan Police Department (MPD) lists the six killings as open cold cases, with a reward of up to $150,000.

According to Wikipedia and a 2025 history by WETA's Boundary Stones, Carol Denise Spinks, 13, left home in Southeast Washington for a 7-Eleven on April 25, 1971, and was found strangled on May 1 behind St. Elizabeths Hospital near I-295. Darlenia Denise Johnson, 16, disappeared on July 8, 1971, and was found on July 19 about fifteen feet from where Spinks had lain. Brenda Faye Crockett, 10, was sent to a store on July 27, 1971, and found the next morning along U.S. Route 50 in Prince George's County. Nenomoshia Yates, 12, vanished walking home from a Safeway on October 1, 1971, and was found within hours off Pennsylvania Avenue in Prince George's County. Most had been strangled and sexually assaulted, and most were missing their shoes.

Brenda Denise Woodard, 18, boarded a bus late on November 15, 1971, and was found hours later on a Baltimore-Washington Parkway ramp near Prince George's County Hospital, stabbed and strangled. A note in her coat pocket read, in part, "this is tAntAmount to my insensititivity to people especiAlly women. I will Admit the others wheN you cAtch me iF you cAn! FRee-wAy PhanTom." According to Wikipedia, authorities concluded from handwriting that Woodard wrote it herself at the killer's dictation. The last victim, Diane Denise Williams, 17, boarded a bus on Martin Luther King Avenue late on September 5, 1972; the Washington Examiner reported she was found strangled the next morning beside southbound I-295 just outside the District line.

The investigation involved MPD homicide and sex-squad detectives, Prince George's and Montgomery County investigators, the Maryland State Police and the FBI, which joined a task force after the fourth killing, according to Boundary Stones. Hairs not belonging to the victims were recovered from three of them, and investigators concluded one offender was likely responsible. Boundary Stones also reported that police at first treated Spinks as a runaway and that in 1974 a Virginia inmate claimed to know the killer's identity but the FBI found his account inconsistent. Wikipedia, citing Washington Post reporting, says detectives interviewed members of a group of convicted rapists at Lorton prison and, in the late 1970s, searched the home of a man with earlier murder charges who had been arrested for an unrelated rape. No evidence was found and he was never charged; he died in federal custody in 2010.

The case files did not survive intact. According to Boundary Stones, when Sergeant Romaine Jenkins reopened the cases in 1987 she found that files and physical evidence had been destroyed or lost; she and the FBI reconstructed part of the record, and in 1990 FBI analysts produced a behavioral profile. The D.C. Council afterward required evidence in unsolved homicides to be kept for 65 years. In 2006 MPD offered a reward of up to $150,000, and in February 2009 the Washington Examiner reported that a DNA discovery could help solve the Williams killing.

The investigation remains formally open. In a December 2017 Freedom of Information Act response released by MPD, the department said the records "pertain to an open investigation" that is "ongoing and active," and that only Spinks and Johnson were found in the District and investigated by MPD, while Prince George's County police are investigating the other four murders. In January 2021 the Mayor's Office of Legal Counsel affirmed MPD's refusal to release the files because disclosure would interfere with an enforcement proceeding. On February 28, 2023, MPD published two sets of FOIA records, mostly correspondence. Boundary Stones, citing a May 2024 Washington City Paper report, noted that a 1974 FBI report could not be located.
The victims were schoolgirls and teenagers from Southeast Washington, most taken within blocks of home. Diane Williams's sister told Boundary Stones, "There is no closure."

Diane Denise Williams, 17, boards a bus on Martin Luther King Avenue; she is found strangled the next morning beside southbound I-295 just outside the District line. She is considered the last victim.

name: Gary Heidnik
victimProfile: Two women murdered (Sandra Lindsay, 24, and Deborah Dudley, 23) among six Black women aged 18 to 25 abducted in North Philadelphia and held captive in his basement; four survived
captureMethod: Captive Josefina Rivera, briefly allowed out of the house, called police, who stopped Heidnik's car and freed the remaining women from his basement
sentence: Death on two counts of first-degree murder, plus a cumulative 150 to 300 years on kidnapping, rape and related counts (jury verdict July 1, 1988; formally sentenced March 2, 1989)
fateDetail: Lethal injection, State Correctional Institution at Rockview, Bellefonte, Pennsylvania, July 6, 1999; the last execution carried out in Pennsylvania
summary: Executed in 1999. Gary Heidnik held six women captive in his Philadelphia basement from November 1986 to March 1987; two died. A jury convicted him of two first-degree murders in 1988.
narrative: Gary Michael Heidnik was a Philadelphia, Pennsylvania, man who from November 1986 to March 1987 abducted six women and held them chained in the basement of his house on North Marshall Street, where two of them died. A Philadelphia jury convicted him on July 1, 1988, of two counts of first-degree murder plus kidnapping, rape, aggravated assault and involuntary deviate sexual intercourse counts, and he was sentenced to death. According to the federal opinion in White v. Horn (E.D. Pa. 1999), the Pennsylvania Supreme Court affirmed the death sentences in Commonwealth v. Heidnik, 526 Pa. 458 (1991). Heidnik was executed by lethal injection on July 6, 1999, and remains the last person put to death by Pennsylvania.

The captives, all Black women, were Josefina Rivera, Sandra Lindsay, Lisa Thomas, Deborah Dudley, Jacqueline Askins and Agnes Adams, as named in CNN reporting carried by CBS News and in a Philadelphia magazine oral history. Rivera, taken first, said Heidnik picked her up on November 25, 1986. Lindsay, who her sister told CNN was intellectually disabled, disappeared the day after Thanksgiving 1986. Thomas was taken shortly before Christmas, Dudley around New Year's Day 1987 and Askins in January 1987. Survivors said the women were chained, kept in a pit dug in the basement floor, starved, beaten and raped.

Lindsay died in February 1987 after being left suspended by her wrists; the prosecutor and defense lawyer both described her death to Philadelphia magazine as suffocation. Heidnik dismembered her body; remains were later found in the house. Dudley died in March 1987 when Heidnik ran an electric current to her chains while she lay in the water-filled pit, according to the Daily Pennsylvanian's account of the Supreme Court record; her body was left in a New Jersey state forest.

The case came to light on March 24, 1987. Heidnik took Rivera out that night to help him pick up Agnes Adams, then let her leave briefly; she called police and said she had been held for four months and that other women remained in the basement. Officers stopped Heidnik's car near 6th and Girard, Rivera identified him, and police entering the house found two women chained in the basement, a third in the pit and human remains in the kitchen. Heidnik was arrested that night.

At trial before Judge Lynne Abraham, defense lawyer A. Charles Peruto Jr. argued insanity; prosecutor Charles Gallagher countered with evidence that Heidnik had grown a $1,500 brokerage deposit into a portfolio worth more than $500,000. The jury rejected the defense and on July 1, 1988, convicted him of two counts of first-degree murder, six of kidnapping, five of rape, four of aggravated assault and two of involuntary deviate sexual intercourse, as summarized by Wikipedia and the Daily Pennsylvanian. UPI reported two death sentences plus a cumulative 150 to 300 years; White v. Horn gives the sentencing date as March 2, 1989.

Heidnik never challenged his sentence and asked the Pennsylvania Supreme Court to skip its mandatory review, which the court said the law did not permit. In March 1991 the court, in an opinion by Justice Rolf Larsen, found the evidence sufficient and the death sentences not disproportionate. In April 1997 he came within hours of execution before an anti-death-penalty group and his daughter, Maxine Davidson White, won stays over his competency. A state judge found him competent, the Pennsylvania Supreme Court upheld that finding on August 19, 1998, and in June 1999 it held that White lacked next-friend standing. On July 3, 1999, the federal district court denied her petition for a stay. He was executed at the State Correctional Institution at Rockview in Bellefonte on July 6, 1999.

Heidnik was born on November 22, 1943, in Eastlake, Ohio. According to Wikipedia, he enlisted in the Army at 17, trained as a medic, and was discharged in 1962 after a diagnosis of schizoid personality disorder. In 1971 he incorporated a church and later posed as a bishop, holding services at his home for a congregation largely of people with intellectual disabilities. In 1978 he was convicted of kidnapping and rape after taking a woman from a state hospital on day leave; he was released in April 1983.

name: Gary Michael Hilton
victimProfile: Hikers and forest visitors, an elderly couple and two women aged 24 and 46, abducted on or near national forest and state park land and robbed of their bank cards
captureMethod: Arrested in the Atlanta area after authorities publicized his description and received numerous calls; the arrest warrant said he was caught after trying to use Meredith Emerson's credit card
sentence: Georgia: life with parole eligibility after 30 years for the Emerson murder (January 31, 2008); Florida: death for the Dunlap murder (April 21, 2011); federal: life without parole under a March 2012 plea agreement for the Bryant murders
fateDetail: On Florida death row since April 2011; Union Correctional Institution, Raiford, Florida, according to the Wikipedia article
summary: Imprisoned. Gary Michael Hilton was convicted of killing four people on forest land in 2007 and 2008: Meredith Emerson in Georgia, Cheryl Dunlap in Florida and John and Irene Bryant in North Carolina. He is under a Florida death sentence.
narrative: Gary Michael Hilton is an American serial killer, often called the National Forest Serial Killer, who was convicted of four murders committed on or near public forest land in North Carolina, Florida and Georgia between October 2007 and January 2008. He pleaded guilty in Georgia in January 2008 to the murder of hiker Meredith Emerson and received life in prison; a Leon County, Florida jury convicted him in 2011 of murdering Cheryl Dunlap and he was sentenced to death; and in March 2012 he pleaded guilty in federal court in Asheville, North Carolina, to murdering John and Irene Bryant. He remains on Florida's death row.

The first known killings were of John and Irene Bryant, a couple in their 80s from western North Carolina who disappeared in October 2007 while hiking in Pisgah National Forest. According to the Wikipedia article, Irene Bryant's body was found near a trail in November 2007 and she had been beaten to death. Skeletal remains found by a hunter in Macon County in early February 2008 were identified as John Bryant on February 4, 2008, when Transylvania County Sheriff David Mahoney said he believed Hilton was responsible for both deaths, CBS News reported. In his later federal plea, Hilton admitted shooting John Bryant within the Nantahala National Forest in Macon County and killing Irene Bryant within the Pisgah National Forest in Transylvania County, according to the U.S. Attorney's Office.

Cheryl Dunlap, 46, a nurse and Sunday school teacher from the Tallahassee area, was last seen alive on December 1, 2007, at Leon Sinks, according to the Florida Supreme Court. Her car was found on December 3 with a tire punctured by a bayonet, and a hunter found her body in the Apalachicola National Forest on December 15. The court recounted that her ATM card was used on December 2, 3 and 4 to withdraw $700, that witnesses placed Hilton near Leon Sinks and in the forest that month, that a bayonet recovered in Georgia was matched to the tire punctures, and that her DNA was found on items taken from his van.

On New Year's Day 2008, Meredith Emerson, 24, was hiking with her dog in the north Georgia mountains near Blood Mountain in Union County. The Associated Press reported that Hilton abducted her and spent three days trying to drain her bank accounts while she gave him incorrect PIN numbers, and that he killed her on January 4 by striking her in the head. He was arrested after authorities released his description and received numerous calls; the AP, citing the arrest warrant, said he was caught after trying to use her credit card. The Florida Supreme Court described a witness calling police after seeing him near a convenience store's dumpsters. Accounts differ on whether the arrest was made on January 4 or January 5.

Hilton, then 61, agreed through his lawyer to lead investigators to Emerson's body, which was found nearly 50 miles from where she disappeared, in exchange for prosecutors not seeking the death penalty. On January 31, 2008, a specially called Dawson County grand jury indicted him and he pleaded guilty to murder the same day before Judge Bonnie Oliver of Dawson County Superior Court, who imposed life in prison with the possibility of parole after 30 years. The judge said she accepted the deal because Hilton would likely die before any execution could be carried out, the AP reported. In interviews later released by the Georgia Bureau of Investigation, he described Emerson resisting him throughout.

A Leon County grand jury indicted Hilton on February 28, 2008, for first-degree murder, kidnapping and two counts of grand theft in the Dunlap case, and he was driven from Georgia to Florida on June 6, 2008. His trial began on February 2, 2011. The jury unanimously recommended death on February 21, 2011, and the trial court sentenced him to death on April 21, 2011, finding six aggravating circumstances, including that the murder was especially heinous, atrocious or cruel and was cold, calculated and premeditated. The Florida Supreme Court affirmed the conviction and sentence on March 21, 2013, and in August 2021 rejected his postconviction claims of ineffective counsel, according to UPI and WCTV.

A federal grand jury returned a five-count indictment in June 2011 charging Hilton with the kidnapping, robbery and murder of the Bryants on national forest land. On March 27, 2012, he pleaded guilty to their murders and to related robbery, kidnapping and firearms offenses under an agreement providing for life in prison without parole. According to the Wikipedia article, Hilton was born on November 22, 1946, in Atlanta, and he has been examined as a possible suspect in several other deaths and disappearances in the Southeast, none of which has led to a charge.

name: Gary Ridgway

victims.suspected: At least 71 (49 confirmed plus about 22 additional suspected)

victimProfile: Women and teenage girls, most of them sex workers or runaways picked up along Pacific Highway South in King County
captureMethod: DNA from a saliva sample police had collected from him in 1987 was matched to evidence recovered from three of the earliest victims.
sentence: 48 consecutive life sentences without parole (2003); a 49th consecutive life sentence (2011)
fateDetail: Washington State Penitentiary, Walla Walla
summary: Imprisoned. Gary Ridgway, the Green River Killer, pleaded guilty in 2003 to 48 murders of women and girls in King County, Washington, between 1982 and 1998, and to a 49th in 2011. He is serving 49 consecutive life sentences without parole.
narrative: Gary Leon Ridgway, known as the Green River Killer, is an American serial killer who murdered women and teenage girls in King County, Washington, between 1982 and 1998. He pleaded guilty in King County Superior Court on November 5, 2003, to 48 counts of aggravated first-degree murder, and on February 18, 2011, to a 49th. He is serving 49 consecutive life sentences without parole at the Washington State Penitentiary in Walla Walla. In taped interviews he claimed as many as 71 victims, and investigators continue to examine other cases as possibly connected.

The killings began in the summer of 1982. According to the victim list published by The Seattle Times when Ridgway entered his pleas, the first, Wendy Lee Coffield, 16, disappeared on July 8, 1982; her body was found in the Green River near Kent on July 15. Most of the 48 women and girls he admitted killing disappeared in 1982 and 1983 from the Pacific Highway South corridor between Seattle and Tacoma, where many were working as prostitutes or living as runaways. Ridgway strangled his victims, by hand or with a ligature, and left their bodies in wooded areas south and east of Seattle. Later admitted killings were sporadic: Patricia Barczak in 1986, Roberta Hayes in 1987, Marta Reeves in 1990 and Patricia Yellow Robe in 1998.

The King County Sheriff's Office formed the Green River Task Force in 1982, and Ridgway came to its attention early. The Associated Press reported that in 1983 the boyfriend of victim Marie Malvar told police he had seen her get into Ridgway's pickup; Ridgway denied knowing her and was cleared. In 1984 he contacted the task force himself, passed a polygraph examination and was cleared again. Police collected hair and saliva samples from him in April 1987, but DNA technology of the time could not produce a match.

The break came nearly two decades later. According to The Associated Press, advances in DNA analysis allowed the 1987 saliva sample to be matched to DNA recovered from the bodies of three of the earliest victims. Ridgway, then 52, was arrested on November 30, 2001, as he left his longtime job as a painter at the Kenworth truck plant in Renton.

Facing the death penalty, Ridgway signed a plea agreement with King County prosecutors on June 13, 2003. In exchange for his life, he agreed to confess, to help investigators find victims whose remains had never been located and to plead guilty to any future King County charge corroborated by reliable evidence. He led investigators to the remains of Pammy Avent, Marie Malvar and April Buttram. On November 5, 2003, he pleaded guilty to 48 counts of aggravated first-degree murder, four of them for victims known only as Jane Doe. On December 18, 2003, Judge Richard A. Jones sentenced him to 48 consecutive life terms without parole; The Seattle Times reported a $480,000 fine, $10,000 per victim, and 48 seconds of courtroom silence.

The agreement was invoked again in 2011. On December 21, 2010, teenagers found a skull in a ravine near Auburn that was identified as Rebecca Marrero, 20, last seen leaving a motel in 1982. Ridgway had confessed to killing her in 2003 but was not charged for lack of conclusive evidence. On February 18, 2011, he pleaded guilty to her murder in Kent, and Judge Mary E. Roberts imposed a 49th consecutive life sentence. In September 2024 Ridgway was briefly booked into the King County jail on an investigative hold; KOMO News reported the sheriff's office was still examining potentially related cases. In December 2025 the Department of Corrections denied reports that he was receiving end-of-life care.

Ridgway was born in Salt Lake City, Utah, on February 18, 1949, grew up in the SeaTac area and graduated from Tyee High School in 1969. He served in the U.S. Navy, including a deployment to Vietnam, was married three times, and worked for about three decades as a spray painter at the Kenworth plant before his arrest.

name: Gary Schaefer
victimProfile: Girls aged 11 to 13 from Springfield, Vermont, abducted from roads near their homes
captureMethod: A friend who escaped the Richards abduction described the abductor and his car, and the description and other evidence led Springfield police to Schaefer
sentence: 30 years to life on a no contest plea to kidnapping, sexual assault and second-degree murder of Catherine Richards, together with a kidnapping charge from a 1982 abduction (sentenced January 1984)
fateDetail: Kentucky State Penitentiary, Eddyville, Kentucky, where he had been held under the Interstate Corrections Compact since May 1985; acute medical event, death not considered suspicious
summary: Died in prison. Gary Schaefer was convicted of the 1983 murder of 11-year-old Katy Richards in Springfield, Vermont, confessed to a 1981 killing and was charged in a third. Serving 30 years to life, he died in a Kentucky prison in 2023.
narrative: Gary Lee Schaefer was a Springfield, Vermont, auto mechanic who was convicted of the 1983 kidnapping, sexual assault and murder of 11-year-old Catherine "Katy" Richards and was the prime suspect in the killings of two other Springfield girls between 1979 and 1983. Under a plea agreement he confessed to the 1981 murder of 12-year-old Theresa Fenton, and he was charged with, but never tried for, the 1979 murder of 13-year-old Sherri Nastasia. Sentenced to 30 years to life, he spent most of his sentence at the Kentucky State Penitentiary in Eddyville, where he died on November 26, 2023, at age 72, according to the Vermont Department of Corrections.

According to the Wikipedia article, Schaefer was born in 1951 in Allentown, Pennsylvania, and grew up in Springfield, where his family belonged to a Christadelphian congregation. He served in the Navy and, after returning to Springfield, worked as a mechanic at a local car dealership and lived in the family farmhouse. Acquaintances described him at the time of his arrest as quiet and religious; a forensic psychologist who studied the case, Tom Powell, told WCAX in 2023 that Schaefer presented himself as a fundamentalist Christian and was able to deceive the people around him.

The first of the three deaths later linked to him was that of Sherri Nastasia, who disappeared from Springfield in late August 1979. The Wikipedia article says she was last seen getting into a man's car and that her skeletal remains were found near a highway rest area in Rockingham several months later and identified through dental records. On August 31, 1981, Theresa Fenton was abducted while riding her bicycle in Springfield and beaten in a wooded area; she was found alive but died the next day at a hospital in Hanover, New Hampshire, according to the Wikipedia article. Both investigations stalled without an arrest.

On April 9, 1983, Katy Richards was walking with a friend in Springfield when a man forced her into his car with threats; the friend ran for help. Richards was found dead in woods near the town the next day, about 18 hours after she was last seen, WCAX reported. The friend's description and other evidence led police to Schaefer, then 31, and he was arraigned on kidnapping charges in Windsor County District Court on April 11, 1983, according to the Brattleboro Reformer. Investigators also tied him to the November 1982 abduction of a 17-year-old Brattleboro girl, who had escaped from his car in White River Junction.

Schaefer was charged with the Richards murder in June 1983 and initially pleaded not guilty. He later changed his plea to no contest and, under a plea agreement, was convicted of kidnapping, sexual assault and second-degree murder in the Richards case and of kidnapping in the 1982 abduction; he was sentenced to 30 years to life, VTDigger and the Department of Corrections reported. VTDigger reported that the agreement also required him to confess to the kidnapping, sexual assault and murder of Theresa Fenton, and the Wikipedia article says the deal protected him from prosecution in her death. He was never charged with that killing.

Prosecutors did charge Schaefer with first-degree murder in the death of Sherri Nastasia, but the charge was dropped after a judge ruled that a confession he had given police was improper evidence because it was obtained under hypnosis. VTDigger dates the dismissal to 1985; the Wikipedia article cites a Brattleboro Reformer report from April 1986. The Nastasia killing has never been resolved in court. Prosecutor William Bos explained the limits of the earlier investigations by saying a man could not be charged with murder merely because one crime resembled another, WCAX reported.

Vermont has no maximum-security prison, and in May 1985 Schaefer was transferred to the Kentucky State Penitentiary under the Interstate Corrections Compact. VTDigger reported that although he had served his minimum term, he was not eligible for release because he had not completed required treatment and rehabilitation programs. Just after midnight on November 26, 2023, staff found him experiencing an acute medical event during a routine cell check; he was taken to a hospital, where efforts to save him failed. Corrections officials said the death did not appear suspicious, and the state Defender General's office said it would conduct its own review.

name: Genene Jones

victims.suspected: more than a dozen to as many as 60

victimProfile: Infants and young children in her care, aged about 3 months to 2 years, in a pediatric intensive care unit and a pediatric clinic
captureMethod: Clinic staff tied a cluster of respiratory arrests to Jones and found a tampered vial of succinylcholine, prompting a grand jury investigation and her arrest
sentence: 99 years for the murder of Chelsea McClellan and a concurrent 60 years for injury to a child (1984); life, parole-eligible after 20 years, for the murder of Joshua Sawyer (2020)
fateDetail: Texas Department of Criminal Justice, Dr. Lane Murray Unit, Gatesville, Texas
summary: Imprisoned. Texas pediatric nurse convicted by a jury in 1984 of murdering 15-month-old Chelsea McClellan and injuring another child; pleaded guilty in 2020 to the 1981 murder of 11-month-old Joshua Sawyer. Suspected in up to 60 infant deaths.
narrative: Genene Jones is a former licensed vocational nurse from San Antonio, Texas, who was convicted by a jury in 1984 of murdering a 15-month-old patient at a Kerrville pediatric clinic and of injuring a second child in San Antonio. Her known crimes span 1981 to 1982, at Bexar County Hospital (now University Hospital) in San Antonio and at a small clinic in Kerrville. She was sentenced to 99 years and a concurrent 60 years in 1984. Facing mandatory release in 2018 under an old Texas good-time law, she was indicted in 2017 for five more infant deaths and, on January 16, 2020, pleaded guilty to one of them, the 1981 murder of 11-month-old Joshua Sawyer, receiving a life sentence. Courts have convicted her of two murders. Prosecutors have suspected her in far more: ABC News reported that prosecutor Ron Sutton estimated between 11 and 46 infant deaths in Bexar County from 1978 to 1982, and NBC News reported in 2017 that she was suspected of killing as many as 60 infants in Bexar and Kerr counties. Those figures are suspicion, not findings of any court.

According to ProPublica, Jones worked the 3 p.m. to 11 p.m. shift in the pediatric intensive care unit at Bexar County Hospital in the early 1980s, a shift that colleagues came to call "the Death Shift" because of the number of children who died on it. The five children named in the 2017 indictments, four boys and one girl aged three months to two years, died between July 1981 and January 1982; prosecutors alleged overdoses of the anti-seizure drug Dilantin, the blood thinner heparin, or an unknown substance. ProPublica reported that the hospital conducted internal probes and ousted Jones without alerting criminal authorities, then gave her a good recommendation.

In 1982 Jones went to work for pediatrician Kathleen Holland's new clinic in Kerrville. ProPublica reported that eight children with routine medical problems stopped breathing there in a single month and one died: Chelsea McClellan, 15 months old, who was injected with the paralyzing muscle relaxant succinylcholine on September 17, 1982. Wikipedia's account, citing contemporary reporting, states that suspicions at the clinic centered on a vial of succinylcholine that had been tampered with, that Jones failed a polygraph and was fired by Holland in September 1982, and that she was arrested at her San Angelo home on May 24, 1983, charged with McClellan's murder.

The murder trial was moved on a change of venue to Georgetown, in Williamson County. A jury convicted Jones of murder in February 1984, and on May 14, 1984, she was sentenced to 99 years in prison, according to ABC News. Later in 1984 she was sentenced to a concurrent 60 years for injury to a child: ProPublica reported the conviction concerned 1-month-old Rolando Santos, who nearly died from repeated heparin overdoses at the San Antonio hospital but survived. In the 1980s the Bexar County district attorney suspected Jones in other child deaths but did not charge her.

Texas's 1977 Mandatory Supervision law, meant to ease prison overcrowding, awarded good-time credit that required Jones's release after she had served roughly a third of her sentence. ABC News reported in 2013 that the Texas Department of Criminal Justice then projected her release for February 2018; ProPublica later gave the scheduled date as March 2018, after 34 years and eight months served. The Texas Board of Nursing revoked her license on June 10, 2011, after she wrote the board a letter apologizing for "the damage I did to all because of my crime" and calling her conduct heinous, ProPublica reported. Prosecutors also cited a 1998 parole interview in which, according to the parole officer, Jones said, "I really did kill those babies."

To prevent her release, Bexar County District Attorney Nico LaHood's office obtained new murder indictments. ProPublica reported the first, returned May 25, 2017, charged her in the December 1981 death of Joshua Sawyer, 11 months, from a Dilantin overdose; further indictments followed for Rosemary Vega, 2, who died September 16, 1981, Richard "Ricky" Nelson, 8 months, who died in July 1981, Patrick Zavala, 4 months, who died in January 1982, and Paul Villareal. Each carried a $1 million bond, and Jones was moved to the Bexar County jail when her state sentence ended. NBC News quoted LaHood saying his office aimed to hold her "accountable for as many children's deaths as the evidence will support."

On January 16, 2020, Jones, then 69, pleaded guilty before state District Judge Frank Castro to the murder of Joshua Sawyer and was sentenced to life in prison; the other four murder counts were dismissed under the plea agreement, ProPublica reported. She must serve 20 years before becoming eligible for parole, with credit for about two years in jail awaiting trial, which places her first eligibility around 2038, when she would be 87. Wikipedia, citing Texas Department of Criminal Justice records, lists her at the Dr. Lane Murray Unit in Gatesville.

Jones was born on July 13, 1950, in Texas, and was adopted and raised in San Antonio, according to Wikipedia. She graduated from high school in 1968, married and later divorced, had two children, and became a licensed vocational nurse in 1977, joining the Bexar County Hospital pediatric ICU in October 1978. Her case prompted a 1983 Texas Monthly investigation and the 1989 book The Death Shift, both by journalist Peter Elkind, who continued covering her prosecution for ProPublica.

name: Gerald Stano

victims.suspected: 9 to 41

victimProfile: Young women and teenage girls in Florida, including hitchhikers, students, sex workers and women with car trouble
captureMethod: Arrested in Daytona Beach for the stabbing of Donna Hensley; a detective linked her wounds to the Mary Carol Maher killing and Stano confessed to it the same day
sentence: Six life sentences on guilty pleas (1981 to 1983); death sentences for the murders of Susan Bickrest and Mary Kathleen Muldoon (guilty pleas, June 1983) and Cathy Lee Scharf (jury trial, December 1983)
fateDetail: Electrocuted at Florida State Prison on March 23, 1998, for the murder of Cathy Lee Scharf
summary: Executed. Gerald Stano was convicted of nine murders of young women in Florida between 1973 and 1980 and confessed to about 41 in three states, though police doubted several confessions. He died in Florida's electric chair in March 1998.
narrative: Gerald Eugene Stano was a Florida serial killer who was convicted of nine first-degree murders of young women committed between 1973 and 1980, mostly in and around Daytona Beach in Volusia County. He confessed to killing about 41 women in Florida, New Jersey and Pennsylvania, but no killing outside Florida was ever charged, and police were skeptical of several of his confessions. Stano pleaded guilty to eight of the murders and was convicted by a jury of a ninth, the killing of 17-year-old Cathy Lee Scharf in Brevard County. He received six life sentences and three death sentences, and was executed in Florida's electric chair at Florida State Prison on March 23, 1998, aged 46.

Stano was born in Schenectady, New York, in 1951, according to the Wikipedia article. The Tampa Bay Times reported at his execution that social workers said his birth mother abused and neglected him, that he went to a foster home at six months and was adopted at 13 months although a psychiatrist had called him unadoptable, and that he had serious behavior problems as a child and was often in trouble with the law as an adult. He later lived in Ormond Beach and worked as a short-order cook.

The case opened on April 1, 1980, when Daytona Beach detective James Gadberry arrested Stano for the aggravated battery of Donna Hensley, a woman who had been stabbed. According to findings of fact by a federal district court, later reproduced by the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Eleventh Circuit, Gadberry noticed that her wounds resembled those of Mary Carol Maher, a 20-year-old whose killing his department was investigating, and Stano confessed to the Maher murder that day. Sergeant Paul Crow of the Daytona Beach police then took charge of questioning. Under a plea agreement with Seventh Judicial Circuit prosecutors that ruled out the death penalty for killings with bodies found in that circuit, Stano pleaded guilty on September 2, 1981, to the Volusia County murders of Maher, Toni Vann Haddocks and Nancy Heard and was sentenced to life in prison.

In 1982 Stano confessed to many more killings. On August 15 and October 8, 1982, he confessed to Crow the murders of Susan Bickrest, found in Spruce Creek in December 1975, and Mary Kathleen Muldoon, killed in November 1977. A Volusia County grand jury indicted him on January 18, 1983. United Press International reported that he had by then pleaded guilty to eight murders in Volusia, Alachua and Bradford counties and was serving six life terms. He pleaded guilty to the Bickrest and Muldoon murders on March 11, 1983, and on June 13, 1983, Circuit Judge S. James Foxman sentenced him to death in both cases, citing his prior convictions and lack of remorse.

The Scharf case was the only one tried before a jury. Scharf, of Port Orange, disappeared in December 1973 and her skeletal remains were found the next month in the Merritt Island National Wildlife Refuge, UPI reported. The first trial ended with a hung jury. On retrial in Titusville, the state introduced a taped 1982 confession to a Brevard County detective and testimony from jailhouse informant Clarence Zacke. Stano was convicted in December 1983 and a jury recommended death by 10 to 2; he was sentenced to death. The Florida Supreme Court affirmed the conviction and sentence in 1985.

Questions about the reliability of Stano's confessions run through the record. In December 1986 he recanted his confessions to the Bickrest and Muldoon murders, describing himself as a compulsive confessor, UPI reported. His lawyers argued that Crow had coerced the confessions while pursuing a book about the case; a book with a foreword by Crow appeared in 1993. After a lengthy evidentiary hearing, a federal judge found no collusion and found that Crow had not fed Stano information, and the Eleventh Circuit affirmed in 1995. In 1998 Stano presented an affidavit from a freelance writer saying Zacke had recanted his testimony, affidavits from officers attacking Crow's credibility, and tapes in which Crow allegedly said he had heard Stano confess to a crime Crow did not believe he committed. The Florida Supreme Court rejected these claims on March 20, 1998, noting that Stano had also confessed to two officers. The Tampa Bay Times reported that police never found physical evidence linking him to the bodies he described and that the true total was unknown.

Three governors signed death warrants for Stano, and his execution was stayed several times, including in July 1986, when he had been scheduled to die alongside Ted Bundy. He was electrocuted on the morning of March 23, 1998, and pronounced dead at 7:15 a.m. In a final statement released by one of his lawyers, Stano maintained that he was innocent.

name: H. H. Holmes (Herman Webster Mudgett)

victims.suspected: About 9 (8 confirmed, 1 probable); claims of 27 to 200 or more are not supported by the record

victimProfile: Business associates, employees, lovers and their children, drawn into his insurance and property frauds; three victims were children aged 8 to 15
captureMethod: Arrested in Boston by Pinkerton detectives after the Fidelity Mutual Life Association, tipped by a fellow prisoner, questioned the staged death of Benjamin Pitezel.
sentence: Death; convicted by a Philadelphia jury of first-degree murder in the death of Benjamin F. Pitezel (1895), affirmed by the Pennsylvania Supreme Court on March 4, 1896
fateDetail: Hanged at Moyamensing Prison, Philadelphia, on May 7, 1896; buried at Holy Cross Cemetery, Yeadon, Pennsylvania; remains exhumed and identified in 2017
summary: Executed in 1896. Herman Webster Mudgett, alias H. H. Holmes, was convicted in Philadelphia of murdering Benjamin Pitezel and is tied to about nine deaths in Chicago, Indianapolis and Toronto. He confessed to 27, a figure the record does not support.
narrative: H. H. Holmes, born Herman Webster Mudgett, was a swindler and murderer active in Chicago, Philadelphia, Indianapolis and Toronto between 1891 and 1894. He was convicted of one murder, that of his business associate Benjamin F. Pitezel, by a Philadelphia jury in 1895. The Pennsylvania Supreme Court affirmed the first-degree murder verdict on March 4, 1896, and he was hanged at Moyamensing Prison on May 7, 1896. He confessed to 27 murders, but several people he named were later found alive, and historians count about nine confirmed or probable victims.

According to the Wikipedia article and Smithsonian magazine, the earliest confirmed victims were Julia Conner, who worked in Holmes's Englewood drugstore, and her daughter Pearl, last seen shortly before Christmas 1891. Emeline Cigrand disappeared in 1892 and the sisters Minnie and Nannie Williams in 1893. Smithsonian reported that most of his victims were people he had befriended or employed and whose deaths served his frauds.

The case that ended his career was an insurance fraud. According to the Pennsylvania Supreme Court opinion in Commonwealth v. Mudgett, Pitezel was insured for $10,000 with the Fidelity Mutual Life Association, and Holmes had arranged with him to fake his death. Instead, Pitezel's body was found on September 4, 1894, at 1316 Callowhill Street in Philadelphia, where he had been living as B. F. Perry. Medical witnesses testified that he died of chloroform poisoning that could not have been self-administered, and the prosecution argued that Holmes burned the body to make the death look accidental. Holmes identified the body and the insurer paid the claim.

Holmes then took custody of three Pitezel children. According to the Wikipedia article, Howard Pitezel was killed in Indianapolis on October 10, 1894, and Alice and Nellie Pitezel in Toronto on October 25, 1894. Holmes was arrested in Boston on November 17, 1894, after a Pinkerton pursuit; the article credits a convict, Marion Hedgepeth, with alerting the insurer. Smithsonian reported that Philadelphia detective Frank Geyer found the girls' bodies in a Toronto cellar in July 1895 and that charred remains of their brother were found at a cottage Holmes had rented in Indianapolis.

A Philadelphia grand jury indicted Holmes on September 12, 1895, and the trial opened on October 28, 1895. According to the Supreme Court opinion, Holmes dismissed his lawyers after jury selection had begun and conducted part of his own defense. The jury found him guilty of murder in the first degree. On appeal the court overruled all 13 assignments of error, held that he 'had a fair trial, and that is all he has a right to demand', and affirmed the judgment. Before his execution he sold the Hearst newspapers a confession claiming 27 murders; the Wikipedia article and historian Adam Selzer, writing in Time Out Chicago, note that some of those named were still alive. The Philadelphia Inquirer reported that he took more than 15 minutes to die on the gallows and was buried, at his request, in a concrete-filled coffin at Holy Cross Cemetery in Yeadon, Pennsylvania.

The 'Murder Castle' at 63rd Street and Wallace Avenue in Chicago is the most contested part of the story. Smithsonian and Time Out Chicago reported that Selzer's research found the first floor held shops, the second long-term apartments, and the unfinished third floor was never opened; the Chicago press described the hidden rooms in 1893 as places where Holmes concealed furniture bought on credit. Reports of torture chambers and a crematorium came from the yellow press of 1895 and were largely debunked at the time; the claim that he killed hundreds first appeared in 1930s pulp magazines. The building burned in August 1895 and was demolished in 1938.

In 2017 a Delaware County judge allowed the grave to be opened at a descendant's request. PhillyVoice and NBC Philadelphia reported that University of Pennsylvania Museum researchers recovered the remains, that dental records and DNA identified them as Holmes, and that they were reburied on August 30, 2017. Mudgett was born in Gilmanton, New Hampshire, on May 16, 1861, graduated from the University of Michigan medical program in June 1884, and moved to Chicago in 1886, where he adopted the Holmes name.

name: Henry Lee Lucas

victims.suspected: Disputed: a Texas task force once attributed 200 or more killings to him; the Texas Attorney General's 1986 report found most of his confessions false, and DNA later excluded him from at least one murder he was convicted of

victimProfile: No consistent profile; the murders he was convicted of include his mother, an elderly woman he was hired to care for, a child in his care, and women and girls aged 16 to 65 killed along Texas highways
captureMethod: Arrested in Montague County, Texas, in June 1983 on a firearm charge while under suspicion in the disappearances of Kate Rich and Becky Powell, after which he began confessing in custody
sentence: Death for the 1979 "Orange Socks" murder (1984), commuted to life in 1998; six other life sentences plus 210 years in Texas for nine more murders; up to 40 years in Michigan for killing his mother (1960)
fateDetail: Ellis Unit, Huntsville, Texas; found dead of apparent heart failure on March 12, 2001
summary: Died in prison in 2001. Texas drifter convicted of 11 murders who confessed to about 600 killings in 1983 to 1985 and then recanted; a 1986 Texas Attorney General report found most confessions false, and his death sentence was commuted in 1998.
narrative: Henry Lee Lucas was a drifter convicted of eleven murders: his mother in Michigan in 1960, a West Virginia patrolman, and nine killings in Texas between 1970 and 1983 (Wikipedia; Associated Press, 1998). He claimed roughly 600 murders in 1983 to 1985 before recanting almost all of them, and the Texas Attorney General concluded in 1986 that most of the confessions were false. His only death sentence, in the Williamson County "Orange Socks" case, was commuted to life by Governor George W. Bush in June 1998, and he died in a Texas prison in March 2001.

The first killing in the record was that of his mother, Viola Lucas, in Michigan on January 11, 1960. Lucas, then 23, stabbed her in the neck after an argument, claimed self-defense, and was convicted of second-degree murder and sentenced to up to 40 years; United Press International reported that he was released on June 3, 1970. On August 9, 1970, schoolteacher Linda Jane Phillips, 26, was abducted while driving home from a party near Richardson, Texas, and stabbed to death. Lucas pleaded guilty to that murder in Kaufman County in May 1984 and received a life term under a plea bargain.

By the late 1970s Lucas was travelling with Florida drifter Ottis Toole and later with Toole's young niece, Frieda "Becky" Powell. In 1982 Lucas and Powell were hired to care for Kate Rich, 82, of Ringgold, Texas. Powell disappeared in August 1982 and Rich in September. Lucas was arrested in Montague County in June 1983 on a firearm charge and soon told authorities he had killed both. In November 1983 he pleaded guilty to both murders. Neither body was ever positively identified.

His confessions then multiplied to roughly 600. The Texas Department of Public Safety set up a Lucas Task Force after confessions to 28 unsolved murders appeared to check out, and hundreds of homicides were marked cleared on his word; the Wikipedia article says at least 200 were attributed to him. He was given access to case files, which investigators later concluded shaped what he said.

The most consequential confession concerned an unidentified woman found strangled in a ditch off Interstate 35 in Williamson County on October 31, 1979, wearing only orange socks. A jury convicted Lucas of capital murder and he was sentenced to death in 1984, in a case the Fifth Circuit said rested "primarily, upon Lucas's confessions of guilt"; the state never identified the victim. His defense was that he was working a construction job in Jacksonville, Florida, that day; work records and a cashed paycheck supported the alibi, which the jury rejected.

In April 1985 the Dallas Times Herald showed that many confessions were physically impossible, and Lucas recanted. Attorney General Jim Mattox's April 1986 "Lucas Report" compared his claims with documented whereabouts, concluded he had falsely confessed to most of the murders, and suggested some agencies had cleared cases to close them. The Texas Court of Criminal Appeals nonetheless affirmed the Orange Socks conviction in 1989, and on January 9, 1998 the Fifth Circuit held that a bare claim of actual innocence was not a ground for federal habeas relief and that the new evidence did not prove him innocent.

On June 26, 1998, days before a scheduled execution, Governor Bush accepted the Board of Pardons and Paroles' recommendation and commuted the sentence to life, saying serious concerns had been raised about his guilt, the Associated Press reported. He remained under six other life sentences and 210 years for nine further murders. He died at the Ellis Unit in Huntsville late on March 12, 2001, at 64, of apparent heart failure, ABC News reported. According to the Wikipedia article, the Orange Socks victim was identified as Debra Jackson, 23, in 2019.

In the 1983 Montgomery County murder of Laura Purchase, to which Lucas confessed and for which he was convicted in 1986, DNA testing in 2008 excluded both Lucas and Toole, and in May 2021 Thomas Elvin Darnell of Kansas was charged with capital murder after a genealogy-assisted DNA match, the AP and KPRC reported. Lucas was born on August 23, 1936, in Blacksburg, Virginia; the Wikipedia article describes a childhood of abuse and head injuries.

name: Henry Louis Wallace
victimProfile: Young women aged 18 to 35, most of them Black women in Charlotte whom he knew through work or acquaintances, killed in their homes
captureMethod: Detectives listed people the victims had let into their apartments, matched his palm print to a victim's car, and arrested him on an outstanding misdemeanor larceny warrant, after which he confessed
sentence: Nine death sentences (January 29, 1997) for nine counts of first-degree murder, plus consecutive prison terms including eight life sentences for first-degree rape
fateDetail: On death row at Central Prison, Raleigh, North Carolina; not among the death sentences commuted by Governor Roy Cooper in December 2024
summary: On death row. Henry Louis Wallace was convicted in 1997 of murdering nine young women in Charlotte, North Carolina, between 1992 and 1994 and received nine death sentences. He also confessed to a 1990 killing in South Carolina and a 1992 Charlotte killing that were never tried.
narrative: Henry Louis Wallace is an American serial killer who was convicted in January 1997 of murdering nine young women in Charlotte, North Carolina, between June 1992 and March 1994. A Mecklenburg County jury returned nine first-degree murder verdicts on January 7, 1997, and he received nine death sentences on January 29. After his arrest in March 1994 he also confessed to two killings that were never tried: one in Charlotte in 1992 and one in his hometown of Barnwell, South Carolina, in 1990. The North Carolina Supreme Court upheld the convictions and sentences in 2000, and as of the most recent reporting he remains on death row at Central Prison in Raleigh.

Wallace was born in Barnwell, South Carolina, in November 1965, according to the Wikipedia article. He served in the U.S. Navy in the late 1980s; the Seattle Times reported in 1994 that he had been a weapons technician assigned to the USS Nimitz when he was arrested for a burglary in Bremerton, Washington,. He settled in Charlotte around 1991. The North Carolina Supreme Court noted that he held a number of jobs with management responsibilities during the period of the crimes, and Fox News reported that the nickname the Taco Bell Strangler came from his work as a manager at a Charlotte Taco Bell, where he met several of the women he later killed.

According to the Charlotte Observer, the first killing was that of Tashanda Bethea, 18, a Barnwell high school student who disappeared on March 8, 1990; her body was found in a pond on April 1. Wallace was questioned but never charged. In Charlotte, Sharon Nance, 33, was killed in May 1992. The nine victims named in the murder convictions were Caroline Love, 20, in June 1992; Shawna Hawk, 20, on February 19, 1993; Audrey Spain, 24, in June 1993; Valencia Jumper, 21, in August 1993, whose apartment was set on fire; Michelle Stinson, 20, in September 1993; Vanessa Mack, 25, found on February 20, 1994; Betty Baucom, 24, and Brandi Henderson, 18, who lived in the same east Charlotte apartment complex and were killed in March 1994; and Deborah Slaughter, 35, found on March 12, 1994. Most were strangled in their own homes, and according to the Seattle Times police said he knew the women, several through work. Henderson's infant son was choked during the attack on her and survived.

Charlotte police were slow to connect the deaths. Retired homicide detective Garry McFadden told Fox News in 2018 that investigators treated the killings as separate homicides and did not recognize a serial killer until a couple of days before the arrest and that police were slow to recognize that lower-income Black women were being targeted. Wallace had been arrested for shoplifting on February 4, 1994, without being linked to the murders. According to the court's account, detectives drew up lists of people who had been let into the victims' apartments, and Wallace's name appeared. On March 11 a palm print from Baucom's car was matched to him, and on the evening of March 12 he was arrested at a friend's apartment on an outstanding misdemeanor larceny warrant.

Over the following hours Wallace gave recorded confessions. The court opinion says he admitted all nine murders later tried, along with related rapes, sexual offenses and robberies, and also admitted killing Bethea in South Carolina and Nance in North Carolina. The Seattle Times reported on March 14 that he had been charged with ten counts of murder, including Nance's, and that he had told investigators where to find the remains of Caroline Love, who had been missing since June 1992.

After more than two years of pretrial litigation, jury selection began on September 30, 1996, on nine murder charges; the Bethea and Nance killings were not part of the trial. Defense experts argued that his mental illness and childhood abuse mitigated against a death sentence, and the state cross-examined them about the two uncharged killings. Besides the murder verdicts, the jury convicted him of multiple counts of rape, sexual offense and robbery, and he received consecutive prison terms on those counts.

On May 5, 2000, in State v. Wallace, the North Carolina Supreme Court found no prejudicial error and held that the nine death sentences were not disproportionate, observing that the number of victims and serial nature of the crimes set the case apart from any other in the state's history. The U.S. Supreme Court declined review in 2001, and a Superior Court judge rejected a further challenge in 2005, according to the Wikipedia article. Wallace was not among the 15 death row prisoners whose sentences Governor Roy Cooper commuted on December 31, 2024, according to WTVD. The Charlotte Observer reported in 2023 that he had been on death row for more than 26 years.
