name: Herb Baumeister

victims.suspected: At least 11 at Fox Hollow Farm (coroner estimates up to 25 or more), plus 9 deaths in Indiana and Ohio from 1980 to 1990 linked by sheriffs in 1998

victimProfile: Men and teenage boys aged about 15 to 34, most of them gay men met at Indianapolis bars and a gay theater
captureMethod: Never arrested: a would-be victim recorded his licence plate in 1995, his wife consented to a search of Fox Hollow Farm in June 1996, and he died by suicide in Ontario before he could be questioned or charged.
fateDetail: Shot himself at Pinery Provincial Park, Ontario, Canada, on July 3, 1996, aged 49
summary: Died by suicide before charges. Indianapolis thrift-store owner whose Westfield estate, Fox Hollow Farm, yielded the remains of at least 11 men in 1996; sheriffs later linked him to nine more deaths along I-70. Identifications continue.
narrative: Herbert Richard Baumeister (1947 to 1996) was an Indianapolis businessman suspected of killing men at Fox Hollow Farm, his 18-acre estate in Westfield, Hamilton County, Indiana, in the mid-1990s, and of further killings in central Indiana and western Ohio between 1980 and 1990. He was never arrested, charged or tried. In June 1996 investigators recovered thousands of burned and crushed bone fragments from his property, representing at least 11 people; he fled to Canada and shot himself on July 3, 1996. The Hamilton County coroner has said the roughly 10,000 fragments could represent 25 or more victims, and identification work continued in 2025.

Per the Wikipedia article, Marion County and Indianapolis police began investigating the disappearances of gay men in the early 1990s. The men later tied to Fox Hollow Farm vanished between May 1993 and March 1995; the eight identified by 1999, as listed by WRTV, were Johnny Bayer, Allen Wayne Broussard, Roger Allen Goodlet, Richard D. Hamilton, Steven S. Hale, Jeff Allen Jones, Michael Keirn and Manuel Resendez. Police believed Baumeister met young men at gay bars, strangled them at home, then burned the bodies and scattered the crushed bones on the farm, WRTV reported.

The break came from a survivor. In 1994 Tony Harris told police that a man calling himself "Brian Smart" had tried to strangle him and, he believed, had killed his friend Roger Goodlet, according to the Wikipedia account. In August 1995 Harris saw the man again and recorded his licence plate, which led investigators to Baumeister. He and his wife initially refused a search. WRTV reported that his wife, Juliana, filed for divorce in January 1996 and told investigators that a child had found a human skull on the farm in December 1994, which Baumeister called a medical specimen from his late father, an anesthesiologist.

In June 1996, while Baumeister was away, his wife consented to a search. Investigators recovered bone fragments from at least 11 people; the Wikipedia article dates the recovery to June 24, 1996. A warrant was issued, but Baumeister drove to Ontario and shot himself at Pinery Provincial Park on July 3, 1996, aged 49. WRTV reported that his three-page note apologised for his failing marriage and businesses but did not mention the missing men. He died before any charge was filed, so no court ever ruled on his responsibility for the deaths.

United Press International reported on April 28, 1998, that sheriffs in Indiana and Ohio had linked nine further deaths to Baumeister: men aged 15 to 29, strangled between 1980 and 1990 and left in streams or culverts in Hancock, Hamilton and Shelby counties in Indiana and Darke and Preble counties in Ohio, all within 70 miles of the farm. A friend of 1983 victim Michael Riley identified Baumeister as the last man seen with Riley outside an Indianapolis gay theater, UPI reported. CBS News reported that by 1999 authorities had linked him to at least 16 disappearances since 1980.

The case was revived in 2022 when Hamilton County Coroner Jeff Jellison reopened the effort to name the remains, in storage for 26 years. On December 4, 2022, coroner's staff and cadaver dogs searched the property, found one more bone and flagged about 20 locations, WRTV reported. Jellison asked relatives of men missing from the mid-1980s to mid-1990s for DNA swabs; per CBS News, 44 bones went to the Indiana State Police laboratory and more than 30 families gave samples.

On October 17, 2023, Jellison announced that forensic genetic genealogy had identified Allen Lee Livingston, 27 when reported missing in August 1993, as the ninth presumed victim, CBS News reported. In January 2024 remains were matched to Manuel Resendez, missing since the same day as Livingston. On April 29, 2025, the coroner's office and Othram announced the identification of Daniel Thomas Halloran, born May 10, 1972, missing since 1994; ABC-affiliate reporting called him the tenth victim identified.

Baumeister was born in Indianapolis on April 7, 1947, the eldest of four children of an anesthesiologist. He married Juliana Saiter in November 1971; they had three children. Per the Wikipedia article, he bought Fox Hollow Farm in May 1988 and founded the Sav-A-Lot thrift stores the same year.

name: Herbert Mullin
victimProfile: Men, women and children aged 3 or 4 to 72, including a drifter, a hitchhiker, a priest, a former classmate and his wife, a mother and her two sons, four teenage campers and a retired fisherman
captureMethod: A neighbor who saw Fred Perez shot in his Santa Cruz driveway noted the gunman's car, and a patrol officer stopped Mullin minutes later with a pistol on the seat beside him
sentence: Santa Cruz County (1973): two concurrent terms of life with the possibility of parole for two first-degree murders and eight concurrent terms of five years to life for second-degree murder; Santa Clara County (December 21, 1973): a consecutive term of five years to life for second-degree murder
fateDetail: California Health Care Facility, Stockton; died August 18, 2022, aged 75, of what the California Department of Corrections and Rehabilitation described as natural causes
summary: Died in prison. Herbert Mullin admitted killing 13 people in Santa Cruz County and Los Gatos, California, in 1972 and 1973. Convicted of 11 murders in two counties, he was repeatedly denied parole and died at a Stockton prison medical facility in 2022.
narrative: Herbert William Mullin was an American serial killer who admitted killing 13 people in and around Santa Cruz, California, between October 1972 and February 1973. A Santa Cruz County jury convicted him in August 1973 of two counts of first-degree murder and eight of second-degree murder, and in December 1973 he pleaded guilty in Santa Clara County to the second-degree murder of a Los Gatos priest. Serving life terms, he was denied parole repeatedly and died at the California Health Care Facility in Stockton on August 18, 2022, aged 75, of natural causes according to the state prison system.

Mullin was born on April 18, 1947, in Salinas and grew up partly in the San Lorenzo Valley, graduating from San Lorenzo Valley High School. According to the Wikipedia article, his mental health declined in his late teens and early twenties; he was admitted to Mendocino State Hospital in 1969 and passed through several psychiatric hospitals over the following years, being released each time when he was judged not to be a danger to himself or others. He was diagnosed with paranoid schizophrenia, and the article says his use of LSD worsened his condition. He later told investigators he killed to prevent a catastrophic earthquake in California, a belief he said was directed by voices.

The San Francisco Sunday Examiner and Chronicle, profiling the victims in August 1973, reported that the first was Lawrence White, 55, a drifter struck with a baseball bat on Highway 9 south of Felton in October 1972; the paper dated it October 12, while the Wikipedia article and later reporting give October 13. Mary Guilfoyle, 24, a student picked up while hitchhiking near Cabrillo College on October 24, was stabbed and her remains were not found until months later. On November 2, All Souls' Day, the Rev. Henri Tomei, 64, associate pastor of St. Mary's Catholic Church in Los Gatos, was stabbed in a confessional. The Valley Press reported in February 1973 that fingerprints and a palm print on the confessional door matched Mullin's, according to Los Gatos police.

On January 25, 1973, Mullin shot Jim Gianera, 25, a former high school classmate, and his wife Joan, 21, at their Santa Cruz home. The same day he killed Kathy Francis and her sons, David Hughes, 9, and Daemon Francis, in a cabin on Mystery Spot Road; the Examiner gave their ages as 28 and 3, the Wikipedia article as 29 and 4. In February he shot four teenagers camping in a shelter in Henry Cowell Redwoods State Park: David Oliker and Robert Spector, both 18, Brian Scott Card, 19, and Mark Dreibelbis, 15. On February 13 he shot Fred Perez, 72, a retired fisherman, as Perez worked in a driveway near Lighthouse Avenue in Santa Cruz.

A neighbor saw the Perez shooting and noted Mullin's car, and a patrol officer stopped him within minutes, according to the Wikipedia article; he made no attempt to use the pistol on the seat beside him. Investigators then connected him to the earlier deaths, which police had initially not linked, in part because Edmund Kemper was killing in the same county at the same time. By February 21 he had been arraigned on six counts of murder, the Valley Press reported, and the district attorney was asked to charge him with the deaths of the four campers.

Mullin's Santa Cruz trial, on 10 murder counts, began with jury selection in July 1973. He did not dispute the killings, and the case turned on his sanity. The defense, led by public defender James Jackson, argued that his delusions drove the killings, while prosecutors pointed to planning and efforts to avoid detection. The Wikipedia article says the jury returned its verdicts on August 19, 1973: first-degree murder for Jim Gianera and Kathy Francis, treated as premeditated, and second-degree murder for the other eight. He was admitted to state prison on September 18, 1973. In the Tomei case he withdrew an insanity plea and admitted second-degree murder, receiving a consecutive term of five years to life on December 21, 1973.

Only 11 of the 13 killings reached a courtroom: the Associated Press reported in 2022 that prosecutors said he committed two murders for which he never faced charges. At a 2021 parole hearing he again admitted all 13 killings but blamed his upbringing and family, and Santa Cruz County District Attorney Jeff Rosell argued he showed no true remorse; parole was denied. CDCR said the San Joaquin County medical examiner would determine the official cause of his death.

Jury selection under way in his Santa Cruz County trial, KPIX reports.
Jury convicts him of two counts of first-degree and eight of second-degree murder, according to the Wikipedia article.

name: Honolulu Strangler

victims.suspected: 5 (attributed by the Honolulu Police Department task force)

victimProfile: Women aged 17 to 36 on Oahu, several abducted while waiting for buses or near Honolulu International Airport
summary: Unidentified. An unknown man sexually assaulted, bound and strangled five women on Oahu, Hawaii, between May 1985 and April 1986, leaving them near waterways around Honolulu airport. One suspect was arrested and released in 1986; the case remains open.
narrative: The Honolulu Strangler is the name given to an unidentified man believed to have murdered five women on Oahu, Hawaii, between May 1985 and April 1986. All five were sexually assaulted, strangled and left with their hands bound behind their backs, and all were found in or near waterways around Honolulu International Airport. No one has been charged. One man was arrested in May 1986 and released without charge. The case is commonly described as Hawaii's first serial murder investigation, although the Wikipedia article counts the killer as the state's second known serial killer, after Eugene Barrett. Hawaii News Now reported in 2006 that the cases remain open with the Honolulu Police Department.

According to the Wikipedia article and a KHON2 archival report, the first victim was Vicki Gail Purdy, 25, of Mililani, the wife of an Army helicopter pilot. She went out to Waikiki nightclubs on May 29, 1985, and a taxi dropped her at the Shorebird Hotel around midnight; her body was found the next morning on an embankment at Keehi Lagoon. On January 14, 1986, Regina Sakamoto, 17, a Leilehua High School student, missed her bus in Waipahu; her body was found the next day in Keehi Lagoon near the airport's reef runway. On January 30, 1986, Denise Hughes, 21, a telephone company secretary who commuted by bus, failed to arrive at work. Three youths found her body on February 1 in the Moanalua stream drainage canal.

The Hughes killing prompted the Honolulu Police Department to form a 27-member serial killer task force on February 5, 1986, with help from the FBI and Washington State's Green River task force, according to Wikipedia. The FBI profile described an opportunist who picked up vulnerable women, often at bus stops, and who probably lived or worked near Waipahu or Sand Island. Policewomen ran sting operations near Keehi Lagoon and the airport. The killings continued. Louise Medeiros, 25, who was three months pregnant, flew back from Kauai late on March 26, 1986, and disappeared after leaving the airport; police believe she was taken while waiting for a bus. Road workers found her body on April 2 near Waikele stream.

The last known victim was Linda Pesce, 36, who left home on April 29, 1986, for an evening work meeting. Her car was found abandoned on the Nimitz-H-1 viaduct near the airport. Police set up roadblocks to question commuters. Her body was found on Sand Island on May 3, 1986, according to KHON2. Wikipedia reports that a 43-year-old man had approached police saying a psychic had told him where the body was, and that the search he directed initially found nothing.

On May 9, 1986, police arrested Howard Gay, an Ewa Beach mechanic who worked overnight shifts at an air freight carrier on Lagoon Drive, as the primary suspect in the Pesce case. According to Wikipedia and the Honolulu Star-Bulletin coverage it cites, he was questioned from about 8 p.m. until 3 a.m., failed a polygraph examination and was released without charge; police kept him under surveillance. His girlfriend told investigators he had left the house after arguments on the nights of the murders. About two months later, a woman who had seen a man with Pesce picked Gay from a photo lineup but was reluctant to testify. Prosecutors never charged him. Hawaii News Now reported in 2025 that he died in 2003 in California.

Retired HPD Major Louis Souza told Hawaii News Now in 2006 that investigators had looked for a connection among the victims and found none, and that while the arrest was "satisfaction," it was "frustrating that the state didn't feel that they had enough to prosecute him." Retired deputy chief John McCarthy told the station in 2025 that police "were finding a dead female and there were no witnesses," and that investigative techniques were far more limited in 1986 than today.

The killings stopped after Pesce's death. Howard Gay was investigated and never charged, and no other person has been publicly named. The five murders remain unsolved and open with the Honolulu Police Department; none of the reporting reviewed for this profile records a DNA identification or new charges.

timeline.text: Vicki Gail Purdy, 25, is last seen in Waikiki around midnight; her body is found the next morning on an embankment at Keehi Lagoon.

Linda Pesce, 36, leaves for an evening work meeting; her car is found abandoned on the Nimitz-H-1 viaduct near the airport.
Pesce's body is found on Sand Island; she is the last known victim.
Police arrest Howard Gay, 43, an Ewa Beach mechanic, in the Pesce case; he fails a polygraph and is released without charge.
Howard Gay dies in California, never having been charged in any of the five murders.
Retired HPD Major Louis Souza tells Hawaii News Now the state did not believe it had enough evidence to prosecute; the cases remain open.
Hawaii News Now revisits the case; retired deputy chief John McCarthy says the investigation was hampered by a lack of witnesses. No one has been charged.

name: I-70 Killer

victims.suspected: 6 killed in 1992; 2 more killed and 1 wounded in Texas in 1993 to 1994 are a disputed possible link

victimProfile: Lone clerks and owners of small specialty shops near Interstate 70, five women aged 23 to 37 and one man aged 40
summary: Unidentified. Six shop workers were shot in the head in small stores in Indiana, Kansas and Missouri between April 8 and May 7, 1992, all linked by a .22-caliber weapon. Police released an age-enhanced sketch in 2022; a $25,000 reward stands.
narrative: The I-70 Killer is the name given to an unidentified man who shot six people working in small retail stores in Indiana, Kansas and Missouri between April 8 and May 7, 1992. The name refers to Interstate 70, which runs near most of the stores. No one has been charged. Police linked the six killings through ballistics on a .22-caliber weapon. Investigators in Texas later examined three 1993 and 1994 shootings as possible related attacks, a link that ballistics testing did not confirm.

The first killing came on April 8, 1992, in Indianapolis, where Robin Fuldauer, 26, the manager of a Payless ShoeSource on Pendleton Pike, was working alone. According to KMOV, police believe the killer entered around 1:15 p.m., took her to a back storage room and shot her; less than $100 was taken. On April 11, Patricia Magers, 32, owner of the La Bride d'Elegance bridal shop in Wichita, Kansas, and her employee Patricia Smith, 23, were shot in the back of the store around closing time. On April 27, Michael McCown, 40, was shot while stocking shelves at Sylvia's Ceramics, his mother's shop in Terre Haute, Indiana; he was the only male victim. On May 3, Nancy Kitzmiller, 24, was killed at Boot Village in St. Charles, Missouri, and on May 7, Sarah Blessing, 37, was shot at a gift shop in Raytown, Missouri.

According to KMOV and WTWO, the pattern was consistent: small specialty shops holding little cash, a victim alone at a slow time of day, a walk to a back room and a shot to the head, with little or nothing taken. Ballistics tied the Indianapolis and Wichita shootings to one gun within days. Investigators identified the weapon as a .22-caliber pistol, most probably an Erma Werke ET22, with an Intratec Scorpion not ruled out, and found traces of jeweler's rouge on the casings. In Wichita, a customer who returned to the bridal shop after closing met a man carrying a small rifle, refused to go to the back and left; retired Wichita Lieutenant Michael Hennessy told FOX59 the encounter gave police their first eyewitness, and it produced the original sketch of a thin white man, 5 feet 7 to 5 feet 9, with sandy blond or reddish hair.

In 1993 and 1994, three women were shot in the head in small shops in Texas: Mary Ann Glasscock, 51, at a Fort Worth antiques store on September 25, 1993; Amy Vess, 22, at an Arlington dance apparel store on November 1, 1993; and Vicki Webb, who survived a shooting at a Houston gift shop on January 15, 1994. According to KMOV, Texas authorities at first called a connection a definite possibility, but ballistics testing found the Texas gun did not match the I-70 weapon, and police came to doubt the link.

Suspect reviews over the following decades produced no charges. KMOV reported that investigators cleared several men, including a Tennessee man sought in 1992 for unrelated killings who resembled the sketch; police ruled him out in 2012. In January 2022, KMOV reported that investigators were also examining the November 30, 2001, shooting of liquor store clerk Billy Brossman in Terre Haute, seven blocks from the McCown scene; Terre Haute police confirmed similarities but did not publicly connect the cases.

In October 2021, authorities released a new sketch, credited to the St. Charles Police Department, describing a white man who was 22 to 40 in 1992, 5 feet 7 to 5 feet 9 and 140 to 160 pounds, with sandy blond hair with a red tint; Crime Stoppers of Central Indiana took tips. KTVI reported that in 2021 the five departments met with the FBI to review the evidence with newer forensic technology. On January 20, 2022, St. Charles police released an age-enhanced sketch estimating the killer would now be 52 to 70 and announced a review of the files with every agency involved plus the FBI and ATF. As of August 2025, KTVI reported that St. Charles police lead the case and a $25,000 reward remains on offer.

name: Israel Keyes
victimProfile: Strangers chosen at random, including a teenage barista in Anchorage and a married couple in their fifties in Vermont
captureMethod: Stopped by Texas Highway Patrol near Lufkin while driving a rental car matching a bulletin, after ransom money deposited into Samantha Koenig's account was tracked to ATM withdrawals in Alaska, New Mexico, Arizona and Texas.
fateDetail: Found dead in his cell at the Anchorage Correctional Complex on the morning of December 2, 2012, while awaiting a March 2013 federal trial
summary: Died before trial. Israel Keyes was indicted for the 2012 kidnapping and killing of Samantha Koenig in Anchorage, confessed to murdering Bill and Lorraine Currier in Vermont and five others, and died by suicide in custody in December 2012.
narrative: Israel Keyes was an Anchorage contractor and Army veteran indicted in federal court in April 2012 for the kidnapping and killing of 18-year-old Samantha Koenig. In custody he confessed to killing William and Lorraine Currier of Essex, Vermont, in June 2011. He was never convicted: he died by suicide in the Anchorage Correctional Complex in December 2012, about three months before trial. According to U.S. Attorney Karen Loeffler, quoted by the Anchorage Daily News, Keyes said he had killed Koenig, the Curriers and five others. In August 2013 the FBI said it had linked 11 killings to him based on his statements, most unnamed and unverified.

The Vermont State Police record that Bill Currier, 50, and Lorraine Currier, 55, were last seen at their Essex home on the evening of June 8, 2011, and that evidence at the house suggested they had not left voluntarily. According to the Anchorage Daily News, Keyes later said he had flown to Chicago, driven to Vermont, taken the couple in their own car to an abandoned farmhouse, shot Bill Currier and strangled Lorraine Currier. The farmhouse had been demolished before investigators arrived, and the bodies have not been located. Keyes was never charged in Vermont.

Samantha Koenig was abducted from the Common Grounds coffee stand in Anchorage on February 1, 2012. According to the account released by Anchorage police and the FBI in December 2012, reported by Alaska Public Media, Keyes approached in a ski mask near closing, bound her with zip ties and drove her to a shed at his home, where he sexually assaulted and strangled her. The next day he left on a pre-planned cruise from New Orleans. After returning on February 17 he photographed the body with a dated newspaper and left a typed $30,000 ransom demand in a city park. The remains were placed under the ice of Matanuska Lake; FBI divers recovered them in early April.

The ransom led to his arrest. The U.S. Attorney's Office stated that Koenig's family deposited reward money into the account linked to her stolen debit card so withdrawals could be tracked, and that Keyes withdrew money from ATMs in Alaska, New Mexico, Arizona and Texas. On March 13, 2012, a Texas Highway Patrol corporal stopped a white Ford Focus matching a bulletin near Lufkin, Texas; officers found Koenig's phone and ATM card. Returned to Alaska on a federal access-device fraud charge, the Anchorage Daily News reported, he soon confessed and told investigators where to find her body.

On April 18, 2012, the U.S. Attorney announced a federal grand jury indictment on three counts: kidnapping resulting in death, receiving and possessing ransom money, and access device fraud. The kidnapping count carried a maximum penalty of death or life imprisonment. Keyes pleaded not guilty to all three counts before U.S. District Judge Michael Thompson. In May 2012 he tried to escape by vaulting the courtroom rail and was subdued with a Taser. Trial was set for March 2013.

In FBI interviews Keyes described other killings. According to the Anchorage Daily News, he admitted to four murders in Washington state, where he lived from about 2001 to 2007, and one on the East Coast in 2009, with the body left in New York. He named none of those victims, and none has been identified. The FBI said he buried caches of weapons and body-disposal items, two of which were recovered in Alaska and New York, and that he financed his travel partly through bank robberies.

Keyes was found dead in his cell on the morning of December 2, 2012; Alaska State Troopers called it an apparent suicide, and Wikipedia gives the date of death as December 1. Because he died before trial, no court ever ruled on the Koenig charges or any other killing. In August 2013 the FBI released a timeline of his travels and said three further killings had been added based on his statements.

Keyes was born on January 7, 1978, in Richmond, Utah, according to Wikipedia. He served in the U.S. Army from 1998 to 2001, lived in Neah Bay, Washington, and moved to Anchorage in March 2007, where he ran a construction business and lived with his partner and daughter.

name: Jane Toppan
victimProfile: Mostly elderly or ill patients in her care as a private nurse, along with landlords, a foster sister, friends and members of a family who employed her
captureMethod: Relatives of the Davis family pressed for an inquiry after four deaths at Cataumet; exhumations and toxicology found poison, and she was arrested in Amherst, New Hampshire
legalStatus: Not guilty by reason of insanity
sentence: None; found not guilty by reason of insanity on the murder of Mary Gibbs (June 1902) and committed for life to the Taunton Insane Hospital
fateDetail: Taunton State Hospital (then Taunton Insane Hospital), Taunton, Massachusetts; died in August 1938 while committed
summary: Died (other). Massachusetts nurse Jane Toppan confessed in 1902 to poisoning 31 people from 1895 to 1901. A Barnstable jury found her not guilty by reason of insanity, and she died in 1938 at the Taunton state hospital, where she had been committed for life.
narrative: Jane Toppan was a private nurse in Massachusetts who confessed in 1902 to poisoning 31 people between 1895 and 1901, most of them patients in her care. She was indicted for three deaths that occurred in the summer of 1901 at Cataumet, a village of Bourne on Cape Cod, and was tried at Barnstable in June 1902 on a single count, the murder of Mary "Minnie" Gibbs. A jury found her not guilty by reason of insanity, so she was never convicted of any killing. She was committed for life to the state insane hospital at Taunton, where she died in August 1938.

Toppan was born Honora Kelley in Boston, in 1854 according to the Wikipedia article and People magazine; some accounts, including the West End Museum's, give 1857. After her mother's death her father could not care for the children, and she was placed in the Boston Female Asylum. She was later sent to the Toppan family of Lowell as an indentured servant and took their surname, though she was never formally adopted. In the 1880s she trained as a nurse at Cambridge Hospital and then at Massachusetts General Hospital, which, according to the West End Museum, dismissed her in 1890 without a diploma. She went on to work as a private nurse for families in Cambridge, Boston and Lowell, where colleagues and clients knew her as "Jolly Jane."

The Wikipedia article lists twelve deaths that have been linked to her by name. The earliest were her landlords, Israel Dunham, who died in May 1895, and his wife Lovey Dunham, who died in September 1897. Her foster sister, Elizabeth Brigham, died in August 1899; Boston Magazine reported that she fell ill after an outing with Toppan at Buzzards Bay. Mary McNear, Florence Calkins, William Ingraham and Myra Connors died between December 1899 and February 1900, and Edna Bannister died in June 1901. Contemporary reporting and later accounts agree that her principal method was morphine, often combined with atropine, given in drinks or by injection. People magazine reported that she later said some of the killings gave her sexual gratification.

The deaths that led to her arrest came in 1901 in the family of Alden P. Davis of Cataumet. His wife, Mattie Davis, died on July 4, 1901; the Wikipedia article places the death at Cataumet, while IrishCentral and the West End Museum say she died in Cambridge. Toppan then stayed on as nurse at the family's summer home. A daughter, Genevieve Gordon, died on July 30, Alden Davis on August 8, and a second daughter, Mary Gibbs, on August 13. According to the West End Museum, Gibbs's father-in-law, Captain Paul Gibbs, pressed for an inquiry; exhumations and toxicology found poison, and a Falmouth chemist said he had sold Toppan morphine before the deaths. She was arrested on October 29, 1901, in Amherst, New Hampshire.

The Batesburg Advocate of South Carolina reported in July 1902 she had been indicted for the murders of Mary Gibbs, Mrs. Harry Gordon of Chicago (Genevieve Gordon) and Alden Davis, and that the state chose to try her on one count. The West End Museum says she spent about six months in the Barnstable County jail and that examining physicians declared her insane in April 1902. At the trial, alienists, as psychiatrists were then called, testified that she was insane. The Wikipedia article gives June 23, 1902, as the date of the verdict. Some later accounts, including People's, say she was charged with twelve murders; the 1902 report gives three indictments.

According to the same 1902 report, she gave her senior counsel, Judge Fred M. Bixby of Brockton, a confession naming 31 people she said she had poisoned during her career as a nurse. The Wikipedia article notes that a fuller confession later printed by the New York Journal claimed more killings, and its authenticity is uncertain. Estimates of her total, as given by Boston Magazine, IrishCentral and the Wikipedia article, range up to about 100, but no court ever examined those claims, and the confessed and suspected counts remain unverified.

At Taunton she was diagnosed with what was then called moral insanity. People and the West End Museum report that in 1904 she refused food, believing staff were trying to poison her, and lost about 80 pounds before recovering. She remained there for the rest of her life. The Wikipedia article gives her death as August 17, 1938, aged 84; the West End Museum gives August 18, and People and Boston Magazine give her age as 81, reflecting the disagreement over her birth year.

name: Jeffrey Dahmer
victimProfile: Men and boys aged 14 to 32, most of them Black, Hispanic or Asian, met at bars, malls and bus stops in Milwaukee
captureMethod: Tracy Edwards escaped Dahmer's Milwaukee apartment in handcuffs and flagged down police officers, who searched the apartment and found evidence of the killings.
sentence: 15 consecutive life terms in Wisconsin (February 17, 1992); a 16th consecutive life term without parole in Ohio (May 1, 1992)
fateDetail: Beaten to death by inmate Christopher Scarver at Columbia Correctional Institution, Portage, Wisconsin, November 28, 1994
summary: Died in prison. Jeffrey Dahmer murdered 17 men and boys in Ohio and Wisconsin between 1978 and 1991. A jury found him sane on 15 counts in 1992; he received 16 life terms and was killed by a fellow inmate in 1994.
narrative: Jeffrey Lionel Dahmer, known as the Milwaukee Cannibal, murdered 17 men and boys in Ohio and Wisconsin between 1978 and 1991 and was convicted of 16 of the killings. After he pleaded guilty but insane to 15 Wisconsin murders, a Milwaukee County jury found him sane on every count in February 1992 and he received 15 consecutive life terms; in May 1992 he pleaded guilty in Ohio to a 16th murder and received another life term. He was beaten to death by a fellow inmate at Columbia Correctional Institution in Portage, Wisconsin, on November 28, 1994.

According to the Wikipedia article, the first killing took place on June 18, 1978, three weeks after Dahmer's high school graduation, when he picked up an 18-year-old hitchhiker, Steven Hicks, and killed him at his family's home in Bath Township, Ohio. The second murder, of Steven Tuomi in a Milwaukee hotel room, came nine years later in 1987. Three further victims were killed at his grandmother's house in West Allis and twelve at the Oxford Apartments on North 25th Street in Milwaukee, where he moved in 1990. He met his victims, aged 14 to 32, at bars, malls and bus stops, offered them money to pose for photographs, and drugged and strangled them. In January 1989 he had pleaded guilty to second-degree sexual assault of a 13-year-old boy and served a work-release term followed by probation.

On May 27, 1991, Milwaukee police officers found 14-year-old Konerak Sinthasomphone, the older brother of the 1989 case's victim, naked and disoriented outside Dahmer's building. Dahmer told them the boy was his adult boyfriend, and the officers returned him to the apartment, where he was killed that day. Wikipedia, citing the federal district court's opinion in Estate of Sinthasomphone v. City of Milwaukee, notes that the family's civil claims against the city and officers were dismissed.

The killings ended on July 22, 1991, when Tracy Edwards, who had been handcuffed in the apartment, escaped and flagged down two patrol officers. They searched the apartment, found evidence of the murders and arrested Dahmer, who confessed to 17 killings over more than 60 hours of interviews, according to Wikipedia. He was charged with four counts of first-degree murder on July 25, 1991, and eleven more by August 22. UPI reported that Summit County prosecutors charged him in September 1991 with aggravated murder in the Hicks case.

Dahmer pleaded guilty but insane to the 15 Wisconsin counts on January 13, 1992, so the trial that began January 30 before Judge Laurence C. Gram Jr. concerned only his sanity. On February 15, 1992, the jury found him sane on each count, with two of twelve jurors dissenting. On February 17 Gram imposed mandatory life plus ten years on the first two counts and consecutive life terms on the other thirteen; Wisconsin has no death penalty. UPI and the Deseret News quoted Dahmer telling the court, "I hope that God can forgive me." On May 1, 1992, in Summit County Common Pleas Court in Akron, he pleaded guilty to the aggravated murder of Steven Hicks and was sentenced to life without parole, consecutive to the Wisconsin terms, UPI reported.

Dahmer was held at Columbia Correctional Institution in Portage, where UPI reported in July 1992 that he was in administrative confinement with a daily cleaning detail. On November 28, 1994, while cleaning a bathroom on a work detail, he was beaten by inmate Christopher Scarver, 25, and died on the way to hospital, UPI reported; inmate Jesse Anderson, attacked at the same time, died two days later. Scarver received two additional life terms in May 1995. In June 1995 a Wisconsin Department of Corrections panel found that Scarver had acted alone after a lapse in supervision, and four staff members were suspended, the Spokesman-Review reported.

The Oxford Apartments were demolished in November 1992, and a civic group bought and destroyed Dahmer's possessions. His remains were cremated in 1995. Dahmer was born in Milwaukee on May 21, 1960, and grew up in Bath Township, Ohio. He briefly attended Ohio State University, served in the Army in West Germany, and later lived with his grandmother in West Allis before renting the Milwaukee apartment.

name: Jerry Brudos
victimProfile: Young women aged 19 to 23, abducted from parking areas, a shopping center, a roadside and a door-to-door sales call in the Salem and Portland areas
captureMethod: Identified after an Oregon State University student he had phoned reported his call to police, then confirmed through a search warrant on his home and his confession
sentence: Three consecutive life terms with the possibility of parole, on guilty pleas to three counts of first-degree murder (Marion County Circuit Court, June 27, 1969); affirmed on appeal in 1970
fateDetail: Oregon State Penitentiary, Salem; died of liver cancer after nearly 37 years in custody
summary: Convicted on guilty pleas to three first-degree murders in Oregon in 1969 and sentenced to three consecutive life terms. Jerry Brudos confessed to four killings of young women in 1968 and 1969 and died in the Oregon State Penitentiary in 2006.
narrative: Jerome Henry Brudos, known as Jerry Brudos, pleaded guilty in June 1969 to three counts of first-degree murder for the killings of young women in the Salem and Portland areas of Oregon in 1968 and 1969. According to the Oregon Court of Appeals in State v. Brudos (1970), he entered the pleas orally and in writing with the advice of counsel and received three consecutive life sentences. Police attributed four murders to him and he admitted all four, but he was never tried for the fourth because the victim's body was not recovered. He died in the Oregon State Penitentiary in 2006.

According to the Wikipedia article and Biography.com, the first victim was Linda Slawson, a 19-year-old encyclopedia saleswoman from Aloha, who called at Brudos's home in the Portland area on January 26, 1968, and was killed there; her body was never found. On November 26, 1968, Jan Whitney, 23, disappeared after her car broke down on Interstate 5 between Salem and Albany. Brudos later admitted stopping for her and strangling her in his car. Her remains were recovered from the Willamette River near Independence after his conviction and identified by dental records.

Karen Sprinker, an 18-year-old Oregon State University student, was abducted at gunpoint from a department store parking garage in downtown Salem on March 27, 1969. Linda Salee, 22, of Beaverton, was taken from the Lloyd Center shopping area in Portland on April 23, 1969. In May 1969 both bodies were found in the Long Tom River, weighted with automobile parts and bound with cord. In the same week as the Salee abduction, two other young women escaped attempted abductions in Portland; one later identified Brudos.

Investigators noticed that the knots on both river victims matched and, because Sprinker was an OSU student, interviewed women on the Corvallis campus. One student reported that a caller had asked her for a date, and police asked her to report any further contact. When Brudos called again, officers were present at the meeting. According to the Wikipedia article, his home was searched under warrant on May 26, 1969, yielding nylon rope and photographs of the victims, and Oregon state troopers took him into custody on May 29 after finding him hiding in the family station wagon. In early June he confessed to the four murders and to earlier assaults.

Brudos was arraigned on June 4, 1969, in Marion County and initially pleaded not guilty by reason of insanity. Court-appointed psychiatrists found him legally sane. On June 27, 1969, before Circuit Judge Val D. Sloper, he pleaded guilty to the first-degree murders of Sprinker, Whitney and Salee and was sentenced to three consecutive life terms with the possibility of parole. His wife, Ralphene Brudos, was indicted in August 1969 in connection with the Sprinker murder and was acquitted at trial.

The Oregon Court of Appeals affirmed the convictions and sentences on July 9, 1970, holding that consecutive life terms were permissible and that any challenge to the pleas had to be raised through post-conviction relief; the Oregon Supreme Court denied review that September. Brudos then sought post-conviction relief, arguing his pleas were not knowing and voluntary. According to Brudos v. Cupp (1977), the post-conviction court rejected that claim and the Court of Appeals upheld the denial of his request to move the hearing out of Marion County. The Wikipedia article reports that later appeals failed and parole was repeatedly denied over the objections of the victims' families.

Brudos spent nearly 37 years at the Oregon State Penitentiary in Salem, where he held clerical jobs. He died there of liver cancer on March 28, 2006, at age 67, described by state officials as the longest-held inmate in the Oregon prison system.

Brudos was born on January 31, 1939, in Webster, South Dakota, and grew up in Oregon. According to the Wikipedia article, he was arrested in 1956 at age 17 for assaulting a girl and spent nine months under psychiatric evaluation at the Oregon State Hospital, graduated from Corvallis High School in 1957, was discharged from the Army in 1959 and married in 1961. He was living in Salem with his wife and two children at the time of the 1969 murders.

name: Joel Rifkin
victimProfile: Women aged roughly 21 to 41, most of them sex workers picked up in Manhattan
captureMethod: Stopped by state troopers for a missing rear license plate, fled, crashed, and was found with a victim's body in his pickup truck
sentence: Aggregate 203 years to life: 25 years to life by jury verdict in Nassau County (1994) plus consecutive terms on guilty pleas in Suffolk, Kings, Bronx and Queens counties (1995 to 1996)
fateDetail: Clinton Correctional Facility, Dannemora, New York
summary: Imprisoned. Joel Rifkin, a Long Island landscaper, confessed to killing 17 women in New York between 1989 and 1993 and was convicted of nine murders after a 1993 traffic stop revealed a body in his truck.
narrative: Joel David Rifkin is a convicted serial killer who murdered women in New York City and on Long Island between 1989 and 1993. According to the New York State Police, he admitted to 16 murders beyond the one for which he was arrested, 17 in all. He was convicted of nine murders in jury and plea proceedings in Nassau, Suffolk, Kings, Bronx and Queens counties between 1994 and 1996 and, according to NBC News, is serving an aggregate sentence of 203 years. He is held at Clinton Correctional Facility.

The known victims were women, most of them sex workers picked up in Manhattan, who were strangled after sexual encounters and whose bodies were left in waterways, wooded areas and other sites around the region. According to the Wikipedia article, the first killing was that of Heidi Balch, 25, in early 1989; a head found at a Hopewell Township, New Jersey golf course in March 1989 was identified as hers only in 2013. Other bodies were recovered from New York City rivers and creeks, upstate New York and Long Island between 1991 and 1993. Two victims were never found, and a woman found in a drum in Newtown Creek in May 1992 has never been identified.

The series ended with a traffic stop. According to the New York State Police, at about 3:15 a.m. on June 28, 1993, troopers Deborah Spaargaren and Sean Ruane tried to pull over a 1984 Mazda pickup on the Southern State Parkway because it had no rear plate. The driver fled at up to 90 mph, struck a light pole on Old Country Road after a 20 to 25 minute chase and was taken into custody. An inventory search of the truck found the body of Tiffany Bresciani, 22, who had disappeared four days earlier. At the station house Rifkin admitted to 16 further killings; a task force recovered the remains of 15 victims across 10 jurisdictions.

Rifkin was tried first in Nassau County for Bresciani's murder and raised an insanity defense. According to United Press International, on May 9, 1994 a jury deliberated just over two hours before convicting him of second-degree murder and first-degree reckless endangerment arising from the chase. Judge Ira Wexner sentenced him on June 8, 1994; wire reports described the combined term as 27 years to life. In December 2001 the Appellate Division, Second Department, held that statements Rifkin made at the crash scene after being handcuffed should have been suppressed because they preceded Miranda warnings, but affirmed the conviction in light of the otherwise overwhelming evidence, finding the later station-house confession voluntary.

The other convictions came by plea. In Suffolk County he admitted murdering Leah Evens and Lauren Marquez, both 28, and on September 18, 1995 Judge John Jones imposed two consecutive terms of 25 years to life, according to wire reports in The Spokesman-Review. In Brooklyn he pleaded guilty on December 1, 1995 to three counts of second-degree murder for Lorraine Orvieto, Mary Ann Holloman and an unidentified woman; UPI reported that on December 12 he received life with a 75-year minimum, consecutive to his earlier terms. According to Wikipedia, a further life sentence followed in January 1996 in the Bronx for the murder of Jenny Soto.

On January 25, 1996, Queens Supreme Court Justice Robert Hanophy added 25 years for the murder of Iris Sanchez, 25, whose body had been found under mattresses near Kennedy Airport. UPI reported that Rifkin, who by then had accumulated 177 years for seven murders, apologized to the victims' families and called himself a monster; the judge noted he was not eligible for New York's newly restored death penalty. In March 2013 Hopewell Township police announced that the 1989 remains had been identified through DNA from the victim's mother as Heidi Balch; NBC News reported that Rifkin would not be charged in New Jersey.

Rifkin was born in New York City on January 20, 1959, and was adopted as an infant by Bernard and Jeanne Rifkin of East Meadow, Long Island, according to Wikipedia. He graduated from East Meadow High School in 1977, attended several colleges without earning a degree and worked as a self-employed landscaper. He was 34 when arrested.

name: John Wayne Gacy

victims.suspected: 33 confirmed; Cook County Sheriff Tom Dart has said he suspects Gacy also killed while travelling for work, which the trial prosecutor disputes

victimProfile: Boys and young men aged 14 to 21, several of them runaways, hitchhikers or job applicants to his contracting business
captureMethod: Des Plaines police investigating the disappearance of 15-year-old Robert Piest traced him to Gacy, who confessed after a search of his home turned up evidence tied to Piest.
sentence: Death on 12 murder counts and natural life on the remaining 21 (March 1980)
fateDetail: Lethal injection at Stateville Correctional Center, Illinois, May 10, 1994
summary: Executed in 1994. John Wayne Gacy was convicted by a Cook County jury in 1980 of murdering 33 boys and young men in suburban Chicago between 1972 and 1978; 29 were found at his home. Five victims remain unidentified.
narrative: John Wayne Gacy was a Chicago-area building contractor who murdered boys and young men at his home in Norwood Park Township, Cook County, Illinois, between 1972 and 1978. According to the Illinois Supreme Court's 1984 opinion in People v. Gacy, a Cook County jury convicted him of 33 counts of murder, one count of deviate sexual assault and one count of indecent liberties with a child, and sentenced him to death on 12 murder counts and to natural life on the rest. Illinois executed him on May 10, 1994. The opinion recites that his confession put the number at about 30; police recovered 33 bodies. Three of the eight victims buried unidentified have been named since the Cook County Sheriff's Office reopened the identification effort in 2011, and five remain unidentified.

The first known victim, Timothy McCoy, was killed on January 3, 1972, according to the victim list in the Wikipedia article. Over the next six years Gacy brought young men to the house, many of them employees or job applicants at his remodelling company, runaways or hitchhikers. NBC Chicago, in a 40th-anniversary report, described a handcuff and rope trick used to restrain and then strangle the victims, who ranged in age from 14 to 21. Twenty-six bodies were buried in the crawl space under the house, three elsewhere on the property, and four were thrown into the Des Plaines River.

The case broke on December 11, 1978, when 15-year-old Robert Piest left the Des Plaines pharmacy where he worked to talk to a contractor about a summer job and never returned. The Illinois Supreme Court opinion records that Gacy had been at the pharmacy that evening, that his truck was seen outside, and that police learned of his Iowa conviction for assaulting a teenage boy. Investigators obtained a search warrant for his home and vehicles on December 13, kept him under surveillance, and arrested him on December 21, 1978. Early on December 22 he confessed, saying bodies were buried under the house and five had been thrown into the river. Excavation recovered 29 bodies from the property; four more were pulled from the Des Plaines and Illinois rivers.

The trial opened on February 6, 1980, before Judge Louis Garippo with a jury drawn from Rockford. The defence argued insanity; the State's experts said Gacy had a personality disorder and was legally responsible. On March 12, 1980, after under two hours of deliberation, the jury found him guilty of all 33 murders. At sentencing the jury returned death sentences for the 12 murders committed after Illinois's 1977 death penalty statute took effect, and the court imposed natural life for the other 21.

The Illinois Supreme Court affirmed the convictions and sentences on June 6, 1984, rejecting challenges to the search warrants, jury selection and the insanity verdict, and the U.S. Supreme Court denied review in 1985. The Illinois Supreme Court upheld the dismissal of a post-conviction petition on September 29, 1988, and the Seventh Circuit, in Gacy v. Welborn on April 12, 1993, affirmed the denial of federal habeas relief. After 14 years on death row at Menard, Gacy was executed by lethal injection at Stateville Correctional Center shortly after midnight on May 10, 1994.

Eight victims were buried without names. In 2011 Cook County Sheriff Tom Dart had the remains exhumed and asked families of young men who vanished in the Chicago area in the 1970s to submit DNA. William Bundy, 19, was identified in November 2011. James Byron Haakenson, a 16-year-old runaway from Minnesota, was identified through a sister's DNA in July 2017, CBS Minnesota reported. On October 25, 2021, the sheriff's office announced that Victim No. 5 was Francis Wayne Alexander, a North Carolina native killed between early 1976 and early 1977 and identified through genetic genealogy with the DNA Doe Project, according to CBS News and ABC7. Five victims remain unidentified.

Gacy was born in Chicago on March 17, 1942. In 1968 he was convicted in Waterloo, Iowa, of sodomy involving a teenage boy; paroled on June 18, 1970, he returned to the Chicago area, ran a contracting business, was active in local Democratic politics and performed at events as a clown called Pogo.

name: Joseph James DeAngelo

victims.suspected: 13 murders; prosecutors also attribute about 50 rapes and more than 120 burglaries

victimProfile: Men and women attacked in their homes at night, often couples; earlier victims were women and girls raped during home invasions
captureMethod: Forensic genetic genealogy on the GEDmatch database pointed investigators to his family, and crime-scene DNA was then matched to samples taken from his car door handle and a discarded tissue.
sentence: 11 consecutive life terms without parole for 13 murders, plus further life terms for 13 kidnapping counts and eight years for enhancements (August 21, 2020)
fateDetail: California State Prison, Corcoran (protective custody)
summary: Imprisoned for life. Joseph DeAngelo, the Golden State Killer, pleaded guilty in 2020 to 13 California murders committed from 1975 to 1986 and admitted dozens of rapes; he was identified in 2018 through forensic genetic genealogy.
narrative: Joseph James DeAngelo is the former California police officer identified in 2018 as the Golden State Killer, the offender earlier known as the Visalia Ransacker, the East Area Rapist and the Original Night Stalker. On June 29, 2020, he pleaded guilty in Sacramento County Superior Court to 13 counts of first-degree murder with special circumstances and 13 counts of kidnapping, and under the plea he admitted dozens of uncharged rapes. NBC News reported that prosecutors described crimes against 87 victims at 53 crime scenes in 11 California counties between 1975 and 1986. On August 21, 2020, Judge Michael Bowman sentenced him to consecutive life terms without the possibility of parole.

The first killing DeAngelo admitted was the September 11, 1975 shooting of Claude Snelling in Visalia, Tulare County, during the period when the Visalia Ransacker was burglarizing homes there. According to the Wikipedia article, the East Area Rapist home-invasion attacks began in Rancho Cordova, near Sacramento, on June 18, 1976, and continued into 1979; Brian and Katie Maggiore were shot to death in Rancho Cordova on February 2, 1978. The attacks then moved to Southern California. According to the Wikipedia article and charges reported by NBC News, Robert Offerman and Debra Manning were killed in Goleta on December 30, 1979; Lyman and Charlene Smith in Ventura on March 13, 1980; Keith and Patrice Harrington in Dana Point on August 19, 1980; Manuela Witthuhn in Irvine on February 6, 1981; Cheri Domingo and Gregory Sanchez in Goleta on July 27, 1981; and Janelle Cruz in Irvine in May 1986. The later victims were bludgeoned in their homes after being bound.

DNA testing eventually linked the Southern California murders to the East Area Rapist attacks. In 2018 investigators uploaded a DNA profile from crime-scene evidence to the public genealogy database GEDmatch, built family trees from distant relatives who matched, and narrowed the candidates to DeAngelo. NBC News reported that Sacramento County Sheriff Scott Jones said investigators confirmed the match with discarded DNA after six days of surveillance; according to the Wikipedia article the samples came from his car door handle and a tissue in his trash. He was arrested at his Citrus Heights home on April 24, 2018, at age 72, in the first widely publicized arrest made through forensic genetic genealogy.

NBC News reported that at an August 2018 arraignment DeAngelo faced 13 murder counts across Sacramento, Santa Barbara, Tulare, Ventura and Orange counties and 13 kidnapping counts in Sacramento and Contra Costa counties; the kidnapping charges were used because California's statute of limitations barred prosecution of the rapes themselves. The district attorneys agreed to consolidate all of the cases in Sacramento.

The 2020 plea agreement spared DeAngelo the death penalty. The Associated Press, in a report carried by PBS NewsHour, said prosecutors had initially sought death but accepted life terms, citing California's execution moratorium, the pandemic and the ages of the defendant, victims and witnesses. Sentencing followed three days of victim impact statements in a university ballroom. DeAngelo, then 74, rose from a wheelchair and told the court he was sorry to everyone he had hurt, ABC News reported. The AP reported that Judge Bowman imposed 11 consecutive life terms without parole on the murder counts, additional life terms on the remaining counts and eight years for enhancements. He waived his right to appeal.

According to the Wikipedia article, DeAngelo is held in protective custody at California State Prison, Corcoran, and DNA testing has excluded him from several other unsolved killings once speculatively linked to the case.

DeAngelo was born on November 8, 1945, in Bath, New York, according to the Wikipedia article. He served in the Navy during the Vietnam War, studied police science and criminal justice, and worked as a police officer in Exeter from 1973 to 1976 and in Auburn from 1976 to 1979. NBC News reported that he was fired from the Auburn department in 1979 after being arrested for shoplifting a hammer and dog repellent. He raised three daughters in Citrus Heights and later worked as a truck mechanic. His wife filed for divorce after his arrest.

name: Joseph Paul Franklin

victims.suspected: 8 to 22

victimProfile: Mostly Black men, Jewish worshippers and interracial couples, chosen for race or religion and shot from concealment, often with a high-powered rifle
captureMethod: Arrested in Kentucky in September 1980 after Salt Lake City police traced his car, he escaped from an interrogation room and was recaptured about a month later in Lakeland, Florida, while selling blood
sentence: Death for the 1977 capital murder of Gerald Gordon in St. Louis County, Missouri (1997); life sentences in Utah (state and federal, 1981), Wisconsin (1986) and Ohio (1998); also convicted of a Chattanooga, Tennessee killing
fateDetail: Lethal injection of pentobarbital, Eastern Reception, Diagnostic and Correctional Center, Bonne Terre, Missouri; pronounced dead at 6:17 a.m. on November 20, 2013
summary: Executed. Joseph Paul Franklin, a white supremacist sniper, was convicted of eight murders in Utah, Missouri, Wisconsin, Ohio and Tennessee committed between 1977 and 1980. He was executed in Missouri in 2013 for a synagogue shooting.
narrative: Joseph Paul Franklin was a white supremacist drifter who was convicted of eight murders committed in five states between 1977 and 1980, most of them sniper shootings of Black men, Jewish worshippers and interracial couples. He received life sentences in Utah, Wisconsin, Ohio and Tennessee and a death sentence in Missouri for the 1977 killing of Gerald Gordon outside a synagogue in Richmond Heights, a St. Louis suburb. Missouri executed him by lethal injection at Bonne Terre on November 20, 2013, when he was 63.

Franklin was born James Clayton Vaughn Jr. in Mobile, Alabama, on April 13, 1950, and later changed his name. A 1995 Deseret News chronology says he joined the American Nazi Party in Virginia in the late 1960s and later sold a fascist party newspaper in Atlanta. According to Associated Press reporting carried by the Christian Science Monitor, he began drifting across the country in the mid-1970s and robbed as many as 16 banks to pay his way. In July 1977 he bombed a synagogue in Chattanooga, Tennessee; no one was hurt, and he was later sentenced to federal prison for it.

The killings began weeks later. On August 7, 1977, he shot dead Alphonce Manning Jr. and Toni Schwenn, an interracial couple, in Madison, Wisconsin. On October 8, 1977, he fired five shots from about 100 yards at guests leaving a bar mitzvah at Brith Sholom Kneseth Israel Congregation in Richmond Heights, according to the Missouri Supreme Court. Gerald Gordon, 42, was killed and two other men were wounded. AP reporting says he was convicted of a further killing in Chattanooga, and that his victims also included two children in Cincinnati. On June 8, 1980, cousins Dante Evans Brown, 13, and Darrell Lane, 14, were shot from a railway trestle on Reading Road in Cincinnati; Dante died at the scene and Darrell three days later, WCPO reported.

On August 20, 1980, Ted Fields, 20, and David Martin, 18, two Black men, were shot dead while jogging with two white women in Liberty Park, Salt Lake City. Retired detective Don Bell told the Deseret News that motel registrations placed Franklin in the city for 10 days, and a motel owner's note of his real licence plate led to a warrant that caused his arrest in Kentucky. He escaped from an interrogation room there and was captured about a month later in Lakeland, Florida. Utah was the first jurisdiction to convict him: a federal civil rights verdict in March 1981 brought two consecutive life terms, and a state jury convicted him of both murders in August 1981 but could not agree on death, according to the Deseret News.

Other convictions followed over the next two decades. Wisconsin convicted him of the Madison killings in February 1986. In 1994 he told FBI agents he was responsible for the Richmond Heights shooting, and in 1997 a St. Louis County jury convicted him of capital murder and two counts of felonious assault and he was sentenced to death. The Missouri Supreme Court affirmed the death sentence on June 16, 1998, after Franklin said he did not wish to appeal. In 1997 a Hamilton County assistant prosecutor, Melissa Powers, obtained a taped confession to the Cincinnati killings, and in 1998 a jury convicted him of two counts of aggravated murder; FOX19 reported he received two life sentences.

Franklin also claimed responsibility for shooting Hustler publisher Larry Flynt in Georgia in 1978 and Urban League president Vernon Jordan in Fort Wayne, Indiana, in 1980. He was acquitted of the Jordan shooting, and the Wikipedia article says no one was ever charged over the Flynt attack. Counts of his killings vary by source: AP reporting said he claimed up to 20, the Deseret News said he told CNN in 2013 that he had killed about 22 people, and the Wikipedia article lists further admitted killings in Georgia, Virginia, Oklahoma, Pennsylvania and West Virginia for which he was not convicted.

His execution was delayed by two federal stays granted on November 19, 2013, including one over Missouri's new single-drug protocol, but an appeals court lifted them and the U.S. Supreme Court declined to intervene. He was pronounced dead at 6:17 a.m. after five grams of pentobarbital, the first Missouri execution with that drug, according to the AP and the BBC. Flynt had publicly opposed the execution. In final interviews Franklin said he regretted his crimes and had renounced racism; defence lawyers had long argued that he was a paranoid schizophrenic.

name: Joshua Wade
victimProfile: Strangers or near-strangers in the Anchorage area: two mentally ill men, an Alaska Native woman, an unidentified man and a 52-year-old neighbor
captureMethod: Identified from ATM security footage using the victim's card, he was arrested by Anchorage police and the FBI after a standoff at a south Anchorage apartment
sentence: 99 years (Alaska, first-degree murder of Mindy Schloss, parole barred for at least 66 years) plus consecutive federal life sentence for carjacking resulting in death (February 17, 2010)
fateDetail: Indiana State Prison, Michigan City, Indiana; found unresponsive in his cell, cause not publicly reported
summary: Died in prison. Joshua Wade pleaded guilty in 2010 to murdering his Anchorage neighbor Mindy Schloss and admitted the 2000 killing of Della Brown; in 2014 he confessed to three more Alaska killings. He died in an Indiana prison in 2024.
narrative: Joshua Alan Wade was an Anchorage, Alaska, man who in February 2010 pleaded guilty in state court to the 2007 first-degree murder of his neighbor, nurse practitioner Mindy Schloss, and in federal court to carjacking resulting in her death. Under the plea agreements he also admitted killing Della Brown in 2000, a murder of which an Anchorage jury had acquitted him in 2003. In 2014 he told state and federal investigators he had killed three more men in Alaska between 1994 and 2000, bringing the total he claimed to five. Serving a 99-year state term and a consecutive federal life sentence, he died at the Indiana State Prison in Michigan City on June 14, 2024, aged 44.

The earliest killing Wade later claimed was that of John Michael Martin, 38, who was found shot in the back of the head beside a bike trail along Northern Lights Boulevard in Anchorage in May 1994, shortly after leaving a Village Inn restaurant where he regularly had coffee with friends. Wade was 14 at the time. The Anchorage Daily News reported that Martin had schizophrenia and that the detective on the case had exhausted all leads. In December 1999 Henry Ongtowasruk, 30, originally from the village of Wales, was found dead in a room at the Alaska Budget Motel in the Fairview neighborhood of Anchorage; the state medical examiner ruled the death a homicide. Both men were mentally ill and, according to the newspaper, had no known link to Wade.

In September 2000 Della Brown, a 33-year-old Alaska Native woman, was found in an abandoned shed in Spenard. Prosecutors said Wade had struck her in the head with a rock and then shown the body to a series of acquaintances. At the 2003 trial his lawyers portrayed him as a boastful talker, and witnesses who had seen the body were themselves involved in crime. The jury acquitted him of murder, sexual assault and robbery and convicted him only of tampering with evidence, for which he served six and a half years. The Anchorage Daily News later noted that the verdict was widely seen as highlighting injustices against Alaska Native crime victims.

Months after completing probation, Wade lived next door to Mindy Schloss, 52, a nurse practitioner. She was last seen on August 3, 2007, and missed a scheduled flight to Fairbanks two days later. According to court testimony reported by the Anchorage Daily News, Wade entered her home at night, bound her with zip ties, obtained her ATM card and PIN, and drove her in her own car to a wooded area near Wasilla, where he shot her and burned her body. On August 29 police said a security photo showed him using an ATM the weekend she vanished, and the FBI sought him for bank fraud. He was taken into custody on September 2, 2007, after a standoff at a south Anchorage apartment, Alaska Public Media reported. Schloss was found more than a month after she disappeared.

Because Schloss died during a carjacking, Wade faced a possible federal death sentence, although Alaska has no death penalty. On February 17, 2010, he pleaded guilty before Superior Court Judge Phillip Volland, who imposed 99 years and barred parole for at least 66 years, and before Chief U.S. District Judge Ralph Beistline, who sentenced him to life to be served consecutively, according to the U.S. Attorney's Office for Alaska. When Beistline called him a coward who preyed on women, Wade interrupted with a remark about the men he had killed, which officials at the time could not explain.

In 2014, after a failed attempt to withdraw his earlier admissions, Wade offered investigators new information in exchange for a transfer out of the Alaska prison system. At a press conference on June 20, 2014, authorities said he had admitted killing Martin, Ongtowasruk and an unidentified man on the night Brown died, whom he said he beat and then shot in the Matanuska-Susitna Valley. Assistant Attorney General John Novak said not all claims were equally confirmed and that no decision on new charges had been made. Wade had already been moved from Spring Creek Correctional Center in Seward to the federal penitentiary in Terre Haute, Indiana.

He was later held in the Indiana state prison system. On June 14, 2024, the Indiana Department of Correction said, he was found unresponsive in his cell and could not be revived; an autopsy was ordered. Wade was born in Great Falls, Montana, and, according to the Wikipedia article, on March 18, 1980; he grew up in Anchorage, and in court he described being sexually abused from the age of five. His case is the subject of Monte Francis's 2016 book Ice and Bone.

name: Juan Corona
victimProfile: Itinerant male farmworkers, mostly middle-aged or older, who had been seen with Corona or hired through his Sutter County labor contracting business
captureMethod: A rancher reported a freshly dug hole in his peach orchard on May 19, 1971; as more graves were found, receipts and witness accounts led police to Corona, who was arrested a week later and whose home yielded a ledger listing victims' names
sentence: 25 concurrent life terms for 25 counts of first-degree murder on reconviction in 1982; the 1973 conviction, which the Wikipedia article says carried 25 consecutive life terms, was reversed in 1978
fateDetail: Held at California State Prison-Corcoran from 1992; died of natural causes at an outside hospital on March 4, 2019, aged 85
summary: Died in prison. Labor contractor Juan Corona was convicted of murdering 25 farmworkers buried in orchards near Yuba City, California, in 1971. His 1973 conviction was reversed in 1978, he was convicted again in 1982, and he died in custody in 2019.
narrative: Juan Vallejo Corona was a farm labor contractor in Sutter County, California, convicted of murdering 25 itinerant farmworkers whose bodies were found buried in orchards along the Feather River near Yuba City in May and June 1971. A jury in Fairfield found him guilty of 25 counts of first-degree murder in January 1973; a state appeals court reversed that verdict in 1978 because of his lawyer's conflict of interest and inadequate defense, and a second jury convicted him again on all 25 counts in 1982. Serving 25 concurrent life terms, he died of natural causes on March 4, 2019, aged 85, while in the custody of California State Prison-Corcoran, according to the California Department of Corrections and Rehabilitation.

Corona was born on February 7, 1934, in Jalisco, Mexico, and came to the United States in 1950 to pick crops, following older brothers, KQED reported. After the 1955 Sacramento Valley flood he was committed to a state hospital and diagnosed with schizophrenia; the 1978 appeals court opinion records a stay at DeWitt State Hospital from January to April 1956. By the mid-1960s he and his brothers were established labor contractors who recruited workers for ranches around Yuba City and Marysville. His business hired the men who later became his victims, and each victim had either been seen with him or hired through that business, according to the corrections department.

The case began on May 19, 1971, when a rancher named Kagehiro noticed a hole in the corner of his peach orchard and called police. The next morning officers uncovered the body of Kenneth Whitacre. Further graves were found on the Kagehiro and Sullivan ranches between May 20 and June 4, 1971, until 25 bodies had been recovered; according to KQED, receipts made out to Corona were found with bodies in a second orchard. The appeals court opinion states that all but one victim had chopping-type head wounds, many also had stab wounds to the chest, and one man, William Kamp, had been shot in the head. Four victims were never identified, and KQED reported that 14 of the dead, including the four unknown men, were buried in a common grave in Sutter.

Corona was arrested on May 26, 1971. Searches of his home, vehicles and property produced knives, a machete, a pistol, a post-hole digger and bloodstained items, and a green ledger in his bedroom with handwritten names and dates. The appeals court found that seven of the names matched identified victims; the Wikipedia article says the prosecution called it a death list. The trial was moved out of Sutter County to the Solano County courthouse in Fairfield, where, after about four months, a jury convicted him on all 25 counts on January 18, 1973, as KPIX-TV news footage of that day records. His lawyer, Richard Hawk, had called no defense witnesses, according to UPI.

Corona was sent to state prison in February 1973. Later that year he was stabbed repeatedly in his cell at the California Medical Facility in Vacaville and lost the sight of his left eye. On May 8, 1978, the California Court of Appeal, First District, reversed the judgment and granted his petition for habeas corpus. It found that Hawk had taken the literary and dramatic rights to Corona's life story as his fee, creating a conflict of interest, and had failed to investigate defenses based on Corona's mental state.

The retrial took place in Hayward, Alameda County, in 1982. Over 28 weeks of testimony from 212 witnesses, at a cost UPI put at 5.2 million dollars, the new defense team argued that Corona's half-brother Natividad, a former Marysville cafe owner believed to have died in Mexico in 1973, was the killer; prosecutors said Natividad was in Mexico at the time. Corona testified that he had killed no one. On September 23, 1982, the jury again convicted him of all 25 murders, and its foreman told UPI that the ledger was the deciding evidence. He was sentenced to 25 concurrent life terms and began serving the Sutter County commitment in December 1982.

Corona was moved in 1992 to the Protective Housing Unit at Corcoran. He was denied parole eight times, at hearings between 1984 and 2016. KQED reported that prosecutors said he admitted the killings at a 2011 hearing, describing the victims as trespassers, while at his last hearing in 2016 he said he could not recall killing anyone. His family maintained his innocence, and neither side ever established a motive. At the time of the 1971 discovery, the number of victims was a United States record, according to the corrections department.

name: Judy Buenoano
victimProfile: Her husband, her 19-year-old son and men she lived with or was engaged to, each insured with her as beneficiary
captureMethod: Investigators looking into the 1983 car bombing that injured her fiance John Gentry found poisoned capsules she had given him, then exhumed her husband James Goodyear and found arsenic
sentence: Life imprisonment for the first-degree murder of her son Michael (1984); 12 years for the attempted murder of John Gentry (1984); death for the first-degree murder of James Goodyear (1985)
fateDetail: Electrocuted at Florida State Prison, Raiford, on March 30, 1998, aged 54; the first woman executed in Florida since 1848
summary: Executed. Judy Buenoano was convicted of poisoning her husband James Goodyear with arsenic in Orlando in 1971 and of murdering her son Michael, who drowned in 1980. She was electrocuted at Florida State Prison in March 1998.
narrative: Judias "Judy" Buenoano was a Florida woman convicted of two murders committed years apart for insurance money: the 1971 arsenic poisoning of her husband, Air Force Sergeant James Goodyear, in Orlando, and the 1980 drowning of her 19-year-old son, Michael. She was also convicted of attempting to murder her fiance, John Gentry, whose car exploded in Pensacola in 1983. Sentenced to death for Goodyear's killing, she was electrocuted at Florida State Prison on March 30, 1998, the first woman executed in Florida since 1848. She maintained her innocence to the end, CBS News reported.

She was born Anna Lou Welty on April 4, 1943, in Quanah, Texas, according to the Wikipedia article and the Florida Sheriffs Association. She married Goodyear in 1962, according to the federal court in the Middle District of Florida and the sheriffs association (the Wikipedia article gives 1963), and in 1978 legally changed her surname to Buenoano, a name investigators later learned was a Spanish rendering of Goodyear. According to the Florida Supreme Court, Goodyear returned to Orlando from a tour of duty in South Vietnam in 1971, fell ill with nausea and vomiting, was admitted to the naval hospital there on September 13 and died on September 16 of cardiovascular collapse and renal failure. No toxicology test was done at the time. She collected about $33,000 in life insurance and $62,000 from the Veterans Administration.

After Goodyear's death she lived with Bobby Joe Morris and moved with him to Colorado. Morris became ill with symptoms like Goodyear's and died; the Wikipedia article dates his death to January 1978 in Trinidad, Colorado, while CBS News gives 1977. She collected about $23,000 from three insurance policies on his life, the Florida Supreme Court found. When his remains were exhumed in 1984, tissue analysis showed acute arsenic poisoning. She was never charged with his death, which came to light after she had already been sentenced to death in Florida, CBS News and the Deseret News reported. The Wikipedia article and the sheriffs association also say she was believed to be involved in the 1980 death of a man named Gerald Dossett and a 1974 killing in Alabama; no charges were brought in either.

Her son Michael, who had been adopted by Goodyear, joined the Army in 1979, became ill and was diagnosed with arsenic poisoning, according to the federal court account. Fitted with heavy metal leg braces, he was discharged into his mother's care. On May 13, 1980, he drowned when a canoe carrying the two of them capsized on the East River near Milton, Florida, weighed down by his braces. Prosecutors argued that she had caused his paralysis with arsenic. She collected about $20,000 from his military life insurance.

In 1982 she was living with John Gentry in the Gulf Breeze area and engaged to him. According to the Florida Supreme Court, she began giving him Vicon C vitamin capsules in November 1982 for a cold; he became so ill that he was hospitalized on December 15, and the sickness returned after she gave him the capsules again. Analysis found they contained paraformaldehyde. She had been telling associates he had terminal cancer, and she held $510,000 in life insurance on him. In 1983 his car exploded in Pensacola, seriously injuring him. A search of her home found wire and tape matching the bomb remains, the federal court account says. The investigation led to the exhumation of Goodyear, whose body contained arsenic. Her son James Goodyear Jr., charged as an accomplice in the bombing, was acquitted at a separate trial.

In 1984 she was convicted of first-degree murder in Michael's death and sentenced to life in prison, and of attempted murder of Gentry, receiving 12 years. A grand jury indicted her on August 31, 1984, for Goodyear's murder. At her trial, where evidence of the Morris death and the Gentry poisoning was admitted as similar-fact evidence, two acquaintances testified that she had discussed killing someone with arsenic, and two witnesses said she admitted killing Goodyear. The jury convicted her and recommended death, and she was sentenced to death in November 1985. The Florida Supreme Court affirmed on June 23, 1988.

Her later appeals, including claims about FBI laboratory testimony concerning the Gentry capsules and an undisclosed juror conviction, were rejected by the Florida Supreme Court on March 26, 1998, and by the Eleventh Circuit on March 29, which found the remaining evidence of guilt strong. She was electrocuted the next morning and pronounced dead at 7:13 a.m., aged 54, the third woman executed in the United States after 1976, according to CBS News.
