name: Keith Hunter Jesperson
victimProfile: Women, several of them hitchhikers, sex workers or acquaintances he met while working as a long-haul truck driver, including a former girlfriend
captureMethod: Clark County, Washington, investigators traced him through Julie Winningham's car; after police questioned him and he made two suicide attempts, he surrendered and was arrested
sentence: Washington (1995): 34 years and 4 months for the first-degree murder of Julie Winningham; Oregon (1995): life with a 30-year minimum for Taunja Bennett (no contest) and life for Laurie Ann Pentland (guilty plea), run consecutively; Wyoming: a life sentence, per a 2008 Spokesman-Review report; California (2010): 15 years to life for the woman later identified as Lydia Jane Wade McWhorter
fateDetail: Oregon State Penitentiary, Salem
summary: Serving life. Long-haul trucker Keith Hunter Jesperson, the Happy Face Killer, is held at the Oregon State Penitentiary for murders of women committed between 1990 and 1995; eight killings in six states are considered confirmed.
narrative: Keith Hunter Jesperson is a former long-haul truck driver known as the Happy Face Killer, a name taken from the smiley faces he drew on confession letters sent to newspapers and police. Eight killings of women between January 1990 and March 1995 are considered confirmed, in Oregon, Washington, California, Florida and on the Wyoming-Nebraska line. He pleaded guilty or no contest in Washington and Oregon in 1995, was later sentenced in Wyoming and, in 2010, in California, and was charged in Florida in 2023. He is serving his sentences at the Oregon State Penitentiary in Salem.

His first known victim was Taunja Bennett, 23, who was strangled near Portland, Oregon, in January 1990. Two other people were convicted of her murder: Laverne Pavlinac, who had falsely told police that she and her boyfriend John Sosnovske killed Bennett, and Sosnovske, who pleaded no contest to avoid a possible death sentence. Pavlinac later said she invented the story to escape an abusive relationship, the Wikipedia article says, and Jesperson later led police to Bennett's purse, a detail that only the killer was likely to know. Jesperson has said he wrote a confession on a truck stop restroom wall after the killing and later sent anonymous letters, including a six-page letter to The Oregonian; a columnist there gave the writer his nickname, the Wikipedia article says.

Over the next five years he killed women he met on the road. According to the Wikipedia article, the body of a woman he called Claudia was found near Blythe, California, on August 30, 1992; the body of Cynthia Lyn Rose was found in Turlock, California, about a month later; and Laurie Ann Pentland was found dead in Oregon in November 1992. A woman found in Santa Nella, California, in 1993 was initially thought to have died of an overdose and was identified in 2022 as Patricia Skiple. The remains of a woman found off Interstate 10 in Okaloosa County, Florida, in September 1994 were identified in October 2023 as Suzanne Kjellenberg, who was 34. Angela May Subrize, 21, of Oklahoma City, was killed in late January 1995 near Cheyenne, Wyoming, and her body was found in western Nebraska, Laramie County sheriff's detectives told the Associated Press in October 1995.

The last killing was that of Julie Ann Winningham, 41, a former girlfriend, whose body was found in March 1995 below a viewpoint off Washington 14 near Washougal, Washington. Clark County investigators traced him through a car she had wrecked and sold. According to the Wikipedia article, police questioned him about a week before his arrest; after two suicide attempts he surrendered, and he was arrested on March 30, 1995. Before and after his arrest he wrote letters, decorated with smiley faces, claiming eight killings in five states. He later claimed far more, as many as 160 according to the Wikipedia article, most of which investigators have not confirmed or he has withdrawn.

In October 1995 Jesperson pleaded guilty in Clark County Superior Court to the first-degree murder of Winningham, and prosecutors dropped rape and kidnapping charges. Judge Robert Harris sentenced him in December to 34 years and four months. In Portland in November 1995 he pleaded no contest to Bennett's murder and was sentenced to life with a 30-year minimum; prosecutors agreed not to seek death partly to speed the release of Pavlinac and Sosnovske, who were later freed. In December 1995 he pleaded guilty in Hillsboro, Oregon, to strangling Pentland, 23, of Carlton, and received a further life term, with all three sentences to run consecutively.

Prosecutors in Cheyenne rejected an offer from his lawyer, made in late 1995, to help solve the Subrize killing in exchange for not seeking the death penalty. A 2008 Spokesman-Review article described him as serving life sentences for killings in Oregon and Wyoming. On January 8, 2010, he pleaded guilty in Riverside County, California, to the murder of the woman he called Claudia and was sentenced to 15 years to life, according to the Riverside County District Attorney's Office. In October 2023 the Okaloosa County Sheriff's Office announced that Kjellenberg had been identified through forensic genetic genealogy and that Jesperson had been charged with her murder; KPTV did not report a resolution of that charge.

Jesperson was born on April 6, 1955, in Chilliwack, British Columbia. The last of the confirmed victims to be named, Claudia, was identified in 2026 as Lydia Jane Wade McWhorter, who had reportedly disappeared from Texas, after DNA and genealogy research, KTLA reported; the district attorney's cold case team said her identification closed the final case tied to his convictions. His daughter, Melissa Moore, has spoken and written publicly about growing up as his child.

name: Kenneth Bianchi

victims.suspected: 12 (10 in Los Angeles with Buono, 2 in Bellingham)

victimProfile: Girls and young women aged 12 to 28 in Los Angeles, lured by the cousins posing as police officers; two university students aged 22 and 27 in Bellingham
captureMethod: Taken into custody by Bellingham police the day after two students he had hired to watch a house were found strangled; a note in the victim's car and his security job pointed to him, and jewelry and fiber evidence then tied him to the Los Angeles killings
sentence: Two consecutive life terms in Washington (1979) and five concurrent life terms in California (1979); Washington parole board set a 116.5-year minimum term in 1990
fateDetail: Washington State Penitentiary, Walla Walla; parole denied by California boards in 2010 and 2025
summary: Imprisoned for life. Kenneth Bianchi, one of the two Hillside Stranglers, pleaded guilty in 1979 to five Los Angeles murders and two Bellingham, Washington murders; his cousin Angelo Buono was convicted of nine killings in 1983.
narrative: Kenneth Alessio Bianchi is one of the two Hillside Stranglers who, with his cousin Angelo Buono Jr., murdered girls and young women in the Los Angeles area between October 1977 and February 1978. He then killed two university students alone in Bellingham, Washington, in January 1979. In October 1979 he pleaded guilty in Washington to two counts of first-degree murder and in Los Angeles to five murders, conspiracy and sodomy. Courts have convicted him of seven murders; he confessed to those seven; police attribute twelve killings to the Hillside Strangler cases. He is serving life sentences at the Washington State Penitentiary in Walla Walla.

According to UPI and the Wikipedia article, Bianchi and Buono posed as police officers to lure victims, took them to Buono's upholstery shop in Glendale, strangled them and left the bodies on hillsides around Los Angeles. The ten Los Angeles victims named in the Wikipedia article were Yolanda Washington, 19; Judith Miller, 15; Lissa Kastin, 21; Jane King, 28; Dolores Cepeda, 12; Sonja Johnson, 14; Kristina Weckler, 20; Lauren Wagner, 18; Kimberly Martin, 17; and Cindy Hudspeth, 20. The first body was found on October 17, 1977, and the last on February 17, 1978.

According to HistoryLink, Bianchi was working for a Bellingham security company when, on January 11, 1979, he offered Western Washington University students Karen Mandic, 22, and Diane Wilder, 27, money to watch a house he was guarding. Both were found strangled in Mandic's car on January 12, 1979. A note in the car naming the house and "Ken" led Bellingham police to take him into custody that day. HistoryLink reports that jewelry in his home resembled items worn by Los Angeles victims, that FBI laboratory work matched fibers and hair to the house and to Bianchi, and that a Los Angeles task force detective recognized his name on January 13.

Charged on January 26, 1979, Bianchi pleaded not guilty and then, on March 30, 1979, not guilty by reason of insanity, claiming under hypnosis that a second personality named Steve had committed the crimes. According to the Wikipedia article, psychiatrist Martin Orne concluded he was simulating, and Bianchi later admitted faking the disorder. After being found competent, HistoryLink reports, he pleaded guilty on October 19, 1979, to both Bellingham murders under an agreement in which the prosecutor withdrew the death penalty request and Bianchi agreed to testify against Buono; Judge Jack Kurtz imposed two consecutive life terms. On October 22, 1979, in Los Angeles, he pleaded guilty to five Hillside Strangler murders, conspiracy to commit murder and sodomy, receiving concurrent life terms.

Buono was arrested in October 1979, and his trial became the longest criminal trial in United States history to that point. UPI reported that Bianchi testified for 80 days but that Judge Ronald George found he had not testified truthfully and completely, and ordered him to serve his sentence in Washington rather than California. A jury convicted Buono in November 1983 of nine of the ten Los Angeles murders; in January 1984 he received nine concurrent terms of life without parole. Bianchi was moved to Walla Walla on January 10, 1984. Buono died at Calipatria State Prison on September 21, 2002, according to the Wikipedia article and AP reporting cited by CBS News.

HistoryLink reports that in July 1990 the Washington parole board set Bianchi's minimum term at 116.5 years, with eligibility in 2059. CBS News, citing the Associated Press, reported that a California board denied him parole on August 18, 2010. The Los Angeles Times reported that the California Board of Parole Hearings denied parole again on July 10, 2025 with eligibility again in ten years, and that he maintains in appeals that his confession and pleas were coerced through hypnosis. Fox News reported that he changed his name to Anthony D'Amato in 2023 and that a Washington parole review was pending in July 2025.

Bianchi was born on May 22, 1951, in Rochester, New York, and was adopted as an infant. According to the Wikipedia article, he was a suspect but never charged in the 1971 to 1973 Rochester Alphabet murders, which he denies, and moved to Los Angeles in 1976 to live near Buono.

name: Kenneth McDuff

victims.suspected: 9 to 14 or more

victimProfile: Three teenagers in 1966; young women aged 21 to 36 in 1989 to 1992, including sex workers and a convenience store clerk
captureMethod: A Kansas City co-worker recognized him from America's Most Wanted; police confirmed his identity by fingerprints and arrested him under an alias
sentence: Death for three 1966 murders, commuted to life after Furman v. Georgia (1972); death for the murder of Melissa Northrup (1993); death plus two life terms for the murder of Colleen Reed (one life term later reversed)
fateDetail: Lethal injection, Huntsville Unit, Texas, November 17, 1998
summary: Executed 1998. Texas killer sentenced to death for three 1966 murders, released on parole in 1989 after his sentence was commuted, and convicted of two 1991 to 1992 murders; his case drove Texas parole reform.
narrative: Kenneth Allen McDuff was a Texas murderer whose two killing periods, 1966 and 1989 to 1992, were separated by a death sentence, a commutation and a parole. Courts convicted him of five murders: three teenagers killed near Fort Worth in 1966, and Colleen Reed and Melissa Northrup, killed in 1991 and 1992. Texas executed him on November 17, 1998. Wikipedia's summary of the reporting puts the attributed toll at nine to fourteen or more. According to the University of North Texas Press, anger that a condemned man had been freed to kill again produced parole reforms and prison construction known collectively as the "McDuff Rules."

The 1966 crimes appear in testimony recited by the United States Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit. Roy Dale Green testified that on August 6, 1966, McDuff locked two teenage boys and a girl in the trunk of a parked car, shot the boys through the trunk, raped the girl and choked her with a broomstick; Green later turned him in. Wikipedia names the victims as Robert Brand, 17, Mark Dunnam, 15, and Edna Louise Sullivan, 16, abducted at Everman. McDuff was convicted of murder with malice and sentenced to death. After the Supreme Court's 1972 Furman v. Georgia decision the sentence became life imprisonment. The board paroled him in October 1989. Wikipedia also lists four deaths attributed to him after release for which he was never charged: Sarafia Parker in Temple in October 1989; Brenda Thompson and Regenia Moore, who vanished near Waco in October 1991 and whose remains were found in 1998; and Valencia Joshua, found in Waco in March 1992.

The two capital cases are described in court opinions. The Texas Court of Appeals in Austin recorded that Colleen Reed was abducted from an Austin car wash in late December 1991 and that her body had not been found at trial. The Fifth Circuit summarized the Texas Court of Criminal Appeals' findings on Melissa Northrup: around 4 a.m. on March 1, 1992, she was taken from the Waco Quik Pak where she worked and where McDuff had briefly been employed; a witness saw him driving her car with a frightened woman beside him; and her bound body was later found in a water-filled gravel pit. State experts linked hairs on her body and in her car to him.

McDuff abandoned his car in Waco and fled to Kansas City, Missouri, where, the Austin court noted, he lived under an alias from March 1992 and was arrested in May 1992 using a false name. Wikipedia reports that a co-worker recognized him from a May 1, 1992 America's Most Wanted broadcast and that he was arrested on May 4, 1992.

A McLennan County jury convicted McDuff of Northrup's capital murder and, according to Wikipedia, returned a death sentence on February 18, 1993. The Reed indictment, returned in Travis County, was tried in Guadalupe County after a change of venue. The Austin court recorded that the jury convicted him of capital murder, aggravated kidnapping and aggravated sexual assault, imposing death on the capital count and life terms on the others. The Court of Criminal Appeals affirmed the Reed death sentence in 1997; the Austin court that year reversed the sexual-assault count because the only witness was the accomplice, Alva Hank Worley, and affirmed the kidnapping count.

The Court of Criminal Appeals affirmed the Northrup conviction in 1997, the Supreme Court denied certiorari in 1998, and state and federal habeas relief were denied. On November 17, 1998, the Fifth Circuit refused a certificate of appealability, rejecting claims that the hair testimony was false and that another man was the killer. McDuff was executed by lethal injection at the Huntsville Unit that evening, aged 52. The Texas Department of Criminal Justice records his last statement as "I'm ready to be released. Release me." Wikipedia and Spectrum News report that in his final weeks he led investigators to Reed's remains.
McDuff was born on March 21, 1946, in Rosebud, Texas. Wikipedia records that in 1964 he was convicted of twelve burglary counts and paroled in December 1965, eight months before the Everman killings.

name: Khalil Wheeler-Weaver
victimProfile: Women aged 19 to 33 whom he contacted through dating and social media apps and arranged to meet for sex in Essex County, New Jersey
captureMethod: Friends of victim Sarah Butler used her social media accounts and a fake profile to lure him to a meeting in Montclair and alerted police; phone location evidence then tied him to the victims
sentence: 160 years in prison, imposed October 6, 2021, for three murders, attempted murder, kidnapping, aggravated sexual assault, aggravated arson and desecration of human remains; parole eligibility after 140 years
fateDetail: New Jersey State Prison, according to the Wikipedia article; a separate 2022 murder charge in the death of Mawa Doumbia was reported as pending
summary: Serving 160 years. Khalil Wheeler-Weaver of Orange, New Jersey, was convicted in December 2019 of murdering three women he met through online apps in 2016 and attempting to kill a fourth. He is charged, but not convicted, in a fourth killing.
narrative: Khalil Wheeler-Weaver is an American serial killer who was convicted by an Essex County, New Jersey, jury in December 2019 of murdering three women in the autumn of 2016 and of attempting to murder a fourth woman, who survived. He was 20 at the time of the killings and lived in Orange, New Jersey. On October 6, 2021, Superior Court Judge Mark S. Ali sentenced him in Newark to 160 years in prison, and a state appeals court upheld the convictions and sentence in January 2024. In 2022 he was also charged with the 2016 murder of a 15-year-old Newark girl; that charge is an allegation only, he is presumed innocent of it, and it was reported as pending in 2024. He has denied all of the killings and said he was framed.

According to the Essex County Prosecutor's Office, the three women he was convicted of killing were Robin West, 19, a Philadelphia native living in Union Township; Joanne Brown, 33, of Newark; and Sarah Butler, 20, a Montclair resident who was a college student in Jersey City. Prosecutors said he contacted the women through dating and social media apps and arranged to meet them for sex. The Associated Press, in reporting carried by NBC News, said West was seen getting into his car on August 31, 2016, and was killed within hours; the prosecutor's office gives her date of death as September 1. Her body was left in a vacant house in Orange near his home, and the house was set on fire. Identifying her remains took about two weeks.

Brown was killed on October 22, 2016, and her body was found on December 5 in a vacant home in Orange. Butler disappeared around Thanksgiving; the prosecutor's office dates her killing to November 22, 2016, and her body was found on December 1 in Eagle Rock Reservation in West Orange. Both Brown and Butler had been strangled with clothing, according to the AP. The killings spanned 84 days, NorthJersey.com reported. The Wikipedia article states that he wore gloves and condoms and left little physical evidence, although a small amount of his DNA was recovered from one victim.

The case turned on the work of Butler's friends. According to prosecutors and the AP, they got into her social media accounts, set up a fake profile, lured Wheeler-Weaver to a meeting in Montclair, and notified police. Records from his phone then placed him where the victims disappeared and where their bodies were found. He pleaded not guilty in 2017. The surviving victim, Tiffany Taylor, testified at the trial; the prosecutor's office described her as a 34-year-old woman who was kidnapped, sexually assaulted and nearly killed. The Wikipedia article says the attack began at a motel in Elizabeth and that she escaped and called 911, but that police did not initially believe her account.

The trial lasted about two months. At its close, his public defenders argued that he had arranged sexual encounters with the women but dropped them off unharmed. The jury deliberated for less than three hours before convicting him on all counts on December 19, 2019: three counts of murder, three counts of desecration of human remains, aggravated arson, and kidnapping, aggravated sexual assault and attempted murder in the attack on Taylor. At sentencing, West's mother and Butler's father addressed the court, and Taylor said the attack had left her paranoid. The Wikipedia article reports parole eligibility after 140 years.

On appeal, he argued that each victim's case should have been tried separately, that the jury had been wrongly instructed, that police had violated his right to remain silent, and that the sentence was excessive. A three-judge Appellate Division panel rejected those claims in January 2024. It found fault with the judge's Miranda instruction but held that the error did not amount to plain error requiring a new trial, and wrote that the length of the sentence was justified by the nature of the crimes.

In March 2022, Essex County prosecutors charged him with the murder of Mawa Doumbia, 15, of Newark, who was last seen leaving her home on October 7, 2016. Her remains, which showed signs of strangulation, were found in a house in Orange in May 2019 and identified in late 2021. Prosecutors allege he met her online and strangled her. He was due for arraignment in Newark in October 2022, and Patch described the case as pending in January 2024. Wheeler-Weaver grew up in Orange and had worked as a security guard; the Wikipedia article says his stepfather is a police detective in East Orange.

name: Kristen Gilbert

victims.suspected: 4 murders and 3 attempted murders charged; prosecutors noted she was on duty for about half of roughly 350 deaths on her ward between 1989 and 1996, but no further murders were attributed to her

victimProfile: Male veterans aged 35 to 68 who were patients on Ward C of the Veterans Affairs Medical Center in Northampton, Massachusetts
captureMethod: Three fellow nurses reported a pattern of cardiac emergencies on her shifts and missing epinephrine in February 1996, prompting a federal investigation that included exhumations and tissue testing; she was already imprisoned for a 1996 bomb threat when the murder indictment was unsealed in November 1998.
sentence: Life in prison without the possibility of parole (March 27, 2001), after the federal jury declined to impose a death sentence; earlier, 15 months for a 1996 bomb threat (1998)
fateDetail: Federal Medical Center Carswell, Fort Worth, Texas
summary: Imprisoned for life. Former VA nurse convicted by a federal jury in March 2001 of murdering four patients and trying to kill two others with epinephrine injections at the Northampton, Massachusetts, VA Medical Center in 1995 and 1996.
narrative: Kristen Gilbert is a former registered nurse who was convicted in federal court in March 2001 of murdering four patients and attempting to murder two others at the Veterans Affairs Medical Center in Northampton, Massachusetts, between August 1995 and February 1996. A jury found her guilty of three counts of first-degree murder, one count of second-degree murder and two counts of attempted murder, then declined to impose the death penalty. She was sentenced on March 27, 2001, to life in prison without parole and is held at the Federal Medical Center Carswell in Fort Worth, Texas.

According to the First Circuit's October 2000 opinion in United States v. Gilbert, she worked the evening shift on Ward C, which housed the hospital's intensive care unit, from March 1989 until February 1996. The indictment alleged that within six months of beginning an affair with a hospital police officer, James Perrault, in autumn 1995, she killed four Ward C patients and tried to kill three others by injecting them with epinephrine, a heart stimulant with no authorized use on the ward. The Boston Globe identified the four men as Stanley Jagodowski, 66, who went into cardiac arrest on about August 21, 1995; Henry Hudon, 35, who died on December 8, 1995; Kenneth Cutting, 41, who died on February 2, 1996; and Edward Skwira, who died in February 1996.

The investigation began inside the ward. The Globe reported that nurses who had noticed how many emergencies fell on Gilbert's shifts began quietly watching her, and one colleague found epinephrine ampules missing; hospital records could not account for about 88 of 135 ampules dispensed to Ward C over six months, a gap the defense blamed on poor record-keeping. In February 1996 three nurses took their suspicions to supervisors, a formal inquiry opened and Gilbert resigned. The Seattle Times reported that an autopsy of Hudon found epinephrine poisoning. A federal grand jury began a criminal investigation in June 1996.

While that investigation was under way, Gilbert made anonymous threatening calls to the hospital, including a false bomb threat on September 26, 1996 that forced the evacuation of about 50 patients, according to the Globe. She was arrested on October 8, 1996, convicted by a jury and sentenced in April 1998 to 15 months in federal prison. The Globe also reported Perrault's account that Gilbert, calling him from a psychiatric ward in July 1996, told him she had killed the patients. Gilbert denied the killings and pleaded not guilty.

The murder indictment was unsealed on November 24, 1998, while she was still serving the bomb-threat sentence. The Seattle Times reported charges of three murders, two attempted murders, witness retaliation and obstruction of justice; a later indictment added a fourth murder and a third attempted murder. Because the hospital was federal property, prosecutors could seek the death penalty even though Massachusetts has none. Before trial, Judge Michael A. Ponsor excluded evidence of the bomb threat and of a statistical analysis putting the odds of her presence at so many deaths at one in 100 million; the First Circuit largely upheld those rulings.

The trial opened in Springfield in late 2000. Prosecutors argued that Gilbert created emergencies to gain attention, particularly from Perrault; the defense said the men died of natural causes, ABC News reported. On March 14, 2001, the jury convicted her on four murder counts and two counts of attempted murder. After a penalty phase, the jury deliberated about six hours and on March 26 chose life imprisonment, according to CBS News. The judge imposed the sentence the next day; Wikipedia describes it as four consecutive life terms plus 20 years. In July 2003 she abandoned her appeal after a Supreme Court decision raised the prospect of a renewed death-penalty prosecution at any retrial.

Gilbert was born Kristen Heather Strickland in Fall River, Massachusetts, on November 13, 1967, according to the Globe. She earned a nursing diploma from Greenfield Community College in 1988, married Glenn Gilbert that year and had two sons. She joined the Northampton VA hospital on March 6, 1989; the Globe reported some staff privately nicknamed her the Angel of Death. She was living in Setauket, New York, when the murder indictment was announced.

name: Larry Eyler

victims.suspected: 19 to 24 (police estimates, 1983 to 1984)

victimProfile: Teenage boys and young men, several of them hitchhikers or male sex workers, picked up along highways in Illinois and Indiana
captureMethod: A janitor saw Eyler leave garbage bags in a dumpster outside his Chicago apartment building; the bags held the dismembered body of 15-year-old Daniel Bridges.
sentence: Death (Illinois, 1986) for the murder of Daniel Bridges; 60 years (Indiana, 1990) after pleading guilty to the murder of Steven Agan
fateDetail: Died of AIDS-related complications on death row at Pontiac Correctional Center, Illinois, March 6, 1994
summary: Died in prison. Larry Eyler was convicted in Illinois in 1986 of murdering Daniel Bridges and sentenced to death, pleaded guilty in Indiana in 1990 to a second murder, and confessed through his attorney to 21 killings of young men in Illinois and Indiana between 1982 and 1984.
narrative: Larry William Eyler, called the Highway Killer or Interstate Killer, was a house painter who divided his time between Chicago and Terre Haute, Indiana. Between late 1982 and 1984 the bodies of teenage boys and young men were found near highways in Illinois and Indiana. A Cook County jury convicted him in 1986 of the murder of Daniel Bridges in Chicago and he was sentenced to death; he pleaded guilty in Indiana in 1990 to the 1982 murder of Steven Agan; and, in a statement his attorney released after his death, he confessed to 21 killings. He died of AIDS-related complications on death row in March 1994.

United Press International reported in October 1983 that a multi-agency task force was investigating at least 19 similar killings in Illinois and northern Indiana. Victims were typically restrained and stabbed and left in fields or woods near interstate exits. Ralph Calise, 28, of Chicago, was found in a cornfield near Lake Forest, Illinois, on August 31, 1983. By August 1984 UPI reported that police considered Eyler a suspect in as many as 24 slayings in four states.

Indiana State Police stopped Eyler on September 30, 1983, near Lowell, Indiana, and seized items from his truck. On October 28, 1983, Lake County, Illinois, authorities charged him with Calise's murder and held him on $1 million bond. In February 1984 Lake County Circuit Judge William Block ruled that Indiana police had detained Eyler illegally and seized his property without probable cause; the evidence was suppressed, bond was cut to $10,000 and Eyler was released on February 6, 1984, with the charge still pending.

According to the Illinois Supreme Court's 1989 opinion in People v. Eyler, the dismembered body of Danny Bridges, a 15-year-old who worked as a street prostitute in Chicago, was found in eight garbage bags in a dumpster on August 21, 1984. UPI reported that the dumpster stood outside Eyler's apartment building and that a janitor had seen Eyler put bags into it the previous afternoon. Eyler, still free on bond in the Calise case, was arrested that day and charged with murder and concealment of a homicidal death on August 22, 1984.

UPI reported that after about three hours of deliberation a Cook County jury on July 9, 1986, found Eyler guilty of murder committed during a kidnapping and aggravated kidnapping, making him eligible for the death penalty. Eyler waived a jury for the penalty phase and Judge Joseph Urso sentenced him to death on October 3, 1986, with additional terms for aggravated kidnapping and concealment. The Illinois Supreme Court affirmed the convictions and the death sentence on October 25, 1989.

In December 1990 Eyler gave Indiana investigators a statement about the December 1982 killing of Steven Agan, 23, a car-wash worker from Terre Haute. He pleaded guilty to Agan's murder in Vermillion County, Indiana, on December 13, 1990, and was sentenced to 60 years on December 28, 1990. He named Robert David Little, a former Indiana State University professor he had lived with, as a participant and testified against him; a Vermillion County jury acquitted Little on April 17, 1991. Newsweek reported in early 1991 that Eyler, through attorney Kathleen Zellner, offered to confess to as many as 20 further killings in exchange for a life sentence; Cook County State's Attorney Jack O'Malley declined.

Eyler died at Pontiac Correctional Center on March 6, 1994, at age 41. Two days later Zellner announced that he had confessed to killing 21 men and boys in Illinois and Indiana between 1982 and 1984, with an accomplice in four, while still denying that he killed Bridges. The Associated Press reported that a Cook County prosecutor's spokesman cautioned that the confessions did not prove Eyler committed the crimes. The AP reported in July 2023 that DNA genealogy identified Keith Lavell Bibbs, 16, of Chicago, found buried at a farm in Lake Village, Indiana, in 1983, as a victim Eyler had confessed to killing.
Eyler was born on December 21, 1952, in Crawfordsville, Indiana. Before his arrest he worked as a house painter and, briefly in 1984, at a Chicago group home for disabled children.

name: Lawrence Bittaker
victimProfile: Teenage girls aged 13 to 18, abducted while walking or hitchhiking in the South Bay and San Fernando Valley areas of Los Angeles County
captureMethod: A former fellow inmate to whom Roy Norris had described the killings went to police, and a surviving rape victim identified Bittaker from a photographic lineup, leading to both men's arrests on November 20, 1979.
sentence: Death (March 1981) for five counts of first-degree murder; affirmed by the California Supreme Court in 1989
fateDetail: Died of natural causes on death row at San Quentin State Prison on December 13, 2019, aged 79
summary: Died on death row in 2019. Lawrence Bittaker and accomplice Roy Norris, the 'Tool Box Killers', kidnapped and murdered five teenage girls in Los Angeles County in 1979. A jury convicted Bittaker in 1981 and he was sentenced to death.
narrative: Lawrence Sigmund Bittaker (1940-2019) was an American serial killer who, with accomplice Roy Lewis Norris, kidnapped and murdered five teenage girls in Los Angeles County, California, between June and October 1979. Because of the hand tools used on the victims, the pair became known as the "Tool Box Killers." A Los Angeles County jury convicted Bittaker in February 1981 of five counts of first-degree murder and 21 related felonies, and he was sentenced to death in March 1981. The California Supreme Court affirmed in 1989. He was never executed: the California Department of Corrections and Rehabilitation (CDCR) reported that he died of natural causes on death row at San Quentin State Prison on December 13, 2019, aged 79.

According to the California Supreme Court's opinion in People v. Bittaker (1989), Bittaker bought a van with sliding doors to make seizing victims easier. The victims, as named by CDCR and the court record, were Lucinda Lynn Schaefer, 16, abducted on June 24, 1979, in Redondo Beach; Andrea Joy Hall, 18, picked up while hitchhiking on Pacific Coast Highway on July 8; Jacqueline Doris Gilliam, 15, and Jacqueline Leah Lamp, 13, taken from a bus stop near Hermosa Beach on September 2; and Shirley Lynette Ledford, 16, abducted on October 31 while hitchhiking home in Sunland-Tujunga. The girls were driven into the San Gabriel Mountains, sexually assaulted and killed. Ledford's body was found on a Sunland lawn the next morning. The bodies of Schaefer and Hall were never recovered; the remains of Gilliam and Lamp were found in February 1980 after Norris agreed to help locate them.

The investigation began in November 1979 when, according to the Wikipedia article, Norris described the killings to a former fellow inmate, who consulted an attorney and then went to the police. The court opinion records that a woman who had survived an abduction and rape in September 1979 identified Bittaker from a photographic lineup, supporting the arrest warrant. Norris was arrested in Hermosa Beach on November 20, 1979, and Bittaker the same day at a Burbank motel. A tape recording of Ledford's abuse and photographs of victims, found in the van, were later used at trial.

Under a plea agreement described in the court opinion, Norris pleaded guilty to five counts of murder without special circumstances, two counts of rape and one count of robbery, agreed to help locate the bodies and to testify against Bittaker, and, prosecutors having agreed not to seek death, was sentenced to 45 years to life.

Bittaker's trial opened in Los Angeles County Superior Court in Torrance on January 19, 1981, before Judge Thomas Fredericks. United Press International reported the guilty verdicts on February 17, 1981; CDCR recorded convictions on all 26 counts, including kidnapping, conspiracy, rape, sodomy and firearm possession. The jury found 38 special circumstances true and returned a death verdict a week later. Bittaker testified that Norris had framed him and that he did not learn the girls had died until after his arrest. Judge Fredericks sentenced him to death on March 24, 1981 (CDCR lists March 22), and he was received on San Quentin's death row on March 30.

On June 22, 1989, a unanimous California Supreme Court, in an opinion by Justice Allen Broussard, affirmed the conviction and death sentence, holding that a restriction on death-penalty questioning of prospective jurors was erroneous but not prejudicial. According to the Wikipedia article, the United States Supreme Court declined to review the case in June 1990, execution dates set for 1989 and 1991 were stayed, and in 1993 a court declared Bittaker a vexatious litigant after he filed dozens of lawsuits. Norris died of natural causes on February 24, 2020, aged 72, at the California Medical Facility in Vacaville, the Associated Press reported.

Bittaker was born on September 27, 1940, in Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania. According to the Wikipedia article, he met Norris in 1977 at the California Men's Colony in San Luis Obispo, where Norris was serving a sentence for rape; Bittaker was paroled in October 1978 and Norris in January 1979. The court opinion notes that Bittaker was known in prison as "Pliers Bittaker" for the stories he told about torturing women.

name: Lonnie Franklin Jr.
victimProfile: Black women and girls aged 15 to 35 in South Los Angeles, many of them poor, drug users or sex workers
captureMethod: A familial DNA search matched crime-scene evidence to his son's profile; an undercover officer then collected discarded pizza crust and utensils at a restaurant, and the DNA matched
sentence: Death (August 10, 2016) on 10 counts of first-degree murder with a multiple-murder special circumstance, plus one count of attempted murder
fateDetail: Found unresponsive in his cell on death row at San Quentin State Prison; CDCR later listed the cause as natural causes
summary: Died on death row in 2020. Lonnie Franklin Jr., the Grim Sleeper, was convicted by a Los Angeles jury in 2016 of 10 murders and one attempted murder in South Los Angeles between 1985 and 2007, and was caught in 2010 through familial DNA.
narrative: Lonnie David Franklin Jr., known as the Grim Sleeper, was convicted by a Los Angeles County jury on May 5, 2016, of 10 counts of first-degree murder and one count of attempted murder for attacks on women and girls in South Los Angeles between 1985 and 2007. According to the Los Angeles County District Attorney's Office, the jury found true the special circumstance of multiple murders, and Superior Court Judge Kathleen Kennedy sentenced him to death on August 10, 2016. He died on death row at San Quentin State Prison on March 28, 2020, at age 67. Prosecutors presented evidence of four uncharged killings at the penalty phase, and CBS Los Angeles reported that prosecutors said he may have had as many as 25 victims. Franklin never confessed.

The District Attorney's conviction announcement lists the 1980s victims by the date their bodies were found: Debra Jackson, 29, on August 10, 1985; Henrietta Wright, 34, on August 12, 1986; Barbara Ware, 23, on January 10, 1987; Bernita Sparks, 26, on April 16, 1987; Mary Lowe, 26, on November 1, 1987; Lachrica Jefferson, 22, on January 30, 1988; and Alicia Alexander, 18, on September 11, 1988. Eight of the ten victims were shot with the same .25-caliber firearm; two were strangled. On November 19, 1988, Enietra Washington, 30, was shot and pushed from Franklin's car; she survived and testified at trial as the attempted-murder victim.

The killings linked to the gun then stopped for roughly 13 years, the gap behind the nickname. The District Attorney identifies the later victims as Princess Berthomieux, 15, found strangled on March 9, 2002; Valerie McCorvey, 35, found on July 11, 2003; and Janecia Peters, 25, found shot inside a trash bag in a dumpster on January 1, 2007. According to Wikipedia, DNA from the Peters scene was connected to the earlier series in 2007, and the LAPD formed a task force.

The break came through familial DNA searching. An Associated Press report published by NBC News on July 7, 2010, said a DNA profile from Franklin's son, taken after a felony weapons conviction, closely resembled the crime-scene profiles. An undercover officer posing as a busboy collected items Franklin discarded at a pizza restaurant, and the DNA matched. Franklin, 57, was arrested at his home on 81st Street on July 7, 2010. The District Attorney's Office said the pistol used to kill Peters was recovered from his home under a search warrant.

The trial opened in February 2016. Deputy District Attorneys Beth Silverman and Marguerite Rizzo told jurors every victim was tied to the same killer through DNA, firearms evidence, or both; the defense argued an unidentified man was responsible. The jury deliberated about a day and a half before convicting Franklin on all counts. In the penalty phase, a woman testified that Franklin and two fellow soldiers had kidnapped and raped her in Germany in 1974. The jury recommended death on June 6, 2016. At sentencing, more than 15 family members addressed the court; CBS Los Angeles reported that Judge Kennedy denied a motion for a new trial.

The California Department of Corrections and Rehabilitation (CDCR) said Franklin arrived on death row on August 17, 2016; CDCR reported that staff found him unresponsive in his cell at about 7:20 p.m. on March 28, 2020, and that he was pronounced dead at 7:43 p.m. with no signs of trauma; the department's register of condemned inmates who have died later recorded the cause as natural causes. NBC News reported that community members had long said police were slow to act because the victims were Black, poor and often drug users or sex workers.

Franklin was born in Los Angeles on August 30, 1952, according to Wikipedia, and served in the U.S. Army, where a West German court convicted him in 1974 over the kidnapping and rape of a teenage girl; he was dishonorably discharged in 1975. The AP reported that he worked as an LAPD garage attendant from 1981, became a city refuse collector in 1982, and left city employment in 1989. He lived for decades in the neighborhood where the bodies were found.

name: Lorenzo Gilyard
victimProfile: Women and girls aged 15 to 36 in Kansas City, most of them sex workers, whose bodies were left outdoors, in vacant buildings or in vehicles
captureMethod: A Kansas City crime lab retesting old evidence under a federal grant matched DNA from the victims to a blood sample taken from him in 1987, when he was questioned as a suspect in one of the deaths
sentence: Six terms of life imprisonment without parole (April 13, 2007) for the first-degree murders of Catherine Barry, Naomi Kelly, Ann Barnes, Kellie Ford, Sheila Ingold and Carmeline Hibbs; acquitted of the murder of Angela Mayhew
fateDetail: Serving life without parole in the Missouri prison system; according to the Wikipedia article he was held at Western Missouri Correctional Center and moved to Crossroads Correctional Center in July 2019
summary: Serving life. Lorenzo Gilyard, a Kansas City trash company supervisor, was linked by DNA in 2004 to the strangling of 12 women and girls and convicted in 2007 of six 1986-1987 murders. He was sentenced to life without parole and maintains his innocence.
narrative: Lorenzo Gilyard is a former trash company supervisor from Kansas City, Missouri, who was convicted in March 2007 of murdering six women whose strangled bodies were found around the city in 1986 and 1987. Arrested in April 2004 after a DNA match, he was at one point charged with 13 killings of women and girls dating from 1977 to 1993. A Jackson County judge, sitting without a jury, found him guilty on six counts and acquitted him on a seventh, and in April 2007 he was sentenced to life in prison without parole. He has denied killing anyone and remains in prison.

The killings stretched over 16 years. According to court papers listed by the Associated Press, the women and girls named in the charges were Stacie L. Swofford, 17; Gwendolyn Kizine, 15; Margaret J. Miller, 17; Catherine M. Barry, 34; Naomi Kelly, 23; Debbie Blevins, 32; Ann Barnes, 36; Kellie A. Ford, 20; Angela Mayhew, 19; Sheila Ingold, 36; Carmeline Hibbs, 30; Helga Kruger, 26; and Connie Luther, 29. AP reported in 2004 that eight of the original 12 deaths occurred in 1986 and 1987, that 11 of those women were sex workers and the 12th was a mentally ill woman who accepted rides from strangers, and that the victims were strangled with items including nylon stockings, shoestrings and wire. Bodies were found in an abandoned van, a field, a parking lot and, in the last case in 1993, a snowdrift.

Investigators did not connect any of the deaths until 1994, when two were linked, and the remaining connections were made in roughly the 10 months before the arrest, according to the AP. A federal grant funded the Kansas City crime lab to analyze DNA from old unsolved cases, and analysts eventually traced semen from multiple victims to a single unknown man. The identification came from a blood sample taken from Gilyard in 1987, when he was among several men sampled as suspects in one of the killings; the technology to compare it with the crime scene evidence did not exist until 2000. According to a probable cause statement cited by NBC News, the match was made on April 12, 2004.

Gilyard, then 53 and married, was arrested on April 16, 2004, and charged the next day with 10 counts of first-degree murder and two counts of capital murder, the charge in force at the time of two of the deaths. He had worked for Deffenbaugh Disposal Service since 1986, first on a trash crew and later supervising several crews; a company spokesman told reporters the allegations did not match the man his co-workers knew. The AP reported that he had been in and out of jail and prison in the 1970s and 1980s on charges ranging from burglary and assault to molestation. A 13th murder count, involving a 26-year-old woman found dead on a street in 1989, was added in 2006.

In January 2007 prosecutors agreed not to seek the death penalty if Gilyard waived a jury, and his lawyers also gave up nearly all of his appeal rights. When trial opened before Judge John O'Malley on March 5, 2007, prosecutors dropped six counts, including one involving an Austrian woman, saying the remaining seven cases were stronger, and reserved the right to refile them. The state's case rested on DNA: semen linked to Gilyard was found on six of the women, and one of his hairs was found on the sweater of the seventh. Defense attorneys Susan Elliott and Tom Jacquinot argued that the evidence showed only sexual contact, not murder.

On March 16, 2007, O'Malley convicted Gilyard of the first-degree murders of Catherine Barry, Naomi Kelly, Ann Barnes, Kellie Ford, Sheila Ingold and Carmeline Hibbs. He acquitted him of killing Angela Mayhew, the only victim on whom no semen was found, saying the state had offered suspicion rather than convincing proof. Barry, according to her family, was the only one of the six who was not a sex worker. On April 13, 2007, the judge imposed six terms of life without parole, the only sentence available, and said Gilyard had forfeited any right to live among the public. Prosecutor Jim Kanatzar said his office would review the six dismissed cases; no refiling is reported in the sources consulted.

Gilyard was born in Kansas City on May 24, 1950, according to the Wikipedia article. He has consistently maintained his innocence, including, the Wikipedia article says, in a 2018 television interview with Piers Morgan. The same article states that he served his sentence at Western Missouri Correctional Center before being moved to Crossroads Correctional Center in July 2019.

name: Marybeth Tinning

victims.suspected: 8 of the 9 deaths

victimProfile: Her own children, all under age five: eight biological children and one adopted son, who died between 1972 and 1985
captureMethod: After her ninth child died in December 1985, a state police forensic pathologist found the infant had been smothered, and Tinning gave police a written statement admitting it.
sentence: 20 years to life for second-degree murder (depraved indifference) of Tami Lynne Tinning (1987)
fateDetail: Paroled from Taconic Correctional Facility, Bedford Hills, on August 21, 2018; lifetime parole supervision in Schenectady County
summary: Convicted in 1987 of the murder of her infant daughter Tami Lynne; nine of her children died between 1972 and 1985 in Schenectady, New York. Sentenced to 20 years to life, paroled in August 2018.
narrative: Marybeth Tinning is a former nursing assistant from Schenectady, New York, whose nine children all died before the age of five between 1972 and 1985. Only one of those deaths was ever adjudicated: in July 1987 a Schenectady County jury convicted her of second-degree murder in the December 1985 smothering of her four-month-old daughter, Tami Lynne. She was sentenced to 20 years to life, served more than 31 years, and was paroled in August 2018. United Press International reported at the time of the verdict that investigators suspected her in eight of the nine deaths, but she was formally charged only in Tami Lynne's case.

According to the Wikipedia article on the case, the first three deaths came within about two months in early 1972. Jennifer, born December 26, 1971, died on January 3, 1972, of what doctors recorded as meningitis and brain abscesses that developed before birth; investigators later treated that death as natural. Joseph Jr., aged two, died on January 20, 1972, and Barbara, aged four, died on March 2, 1972, after a hospital admission the previous day. Timothy died in December 1973 at about two weeks old, a death attributed to sudden infant death syndrome, and Nathan died in 1975 at five months. Mary Frances died in 1979 after cardiac arrest and brain damage, Jonathan died in March 1980 after four weeks on life support, and Michael, a boy the couple had adopted in 1978, died on March 2, 1981. CBS New York, drawing on Associated Press reporting, listed the recorded causes as meningitis, seizures, cardiac arrest, SIDS, pulmonary edema, pneumonia and, in one case, undetermined.

Tami Lynne, born August 22, 1985, died on December 20, 1985. According to the Wikipedia account, Dr. Michael Baden, a forensic pathologist working for the New York State Police, determined that she had been smothered, and the medical examiner said no suspicion had attached to the family before that death. Social services officials and Schenectady police visited the home the same day, and the Tinnings were questioned separately. In early 1986 Tinning signed a statement admitting that she had smothered Tami Lynne and had also killed her sons Timothy and Nathan. CBS New York reported that prosecutors indicted her in all three deaths but pursued only the Tami Lynne case. She was released on $100,000 bail to await trial.

The trial opened in Schenectady County Court on June 22, 1987, before Judge Clifford Harrigan, with District Attorney John Poersch prosecuting. UPI reported that the defense, led by Paul Callahan, argued that Tami Lynne could have died of natural causes, including a rare hereditary disorder, and that investigators had intimidated Tinning into confessing. Her husband, Joseph Tinning, testified that she had told him privately, "I killed Tami," while saying he still believed she was innocent. On July 17, 1987, after about 23 hours of deliberation over three days, the jury acquitted her of intentional murder but convicted her of second-degree murder on the theory of depraved indifference to human life. Bail was revoked and she was jailed pending sentence.

In October 1987 she was sentenced to 20 years to life, five years less than the maximum, and entered Taconic Correctional Facility in Bedford Hills. On appeal she argued that her confession was involuntary and that the evidence was insufficient; according to the Wikipedia article, the Appellate Division of the New York Supreme Court rejected those arguments in December 1988. The six other children's bodies that were exhumed after Tami Lynne's death showed no physical signs of abuse, and no further charges were ever brought.

Tinning first became eligible for parole in March 2007 and was denied six times. The Associated Press reported that at her second hearing, in January 2011, she began to acknowledge the killing for which she was convicted, and Oxygen quoted her telling the board that after the earlier deaths she had "just lost it" and believed her daughter would die too. Parole boards nonetheless cited superficial remorse and the senseless loss of a young life in denying release in 2009, 2011, 2013, 2015 and 2017. At her seventh hearing, in July 2018, the board granted parole. According to the Associated Press, she walked out of Taconic on Tuesday, August 21, 2018, at age 75, after more than 31 years in custody, and was placed under lifetime parole supervision in Schenectady County, where her husband said she would live with him in Duanesburg.

Born Marybeth Roe on September 11, 1942, in Duanesburg, New York, she married Joseph Tinning in 1965 and worked as a nursing assistant at Ellis Hospital in Schenectady. Commentators cited by the Associated Press and other outlets have described the case as an early example of what became known as Munchausen syndrome by proxy, and it is often credited with prompting hospitals, police and medical examiners to share information about repeated child deaths in a single family. Her 1986 admissions about Timothy and Nathan were never tested in court, and she later maintained that the statement was coerced.

name: Nannie Doss

victims.suspected: up to 11

victimProfile: Members of her own family: four husbands, two daughters, her mother, a sister, a mother-in-law and two grandchildren
captureMethod: After her fifth husband, Samuel Doss, died in Tulsa in October 1954, his physician pressed for an autopsy, which found a large quantity of arsenic; she was arrested and confessed under questioning.
sentence: Life imprisonment (pleaded guilty on May 17, 1955, to the murder of Samuel Doss; the state did not seek the death penalty)
fateDetail: Oklahoma State Penitentiary, McAlester; died of leukemia in the prison hospital ward on June 2, 1965
summary: Died in prison. Nannie Doss pleaded guilty in 1955 to poisoning her fifth husband, Samuel Doss, in Tulsa, Oklahoma, confessed to killing four husbands, and is linked to as many as 11 family deaths from 1927 to 1954. She died at the Oklahoma State Penitentiary in 1965.
narrative: Nannie Doss, born Nancy Agnes Hazel, was a serial poisoner whose victims were members of her own family in Alabama, North Carolina, Kansas and Oklahoma between 1927 and 1954. She was convicted of one murder: on May 17, 1955, she pleaded guilty in Tulsa, Oklahoma, to killing her fifth husband, Samuel Doss, and was sentenced to life imprisonment. According to the Encyclopedia of Alabama, she confessed under interrogation to killing four husbands. The Wikipedia article and an Oklahoma Gazette retrospective attribute as many as 11 deaths to her, among them two of her daughters, her mother, a sister, a mother-in-law and two grandchildren. She was never charged in any death other than that of Samuel Doss.

The Encyclopedia of Alabama records that she married Charles Braggs in 1921, at about 16, after the two met at the Linen Thread Company in Anniston, Alabama. Two of their four daughters died in 1927, with the deaths attributed at the time to food poisoning. The couple divorced in 1928, and Braggs was the only one of her five husbands to survive the marriage. In 1929 she married Frank Harrelson, whom she met through a lonely hearts column. Harrelson died on September 15, 1945; by her later account, she had put rat poison in his whiskey. A grandson, Robert, died of asphyxia at age two while in her care, and she collected a $500 life insurance policy.

Her third husband, Arlie Lanning of Lexington, North Carolina, died of what was recorded as heart failure, with no autopsy performed; the Encyclopedia of Alabama dates his death to 1950, while the Oklahoma Gazette gives 1952. The Wikipedia article states that Lanning's mother died in her sleep while Doss lived in the household, and that her sister Dovie died soon after Doss came to stay with her. In October 1952 she married Richard L. Morton of Emporia, Kansas. Her mother, Louisa Hazle, came to live with the couple and died within days, in January 1953. Morton died on May 19, 1953, after, the Encyclopedia of Alabama reports, drinking coffee laced with arsenic.

In June 1953 she married Samuel Doss, a Nazarene minister, in Tulsa, Oklahoma. In the autumn of 1954 he was hospitalised with a severe digestive illness, was sent home on October 5 and died about a week later, on October 12 according to the Wikipedia article. His physician insisted on an autopsy, which found a large quantity of arsenic. Doss was arrested in Tulsa in October 1954 and, during questioning, confessed to killing four husbands; the Encyclopedia of Alabama reports she did so in exchange for being allowed to keep a romance magazine. Her habit of laughing while recounting the deaths produced the nickname the Giggling Granny. The same source states that exhumations reportedly confirmed rat poison or arsenic in several of the bodies.

Oklahoma prosecuted her for a single count of murder, that of Samuel Doss. The prosecutor, according to the Wikipedia article, was J. Howard Edmondson, later governor of Oklahoma. She pleaded guilty on May 17, 1955, and received a life sentence; the Wikipedia article and a syndicated history column published by the Albuquerque Journal both report that the state did not seek the death penalty because she was a woman. The Encyclopedia of Alabama notes that North Carolina, Kansas and Alabama also brought charges, but she was never tried outside Oklahoma.

She served her sentence at the Oklahoma State Penitentiary in McAlester, where she died of leukemia in the prison hospital ward on June 2, 1965, at age 59. She was buried at Oak Hill Memorial Park in McAlester. The Oklahoma Gazette has written that her case figures in the history of Oklahoma's Office of the Chief Medical Examiner, as an example of suspicious deaths that went uninvestigated before the state had a medical examiner system.

She was born on November 4, 1905, in Blue Mountain, Calhoun County, Alabama, one of five children of Jim and Louisa Hazle. The Encyclopedia of Alabama describes her father as abusive and says he kept the children out of school to work the family farm. At about age seven she suffered a head injury in a train incident, which she later blamed for headaches and blackouts.

name: New Bedford Highway Killer

victims.suspected: 9 to 11

victimProfile: Women aged 19 to 36 with histories of drug use who frequented a New Bedford neighborhood known for prostitution; nine were found beside highways and two remain missing
summary: Unidentified. Nine women who disappeared from New Bedford, Massachusetts, in 1988 were found beside area highways in 1988 and 1989, and two more remain missing. One man was charged in a single death in 1990; the charge was dropped in 1991. No one has been convicted.
narrative: The New Bedford Highway Killer is the name given to an unidentified person or persons blamed for the deaths of at least nine women whose remains were found beside highways around New Bedford, Massachusetts, between July 1988 and April 1989. Two more women who vanished from the same streets in 1988 have never been found. No one has been convicted. A New Bedford lawyer, Kenneth Ponte, was indicted in 1990 for one of the deaths, but the charge was dropped in 1991 for lack of evidence, and the case remains open with the Bristol County District Attorney's Office.

According to the Associated Press, all eleven women had histories of drug use and frequented a New Bedford neighborhood known for prostitution; Brandeis University Press, publisher of a book on the case, describes them as aged 19 to 36. The Wikipedia article lists the recovered victims as Debra Medeiros of Fall River, Nancy Paiva, Debra Greenlaw DeMello, Dawn Mendes, Deborah McConnell of Newport, Rhode Island, Rochelle Clifford Dopierala of Falmouth, Robbin Rhodes, Mary Rose Santos and Sandra Botelho. Christina Monteiro, 19, and Marilyn Cardoza-Roberts, 34, both last seen in 1988, are the two who remain missing.

The women disappeared over roughly six months, from about March to September 1988. Medeiros, reported missing in late May, was the first found, on July 3, 1988, in woods beside Route 140 in Freetown. Paiva was found beside Interstate 195 in Dartmouth on July 30, DeMello near the Reed Road ramp off I-195 on November 8, and Mendes near the same interchange on November 29. McConnell was found off Route 140 in Freetown on December 1 and Dopierala in a gravel pit off Reed Road on December 10. The last three were found in 1989: Rhodes beside Route 140 on March 28, Santos along Route 88 in Westport on March 31, and Botelho in woods along I-195 in Marion on April 24. The Brandeis University Press description says some remains showed signs of strangulation while others were too decomposed for a cause of death to be determined; the Wikipedia article says Dopierala was beaten.

Kenneth Ponte, a New Bedford attorney, is the only person ever charged with any of the deaths. A grand jury indicted him in August 1990 for the murder of Dopierala, with whom he acknowledged a relationship; he also said he had represented three of the other women as their lawyer. He pleaded not guilty and posted bond. According to the ABA Journal, prosecutors had contended he killed Dopierala because she was going to reveal his drug use. A special prosecutor, Paul Buckley, later said there was not enough evidence and called the indictment a fishing expedition, and the charge was dropped in July 1991. Ponte denied any involvement in the killings. He was disbarred in 1997 over misuse of a client's settlement money and was found dead at his New Bedford home in January 2010; authorities said the death did not appear suspicious.

A second man, Anthony DeGrazia, a construction worker, drew attention in 1989 after a woman who had been attacked said he resembled her assailant. According to the Wikipedia article, District Attorney Ronald Pina sought his arrest on a series of assault and attempted rape charges involving other women, and he was held in jail for about 13 months before his release in June 1990. He was never charged with any of the highway killings. He was found dead in Freetown on July 17, 1990; the district attorney's office called the death a suicide, a finding his family has disputed.

In May 2007 the newly elected Bristol County District Attorney, Samuel Sutter, reopened the investigation, pledging to have state police re-examine the evidence with modern DNA and fiber analysis, and investigators dug up the driveway and patio at Ponte's former home, the Associated Press reported. Nothing from that search has been publicly linked to the killings. The Wikipedia article also notes that Daniel Tavares, later convicted of other murders, indirectly claimed responsibility in a letter written in prison; he has not been charged in this case.

In March 2023 a spokesman for the Bristol County District Attorney's Office told WBSM that at least three men had been considered suspects over the years, that investigators were still pursuing a suspect, and that the office would not give up on the case. The State Police Cold Case Unit has also followed leads from the public, according to Maureen Boyle, a former Standard-Times crime reporter whose 2017 book Shallow Graves is the most detailed account of the investigation.

name: Oakland County Child Killer
victimProfile: Children aged 10 to 12, two boys and two girls, abducted from suburbs along the Woodward Avenue corridor north of Detroit
summary: Unidentified. Four children aged 10 to 12 were abducted in Oakland County, Michigan, between February 1976 and March 1977 and found dead days or weeks later. A 200-officer task force closed in 1978; the case remains open with the Michigan State Police.
narrative: The Oakland County Child Killer is the name given to the unidentified person or persons who abducted and killed four children in the northern suburbs of Detroit, Michigan, between February 1976 and March 1977. The victims, Mark Stebbins, 12, Jill Robinson, 12, Kristine Mihelich, 10, and Timothy King, 11, were taken from communities along the Woodward Avenue corridor in Oakland County and found dead between four and nineteen days later. No one has ever been charged. According to the Michigan State Police, quoted by WDIV in February 2026, the investigation remains open and every new tip is examined.

Stebbins was last seen leaving an American Legion hall in Ferndale on February 15, 1976, and was found four days later in a Southfield parking lot; he had been smothered and sexually assaulted. Robinson left her Royal Oak home on December 22, 1976, and was found on December 26 beside Interstate 75 in Troy, killed with a shotgun. Mihelich went missing in Berkley on January 2, 1977, and was found on January 21 in a snowbank in Franklin; she had been suffocated. King left his Birmingham home on March 16, 1977, and was found on March 22 in a ditch in Livonia; he had been suffocated and sexually assaulted. The ABA Journal and WDIV report that the children were fed and bathed while held captive, the detail behind the "Babysitter Killer" label.

After King's disappearance a multi-agency task force led by the Michigan State Police was formed. The ABA Journal reported in 2017 that it drew about 200 local, county and state officers plus the FBI, spent about 2 million dollars and reviewed roughly 20,000 leads. A 1978 U.S. Department of Justice report used the investigation as the model for a manual on interjurisdictional "major case teams". A witness account of a blue AMC Gremlin near the King abduction led police to stop many Gremlin drivers; later reporting has questioned whether that car was involved. The task force was disbanded in December 1978 and the case passed to the Michigan State Police.

The investigation produced persons of interest but no charges. Christopher Busch, a Bloomfield Township man with child sexual assault convictions, was questioned and polygraphed in early 1977 and released; he died of a gunshot wound ruled self-inflicted in November 1978. In June 2012 Oakland County Prosecutor Jessica Cooper and Chief Assistant Prosecutor Paul Walton told WDIV that Busch's DNA did not match the physical evidence and that no evidence connected him to the killings. At a press conference on July 17, 2012, reported by The Associated Press and CBS News, Cooper announced that FBI testing showed hairs found on Stebbins and King came from the same unknown person, the first forensic link between any of the victims, and that a matching hair had been recovered from a 1966 Pontiac Bonneville owned by Arch Edward Sloan, who was serving a life sentence for an unrelated 1983 sexual assault. Cooper said Sloan was not the source of the hair and often lent his car to others; he was investigated repeatedly and never charged. The ABA Journal also reported that a hair from Mihelich's body yielded a mitochondrial DNA profile pointing to another man and his maternal relatives; he was questioned and never charged.

Victims' families pressed the case in court. Timothy King's father, Barry King, sued the Michigan State Police under the Freedom of Information Act in 2010 and obtained more than 3,400 pages of files, according to the ABA Journal. Kristine Mihelich's mother filed a 100 million dollar lawsuit in 2012 alleging the investigation had been mishandled; WDIV reported it was dismissed in 2013. Barry King died in 2020.

In February 2019 WXYZ reported, citing prison records, that Sloan had been interviewed by task force detectives in 2010 and 2012 and had failed a polygraph about the murders. Sloan died in custody on June 12, 2026, according to a Michigan Department of Corrections spokesperson quoted by WXYZ, which reported that detectives questioned him a final time in his last hours. In February 2026 the Michigan State Police told WDIV that the case is open and that evidence is re-evaluated as new technology becomes available. Tips can be submitted at 1-855-MICHTIP.

name: Ottis Toole

victims.suspected: 1 further (Adam Walsh, attributed by Hollywood, Florida police in 2008; never charged)

victimProfile: Adults in Jacksonville and Tallahassee, Florida, including a 64-year-old boarding-house resident and a 19-year-old woman; police attribute the 1981 killing of six-year-old Adam Walsh to him
captureMethod: Already imprisoned in 1983 on an unrelated Jacksonville arson conviction when, questioned at the Lake Butler reception center, he confessed to the 1982 boarding-house fire that killed George Sonnenberg.
sentence: Death (1984, Sonnenberg arson-murder; vacated by the Florida Supreme Court in 1985 and reduced to life); second death sentence (1984, Tallahassee strangulation) also reduced to life; four life sentences on guilty pleas (1991); 20 years for arson (1983)
fateDetail: Florida State Prison, Raiford; liver failure (cirrhosis), aged 49; buried in the prison cemetery after his body went unclaimed
summary: Died in prison 1996. Jacksonville drifter convicted of six Florida murders (1980-1983); two death sentences reduced to life. Confessed with Henry Lee Lucas to many more, then recanted. Named by police in 2008 as Adam Walsh's killer; never charged.
narrative: Ottis Elwood Toole was a Jacksonville, Florida drifter and arsonist convicted of six murders committed in Florida between 1980 and 1983. A jury convicted him in 1984 of the arson death of George Sonnenberg and he was sentenced to death; the Florida Supreme Court affirmed the conviction but vacated the sentence in 1985, and he was resentenced to life. A second 1984 death sentence, for strangling a 19-year-old Tallahassee woman, was also reduced to life, and in 1991 he pleaded guilty to four more Jacksonville murders. With Henry Lee Lucas he confessed to many more killings, most never corroborated and later recanted. He died in Florida State Prison in September 1996.

According to the Florida Supreme Court's opinion in Toole v. State (No. 65,378, November 25, 1985), a Jacksonville boarding house burned on January 4, 1982, and resident George Sonnenberg died of his injuries. Toole, a handyman for the owner, was questioned while incarcerated at Lake Butler on an unrelated offense and confessed to setting the fire after arguing with Sonnenberg; at trial he denied it and said he signed the statement to get back to Jacksonville. UPI reported that Sonnenberg, 64, died a week after the fire and that Toole was already serving 20 years for burning two abandoned Jacksonville houses in 1983.

The jury found Toole guilty of first-degree felony murder on April 28, 1984, and recommended death; Circuit Judge James L. Harrison imposed the sentence in May 1984, UPI reported. The Florida Supreme Court affirmed the conviction but held that the trial judge had wrongly refused a jury instruction on extreme mental or emotional disturbance, given defense evidence of pyromania, borderline intellectual functioning and a personality disorder, and ordered a new sentencing hearing. According to Fox News and the Wikipedia article, this and a second 1984 death sentence, for the February 1983 strangulation of a 19-year-old Tallahassee woman, were both reduced to life imprisonment.

Toole's notoriety rests mainly on his association with Henry Lee Lucas, whom he met in Jacksonville in the 1970s. After Lucas was arrested in Texas in June 1983 and began confessing to hundreds of murders, Toole first denied involvement and then backed many of Lucas's claims. UPI reported in 1984 that authorities said the pair had admitted to more than 300 killings, though investigators doubted many of them; Wikipedia records Toole's own uncorroborated claim of 108 murders with Lucas. Reviewers later concluded that Lucas could not have travelled the distances his confessions required, and both men recanted. The courts convicted Toole of six murders; the confessions remain unverified.

In October 1983, while in prison, Toole confessed to the July 27, 1981 abduction and killing of six-year-old Adam Walsh from a Sears store at a Hollywood, Florida mall. NBC News reported that fishermen found the child's severed head in a canal near Vero Beach two weeks later and that his body was never found. Toole confessed and recanted repeatedly; ABC News counted 24 documented confessions. Authorities lost the bloodstained carpet from Toole's car and then the car itself, preventing DNA testing. He was never charged in the case.

On December 16, 2008, twelve years after Toole's death, Hollywood Police Chief Chadwick Wagner announced that the department considered Toole responsible for Adam Walsh's murder and closed the case, acknowledging missteps and apologizing to the Walsh family, NBC News reported. No new physical or DNA evidence was presented. It is a police conclusion, not a court verdict. Adam's father, John Walsh, has said he believes Toole was the killer.

In 1991 Toole pleaded guilty in Jacksonville to four further murders and received four life sentences, according to Fox News and the Wikipedia article. He died on September 15, 1996, aged 49, at Florida State Prison in Raiford of liver failure; NBC News reported that no relative claimed his body and he was buried on prison grounds. Toole was born in Jacksonville on March 5, 1947. The Wikipedia article reports a childhood of abuse, early arrests and repeated fire-setting.
