name: Paul Dennis Reid
victimProfile: Fast-food and restaurant employees, three of them teenagers, killed during after-hours or opening-time robberies at three restaurants
captureMethod: Arrested in June 1997 after allegedly trying to kidnap the Shoney's manager who had fired him; fingerprints taken then were matched to a card from a Captain D's victim's wallet
sentence: Seven death sentences on seven first-degree murder convictions from three trials (Davidson County, Captain D's and McDonald's cases; Montgomery County, Baskin-Robbins case), plus consecutive prison terms on robbery, kidnapping and attempted murder counts
fateDetail: Died on death row on November 1, 2013, aged 55, at Nashville General Hospital at Meharry after about two weeks in hospital; held at Riverbend Maximum Security Institution
summary: Died in prison. Paul Dennis Reid was convicted of murdering seven workers in robberies at a Captain D's and a McDonald's in Nashville and a Baskin-Robbins in Clarksville, Tennessee, in 1997. Sentenced to death seven times, he died on death row in 2013.
narrative: Paul Dennis Reid Jr., known in press coverage as the Fast Food Killer, was convicted of murdering seven restaurant workers during three robberies in Nashville and Clarksville, Tennessee, between February and April 1997. Across three separate trials he was found guilty of seven counts of first-degree murder and received seven death sentences, which the Wikipedia article describes as the most ever imposed on one person in Tennessee. He was never executed. After years of litigation over his mental competency, he died on November 1, 2013, aged 55, at Nashville General Hospital at Meharry, where he had been a patient for about two weeks, the Associated Press reported.

Reid was born in Texas in 1957 and, according to the Associated Press, was a drifter who had come to Nashville hoping to become a country singer. The Tennessee Supreme Court recorded that he had been convicted in Texas in 1984 of aggravated robbery and that he was 39 when the 1997 crimes were committed. AP reporting states that he had been fired from his job as a dishwasher at a Nashville Shoney's shortly before the first killings.

The first robbery took place on the morning of February 16, 1997, at a Captain D's restaurant on Lebanon Road in the Donelson area of Nashville. According to the Tennessee Supreme Court, Sarah Jackson, 16, and Steve Hampton, 25, were preparing to open the restaurant when they were shot on the floor, and about $7,140 and Hampton's wallet were taken. On March 23, 1997, four employees finishing the night shift at a McDonald's in the Hermitage area were forced into a storage room after the safe was emptied. Ronald Santiago, Robert Sewell and Andrea Brown were shot; Santiago and Sewell died at the scene and Brown died later in hospital. The fourth employee, Jose Ramirez Gonzales, was stabbed repeatedly after the gun jammed, pretended to be dead and then called 911. He survived and later identified Reid from photographs. On April 23, 1997, Angela Holmes, 21, and Michelle Mace, 16, were abducted during a robbery at a Baskin-Robbins in Clarksville; their bodies were found at Dunbar Cave State Natural Area, AP reported.

Reid became a suspect after an unrelated arrest. According to AP reporting, in June 1997 he tried to kidnap the Shoney's manager who had fired him, and he was linked to the restaurant killings after that. The Tennessee Supreme Court's 2002 opinion says police first considered him a suspect on June 12, 1997, after his arrest in Cheatham County, which supplied his fingerprints and photograph. His right thumbprint was found on a video rental card from Hampton's wallet, which had been discarded along Ellington Parkway, and shoe prints at the Captain D's matched the length of shoes taken from his home. Employees also identified him as a man who had asked about a job there the night before the killings. The exact date of his first arrest is given differently across sources.

Reid was tried separately for each robbery. A Davidson County jury convicted him in 1999 of two counts of first-degree murder and especially aggravated robbery in the Captain D's case and imposed death on both murders; the trial court added a consecutive 25-year robbery sentence. In Montgomery County he was convicted of two counts of first-degree murder, two counts of especially aggravated kidnapping and especially aggravated robbery for the Clarksville killings. A second Davidson County jury convicted him on all counts in the McDonald's case, including three premeditated murders and attempted first-degree murder, and sentenced him to death on each murder. The Tennessee Supreme Court affirmed the Captain D's judgment in 2002, the Clarksville judgment in 2005 and the McDonald's judgment in December 2006.

The later years of the case turned on whether Reid was competent to make legal decisions. He dropped his appeals and came within hours of execution in April 2003; U.S. District Judge Todd Campbell found him mentally ill but competent to waive them, AP reported, before he agreed to resume. In 2006 AP described him as having been found brain-damaged and schizophrenic, and reported that he told lawyers and reporters a military government controlled and monitored him. Family members, including his sister, kept filing appeals on his behalf. A January 2008 execution date was stayed by Judge Campbell in December 2007 while Tennessee's lethal injection procedure was under review. In 2013 the Tennessee Supreme Court ruled that relatives and advocates could not pursue appeals against his wishes, finding that they had not proven him incompetent.

Reid was held on death row at Riverbend Maximum Security Institution in Nashville, according to WPLN. He died months after the 2013 ruling, with no execution date pending; the state medical examiner was to determine the cause of death. According to the Wikipedia article, he had at one time also been considered a suspect in the 1993 Brown's Chicken killings in Palatine, Illinois, for which two other men were later convicted.

name: Paul John Knowles
victimProfile: Strangers and brief acquaintances of both sexes and many ages, including older women in their homes, teenage girls, hitchhikers, motorists, a father and daughter who took him in, and a state trooper
captureMethod: After crashing through a police roadblock in Henry County, Georgia, he fled on foot and was cornered by an armed local resident, who held him until Henry County investigators arrived
fateDetail: Shot three times in the chest by GBI Agent Ronnie Angel on Interstate 20 near Lithia Springs, Douglas County, Georgia, during a transfer; authorities said he had grabbed the sheriff's revolver
summary: Killed. Paul John Knowles, the Casanova Killer, was linked to at least 18 killings across several states in 1974 after escaping a Jacksonville jail. Arrested in Georgia, he was shot dead by a GBI agent during a transfer in December 1974 and never tried.
narrative: Paul John Knowles, known in the press as the Casanova Killer, was linked to at least 18 killings committed between late July and mid-November 1974 after he escaped from a jail cell in Jacksonville, Florida. The killings attributed to him took place in Florida, Georgia, Ohio, Nevada, Texas, Connecticut and Virginia, with Georgia accounting for the largest share. He was arrested in Henry County, Georgia, on November 17, 1974, and was charged with murders in Georgia, Florida and Ohio, but he never went to trial: on December 18, 1974, a Georgia Bureau of Investigation agent shot him dead during a transfer, in what authorities described as an escape attempt. Because he was never tried, none of the killings resulted in a conviction.

Knowles was born in Orlando in 1946 and, according to the Wikipedia article, spent much of his childhood in foster homes and in the Florida School for Boys before serving adult prison terms. News4JAX reported in 2022 that in the summer of 1974 he was being held in Jacksonville for stabbing a bartender when he picked a lock and escaped. That same night, according to News4JAX and WGXA, Alice Curtis, a 65-year-old retired teacher in Jacksonville Beach, was bound and gagged during a robbery and died; she is regarded as his first known victim. Marjorie Howie, 49, was later found strangled in her home in Atlantic Beach, and News4JAX reported that Knowles is believed responsible. He also claimed in a letter to have killed two Jacksonville sisters, Annette and Mylette Anderson, who vanished in 1974; prosecutors later concluded he was responsible, but their bodies were never found and some investigators doubted the claim, so they are not included in the count of 18.

In Georgia, the GBI said in 2011 that investigators had found evidence that Knowles murdered Ima Jean Sanders, 13, of Warner Robins, who disappeared on August 1, 1974. Her skeletal remains were found in Peach County in April 1976 and identified through DNA in 2011; a 1975 letter from the U.S. Attorney summarizing Knowles's taped confessions had described a teenage hitchhiker who called herself Alma. Kathy Pierce, 24, was killed in Musella in Crawford County later in August. The Wikipedia article attributes the September 1974 deaths of William Bates near Lima, Ohio, of Emmett and Lois Johnson at a rest stop near Ely, Nevada, and of Charlynn Hicks near Seguin, Texas, to him. Ann Dawson, a Birmingham, Alabama, beautician, disappeared after meeting him in late September; Knowles claimed to have put her body in the Mississippi River, and remains were found in Mississippi in 1977.

On October 16, 1974, Karen Wine, 35, and her 16-year-old daughter were killed in their home in Marlborough, Connecticut, according to the Wikipedia article, and two days later Doris Hosey, 53, was shot with her husband's rifle. News4JAX reported that Knowles's confession tapes described killings in Virginia as well as Connecticut, Nevada and Texas. In early November he was in central Georgia. Two hitchhikers, Edward Hilliard and Debbie Griffin, disappeared near Macon on November 2, and remains were later found in Crawford County; the Wikipedia article says Knowles is reportedly suspected in their deaths. On November 6 in Milledgeville, Carswell Carr was stabbed to death and his 15-year-old daughter Mandy was strangled after Carr invited Knowles to spend the night, according to WGXA and The Atlanta Constitution.

On November 16, near Perry, Florida, Knowles took Florida Highway Patrol Trooper Charles Campbell hostage, used the patrol car to stop motorist James Meyer, a businessman from Wilmington, Delaware, and drove both men into Georgia. They were found handcuffed to a tree in Pulaski County, each shot in the head, the GBI and WGXA reported. The next day Knowles crashed through a police roadblock in Henry County and fled on foot, firing at officers. He was cornered hours later by an armed resident outside the search area and handed over to Henry County investigators, according to the Wikipedia article and the AJC.

Knowles had mailed audio-taped confessions to a Florida attorney. The GBI said litigation over the tapes reached the federal appeals court, that a federal grand jury was allowed to review them in 1975, and that the only copies were later destroyed in a flood at the federal courthouse in Macon. The AJC reported that the tapes described 16 murders and that he claimed between 20 and 35 killings in all; investigators have linked him to at least 18, and the true number is not known.

On December 18, 1974, Douglas County Sheriff Earl Lee and GBI Agent Ronnie Angel were driving Knowles along Interstate 20 to search for Trooper Campbell's missing handgun. Authorities said he freed himself from his handcuffs and grabbed the sheriff's revolver, which fired, and Angel shot him three times in the chest; the car left the road near Lithia Springs. Knowles was 28. His Miami attorney, Sheldon Yavitz, publicly doubted the escape account, the AJC reported. The killings were never tested in court.

name: Randy Kraft

victims.suspected: up to 67

victimProfile: Young men aged roughly 14 to 30, many of them Marines or hitchhikers, picked up along Southern California freeways
captureMethod: California Highway Patrol officers stopped his weaving car on Interstate 5 for suspected drunk driving and found a dead Marine, Terry Gambrel, in the passenger seat.
sentence: Death on 11 murder counts (November 29, 1989); consecutive 25-years-to-life terms on five pre-1978 murder counts, stayed; affirmed by the California Supreme Court August 10, 2000
fateDetail: California's condemned population; held at San Quentin per 2023 and 2025 official and AP reporting, with executions under a statewide moratorium since 2019
summary: On death row in California since 1989. Randy Kraft was convicted by an Orange County jury of murdering 16 young men between 1972 and 1983; a coded list found at his 1983 arrest is believed to reference up to 67 victims in California, Oregon and Michigan.
narrative: Randy Steven Kraft is a California serial killer convicted of murdering 16 young men in Southern California between 1972 and 1983. According to the California Supreme Court's 2000 opinion in People v. Kraft, an Orange County jury convicted him in May 1989 of 16 counts of first-degree murder, one count of sodomy and one count of mayhem, and he was sentenced to death on November 29, 1989. Investigators attribute more deaths to him: the Orange County Sheriff's Department said in 2025 that it believes he is responsible for more than 60 killings in California, six in Oregon and two in Michigan. He has never confessed and, the Associated Press reported in 2025, denies killing anyone.

The court opinion sets out the 16 murders. The earliest victim, Marine Edward Daniel Moore, was found strangled near a Long Beach-area freeway off-ramp on December 26, 1972. Others followed through the 1970s, including Ronald Wiebe, Keith Crotwell, Mark Hall, Scott Hughes, Roland Young, Richard Keith, Keith Klingbeil, Michael Inderbieten, Donald Crisel and Robert Loggins, with a final cluster in 1983 of Eric Church, Geoffrey Nelson and Rodger DeVaul. Most were strangled with a ligature or suffocated after being given alcohol and sedatives, and their bodies were left beside freeways in Orange and Los Angeles counties. The opinion notes that physical evidence, including a thumbprint at the Hall scene and victims' property and photographs found in his home and car, linked Kraft to eight murders; the rest rested on the common method and his written list.

Kraft was arrested early on May 14, 1983. According to the opinion, California Highway Patrol officers saw his car weaving on Interstate 5 in southern Orange County and arrested him for drunk driving; his passenger, 25-year-old Marine Terry Gambrel, was dead of ligature strangulation, with a vial of Kraft's prescription sedative on the floor. A notebook in the car held a sheet of 61 cryptic handwritten entries. Prosecutors linked 13 to the charged murders, eight to Oregon and Michigan killings and 21 to uncharged victims, hence the press name Scorecard Killer.

The trial opened in Orange County Superior Court in September 1988 and ran about 13 months, according to reporting summarized in the Wikipedia article. The jury returned guilty verdicts on May 12, 1989 and a death verdict on August 11, 1989. Death was imposed on the 11 murders committed after 1978; the five earlier murders drew consecutive 25-years-to-life terms, stayed. The CDCR condemned list records the sentence date as November 29, 1989.

In the penalty phase, the opinion records, prosecutors presented eight uncharged murders in Oregon and Michigan. Oregon victims found near Interstate 5 between July 1980 and December 1982 included Michael O'Fallon, Michael Cluck, Brian Whitcher, Anthony Silveira and an unidentified man; travel records placed Kraft in the Portland area on each date, and several victims' belongings were in his home. In Michigan, Dennis Alt and Christopher Schoenborn were found strangled in Kent County on December 9, 1982, last seen at the Grand Rapids hotel where Kraft was staying.

On August 10, 2000, the California Supreme Court unanimously affirmed the judgment in its entirety in an opinion by Justice Werdegar. Kraft remains under sentence of death; California executions have been halted by a gubernatorial moratorium since 2019, and official and AP reporting in 2023 and 2025 placed him at San Quentin.

DNA work has continued to develop the case. In November 2023 the Orange County Sheriff's Department used genetic genealogy to identify a John Doe found in Laguna Hills in 1974 as Michael Ray Schlicht, 17, of Cedar Rapids, Iowa, calling him a presumed early Kraft victim. In May 2025 the department and Oregon State Police identified the 1980 Oregon John Doe as Larry Eugene Parks, a 30-year-old Vietnam veteran, and Oregon State Police named Kraft the sole person of interest.

Kraft was born in Long Beach, California, on March 19, 1945, according to the Wikipedia article, graduated from Claremont Men's College in 1968 and received a general discharge from the U.S. Air Force in 1969. He worked as a computer programmer; the court opinion notes his employment with Lear Siegler from 1980 to 1983, whose business travel coincided with the Oregon and Michigan murders.

name: Rex Heuermann
victimProfile: Women aged 20 to 34, many of them working as escorts or sex workers, whose remains were left on Long Island's South Shore and in eastern Suffolk County
captureMethod: A Suffolk County task force traced a Chevrolet Avalanche seen by a witness, linked burner-phone records to the victims' phones, and matched a hair on burlap to DNA from pizza crusts he discarded
sentence: Guilty pleas to seven murders (April 8, 2026); sentenced June 17, 2026, to three consecutive terms of life without parole plus four consecutive terms of 25 years to life; admitted an eighth killing (Karen Vergata) under the plea agreement
fateDetail: New York State prison system; admitted to Green Haven Correctional Facility, Stormville, for intake processing in June 2026
summary: Serving life. Massapequa Park architect Rex Heuermann pleaded guilty in April 2026 to seven of the Gilgo Beach / Long Island serial killings and admitted an eighth. He was sentenced in June 2026 to life without parole.
narrative: Rex Heuermann, an architect from Massapequa Park on Long Island, New York, pleaded guilty on April 8, 2026, to murdering seven women whose remains were found on Long Island between 1993 and 2010, and admitted in the same hearing to killing an eighth woman, Karen Vergata, whom he had never been charged with killing. The case is known as the Gilgo Beach or Long Island serial killings. On June 17, 2026, he was sentenced in Suffolk County to consecutive terms that keep him in prison for life without the possibility of parole. He is held by the New York State Department of Corrections and Community Supervision, which said in June 2026 that he was undergoing admission processing at Green Haven Correctional Facility.

Heuermann was born in 1963 and grew up in Massapequa Park, according to the Wikipedia article. He studied architecture and, NBC News reported, had worked as an architect and consultant in Manhattan since 1987, receiving his state license in 1996. His listed clients included Catholic Charities and New York City's Department of Environmental Protection. He lived with his family in a small house in Massapequa Park, about a half-hour drive from the stretch of Ocean Parkway where most of the remains were later found.

The investigation began in December 2010, when police searching the brush along Ocean Parkway near Gilgo Beach for Shannan Gilbert, a missing 24-year-old escort, instead found the remains of Melissa Barthelemy, Maureen Brainard-Barnes, Megan Waterman and Amber Costello. Further remains were found along the parkway in 2011. Gilbert's own remains were found in a marsh in Oak Beach in December 2011; Suffolk County medical examiners ruled her death an accidental drowning, and her cause of death has remained listed as undetermined. Heuermann was never charged in her death, and after the plea his lawyer, Michael Brown, said publicly that Heuermann had nothing to do with Gilbert. Her case is linked here because the search for her led to the discovery of the other victims.

The case stalled for more than a decade. According to CBS News, a Suffolk County task force reopened the evidence in 2022 and focused on a Chevrolet Avalanche registered to Heuermann that matched a witness's description from 2010. FBI analysts compared cell-site records from the victims' phones with records from prepaid burner phones linked to him, and a hair found on burlap used to wrap one victim was matched to DNA taken from pizza crusts he discarded in Manhattan. He was arrested on July 13, 2023, and charged with murdering Barthelemy, Waterman and Costello. He pleaded not guilty and was held without bail.

Prosecutors added charges over the next eighteen months. He was indicted in the death of Brainard-Barnes in January 2024. In June 2024, NBC New York reported, he was charged with murdering Jessica Taylor, 20, whose partial remains were found in Manorville in 2003, and Sandra Costilla, 28, whose remains were found by hunters near North Sea in Southampton in November 1993. According to the Wikipedia article, he was indicted in December 2024 for the murder of Valerie Mack, 24, whose partial remains had been found in Manorville in 2000. He pleaded not guilty each time, and a trial was set for September 2026.

Instead, on April 8, 2026, Heuermann appeared before State Supreme Court Justice Timothy Mazzei in Riverhead and pleaded guilty. ABC7 New York reported that he admitted strangling all of the women, and amNY reported that he described luring them with money arranged over burner phones, wrapping the bodies in burlap, and dismembering Taylor, Mack and Vergata. Vergata, 34, was last heard from on Valentine's Day 1996; her legs were found on Fire Island that year and her skull near Tobay Beach in 2011. Under the agreement described by Suffolk County District Attorney Ray Tierney, Heuermann waived his right to appeal, will not be prosecuted further for the eight deaths, and must cooperate with the FBI. amNY reported that he could still face charges if other victims are linked to him, while his lawyer said he denied involvement in the case of an unidentified Asian man found on Ocean Parkway.

At the June 17, 2026, sentencing, victims' relatives addressed him in court. The agreed sentence was three consecutive terms of life without parole for the murders of Barthelemy, Waterman and Costello, followed by four consecutive terms of 25 years to life for Brainard-Barnes, Taylor, Costilla and Mack. Heuermann told the court he was responsible, FOX 5 New York reported. Other remains found along Ocean Parkway, including those of Tanya Jackson and her young daughter, have not been attributed to him in any court record.

name: Richard Chase
victimProfile: Strangers chosen at random in the Sacramento area, among them a man outside his home, a pregnant woman, a mother, her six-year-old son, a family friend and a 22-month-old boy
captureMethod: Detectives identified him through motor vehicle records, a composite drawing and a witness who recognized him, then waited outside his Watt Avenue apartment and arrested him after a brief chase when he came out
sentence: Death, on six counts of first-degree murder; jury verdict of death in May 1979, formally imposed by Judge John Schatz on June 8, 1979
fateDetail: Found dead in his death row cell at San Quentin State Prison on December 26, 1980; the autopsy attributed the death to an overdose of a prescribed antidepressant he had hoarded
summary: Suicide. Richard Chase was convicted in May 1979 of six counts of first-degree murder for killings in Sacramento, California, in December 1977 and January 1978. Sentenced to death, he died of a drug overdose on San Quentin's death row in December 1980.
narrative: Richard Trenton Chase was an American serial killer who shot six people in the Sacramento area of California between December 29, 1977, and January 27, 1978. A Superior Court jury in Palo Alto convicted him in May 1979 of six counts of first-degree murder, rejected his plea of not guilty by reason of insanity, and returned a verdict of death. He never reached execution or the end of his appeals: on December 26, 1980, he was found dead in his cell on death row at San Quentin State Prison, and an autopsy attributed his death to an overdose of medication he had been saving.

Chase was born on May 23, 1950. The Wikipedia article is inconsistent about the place, giving Santa Clara County in one section and Sacramento in another. He attended American River College from 1968 to 1971, according to the college newspaper, and spent much of his adult life in and out of psychiatric care. HISTORY.com reports that he was released from a hospital roughly a year before the killings after a psychiatrist judged his problems to be under control. Trial records cited by the American River Current said he had first sought psychiatric help at 18 and believed he suffered from a blood disorder that only fresh blood could cure.

The first killing took place on December 29, 1977, when Ambrose Griffin, 51, an engineer and father of two, was shot while unloading groceries in the driveway of his home, United Press International reported. On January 23, 1978, Chase entered the home of Teresa Wallin on Tioga Way and killed her. She was pregnant; Wikipedia gives her age as 22 and UPI as 23. Her husband, David Wallin, came home from work and found her, he told CBS Sacramento in 2014. Four days later, on January 27, Chase entered a house on Merrywood Drive and killed Evelyn Miroth, 36; her six-year-old son, Jason; her 22-month-old nephew, David Ferreira; and a family friend, Daniel Meredith, 52. The victims were strangers to him. UPI reported that they were shot and their bodies mutilated, and Sacramento County Sheriff Duane Lowe called the killings the worst he had seen in 28 years of police work.

According to the Wikipedia article, detectives identified Chase through motor vehicle records, a composite drawing and a witness who recognized him, and arrested him on January 28, 1978, outside his apartment on Watt Avenue after a short chase. Other published accounts give slightly different arrest dates. The body of David Ferreira, which had been missing from the Miroth home, was found on March 24, 1978, in a box in an alley, the Wikipedia article says.

Because of heavy pretrial publicity, the case was moved from Sacramento to Palo Alto, where the trial opened on January 2, 1979, before Judge John Schatz, with Ronald Tochterman prosecuting. The defense, led by Farris Salamy, argued that Chase was insane, and testimony over five months centered on his mental illness and his own statements that he had drunk the blood of at least one victim, UPI reported. Chase testified in his own defense in March. The jury found him guilty of six counts of first-degree murder in May 1979, ruled on May 14 that he had been legally sane, and three days later returned a verdict of death. Judge Schatz formally imposed the sentence on June 8, 1979, according to the Wikipedia article, which in its opening section gives the date as May 8.

A San Quentin guard bringing lunch found Chase dead in his cell shortly after 11 a.m. on December 26, 1980. The Marin County coroner estimated that he had died about an hour earlier, UPI reported that day, and officials said an overdose was possible. The Wikipedia article says the autopsy later found that he had taken a large quantity of a prescribed antidepressant that he had hoarded for two to three weeks. UPI gave his age as 29; by the birth date in the Wikipedia article he was 30. The lead homicide detective on the case, Ray Biondi, later co-wrote a book about the investigation.

Relatives of the victims have objected to the way the case is retold. In 2014 the Wallin family's complaints led organizers of a Sacramento haunted house to drop scenes based on the killings, CBS Sacramento reported. In a 2025 opinion piece in the Sacramento Bee, Vern Miroth, who was 12 when his mother, brother and cousin were killed, wrote that true crime presentations had turned his family into props and asked that the victims be remembered as people.

Chase is arrested outside his Watt Avenue apartment after a brief chase, according to the Wikipedia article.

Jury convicts Chase of six counts of first-degree murder.
Jury finds Chase legally sane at the time of the killings.
Jury returns a verdict of death.

name: Richard Cottingham

victims.suspected: 20 attributed by prosecutors (9 convictions plus 11 cleared confessions); Cottingham has claimed 80 to 100

victimProfile: Women and girls aged 13 to 33, including sex workers picked up in Manhattan and teenagers abducted in Bergen County, New Jersey
captureMethod: Arrested at a Hasbrouck Heights, New Jersey motel on May 22, 1980 after a woman he had attacked in his room escaped into the hallway and screamed, and motel staff called police.
sentence: New Jersey: 173 to 197 years (1981) and 25 years to life (1982); New York: 75 years to life (1984); life (2010 plea); two concurrent life terms agreed on 2021 plea; 25 years to life (2022 plea)
fateDetail: South Woods State Prison, Bridgeton, New Jersey
summary: Imprisoned since 1980. Richard Cottingham, the "Torso Killer", was convicted at trials in New Jersey and New York (1981, 1982, 1984) of five murders, later pleaded guilty to four more, and has confessed to 11 others closed without charges.
narrative: Richard Francis Cottingham, known as the "Torso Killer" and the "Times Square Killer", murdered women and girls in New Jersey and New York between 1967 and 1980. Courts have convicted him of nine murders: five by trial verdicts in Bergen County, New Jersey (1981 and 1982) and Manhattan (1984), and four by guilty pleas in 2010, 2021 and 2022. Prosecutors have also accepted his confessions to 11 further killings closed without charges. NBC News reported that he has claimed up to 100 murders, a figure authorities have not confirmed.

The crimes he was tried for surfaced in 1979 and 1980. On December 2, 1979, Deedeh Goodarzi, 22, and an unidentified woman were found decapitated in a burning room at the Travel Inn Motor Hotel in Manhattan, the source of the "Torso Killer" name. In May 1980 Valerie Ann Street, 19, was found strangled under a bed at the Quality Inn in Hasbrouck Heights, New Jersey, and Mary Ann Jean Reyner, 25, was found stabbed and burned at the Seville Hotel in Manhattan. The December 1977 strangling of Maryann Carr, 26, in Little Ferry was later tied to him as well.

On May 22, 1980, Cottingham brought Leslie Ann O'Dell, 18, to the same Hasbrouck Heights motel. According to the Wikipedia account, she escaped into the hallway and screamed, staff called police, and he was arrested as he tried to leave. Two women who survived 1978 attacks, Karen Schilt and Susan Geiger, identified him in a lineup, and he was indicted in Bergen County and charged in New York with the three Manhattan killings.

A Radford University case summary citing New York Times coverage records the three trials. In June 1981 he was convicted in Bergen County of murdering Street and of kidnapping and assaulting Schilt, Geiger and O'Dell, and on July 25, 1981 was sentenced to 173 to 197 years. On October 12, 1982, he was convicted of the Carr murder in what the summary describes as a non-jury trial and sentenced to 25 years to life. On July 9, 1984, a Manhattan jury convicted him of murdering Goodarzi, the unidentified woman and Reyner; he was sentenced to 75 years to life.

Interviews by Bergen County Chief of Detectives Robert Anzilotti produced later admissions. In 2010 Cottingham pleaded guilty to the 1967 strangling of Nancy Schiava Vogel, 29, found in her car in Ridgefield Park, and received a life sentence, according to New Jersey 101.5 and Oxygen. In January 2020 the prosecutor's office announced he had admitted strangling Jacalyn Harp, 13, Irene Blase, 18, and Denise Falasca, 15, in 1968 and 1969; those cases were cleared without charges. On April 27, 2021, he pleaded guilty before Judge Keith Bachmann to murdering Mary Ann Pryor, 17, and Lorraine Marie Kelly, 16, who vanished hitchhiking on August 9, 1974 and were found in Montvale five days later. The prosecutor's office said he admitted drowning them in a motel bathtub; NBC News reported the plea agreement called for two concurrent life sentences.

After a DNA match, Nassau County, New York indicted him in 2022 for the 1968 killing of Diane Cusick, 23, found in her car outside the Green Acres Mall in Valley Stream. On December 5, 2022, he pleaded guilty before Judge Caryn Fink and was sentenced to 25 years to life, and the Long Island Press reported he admitted killing four other Nassau women in 1972 and 1973, Mary Beth Heinz, Laverne Moye, Sheila Heiman and Maria Emerita Rosado Nieves, under a non-prosecution agreement. According to the Wikipedia article, Rockland County accepted confessions to two more killings in 2022 and Bergen County added the 1967 killing of Mary Ann Della Sala in 2023. In January 2026, NBC New York reported that Fair Lawn police had closed the 1965 killing of Alys Eberhardt, 18, on his confession; he was not charged.

Cottingham was born on November 25, 1946 in the Bronx and raised in Bergen County. He worked as a computer operator in Manhattan, married in 1970 and had three children, and lived in Lodi, New Jersey when arrested. He is now held at South Woods State Prison in Bridgeton, according to the Wikipedia article and 2022 court reporting.

name: Richard Ramirez

victims.suspected: 15 or more (13 convictions plus two San Francisco killings attributed by police)

victimProfile: Residents attacked in their homes at night, from a 9-year-old girl to adults in their 60s to 80s; women were often sexually assaulted and men shot
captureMethod: A fingerprint lifted from the rear-view mirror of an abandoned stolen car was matched to his 1984 arrest record, his photograph was released, and residents of East Los Angeles recognized and held him after an attempted carjacking.
sentence: Death (Los Angeles County Superior Court, 1989-11-07); affirmed by the California Supreme Court on 2006-08-07
fateDetail: San Quentin State Prison death row; died at Marin General Hospital, Greenbrae, California, of complications from B-cell lymphoma
summary: Died on death row in 2013. Richard Ramirez, the Night Stalker, was convicted by a Los Angeles jury in 1989 of 13 murders, 5 attempted murders, 11 sexual assaults and 14 burglaries committed in 1984 and 1985, and sentenced to death.
narrative: Richard Ramirez, known as the Night Stalker, carried out a series of night-time home invasions in the Los Angeles area between June 1984 and August 1985, with related attacks in San Francisco and Orange County. On September 20, 1989, a Los Angeles County jury convicted him of 12 counts of first-degree murder, one count of second-degree murder, five counts of attempted murder, 11 sexual assault counts and 14 counts of first-degree burglary, according to the California Supreme Court's 2006 opinion in People v. Ramirez. He was sentenced to death on November 7, 1989, and died of natural causes on June 7, 2013, while on death row at San Quentin.

The first killing in the Los Angeles case was that of Jennie Vincow, 79, found dead in her Glassell Park apartment on June 28, 1984; a fingerprint was recovered from a window screen, the court opinion says. The attacks resumed on March 17, 1985, when Dayle Okazaki was shot dead in Rosemead and her roommate Maria Hernandez survived; within the hour Tsai-Lian Yu was shot dead in Monterey Park. Over the following months Vincent and Maxine Zazzara were killed in Whittier, William Doi in Monterey Park, Mabel Bell in Monrovia, Mary Cannon in Arcadia, Joyce Nelson in Monterey Park, Maxon and Lela Kneiding in Glendale, Chainarong Khovananth in Sun Valley and Elyas Abowath in Diamond Bar on August 8, 1985. Several surviving women were raped, and pentagrams were drawn at some scenes.

Investigators tied the crimes together through ballistics from a .22-caliber pistol, prints from Avia athletic shoes and eyewitness descriptions, according to the opinion. On August 18, 1985, Peter Pan was shot dead in San Francisco and his wife Barbara survived, an attack San Francisco authorities linked to the series. After an August 24 attack in Mission Viejo in which Bill Carns was shot and survived, a witness noted the suspect's car. The stolen Toyota was found abandoned in Los Angeles on August 28, and a fingerprint from its rear-view mirror was matched to Ramirez's record from a 1984 auto-theft arrest, according to Wikipedia's account. Police released his photograph.

On August 31, 1985, Ramirez tried to steal cars in East Los Angeles; residents who recognized him from news reports chased, struck and held him until police arrived, the court opinion records. At the station he made spontaneous statements admitting the killings.

Ramirez was charged with 43 offenses in Los Angeles County; the Los Angeles Times reported in November 1987 that one murder count was dismissed, leaving 13. Jury selection began on July 22, 1988. The jury returned guilty verdicts on all counts on September 20, 1989, found special circumstances of multiple murder, burglary, rape, sodomy and oral copulation true, and returned a death verdict. The judge imposed the death sentence on November 7, 1989.

On August 7, 2006, the California Supreme Court affirmed the convictions and death sentence, rejecting challenges to venue, severance, counsel substitution, competency and the admission of crime-scene photographs. He never went to trial on the San Francisco charges arising from the Pan shooting. In October 2009, San Francisco police said DNA matched Ramirez to the April 10, 1984, killing of nine-year-old Mei Leung in an apartment building basement; CBS News reported the match, and no charges followed. Ramirez married Doreen Lioy at San Quentin on October 3, 1996.

Ramirez died at Marin General Hospital in Greenbrae on June 7, 2013, at age 53. The California Department of Corrections and Rehabilitation lists the death as natural causes, and the Marin County coroner later attributed it to complications of B-cell lymphoma, according to reporting cited by Wikipedia. He had been on death row for more than 23 years.

Ramirez was born Ricardo Leyva Muñoz Ramírez in El Paso, Texas, on February 29, 1960, the youngest of five children of Mexican immigrant parents. Accounts cited by Wikipedia describe childhood head injuries, epilepsy and early drug use. He dropped out of high school, moved to California in 1982 and funded a cocaine habit through burglaries before the murders began.

name: Robert Ben Rhoades
victimProfile: Hitchhikers and runaways picked up along interstate highways, including a teenage girl and a young married couple
captureMethod: An Arizona state trooper checking a truck parked with its hazard lights on beside Interstate 10 near Casa Grande found a chained captive woman in the cab
sentence: Life without parole in Illinois for the first-degree murder of Regina Walters; life sentences without parole in Texas (2012) on two counts of capital murder for Patricia Walsh and Douglas Scott Zyskowski; earlier six-year Arizona term for the 1990 kidnapping
fateDetail: Serving life in the Illinois prison system; listed by Wikipedia at Menard Correctional Center, Chester, Illinois
summary: Serving life. Long-haul trucker Robert Ben Rhoades pleaded guilty to the 1990 murder of 14-year-old Regina Walters in Illinois and, in 2012, to the Texas capital murders of Patricia Walsh and Douglas Scott Zyskowski. Investigators suspect many more victims.
narrative: Robert Ben Rhoades is an American long-haul truck driver convicted of three murders committed in 1990: the killing of 14-year-old Regina Walters in Illinois and the killings of Seattle newlyweds Patricia Candace Walsh and Douglas Scott Zyskowski, who were picked up in West Texas. He was arrested in Arizona on April 1, 1990, after a state trooper found a captive woman in the cab of his truck. He pleaded guilty in Illinois to Walters' murder and received life without parole, and in March 2012 he pleaded guilty in Texas to two counts of capital murder and received further life sentences. He is serving life in Illinois. Investigators have said they believe there were more victims, but no further charges have been brought.

Rhoades was born on November 22, 1945, in Council Bluffs, Iowa, according to the Wikipedia article, and by the late 1980s was living in Houston and driving a tractor-trailer on interstate routes. A 1996 Tucson Weekly investigation reported that his job assignments took him to Tucson or nearby cities 36 times in late 1989 and early 1990. In the early morning of April 1, 1990, Arizona State Trooper Mike Miller stopped to check a Peterbilt rig parked with its hazard lights on beside Interstate 10 at Casa Grande. Inside the cab he found a naked woman chained and shackled, who told investigators she had been whipped and tortured. Rhoades was booked on charges of aggravated assault, sexual assault and unlawful imprisonment. He was convicted in Arizona, and the Tucson Weekly reported a six-year sentence for that kidnapping.

The Arizona arrest led investigators to Houston, where police found another woman who said she had escaped from Rhoades after being held and tortured, the Associated Press reported in 2012. On April 6, 1990, FBI agents searched his Houston apartment and seized restraints, women's clothing and photographs, according to the Tucson Weekly. Among the photographs were images of a bound teenage girl at a barn. She was later identified as Regina Walters, a 14-year-old runaway from Pasadena, Texas, who had disappeared in February 1990 with her 18-year-old boyfriend, Ricky Lee Jones. Walters' body was found in a barn loft at an abandoned farm near Greenville, Illinois; the Wikipedia article dates the discovery to September 29, 1990. Investigators said she had been strangled with baling wire attached to a piece of lumber.

Prosecutors in Bond County, Illinois, charged Rhoades with Walters' murder as his Arizona sentence neared its end. The Tucson Weekly reported that in September 1992, after his court-appointed lawyers reviewed the evidence with him, he pleaded guilty to her killing and was sentenced to life in prison without the possibility of parole. The Wikipedia article instead dates the Illinois conviction to 1994; the record available to us does not settle the year. Jones was never charged as a victim in any case. The 2012 Associated Press and Deseret News reports said his body had never been found, while the Wikipedia article says partial skeletal remains found near Harleton, Texas, in May 1990 were later attributed to him. His death is attributed to Rhoades only as a suspicion.

The case of Walsh, 24, and Zyskowski took years longer. The couple had left Seattle in November 1989 to hitchhike to Georgia to preach, and accepted a ride from Rhoades near El Paso, according to the Associated Press. Zyskowski's age is given as 25 by the Deseret News and 28 by the AP. He was shot, and his body was found in January 1990 along Interstate 10 east of Ozona, Texas, but was not identified until 1992. Deer hunters found Walsh's remains in October 1990 about 22 miles south of Fillmore, Utah. They lay unidentified in the basement of the Millard County Sheriff's Office for 13 years until dental records identified her in 2003. Investigators believe Rhoades held her captive for about a week before shooting her several times.

In 2005, Utah charged Rhoades with murder and aggravated kidnapping in Millard County and sought his extradition from Illinois. The Deseret News reported that Utah later dropped its charge and, at the families' request, allowed Texas to prosecute both killings, since authorities there said the kidnappings had occurred in Texas. Prosecutors in Ozona said they would seek the death penalty, but the trial was repeatedly delayed after 2009. On March 26, 2012, as the trial was due to begin, Rhoades pleaded guilty in Sutton County to two counts of capital murder. In exchange, prosecutors did not seek death; he received life sentences and waived his rights to appeal and to parole.

The full extent of Rhoades' crimes is unknown. The Tucson Weekly quoted FBI Special Agent Mark Young as saying he believed Rhoades had escalated to about three abductions a month by early 1990, and reported that the woman found in his truck said he told her he had been doing this for 15 years. The Wikipedia article says he is suspected in the deaths of more than 50 women between 1975 and 1990, but that figure reflects suspicion, not charges. Steve Smith of the 112th District Attorney's office told ABC News in 2012 that Rhoades would die in prison, and that if he were ever released in Illinois he would return to Texas custody. The Wikipedia article lists him at Menard Correctional Center in Chester, Illinois.

Walters' body is found in a barn loft near Greenville, Illinois, according to the Wikipedia article.

Rhoades pleads guilty in Illinois to Walters' murder and is sentenced to life without parole, per the Tucson Weekly (Wikipedia gives 1994).

name: Robert Berdella
victimProfile: Young men aged 19 to 27, several of them acquaintances or lodgers, held captive at his Kansas City home
captureMethod: A captive escaped from a second-floor window and reached police, who searched the house and found human remains and photographs
sentence: Life without parole for first-degree murder of Larry Pearson (August 1988), plus life and seven years on sodomy and restraint counts; five further concurrent life sentences on one first-degree and four second-degree murder pleas (December 1988)
fateDetail: Missouri State Penitentiary, Jefferson City; heart attack, pronounced dead at a hospital in Columbia, Missouri
summary: Died in prison. Robert Berdella pleaded guilty in 1988 to murdering six young men held captive at his Kansas City, Missouri home between 1984 and 1987. Sentenced to life without parole, he died at the Missouri State Penitentiary in October 1992.
narrative: Robert Berdella is an American serial killer who pleaded guilty in 1988 to murdering six young men in Kansas City, Missouri, between 1984 and 1987. He was never tried: on his pleas he was convicted of two counts of first-degree murder and four counts of second-degree murder, received six life sentences, and died in the Missouri State Penitentiary in October 1992. Prosecutors agreed not to seek the death penalty in exchange for his confessions, according to United Press International reporting at the time.

According to the Wikipedia article, the first victim was Jerry Howell, 19, who died on July 5, 1984, after being held at Berdella's house in the Hyde Park neighborhood. Five more men died there over the next three years: Robert Sheldon, 20, in April 1985; Mark Wallace, 27, in June 1985; Walter Ferris, 25, in September 1985; Todd Stoops, 23, in July 1986; and Larry Pearson, 20, in 1987. Each man was held captive at the house before he died, in most cases of asphyxiation, and the bodies were never recovered. UPI reported in May 1988 that the families of Howell and Ferris had long said the men were last seen with Berdella.

The case broke on April 2, 1988, when a 22-year-old man, later identified as Christopher Bryson, escaped from the house by jumping from a second-floor window and reached police wearing only a dog collar. Berdella was arrested the same day and charged with seven counts of forcible sodomy, one count of first-degree assault and one count of felonious restraint. Police began digging up the yard on April 3 and seized more than 200 photographs of men being abused. A skull found inside the house was identified on May 10, 1988, through hospital X-rays and dental records as Robert Sheldon, and two days later a second skull dug from the back yard was identified by dental records as Larry Pearson, UPI reported.

A grand jury indicted Berdella for Pearson's murder on July 22, 1988. In early August he pleaded guilty to first-degree murder in Pearson's death before Judge Alvin C. Randall and was sentenced to life in prison without parole; later that month he pleaded guilty to forcible sodomy and felonious restraint in the Bryson case, receiving a further life term and seven years, with the remaining counts dropped. In September he pleaded not guilty to five additional murder charges. UPI reported on December 19, 1988, that after a week of meetings with prosecutors, public defenders and detectives at the county jail, Berdella had agreed to confess to the five remaining killings in exchange for prosecutors not recommending death. That day, according to the Wikipedia article, he pleaded guilty before Jackson County Circuit Judge Robert Meyers to first-degree murder in the death of Sheldon and second-degree murder in the deaths of Howell, Wallace, Ferris and Stoops, and received five further concurrent life sentences.

Berdella was sent to the Missouri State Penitentiary in Jefferson City, with a brief period at Potosi Correctional Center for his own protection. He died on October 8, 1992, aged 43, after complaining of chest pains; he was pronounced dead at a hospital in Columbia, Missouri, and the cause was recorded as a heart attack. The Pitch, a Kansas City weekly, reported in 2004 that a minister said Berdella had telephoned him shortly before his death claiming prison officials were withholding his heart medication. His house on Charlotte Street was sold and demolished, and the lot was later deeded to the Hyde Park Neighborhood Association.

Berdella was born on January 31, 1949, in Cuyahoga Falls, Ohio. By the 1980s he ran a stall at the Westport Flea Market in Kansas City, known as Bob's Bazaar Bizarre and lived alone at 4315 Charlotte Street. He was described in court proceedings as having a depressive personality disorder and sexual sadism disorder, according to the Wikipedia article. His case was the subject of Tom Jackman and Troy Cole's book Rites of Burial (1992) and Ben Meade's 2004 documentary Bazaar Bizarre.

name: Robert Charles Browne

victims.suspected: 9 to 48

victimProfile: Mostly girls and young women, including two Colorado Springs-area teenagers, among them a 15-year-old Army wife, and young women from his Louisiana hometown
captureMethod: Crime-scene fingerprints from the Heather Church case were run through fingerprint databases not searched before and matched Browne through earlier felony records
sentence: Life without parole for the kidnapping and murder of Heather Dawn Church (1995 guilty plea); a second life sentence for first-degree murder of Rocio Sperry (2006 guilty plea)
fateDetail: Limon Correctional Facility, Limon, Colorado (per Wikipedia, as of February 2023)
summary: Serving life. Robert Charles Browne pleaded guilty to the 1991 murder of Heather Dawn Church and the 1987 murder of Rocio Sperry near Colorado Springs. He claims 48 killings in nine states; investigators said a few out-of-state claims were corroborated.
narrative: Robert Charles Browne is a Louisiana-born former soldier who is serving two life sentences in Colorado for the murders of two girls in the Colorado Springs area. In 1995 he pleaded guilty to the 1991 kidnapping and murder of 13-year-old Heather Dawn Church and was sentenced to life without parole; in July 2006 he pleaded guilty to first-degree murder in the 1987 death of Rocio Sperry, about 15, and received a second life term. He has claimed responsibility for 48 killings in nine states between 1970 and 1995. Investigators have said a handful of those claims were corroborated, but he has not been charged in any killing outside Colorado.

According to the Wikipedia article, Browne was born on October 31, 1952, in Coushatta, Louisiana, the youngest of nine children. He left high school shortly before turning 17 to join the Army, and the Associated Press reported that he served from 1969 to 1976 before being dishonorably discharged for drug use. Wikipedia says he married five times, with every marriage ending in divorce, and that he worked at various businesses in Louisiana, Texas and Colorado.

Heather Dawn Church disappeared on September 17, 1991, from her family's home in Black Forest, Colorado, where she had been babysitting. According to the Wikipedia article, her remains were found in September 1993 off Rampart Range Road, and the case stayed unsolved until an investigator working for the Colorado Springs police ran crime-scene fingerprints through dozens of fingerprint databases that had not been searched before. The prints matched Browne through earlier felony records, and he was charged with Church's murder on March 28, 1995. Under a plea agreement he pleaded guilty to kidnapping and murder; prosecutors did not seek the death penalty, and he was sentenced to life in prison without parole.

In March 2000, Browne sent El Paso County prosecutors a taunting letter written in cryptic prose; Newsweek reported that it read in part, "The score is you, one, the other team, 48." A group of unpaid retired investigators working with the El Paso County Sheriff's Office, among them former FBI and CIA officer Charlie Hess, retired Colorado Springs detective Lou Smit and former newspaper publisher Scott Fischer, took up the case. The Associated Press reported that Hess corresponded with Browne, and that in early 2003 Browne wrote, "Try the missing persons files on a young Army wife." That pointed investigators to Rocio Sperry, a 15-year-old who was married to a soldier and had vanished from Colorado Springs in 1987. Browne then confessed in a prison interview to killing her. Her remains have never been found.

On July 27, 2006, Browne pleaded guilty in Colorado Springs to first-degree murder in Sperry's death. Newsweek reported that investigators had confirmed details of his account, including a ring he said he took from her and sold, which the sheriff's office traced to the buyer. He received a second life sentence. The same week, El Paso County Sheriff Terry Maketa announced that Browne claimed 48 killings: 17 in Louisiana, nine in Colorado, seven in Texas, five in Arkansas, three in Mississippi, two each in California, New Mexico and Oklahoma, and one in Washington. Some reports gave the figure as 49, counting a claimed killing of a fellow soldier in South Korea in 1970, which the sheriff said had not been verified.

Maketa said authorities had corroborated six of the out-of-state claims, three in Louisiana, two in Texas and one in Arkansas, according to the Associated Press; a later WAFB report put the total at seven when the two Colorado cases were included. Newsweek quoted Maketa as saying Browne had given information on 19 of the 48 claimed killings and was a strong suspect in seven. The Louisiana cases named in reporting are three young women from Coushatta: Wanda Faye Hudson, Faye Self and Katherine Jean Hayes. Published accounts differ on the years of those deaths, which fall in the early 1980s. Reporting also linked Browne to Nidia Mendoza, 17, whose body was found near Houston in 1984, and the Wikipedia article lists further possible victims in Texas, Arkansas and Oklahoma, among them Timothy Lee Warren, found shot in a Tulsa park in March 1992.

Maketa said Browne might be exaggerating but that investigators could not proceed on that assumption, and then-Colorado Attorney General John Suthers said he believed the claims of multiple killings. Others were more doubtful. Criminologist Robert Keppel told the Associated Press that such numbers were "just for media purposes." The Wikipedia article notes that most of the 48 claims remain uncorroborated. As of February 2023, according to Wikipedia, Browne was held at the Limon Correctional Facility in Limon, Colorado.

Heather Dawn Church, 13, abducted from her family's home in Black Forest, Colorado.
Church's remains found off Rampart Range Road.
Browne charged with Church's murder after a fingerprint match.
Pleads guilty to Church's kidnapping and murder; sentenced to life without parole.
Sends a taunting letter to El Paso County prosecutors hinting at 48 killings.
In correspondence with retired investigator Charlie Hess, points to the missing-persons file of a young Army wife; later confesses to killing Rocio Sperry.
Pleads guilty to first-degree murder of Rocio Sperry and receives a second life sentence; sheriff announces his claim of 48 killings in nine states.
Held at Limon Correctional Facility, Colorado, according to Wikipedia.

name: Robert Foley
victimProfile: Adult acquaintances in Laurel County, Kentucky: four people shot in 1989 and two brothers shot at his home in 1991
captureMethod: Arrested in 1991 after the bodies of Rodney and Lynn Vaughn were found in Sinking Creek two days after they were shot; four further bodies were recovered from a septic tank in October 1991
sentence: Death, on two counts of murder (Vaughn brothers, Laurel Circuit Court, 1993) and on four counts of murder (1989 killings, Madison Circuit Court, 1994)
fateDetail: On Kentucky's death row; executions in the state have been halted by court order since 2010, and he was still listed on death row by the Louisville Courier Journal in July 2024
summary: Serving death sentence. Robert Carl Foley was convicted of six murders in Laurel County, Kentucky: four people shot in 1989 and brothers Rodney and Lynn Vaughn in 1991. He holds six death sentences and remains on Kentucky's death row.
narrative: Robert Carl Foley is a Kentucky death row prisoner convicted of six murders committed in Laurel County, in the southeastern part of the state, between 1989 and 1991. A Laurel County jury convicted him in 1993 of killing brothers Rodney and Lynn Vaughn at his home in August 1991, and a jury in Madison County, where the second case was moved, convicted him in 1994 of four killings carried out in 1989. He received a death sentence for each of the six murders. All of his appeals have so far failed, and he remains on death row, where Kentucky executions have been halted by a court order since 2010, according to Associated Press reporting.

According to the Sixth Circuit's 2007 opinion in Foley v. Parker, the Vaughn killings took place on August 17, 1991, at Foley's house in Laurel County. Foley admitted starting a fight by punching Rodney Vaughn, who was intoxicated. After the two were separated, Foley knocked Rodney down several more times, drew a revolver and shot him six times at close range. He then fetched another gun and shot Lynn Vaughn, whose full name the Kentucky Supreme Court gives as Harry Lynn Vaughn, in the back of the head. The court said Foley organized three other men to help dispose of the bodies, which were dumped in Sinking Creek and found two days later. Foley was indicted on two counts of capital murder and related charges.

While the Vaughn case was pending, investigators uncovered the earlier killings. In October 1991, the Sixth Circuit recorded, authorities recovered four bodies from property in the Bald Rock community of Laurel County; they had been covered in lime and placed in a septic tank capped with cement. The victims were Kimberly Bowersock, Lillian Contino, Jerry McMillen and Calvin Reynolds, whose surnames are spelled in slightly different ways across court records. The Associated Press reported that they were shot on October 8, 1989, because Foley believed one of them had reported him to his parole officer. The Kentucky Supreme Court has noted that prosecutors also linked the killings to Foley's alleged trafficking in marijuana and moonshine, and that the Commonwealth's theory placed the shootings inside the home of a man named David Gross.

The Vaughn trial was set for August 11, 1993, in Laurel Circuit Court. The judge refused a last-minute request to move it, despite heavy local coverage that included the septic tank discoveries, and the jury found Foley guilty of both murders and recommended death. The Kentucky Supreme Court affirmed in November 1996. The trial on the four 1989 murders was moved to Madison County and held in April 1994. That case rested largely on two eyewitnesses who were present at the killings and who, according to the state's high court, said Foley spared them to intimidate them into helping cover up the scene. He was convicted of all four murders and given four more death sentences, which the Kentucky Supreme Court affirmed in 1997. The Vaughn convictions were used as an aggravating factor in the second penalty phase.

Foley has maintained that he is innocent of the 1989 killings and has argued that he shot the Vaughns in self-defense. His later challenges have all been rejected. The Sixth Circuit affirmed the denial of his federal habeas petition in 2007 over a dissent that questioned the fairness of the Laurel County jury. In 2009 Attorney General Jack Conway asked Governor Steve Beshear to set an execution date, saying Foley had exhausted his appeals as of right, WUKY reported. In March 2014 the Kentucky Supreme Court unanimously refused to reopen the Vaughn case on the basis of a firearms expert's report, finding nothing new in it. In February 2017 the same court rejected two further challenges in the 1989 case, including affidavits from people who claimed to have seen Calvin Reynolds alive after the killings.

Foley also brought a federal lawsuit over the state's failure to arrange a hip replacement, which a magistrate judge dismissed in 2014. The Associated Press reported that six facilities declined to host the operation, partly because of security concerns about him. With six victims, he has more murder convictions than any other prisoner on Kentucky's death row, according to the AP. The Louisville Courier Journal listed him in July 2024, aged 67, as one of 25 people under a death sentence in the state, after 30 years on death row.

Trial on the 1989 murders, moved to Madison County, ends with convictions on all four counts and four death sentences.
Kentucky Supreme Court affirms the Vaughn convictions and death sentences.
Kentucky Supreme Court affirms the four 1989 murder convictions and death sentences.
Sixth Circuit affirms denial of federal habeas relief in the Vaughn case, over a partial dissent.

name: Robert Hansen
victimProfile: Young women in Anchorage, many of them dancers or sex workers, abducted and flown or driven to remote areas of south-central Alaska
captureMethod: A 17-year-old woman escaped in handcuffs in June 1983 and reported him; a search of his home in October 1983 found victims' jewelry, a Ruger Mini-14 rifle and a marked aviation chart
sentence: 461 years in prison on guilty pleas (February 1984) to four murders and related felonies
fateDetail: Died August 21, 2014, aged 75, at Alaska Regional Hospital, Anchorage, while in Department of Corrections custody; apparent natural causes after a year of declining health
summary: Died in prison. Anchorage baker Robert Hansen pleaded guilty in 1984 to murdering four women in Alaska, confessed to killing 17, and was sentenced to 461 years. He died in custody in Anchorage in August 2014, aged 75.
narrative: Robert Hansen was an Anchorage, Alaska, bakery owner who pleaded guilty in February 1984 to murdering four women in south-central Alaska and later admitted to killing 17. He was never tried: under a plea agreement he was convicted of the four murders, along with related felonies, and was sentenced to 461 years in prison. He died in state custody on August 21, 2014, aged 75, at Alaska Regional Hospital in Anchorage, after a year of declining health, according to the Anchorage Daily News and the Associated Press.

Hansen was born on February 15, 1939, in Estherville, Iowa, and moved to Anchorage in 1967, where he opened a bakery. According to the Wikipedia article, he had earlier served about twenty months of a three-year sentence for arson in Iowa and, in Alaska, had several arrests for theft and a 1971 conviction for assault with a deadly weapon. A woman accused him of rape in 1971, the Anchorage Daily News reported. He was a licensed pilot who owned a Piper Super Cub, and the press later called him the Butcher Baker.

Investigators and later court proceedings described a pattern in which Hansen picked up young women in Anchorage, many of them dancers or sex workers, took them to his home and then flew them to remote areas north and east of the city, where he killed them and buried them in shallow graves. The Associated Press reported in 2021 that he abducted and hunted women in the wilderness north of Anchorage in the early 1980s. His most frequent burial area, according to the AP's 2014 obituary, was along the Knik River northeast of Anchorage. The remains of an unidentified young woman, later known as Eklutna Annie, were found near Eklutna Lake Road in July 1980; Hansen told investigators she was his first victim. Further remains were found along the Knik River in 1982 and 1983.

The case turned in June 1983, when a 17-year-old woman ran into a Fifth Avenue motel in Anchorage wearing handcuffs and told police that Hansen had held her captive, raped her and put her on his plane, the Anchorage Daily News reported. Police did not at first treat him as a serious suspect. Alaska State Trooper investigator Glenn Flothe linked three bodies found in the region, and the FBI helped build an offender profile, according to the Wikipedia article. Hansen was arrested in October 1983. A search of his home turned up jewelry belonging to missing women, firearms including a Ruger Mini-14 rifle, and an aviation chart marked with locations; the Anchorage Daily News described the map as marked with 17 locations.

After ballistics tests matched bullets from crime scenes to his rifle, Hansen agreed to a plea bargain. In February 1984 he pleaded guilty to four murders, those of Sherry Morrow, Joanna Messina, Paula Goulding and the woman known as Eklutna Annie, and received a 461-year sentence. The AP reported that the agreement spared prosecutors 17 separate trials. As part of the deal he confessed to killing 17 women and raping about 30 others over roughly a dozen years, and he showed investigators from a helicopter where he had left bodies. Troopers recovered 12 sets of remains; the rest have never been found. The Anchorage Daily News reported in 2014 that he may have killed as many as 21 women, though that figure is not a confession or conviction count.

Hansen served his sentence first in a federal prison in Pennsylvania and in Minnesota, then at Lemon Creek Correctional Center in Juneau, where officials found escape plans, and finally at Spring Creek Correctional Center in Seward, the Anchorage Daily News reported. On May 11, 2014, he was moved to the Anchorage Correctional Complex for medical care. The Department of Corrections said he appeared to have died of natural causes; a do-not-resuscitate order was on file, according to the AP.

Identification of the victims continued after his death. In October 2021 the Alaska Bureau of Investigation's Cold Case Investigation Unit announced that a woman whose remains were recovered near Horseshoe Lake in 1984, and who had been buried as an unknown under the name Horseshoe Harriet, was Robin Pelkey, a 19-year-old born in Colorado. Her remains were exhumed in 2014, and the identification was made through genetic genealogy and a DNA match with a relative in Arkansas, according to the Associated Press and Alaska Public Media. As of that announcement, Eklutna Annie remained the one recovered victim still unidentified, and troopers said they were working with genealogy laboratories to identify her. Hansen's case was the basis for the 2013 film The Frozen Ground.

name: Robert Lee Yates Jr.

victims.suspected: 16; at his arrest the Spokane County sheriff cited 12 to 18 possible victims

victimProfile: Mostly women aged 16 to 47 working as sex workers in Spokane and Tacoma; also a young couple shot near Walla Walla in 1975 and a 23-year-old woman killed in Skagit County in 1988
captureMethod: Carpet fibers from a white 1977 Corvette he had owned matched fibers found with 16-year-old Jennifer Joseph; a search of the car turned up blood and a button from her jacket, and DNA then linked him to a dozen further victims.
sentence: 408 years and 4 months (Spokane County, 2000, guilty plea to 13 aggravated murders and 1 attempted murder); death (Pierce County jury, 2002, two aggravated murders), converted to life without parole in 2018
fateDetail: Washington State Penitentiary, Walla Walla; death sentence converted to life without parole after Washington's Supreme Court struck down capital punishment in October 2018
summary: Imprisoned for life. Former Army helicopter pilot who pleaded guilty in Spokane County in 2000 to 13 murders (1975 to 1998) and was convicted by a Pierce County jury in 2002 of two more; his death sentence became life without parole in 2018.
narrative: Robert Lee Yates Jr. is a Washington man convicted of 15 murders committed between 1975 and 1998 in Spokane, Tacoma, Walla Walla and Skagit counties. In October 2000 he pleaded guilty in Spokane County Superior Court to 13 counts of aggravated first-degree murder and one count of attempted first-degree murder and was sentenced to 408 years in prison. In 2002 a Pierce County jury convicted him of two further aggravated murders and returned a death verdict. According to the Washington Supreme Court's 2013 order on his personal restraint petition, Yates acknowledged committing 15 murders. His death sentence was converted to life without parole in October 2018, when the state's high court struck down Washington's death penalty.

The earliest killings to which he pleaded guilty were those of Patrick Oliver and Susan Savage, a young couple shot near Walla Walla in July 1975, and of Stacy Hawn, a 23-year-old Seattle woman killed in Skagit County in 1988, as reported by The Seattle Times at his sentencing. Most of the victims were women working as prostitutes in Spokane between 1996 and 1998. Bodies were found at roadsides, in vacant lots and in rural areas around the city: Shannon Zielinski in June 1996; Jennifer Joseph, 16, and Heather Hernandez in August 1997; Darla Sue Scott in November 1997; Shawn Johnson, Laurie Wason and Shawn McClenahan in December 1997; Sunny Oster in February 1998; Linda Maybin in April 1998; and Michelyn Derning in July 1998. The Spokesman-Review reported in December 1997 that Wason and McClenahan were found together in an overgrown gravel pit in southeast Spokane and identified by fingerprints, and that a four-detective task force was examining whether a series of murders of Spokane-area women was the work of one person.

Two victims were found near Tacoma, in Pierce County: Melinda Mercer, 24, in December 1997, and Connie LaFontaine Ellis, 35, in October 1998. According to the Washington Supreme Court's 2013 order, prosecutors argued that Yates was in Pierce County for National Guard duty when he killed them. The Associated Press reported that the Tacoma victims were shot and suffocated with plastic grocery bags placed over their heads. Yates also admitted attempting to kill a woman in Spokane in 1998, the single attempted-murder count in his plea.

The Seattle Times reported in May 2000 that Yates had been interviewed in September 1999 as one of hundreds of suspects and refused to give a blood sample. Investigators then traced a white 1977 Corvette he had owned from 1994 to 1998 and, in January 2000, took carpet fibers from it. In April 2000 the fibers were reported to match fibers found on Jennifer Joseph's shoes and on a towel near her body; a search of the car under a warrant produced a button matching one missing from her jacket and traces of blood. Yates was arrested on April 18, 2000, on his way to work at a Kaiser Aluminum plant, and charged the next day with Joseph's murder. The sheriff said DNA linked him to eight deaths and other evidence to more.

According to the Washington Supreme Court, negotiations in July 2000 produced a Spokane County plea agreement under which Yates would plead guilty and reveal the location of a further victim's body in exchange for life without parole; the body of Melody Murfin was recovered from his own yard. Pierce County declined to join the deal and filed two counts of aggravated murder. On October 26, 2000, Spokane County Superior Court Judge Richard Schroeder sentenced Yates to 408 years and four months and fined him $620,000; The Seattle Times reported that 17 relatives of 11 victims addressed the court and that Yates apologized by name to each victim. A charge in the McClenahan killing was dismissed without prejudice.

A Pierce County jury convicted Yates of the Mercer and Ellis murders on September 19, 2002, and on October 3, 2002, after fewer than five hours of deliberation, unanimously returned a death verdict. The Washington Supreme Court affirmed the convictions and sentence 8-1 in September 2007, rejecting his argument that the state's inconsistent use of capital punishment, including the life sentence given to Gary Ridgway for 48 murders, made his sentence unconstitutional. The court dismissed his 25-ground personal restraint petition in March 2013, and in 2014 declined to let him withdraw his guilty pleas to the 1975 murders, though it agreed that those consecutive 20-year sentences had been miscalculated under pre-1981 law. In October 2018, in State v. Gregory, the court held the death penalty unconstitutional as applied and ordered all death sentences converted to life in prison; the Associated Press listed Yates among the eight men then on death row.

Yates was born on May 27, 1952, and raised in Oak Harbor on Whidbey Island, graduating from Oak Harbor High School in 1970. He worked briefly as a guard at the Washington State Penitentiary in Walla Walla in 1975, enlisted in the Army in 1977 and became a warrant officer and helicopter pilot, serving in Germany, Somalia and Haiti before retiring in 1996. He moved his family to Spokane that spring, joined the Washington National Guard in 1997 and worked at a circuit-board company and later at Kaiser Aluminum. He is married with five children. He is held at the Washington State Penitentiary in Walla Walla, the prison where he once worked.
