name: Rodney Alcala

victims.suspected: 8 charged (one Wyoming charge was never tried); investigators have linked him to further deaths in California, Washington, New York, New Hampshire and Arizona, with published estimates ranging into the dozens

victimProfile: Women and girls aged 12 to 32 in Southern California and Manhattan, several approached under the pretext of being photographed
captureMethod: After the Samsoe abduction, a police sketch of a beach photographer was recognised by his parole officer; a Seattle storage locker he rented held the girl's earrings and hundreds of photographs, and DNA later tied him to four Los Angeles County murders.
sentence: Death (Orange County, 2010) for five first-degree murders; concurrent 25 years to life (New York, 2013) for two murders. Two earlier death sentences in the Samsoe case (1980, 1986) were overturned.
fateDetail: Died of natural causes on 24 July 2021 at a hospital in Kings County, California, while a condemned inmate at Corcoran; never executed
summary: Convicted; died on California's death row in 2021. Rodney Alcala, the Dating Game Killer, was convicted in 2010 of five murders in Southern California (1977-1979) after two overturned Samsoe convictions, and pleaded guilty in 2012 to two 1970s Manhattan murders.
narrative: Rodney James Alcala, known as the Dating Game Killer, was convicted of seven murders committed in California and New York between 1971 and 1979. In February 2010 an Orange County jury found him guilty of five counts of first-degree murder and he was sentenced to death; in December 2012 he pleaded guilty in Manhattan to two further murders and received 25 years to life. He had twice before been convicted and sentenced to death for one of the California killings, the 1979 murder of 12-year-old Robin Samsoe, but both judgments were overturned on appeal. He died of natural causes on California's death row on 24 July 2021.

According to NBC New York's report on the 2013 sentencing, the earliest murder was that of Cornelia Crilley, a 23-year-old flight attendant strangled with a stocking in her Manhattan apartment in June 1971. Ellen Jane Hover, 23, disappeared from Manhattan in July 1977; her remains were found the next year in Westchester County, and her calendar noted a lunch with a photographer using one of Alcala's aliases. In California, the California Department of Corrections and Rehabilitation (CDCR) lists the five 2010 convictions as the murders of Jill Barcomb, 18, and Georgia Wixted, 27, in 1977; Charlotte Lamb, 32, in 1978; and Jill Parenteau, 21, and Robin Samsoe, 12, in 1979.

The Ninth Circuit's 2003 opinion in Alcala v. Woodford describes the Samsoe case. She left a friend's apartment just after 3 p.m. on 20 June 1979 and never arrived; her body was found in a remote ravine about fifty miles away almost two weeks later, too decomposed to establish a cause of death. Alcala was arrested on 24 July 1979. The circumstantial case rested on beachgoers approached by a photographer, a witness who placed him near the body, and earrings identified as Samsoe's, found in a Seattle storage locker he rented after the disappearance. The locker also held a large collection of photographs of women and girls that police later released publicly to identify possible victims.

Alcala was convicted and sentenced to death in 1980. In 1984 the California Supreme Court reversed because the trial court had erroneously admitted evidence of his prior offences, and ordered a new trial. A second jury convicted him in 1986 and he was again sentenced to death; the state supreme court affirmed in 1992. In 2001 a federal district judge conditionally granted his habeas petition, and in June 2003 the Ninth Circuit affirmed, finding ineffective assistance of counsel on his alibi, the wrongful exclusion of a defence expert, and cumulative error that denied him a fair trial.

Before a third trial, DNA evidence connected Alcala to four unsolved Los Angeles County murders. In Alcala v. Superior Court (2008) the California Supreme Court held that those charges could be joined with the Orange County retrial. Alcala represented himself. On 25 February 2010 the jury found him guilty on all five counts, and he was sentenced to death in March 2010. ABC News reported that his closing argument cited his 1978 appearance as a contestant on The Dating Game, the source of his nickname.

Manhattan prosecutors indicted him in January 2011 for the Crilley and Hover murders after a cold-case review. He was extradited in 2012, pleaded guilty in December, and on 7 January 2013 was sentenced to a concurrent 25 years to life. In 2016 Wyoming prosecutors charged him with the murder of Christine Ruth Thornton, 28, whose 1982 remains were identified by relatives' DNA in 2015 after a sister recognised her in a storage-locker photograph, CBS News and CDCR reported; he was never extradited. Investigators have also linked him to other deaths in California, Washington, New York, New Hampshire and Arizona without further convictions.

Alcala was born Rodrigo Jacques Alcala Buquor in San Antonio, Texas, on 23 August 1943, and grew up near Los Angeles. He served in the Army before a medical discharge and later studied fine arts at UCLA. In 1968 he attacked an eight-year-old girl in Hollywood and fled; arrested in New Hampshire in 1971 under an alias, he was convicted in California and paroled in 1974, then paroled again in 1977 after a second assault conviction.

name: Roger Kibbe

victims.suspected: 8 or more

victimProfile: Young women aged 17 to 29, several of them abducted along or near Interstate 5 and other Northern California highways
captureMethod: After a woman he attacked in Sacramento in 1987 escaped, police recovered a parachute-cord garrote whose cord was matched to rope found with Darcie Frackenpohl's body, and he was arrested for her murder in 1988
sentence: 25 years to life for the first-degree murder of Darcie Frackenpohl (El Dorado County, May 1991); six further life sentences with rape and kidnapping enhancements on guilty pleas to six murders (San Joaquin County, 2009)
fateDetail: Strangled by his cellmate, Jason Budrow, at Mule Creek State Prison, Ione, California, on February 28, 2021; autopsy found manual strangulation
summary: Killed in prison. Roger Kibbe, the I-5 Strangler, was convicted in 1991 of murdering Darcie Frackenpohl and pleaded guilty in 2009 to six more killings of women in Northern California. His cellmate strangled him at Mule Creek State Prison in 2021.
narrative: Roger Reece Kibbe, known as the I-5 Strangler, was a former suburban Sacramento furniture maker convicted of seven murders of women in Northern California between 1977 and 1987. A jury convicted him in 1991 of the 1987 killing of 17-year-old Darcie Frackenpohl, and in 2009 he pleaded guilty in San Joaquin County to six further murders under an agreement that removed the death penalty. He was serving multiple life terms when he was strangled in his cell at Mule Creek State Prison in Ione, California, on February 28, 2021, at the age of 81.

The earliest of the killings dates to September 1977. Lou Ellen Burleigh, 21, of Walnut Creek, had gone to meet Kibbe about what she believed was a secretarial job and was never seen again, according to Associated Press reporting. The remaining cases on which he was convicted all date to 1986 and 1987. Barbara Ann Scott, 29, was abducted in Pittsburg on July 3, 1986, and her body was left on a golf course in Contra Costa County, CBS San Francisco reported. Stephanie Brown, 19, was found in a drainage ditch in San Joaquin County in mid-July 1986, and Charmaine Sabrah, 26, of Sacramento, disappeared on August 17, 1986, after her car broke down along Interstate 5; the Wikipedia article says her remains were found near Ione that November. Lora Heedick, whose name and age are given differently across sources (AP reported Lora Heedrick, 20), was last seen in April 1986, and Katherine Kelly Quinones, 25, was found near Lake Berryessa in December 1986.

Frackenpohl, a runaway from Seattle, was found in September 1987 below Echo Summit, west of South Lake Tahoe in El Dorado County. Prosecutors described a consistent pattern: the women were kidnapped, bound with parachute cord, silenced with duct tape, sexually assaulted and strangled, and their clothing was cut with scissors that had belonged to Kibbe's mother. Investigators treated the oddly cut clothing as his trademark, according to the AP.

Kibbe was first identified after a woman he attacked in Sacramento in 1987 escaped. Police recovered a garrote made from two dowels and parachute cord, along with scissors and other items, and investigators later matched the cord to rope found with Frackenpohl's body and at Kibbe's house; all of it carried microscopic dots of red paint, the AP reported. He was arrested in 1988 for Frackenpohl's murder, convicted of first-degree murder in 1991, and sentenced in El Dorado County on May 10, 1991, to 25 years to life. For years prosecutors were unable to file charges in the other deaths.

In 2003 authorities confronted Kibbe with evidence concerning other women, and a San Joaquin County investigator later tied him to six more killings using newer evidence, including DNA. In 2009, at age 70, he pleaded guilty six times before San Joaquin County Judge George Abdallah Jr. to murders in Amador, Contra Costa, Napa, Sacramento, San Joaquin and Stanislaus counties, covering Burleigh, Brown, Heedick, Quinones, Sabrah and Scott. He received six more life sentences with enhancements for rape and kidnapping. Prosecutors said they dropped the death penalty because he was unlikely ever to face execution, and as part of the deal Kibbe agreed to help find Burleigh's body.

Searches with Kibbe were hampered by fires and landslides that had altered the terrain, a former San Joaquin County sheriff's investigator told the AP. In 2011 a Napa County deputy searching on his own time found a bone fragment in a dry creekbed near Lake Berryessa, the only remains of Burleigh ever recovered; she was buried in Klamath County, Oregon, where she was born. Kibbe never admitted to killings beyond those he was charged with, although investigators believed he may have killed others in the decade between his first and last known cases. The Wikipedia article also lists Karen Finch, found near Sloughhouse in June 1987, as a suspected victim for whose death he was never charged.

Shortly after midnight on February 28, 2021, an officer conducting a count at Mule Creek State Prison found Kibbe unresponsive on his cell floor with his cellmate, Jason Budrow, standing nearby. He was pronounced dead at 1:23 a.m. The Amador County Sheriff's Office announced on March 3 that an autopsy showed manual strangulation and classified the death as a homicide. Budrow, already serving life without parole for a 2010 killing in Riverside County, later received an additional consecutive life sentence for killing Kibbe, KTVU reported in 2023.

name: Samuel Little

victims.suspected: about 60 confirmed by the FBI, of 93 confessed

victimProfile: Women, many of them sex workers, drug users or poor women on society's margins, met shortly before they were killed
captureMethod: Arrested at a homeless shelter in Louisville, Kentucky, and extradited to California on a narcotics charge, after which DNA linked him to three Los Angeles killings
sentence: Life sentences in California (2014) for three Los Angeles murders; life in Texas (December 2018) on a guilty plea; in Ohio (August 2019) two consecutive 15-years-to-life terms in Hamilton County and a 40-years-to-life term in Cuyahoga County on guilty pleas
fateDetail: Died at age 80 in a California hospital while serving his sentences in California state custody; officials reported no sign of foul play and the cause was left to the coroner
summary: Died in prison. Samuel Little was convicted of eight murders in California, Texas and Ohio. He confessed to 93 killings from 1970 to 2005, and authorities said nearly 60 were confirmed. He died in December 2020, aged 80.
narrative: Samuel Little was an American serial killer convicted of eight murders of women in California, Texas and Ohio, and who confessed to killing 93 people across the country between 1970 and 2005. A Los Angeles jury convicted him in 2014 of three killings from the late 1980s, and he later pleaded guilty to one murder in Texas and four in Ohio. The FBI described him as the most prolific serial killer in United States history; authorities said at the time of his death that nearly 60 of the confessed killings had been confirmed. He died in California state custody on December 30, 2020, at age 80.

Little was born on June 7, 1940, in Reynolds, Georgia, according to the Wikipedia article, and was raised by his grandmother in Lorain, Ohio. He often went by the name Samuel McDowell. The Boston Globe, reporting the Associated Press account of his death, described him as a former boxer and a career criminal who was jailed repeatedly over decades on charges including larceny, assault and drug offenses. He moved frequently between cities, which the FBI said helped him avoid detection. According to the Wikipedia article, he was acquitted in Florida in January 1984 of a 1982 murder and served about two and a half years for a 1984 attack in California on a woman who survived.

In 2012 Little was arrested at a homeless shelter in Louisville, Kentucky, and extradited to California on a narcotics charge. Los Angeles police then matched his DNA to three women strangled in the Los Angeles area between 1987 and 1989. The Wikipedia article names them as Linda Alford, Audrey Nelson Everett and Guadalupe Duarte Apodaca. Little denied the killings, but a jury found him guilty in September 2014 and he received life sentences, reported as three consecutive life terms.

The wider case opened through Texas. Little was extradited from California in 2018 and charged with the 1994 killing of Denise Christie Brothers, whose body was found in a vacant lot in Odessa. Texas Ranger James Holland interviewed him almost daily, and beginning in May 2018 Little started describing killings across the country, eventually in some 700 hours of interviews. He also drew portraits of many of the women. On December 13, 2018, he pleaded guilty to the Brothers murder in Ector County and received another life term, according to the district attorney. NBC News reported that day that authorities had by then concluded he was the killer in 36 cases.

In August 2019 Little pleaded guilty by video link from a California prison to four Ohio murders. In Hamilton County he admitted killing Anna Stewart, a mother of three, in 1981, and an unidentified woman killed in the Mt. Adams area at an unknown date; Judge Melba Marsh imposed two consecutive terms of 15 years to life. Prosecutor Joe Deters said the Ohio sentences would allow the state to reclaim him if California ever ended his sentence. The same day in Cuyahoga County he pleaded guilty to the strangling deaths of Mary Jo Peyton in 1984 and Rose Evans in 1991 in Cleveland and was sentenced to 40 years to life. The Wikipedia article also lists a 2019 conviction in Arkansas, which the news sources cited here do not confirm.

On October 7, 2019, NBC News reported that the FBI had confirmed 50 of the 93 confessed deaths. FBI crime analyst Christie Palazzolo said Little had believed he would not be caught because no one was accounting for his victims. Most of his victims were women who were sex workers, drug users or otherwise vulnerable, and many deaths had first been recorded as accidents, overdoses or undetermined. He usually strangled them soon after meeting them. By his account the first killing was in Miami at the end of 1970 and the last was in Tupelo, Mississippi, in 2005. According to the Boston Globe, most of the killings took place in Florida and Southern California, and Holland said nothing Little told him had been shown to be false.

Little suffered from diabetes, heart trouble and other ailments. He died at a California hospital on December 30, 2020. The California Department of Corrections and Rehabilitation confirmed the death, officials said there was no sign of foul play, and the cause of death was left to the coroner. At the time, authorities said they had confirmed nearly 60 of his killings and had no reason to doubt the others; many of the remaining victims had not been identified.

name: Scott Lee Kimball
victimProfile: People he knew personally: two women who were girlfriends of former fellow inmates, a 19-year-old woman whose mother he married, and his own uncle
captureMethod: Arrested by U.S. marshals on a federal weapons warrant after a long car chase from Riverside, California; he was later tied to the killings and confessed under a plea agreement
sentence: 70 years in prison on guilty pleas to second-degree murder of four people (Boulder County, October 2009), alongside a 48-year habitual-criminal theft sentence; four concurrent years for attempted escape (2020)
fateDetail: Held at United States Penitentiary, Florence High, Colorado, as of 2023 after a 2021 transfer to USP Coleman, Florida
summary: Serving 70 years. Scott Lee Kimball, a con man released in 2002 to work as a paid FBI informant, pleaded guilty in Boulder County, Colorado, in October 2009 to killing four people, including his uncle, in Colorado and Utah in 2003 and 2004.
narrative: Scott Lee Kimball is a Colorado con man and former paid FBI informant who pleaded guilty in Boulder County District Court on October 8, 2009, to killing four people in 2003 and 2004: LeAnn Emry, Jennifer Marcum, Kaysi McLeod and his uncle, Terry Kimball. Under a plea agreement he was sentenced the same day to 70 years in prison; the Associated Press reported that the pleas were to second-degree murder. Two of the killings took place in Utah and two in Colorado, according to KSL. He remains in custody, held as of 2023 at the federal high-security penitentiary in Florence, Colorado, according to the Wikipedia article.

Kimball was born in Boulder, Colorado, in 1966 and had a long record of check fraud and other theft offenses in Montana, Alaska and Colorado before the killings. In 2002, while held at the federal prison in Englewood, he came to the attention of FBI agent Carle Schlaff, and in December 2002 he was released on an unsecured bond to work as a paid informant in a drug and murder-for-hire investigation, according to reporting by The Atavist magazine. The AP noted in 2010 that all four killings happened after that release. The Wikipedia article says the information he supplied was largely of little use and in some cases false. He pleaded guilty to the Alaska fraud charges in March 2003 and was later sentenced to a fine, restitution and three years of federal probation, which ended his informant work.

The victims were all people Kimball knew. LeAnn Emry, 24, and Jennifer Marcum, 25, were girlfriends of men Kimball had met in prison, KSL reported. Emry disappeared in early 2003, and her car was later found in Moab, Utah. Marcum vanished in February 2003 after a dinner with Kimball, according to The Atavist. Kaysi McLeod, 19, the daughter of a woman Kimball married, went missing in August 2003 after failing to show up for a shift at work. Terry Kimball, his uncle, who had come to stay with the family to help care for Kimball's injured son, disappeared in 2004.

Kimball's freedom ended over a separate matter. On March 14, 2006, U.S. marshals trying to serve a federal weapons warrant pursued him from Riverside, California, in a chase of more than three hours that ended in a farm field, where he surrendered, The Atavist reported. In May 2006 he received 10 months in jail and six months in a halfway house on the weapons charge, and he also served a Montana sentence for violating probation. By 2009 he was also serving 48 years for theft and for being a habitual criminal, according to KSL. In April 2007 a skull found in the Routt National Forest near Walden, Colorado, was identified through DNA as Kaysi McLeod's, which Wikipedia says gave investigators leverage.

Facing possible murder charges, Kimball accepted a deal under which he would lead investigators to bodies. He took them to Emry's remains in the Book Cliffs area of eastern Utah, north of Moab, and admitted shooting her there, KSL reported. He also led them to his uncle's body, buried near Vail Pass in Colorado. He said he had buried Marcum in the Book Cliffs, but the sites he pointed to were empty and her remains have not been found. At the October 2009 hearing, Marcum's father told the court that Kimball had destroyed the family's lives, and her sister asked him to reveal where her body lay. In early 2011 Kimball wrote a letter to his family in which, according to Wikipedia, he described all four deaths and revised several earlier accounts, including saying that Marcum died of a drug overdose he prepared and that McLeod died of an overdose in his presence.

Investigators have examined Kimball in connection with other unsolved cases, but he has not been charged with any further killing. The AP reported in August 2010 that the FBI was investigating several missing-person cases without saying in which states. The Wikipedia article says he has been suspected in as many as 21 other deaths and that the FBI looked at him in the October 2004 killing of Catrina Powell in Westminster, Colorado, though no charge followed. Agent Schlaff was suspended after an internal FBI review and left the bureau in 2013, according to The Atavist.

In October 2017 Logan County prosecutors said Kimball would be charged with attempted escape and solicitation to commit murder over a plot at the Sterling Correctional Facility, CBS Colorado reported. He pleaded guilty to attempted escape in 2020 and received four years, concurrent with his existing terms; the solicitation counts were dropped, according to The Atavist. In 2021 CBS Colorado found that he had been moved under an interstate compact to the federal prison at Coleman, Florida, with a listed release date in 2082.

name: Shawn Grate
victimProfile: Women aged 23 to 43 in north-central Ohio, several of them vulnerable or living on the margins, including a door-to-door magazine seller
captureMethod: A woman he was holding captive in a vacant Ashland house called 911 on his phone while he slept, and police arrested him there and found two bodies
sentence: Death (Ashland County, June 2018), affirmed by the Ohio Supreme Court in 2020; life without parole plus consecutive terms in Richland County (2019) and Marion County (2019)
fateDetail: Ohio death row; held at Chillicothe Correctional Institution according to the state's 2021 U.S. Supreme Court brief
summary: On Ohio's death row. Shawn Grate was convicted of killing five women in Ashland, Richland and Marion counties between 2006 and 2016; a captive's 911 call from his Ashland house led to his arrest in September 2016.
narrative: Shawn Grate is an Ohio man convicted of murdering five women in Ashland, Richland and Marion counties between 2006 and 2016. An Ashland County jury convicted him in May 2018 of the aggravated murders of Stacey Stanley and Elizabeth Griffith, and he was sentenced to death; he later pleaded guilty to three more killings in Richland and Marion counties and received life without parole in each. According to the Ohio Attorney General's 2021 brief to the U.S. Supreme Court, he fully confessed to the two Ashland murders and the kidnapping of a third woman, and the Richland Source reported that authorities said he admitted to killing five women in all. The Ohio Supreme Court upheld the death sentence in December 2020.

Prosecutors consider his first victim Dana Nicole Lowrey, 23, of Louisiana. The Associated Press reported that she was selling magazines door-to-door in Ohio when Grate stabbed her at his home in 2006; her remains were found on Victory Road in Marion in 2007 but went unidentified for more than a decade. Grate confessed in 2016 to killing a woman whose name he did not know, and in June 2019 investigators identified her through a DNA match with one of her daughters, with help from the DNA Doe Project. In Richland County, Rebekah Leicy's body was found in March 2015, about a month after she went missing; her death was initially ruled an overdose, and News 5 Cleveland reported the case was reopened after Grate's Ashland confessions. Candace Cunningham's body was found behind a burned-down house in Madison Township in September 2016.

The Ashland crimes ended on September 13, 2016. According to the state's brief and news reports, a woman Grate had held for days in a vacant house on Covert Court partly freed herself and, while he slept, whispered a 911 call on his phone saying she had been abducted. Ashland police arrested Grate and found in the house the bodies of Stanley, 43, and Griffith, 29, both reported missing. Autopsies found both had been strangled, and prosecutors said Grate confessed to detectives. The survivor has not been publicly named in the sources used here.

An Ashland County grand jury indicted Grate in September 2016 on 23 felony counts, including aggravated murder, kidnapping and rape. His lawyers entered a not guilty by reason of insanity plea but withdrew it in April 2017 after two experts found he was not insane. On May 2, 2018, Grate pleaded guilty to 15 counts, leaving the remaining eight, including the aggravated murders, to a jury. After a trial before Judge Ronald Forsthoefel at which prosecutors played his recorded statements, the jury convicted him on all eight counts on May 7, 2018, after deliberating a little over three hours, CBS News and the AP reported. The jury recommended death, and on June 1, 2018, the court sentenced him to death, according to Wikipedia; an initial September 13, 2018 execution date was stayed by his appeal.

On March 1, 2019, Grate pleaded guilty in Richland County to aggravated murder in Leicy's death and murder in Cunningham's death, plus two counts of gross abuse of a corpse; News 5 Cleveland reported a sentence of life without parole, 15 years to life and two 12-month terms, all consecutive. On September 11, 2019, he pleaded guilty in Marion County to Lowrey's aggravated murder and related counts and was sentenced to life without parole plus 16 years, consecutive to his other sentences; the AP reported that he apologized before sentencing.

On December 10, 2020, the Ohio Supreme Court unanimously affirmed the Ashland County convictions and death sentence in State v. Grate, 2020-Ohio-5584, rejecting claims of trial error and ineffective counsel. Grate petitioned the U.S. Supreme Court in 2021; the state's response noted he then had no scheduled execution date. Wikipedia reports that a March 19, 2025 execution date was later set and delayed amid continuing appeals.

Grate was born in Marion, Ohio, on August 8, 1976. According to Wikipedia, his parents divorced in 1982, he graduated from River Valley High School in 1995 and he had a felony burglary case in 1997. At the time of his arrest he was squatting in the vacant Covert Court house in Ashland.

sentence: 266 months (about 22 years): 164 months for second-degree murder and 102 months for first-degree manslaughter, consecutive, on Alford pleas (August 19, 2004)
fateDetail: Paroled from the Washington Corrections Center for Women, Gig Harbor, on November 8, 2022
summary: Released in 2022 after serving about 19 years. Pleaded guilty (Alford pleas) in 2004 to second-degree murder of Kathy Loreno and first-degree manslaughter of Ron Woodworth, boarders who died in her Pacific County, Washington home; her husband was convicted of killing her nephew.
narrative: Shelly Knotek, legally Michelle Knotek, is a Washington woman convicted in the deaths of two adults who lived in her rural home near Raymond, in Pacific County. On June 18, 2004, she entered Alford pleas in Pacific County Superior Court to second-degree murder in the death of Kathy Loreno, 36, and first-degree manslaughter in the death of Ronald Woodworth, 57, according to the Washington Court of Appeals opinion in State v. Knotek and Associated Press reporting. An Alford plea is a guilty plea in which the defendant maintains innocence while acknowledging a jury would likely convict. She was sentenced to 266 months, about 22 years, and released on November 8, 2022. A third death in the household, that of her nephew Shane Watson, was the subject of her husband David Knotek's separate guilty plea to second-degree murder; she was not convicted of it.

According to the Court of Appeals, in 1991 Knotek invited Loreno, a hairdresser she met at a South Bend salon, to live with her family. The opinion states that Knotek and her husband abused Loreno physically and mentally, causing severe weight loss and hypothermia, and that she died of the prolonged abuse. The Seattle Times reported that charging documents placed her death between April 1990 and December 1993; her mother reported her missing in 1994, and the Knoteks said she had run off with a truck driver. Per the opinion, David Knotek and Shane Watson burned and buried the body, and Knotek sent Loreno's family letters made to look as if they came from her.

Watson, Knotek's nephew, had lived with the family since his teens and vanished around the time of Loreno's disappearance. The Seattle Times reported that prosecutors alleged he was shot in a shed on the property between January 1993 and December 1994, and that the Knoteks had claimed he went to Alaska to fish. The Associated Press reported that David Knotek admitted shooting him.

In October 2001, according to the Court of Appeals, Knotek invited Woodworth, a Vietnam veteran who had helped her care for elderly clients, into the home, and the couple abused him in similar ways. The Seattle Times reported that prosecutors alleged the abuse included scalding his feet and that he died on about July 24, 2003. David Knotek buried the body in the backyard.

The case broke in August 2003 when Knotek's two older daughters contacted police about the treatment of Woodworth, per the Court of Appeals. The daughters, identified in Gregg Olsen's 2019 book If You Tell as Sami and Tori Knotek with their older sister, have since spoken publicly. Officers arrested the couple at their Monohon Landing Road home on August 8, 2003, and unearthed Woodworth's body. On August 13, prosecutors charged Michelle Knotek with two counts of first-degree murder and David Knotek with the first-degree murder of Watson, rendering criminal assistance and unlawful disposal of human remains. The Seattle Times also reported that South Bend police reopened an inquiry into the February 2002 death of James McClintock, 81, a client in Knotek's care; no charge resulted.

After the charges were reduced and the June 2004 Alford pleas entered, Judge Mark McCauley sentenced Knotek on August 19, 2004, to 164 months on the murder count and 102 months on the manslaughter count, consecutive, the top of the standard range and more than the roughly 17 years in the plea agreement. The Court of Appeals noted the judge said he would have gone higher but for Blakely v. Washington, decided six days after the plea. David Knotek was sentenced the following week to 179 months, the Chinook Observer reported. The Court of Appeals affirmed the denial of Knotek's motion to withdraw her plea on December 26, 2006.

The Chinook Observer reported that Knotek, then 68, was paroled from the Washington Corrections Center for Women on November 8, 2022, after just over 19 years, and was not expected to return to Pacific County. Wikipedia states David Knotek was released in 2016. The case was the subject of Olsen's book and of television programs.
Knotek was born Michelle Watson on April 15, 1954, according to Wikipedia.

name: Ted Bundy

victims.suspected: 20 attributed by police before his confessions; the FBI put the total at more than 30, and some estimates run to 36 or more

victimProfile: Young women and girls, mostly college-age, abducted in public places or from their homes; the youngest confirmed victim was 12
captureMethod: Stopped by Pensacola police officer David Lee while driving a stolen car near the Alabama state line on February 15, 1978, six weeks after his second escape from Colorado custody.
sentence: Death, three times: two death sentences in July 1979 for the Chi Omega murders and one in February 1980 for the murder of Kimberly Leach; earlier, one to fifteen years in Utah for aggravated kidnapping (1976)
fateDetail: Electric chair, Florida State Prison, Bradford County, Florida; pronounced dead at 7:16 a.m. on January 24, 1989
summary: Executed in Florida in 1989. Ted Bundy was convicted of three murders in Florida and confessed to 30 killings of young women across Washington, Oregon, Utah, Colorado, Idaho and Florida between 1974 and 1978.
narrative: Ted Bundy, born Theodore Robert Cowell, was an American serial killer who murdered young women and girls in Washington, Oregon, Utah, Colorado, Idaho and Florida between 1974 and 1978. Florida juries convicted him of three murders: two Chi Omega sorority members at Florida State University in Tallahassee (1979) and 12-year-old Kimberly Leach of Lake City (1980), with a death sentence in each case. Before his execution he confessed to 30 homicides in seven states, according to Washington investigator Robert Keppel as quoted by The Associated Press; police had attributed about 20 killings to him before those confessions. Florida executed him on January 24, 1989.

The known crimes began in Seattle. According to the chronology in his Wikipedia article, Lynda Ann Healy, abducted on February 1, 1974, is counted as his first confirmed murder victim. Through 1974 five more young women vanished in Washington, including Georgann Hawkins (June 11) and, on the same July 14 afternoon, Janice Ott and Denise Naslund; Roberta Parks disappeared in Oregon on May 6. In recorded interviews released by the Washington attorney general's office and reported by the Deseret News, Bundy told Keppel how he lured, struck, handcuffed and strangled Hawkins and left her body outside Issaquah. He typically lured women by feigning injury or posing as an authority figure, then bludgeoned them and drove them to a remote site.

After Bundy moved to Utah in the autumn of 1974, Nancy Wilcox, Melissa Smith, Laura Aime and Debra Kent were killed there between October 1 and November 8. On the evening of November 8, at Fashion Place Mall in Murray, a man posing as a police officer lured Carol DaRonch into his car; she fought free. In 1975 Caryn Campbell vanished from Snowmass Village, Colorado, on January 12, followed by further disappearances in Colorado, Idaho and Utah through June 1975.

Utah Highway Patrol officer Bob Hayward arrested Bundy after a traffic stop in Granger, Utah, on August 16, 1975. DaRonch identified him in a lineup on October 2, 1975, and in 1976 a judge found him guilty of aggravated kidnapping after a bench trial; he was sentenced in June 1976 to one to fifteen years. Colorado then charged him with the Campbell murder. On June 7, 1977, he escaped from the Pitkin County Courthouse in Aspen, recaptured six days later. On December 30, 1977, he escaped again from the Garfield County jail in Glenwood Springs and made his way to Tallahassee.

In the early hours of January 15, 1978, an intruder attacked four women at the Chi Omega house, killing Margaret Bowman, 21, and Lisa Levy, 20, and injuring Kathy Kleiner and Karen Chandler; Cheryl Thomas was attacked nearby the same night and survived. On February 9, 1978, Kimberly Leach, 12, was taken from Lake City Junior High School; her remains were found near Suwannee River State Park on April 7. Pensacola officer David Lee arrested him in a stolen car on February 15, 1978.

The Chi Omega trial was moved to Miami before Judge Edward Cowart. Bite-mark testimony linked him to Levy. On July 24, 1979, the jury convicted him of two counts of first-degree murder, three counts of attempted first-degree murder and burglary, and Cowart imposed two death sentences. The Leach case was moved from Suwannee County to Orange County, where, as the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Eleventh Circuit later recounted, jury selection took place in January 1980; Bundy was convicted of first-degree murder and kidnapping and sentenced to death in February 1980.

The Florida Supreme Court affirmed both convictions (Bundy v. State, 1984 and 1985). The U.S. Supreme Court denied review of the Leach conviction on October 14, 1986, over dissents by Justices Brennan and Marshall. On July 7, 1988, the Eleventh Circuit in Bundy v. Dugger rejected his federal habeas petition finding that he had been competent to stand trial. In January 1989 Bundy admitted 30 homicides to Keppel and other investigators. He was executed in the electric chair at Florida State Prison on January 24, 1989.
Bundy was born on November 24, 1946, in Burlington, Vermont, and grew up in Tacoma, Washington. He remains an unconfirmed suspect in the 1961 disappearance of eight-year-old Ann Marie Burr in Tacoma.

name: Phantom Killer of Texarkana

victims.suspected: 5 killed and 3 wounded in 4 attacks

victimProfile: Young couples parked on rural roads outside Texarkana, aged 15 to 29, and a farm couple in their thirties attacked at home
summary: Unidentified. An attacker shot and beat eight people in four attacks around Texarkana, Texas and Arkansas, between February and May 1946, killing five. The Texas Rangers led a huge investigation; a car thief was questioned but never charged. The case remains open.
narrative: The Phantom Killer is the name given to an unidentified attacker who struck four times around Texarkana, on the Texas-Arkansas line, between February 22 and May 3, 1946. Eight people were attacked and five were killed, according to the Encyclopedia of Arkansas and the Texarkana Gazette. Three attacks took place in Bowie County, Texas, and the fourth in Miller County, Arkansas. No one has ever been charged with any of the crimes, and the case was never officially solved.

The first attack came late on February 22, 1946, when Jimmy Hollis, 25, and Mary Jeanne Larey, 19, were parked on a secluded road outside Texarkana, Texas. According to the Encyclopedia of Arkansas, a masked man forced them out of the car at gunpoint, beat Hollis with the gun and sexually assaulted Larey. Both survived. On March 24, Richard Griffin, 29, and Polly Ann Moore, 17, were found dead in Griffin's car on a lovers' lane off Highway 67, each shot in the back of the head with a .32-caliber pistol.

On April 14, Paul Martin, 16, and Betty Jo Booker, 15, were found shot dead near Spring Lake Park; investigators linked the same .32 pistol to both double murders. The Texarkana Gazette, marking the 70th anniversary in 2016, reported that the second double murder sent a shock wave through the twin cities. The final attack, on May 3, was different: farmer Virgil Starks, 37, was shot twice through a window of his farmhouse in Miller County, Arkansas. His wife Katie, 36, was shot twice in the face but escaped and survived. A .22-caliber weapon was used, and the Gazette has reported that some close to the case question whether the Starks attack was the Phantom's work.

The investigation was one of the largest Texas had seen. Texas Ranger Captain Manuel T. "Lone Wolf" Gonzaullas became its public face, working with Bowie County sheriff W. H. Presley, Texarkana police chief Jack Runnels, Miller County sheriff W. E. Davis and the Arkansas State Police, with FBI assistance. Hundreds of suspects were questioned, Rangers used decoy couples in parked cars, rewards passed $10,000, and the Texarkana Gazette coined the name Phantom Killer.

In July 1946, Arkansas State Police officer Max Tackett, who had noticed that a car was stolen and abandoned around the time of each attack, traced a stolen car to a woman connected to Youell Swinney, a 29-year-old car thief and counterfeiter. According to the Encyclopedia of Arkansas, the woman, Peggy, who later became Swinney's wife, gave officers unpublished details of the Booker-Martin murders, but her account changed, and prosecutors concluded she was unreliable and could not be compelled to testify against her husband. Swinney was investigated and never charged with any of the murders. In 1947 he was convicted in Bowie County of automobile theft and, as a habitual criminal, received a mandatory life sentence.

That sentence later unraveled. In Ex parte Swinney, decided September 25, 1973, the Texas Court of Criminal Appeals found that a 1941 Arkansas conviction used to enhance his sentence was void because he had not been shown to have had counsel; without it the maximum term was ten years, long since served, and the court ordered his release. Wikipedia records that he died in Dallas on September 15, 1994, though the Encyclopedia of Arkansas notes conflicting accounts. Tackett and Miller County deputy Tillman Johnson believed to the end of their lives that Swinney was the Phantom, and historian James Presley argued the same in a 2014 book. No court has ever ruled on the question.

Other leads failed, including a 1948 suicide note confessing to the murders that investigators could not corroborate. In February 2020 the FBI released more than 1,100 pages from its 1946-1949 file, the Arkansas Democrat-Gazette reported. The Encyclopedia of Arkansas describes the case as a cold case that is theoretically still open. It inspired Charles B. Pierce's 1976 film The Town That Dreaded Sundown, which, the Wikipedia article notes, is the source of much of the folklore around the case.

name: Timothy Wilson Spencer

victims.suspected: 5 (investigators also attributed the 1984 Arlington murder of Carolyn Hamm to him; he was never charged with it)

victimProfile: Women aged 15 to 44 attacked alone in their homes at night in Richmond and Arlington, Virginia
captureMethod: Arrested in January 1988 for the Arlington murder of Susan Tucker after police tied his Thanksgiving visit to the area to the crime; DNA testing by Lifecodes Corporation then matched his blood to semen from the Richmond-area scenes.
sentence: Four death sentences: Arlington County (Tucker, July 1988), Richmond (Davis, September 1988), Richmond (Hellams, 1989) and Chesterfield County (Cho, affirmed June 1990)
fateDetail: Electrocuted at Greensville Correctional Center, Jarratt, Virginia, on April 27, 1994
summary: Executed in Virginia in 1994. Timothy Spencer, the Southside Strangler, was convicted by juries of raping and strangling four women in Richmond and Arlington in fall 1987, the first U.S. murder convictions won on DNA evidence.
narrative: Timothy Wilson Spencer, known as the Southside Strangler, was convicted by four separate Virginia juries of the rape and murder of four women killed in Richmond, Chesterfield County and Arlington between September and November 1987. Each jury fixed his punishment at death. He was the first person in the United States convicted of murder on the strength of DNA evidence, and his case also led to the pardon of David Vasquez, who had been wrongly convicted of a 1984 Arlington murder that investigators later attributed to Spencer. Spencer never confessed and maintained his innocence. Virginia executed him in the electric chair on April 27, 1994.

The first killing came in Richmond. According to the Fourth Circuit's 1993 opinion in Spencer v. Murray, Debbie Dudley Davis, 35, was killed in her Southside Richmond apartment between the evening of September 18 and the morning of September 19, 1987; the cause of death was ligature strangulation. On the night of October 2 or early on October 3, 1987, Dr. Susan Hellams, a 32-year-old neurosurgery resident at the Medical College of Virginia, was strangled with ligatures in her Richmond home after an intruder cut through a second-story window screen, according to the Fourth Circuit's 1994 opinion. In November 1987, Diane Cho, a 15-year-old high school student, was found dead in her family's apartment in Chesterfield County, just south of Richmond. Days later, around November 27, 1987, Susan Tucker, 44, was killed in her Arlington condominium; her body was found on December 1.

Arlington County police arrested Spencer on January 20, 1988. Police established that he had travelled from Richmond to Arlington over Thanksgiving to stay with his mother, who lived about a mile from Tucker's home. According to the Innocence Project, Spencer had been released on September 4, 1987 from a burglary sentence to a Richmond halfway house, and its sign-out records placed him away from the facility at the times of the murders. The linking evidence was semen recovered at the scenes. The Fourth Circuit recorded that Lifecodes Corporation, a private laboratory, found that DNA from Spencer's blood matched the semen in the Davis case, and an expert put the chance of another Black North American man sharing the pattern at about one in 705 million. A Library of Virginia exhibit notes that experts told a 1988 court the evidence would match only about one in 135 million African American men.

Spencer was tried first in Arlington County. The trial opened on July 11, 1988, and Style Weekly described it as the first capital murder conviction in United States history based on DNA evidence; he was convicted on July 16, 1988 and sentenced to death. On September 22, 1988, a Richmond jury convicted him of the rape, burglary and capital murder of Davis and fixed his sentence at death. His trial for the Hellams murder began on January 17, 1989 in the Circuit Court of the City of Richmond and ended in convictions for capital murder, rape, sodomy and burglary and another death sentence. He was then convicted in the Cho case of capital murder, rape and breaking and entering and received a fourth death sentence, which the Supreme Court of Virginia affirmed on June 8, 1990 in an opinion that accepted DNA analysis as reliable evidence.

His appeals turned largely on the DNA evidence. The Supreme Court of Virginia affirmed each conviction. In federal habeas proceedings, the Fourth Circuit held in September 1993 that the admission of the DNA results in the Davis case did not violate due process, and in February 1994 it rejected his claims in the Hellams case, including an argument that his lawyers were ineffective for not hiring a DNA expert. On April 27, 1994, Spencer, aged 32, was electrocuted at Greensville Correctional Center in Jarratt, Virginia. He declined to make a final statement.

The case had a second consequence. According to the Innocence Project, Carolyn Hamm, a 32-year-old lawyer, was raped and murdered in her Arlington home on January 23, 1984. David Vasquez, whose IQ was below 70, entered an Alford plea to second-degree murder and burglary on February 3, 1985 and was sentenced to 35 years. After Spencer's arrest, Arlington investigators concluded that the Hamm killing fit his pattern; the physical evidence had degraded too far to test, and Spencer was never charged with it. Governor Gerald L. Baliles granted Vasquez an unconditional pardon on January 4, 1989, the first exoneration in the United States brought about by DNA testing, and the General Assembly voted him $117,000 in compensation in 1990.

In 2026 WHRO reported that Spencer's convictions are among eight Virginia executions being reviewed by a State Crime Commission panel as part of a broader reassessment of the work of former state serologist Mary Jane Burton. A review by Shawn Armbrust of the Mid-Atlantic Innocence Project found no evidence that Burton's involvement affected the outcome in any of the eight cases. Spencer's brother, Travis Spencer, has said in a book that his brother told him he was not guilty.

Spencer was born on March 17, 1962 in Arlington, Virginia and raised by a single mother. Wikipedia records that he was sent to juvenile detention as a young teenager for petty theft and truancy, and in his twenties served prison time for burglaries and robberies in the Richmond area. He was serving a sentence for a 1984 burglary conviction until his release to the Richmond halfway house in September 1987, weeks before the first killing.

name: Todd Kohlhepp

victims.suspected: 7; Kohlhepp later claimed additional undisclosed victims, none verified

victimProfile: Four employees of a motorcycle shop shot during a 2003 robbery-style attack, and three people hired to work on his rural property in 2015 and 2016
captureMethod: Deputies tracing the last cellphone signals of a missing couple searched his Woodruff property and found Kala Brown alive, chained inside a storage container
sentence: Seven consecutive life sentences without parole plus 60 years for kidnapping and criminal sexual conduct (May 26, 2017); appeal waived under plea agreement
fateDetail: South Carolina Department of Corrections; Wikipedia, citing the SCDC inmate record, lists Broad River Correctional Institution, Columbia
summary: Imprisoned for life. Todd Kohlhepp, a South Carolina real estate agent, pleaded guilty in May 2017 to seven murders: the 2003 Superbike Motorsports shootings in Chesnee and three people killed on his Woodruff property in 2015 and 2016.
narrative: Todd Kohlhepp is a South Carolina real estate agent who pleaded guilty on May 26, 2017, to seven counts of murder committed in Spartanburg County between 2003 and 2016: the four Superbike Motorsports killings in Chesnee in November 2003 and three people killed on his rural property near Woodruff in 2015 and 2016. He received seven consecutive life sentences without parole under a plea agreement that took the death penalty off the table. No court has attributed further deaths to him, although he has since claimed, without specifics, that there are more victims.

The Superbike Motorsports killings were a cold case for 13 years. According to ABC News, shop owner Scott Ponder, 30, service manager Brian Lucas, 29, mechanic Chris Sherbert, 26, and bookkeeper Beverly Guy, 52, Ponder's mother, were found on the morning of November 6, 2003, and investigators said all four had been shot with the same pistol. NBC News reported that at his plea hearing Kohlhepp admitted shooting the workers after the shop's manager made him angry.

The next known killings came in December 2015. NPR, citing the arrest warrants, reported that Johnny Joe Coxie, 29, was shot on December 19, 2015, and that his wife, Meagan Leigh McCraw Coxie, 25, was kidnapped that day and shot on either December 20 or December 26. The couple had been hired to work on Kohlhepp's property and were reported missing in late December. Their remains were recovered in November 2016 after Kohlhepp led investigators to the graves.

The case broke open in 2016. Kala Brown, 30, and her boyfriend Charles David Carver, 32, disappeared on about August 31, 2016, after going to a cleaning job on Kohlhepp's fenced property of nearly 100 acres near Woodruff. The Associated Press reported that Spartanburg County deputies, led there by the couple's last known cellphone signals, found Brown chained inside a metal storage container on November 3, 2016, after about two months in captivity. Brown told investigators she had watched Kohlhepp shoot Carver, whose body was found in a shallow grave on the property the next day. Brown has spoken publicly about her ordeal.

Kohlhepp was arrested on November 3, 2016, and charged with kidnapping Brown. According to the AP, Sheriff Chuck Wright announced on November 5 that Kohlhepp had voluntarily confessed to the four Superbike murders and pointed out two more graves. On November 28, 2016, prosecutors added three murder counts for Carver and the Coxies with kidnapping and weapons charges, NBC News and NPR reported.

On May 26, 2017, Kohlhepp pleaded guilty in Spartanburg County to seven counts of murder, two counts of kidnapping, one count of first-degree criminal sexual conduct and weapons charges. WLOS reported that under the nine-page agreement, signed by Seventh Circuit Solicitor Barry Barnette, Sheriff Wright and Brown, he received seven consecutive life terms plus 30 years each for the kidnapping and sexual-conduct counts, waived his right to appeal, and agreed never to seek parole. Barnette said the state could have pursued execution but chose a plea in part because South Carolina's lethal-injection drugs had expired, NBC News reported. Through his attorney, Kohlhepp said there were no other victims.

That claim did not hold. The Associated Press reported in December 2017 that Kohlhepp had written an eight-page letter to the Spartanburg Herald-Journal saying he had additional undiscovered victims but saw no reason to give numbers or locations; the FBI's Columbia office confirmed a pending investigation. According to Wikipedia, he was named a person of interest in a 2003 Greer bank triple homicide, which he denied and which has not been linked to him. Brown and victims' relatives have filed civil suits.

Kohlhepp was born Todd Christopher Sampsell in Fort Lauderdale, Florida, on March 7, 1971, according to Wikipedia. As a teenager in Tempe, Arizona, he forced a 14-year-old neighbor into his home at gunpoint and assaulted her; the AP reported he pleaded guilty to kidnapping in 1987, the sexual-assault charge was dismissed, and he served about 15 years and had to register as a sex offender. After his release in 2001 he moved to South Carolina, obtained a real estate license in 2006 and built a brokerage with more than a dozen agents.

name: Tommy Lynn Sells
victimProfile: Mostly children and young women, often attacked in their homes, including the daughter of an acquaintance; his convictions were for the killings of girls aged 13 and 9 in Texas
captureMethod: A surviving 11-year-old victim described her attacker for a composite sketch, from which Sells was identified and arrested two days after the attack
sentence: Death for the capital murder of Kaylene Harris (jury verdict, September 2000); life imprisonment on a 2003 guilty plea to the capital murder of Mary Bea Perez
fateDetail: Executed by lethal injection (pentobarbital) at the Huntsville Unit, Huntsville, Texas; pronounced dead at 6:27 p.m.
summary: Executed. Drifter Tommy Lynn Sells was sentenced to death for the 1999 murder of 13-year-old Kaylene Harris near Del Rio, Texas, and pleaded guilty to a second child killing in San Antonio. He claimed up to 70 killings; Texas executed him in April 2014.
narrative: Tommy Lynn Sells was an American drifter who was convicted of two murders in Texas and claimed responsibility for many more across the country. A Val Verde County jury convicted him in September 2000 of the capital murder of 13-year-old Kaylene Harris, who was stabbed to death in her family's trailer home outside Del Rio at the end of 1999, and he was sentenced to death. In 2003 he pleaded guilty to the 1999 killing of 9-year-old Mary Bea Perez in San Antonio and accepted a life sentence. Texas executed him by lethal injection at Huntsville on April 3, 2014.

Sells was born on June 28, 1964, in Oakland, California, according to Texas Department of Criminal Justice records. The department lists his prior occupations as barber, mechanic and laborer, and records earlier prison terms in Missouri and Wyoming for theft, a drunk-driving conviction and malicious wounding, with at least one return to prison as a parole violator. The Associated Press described him as a former carnival roustabout who hopped trains around the country.

The facts of the Harris case are set out in a July 2013 opinion of the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit. Sells knew Kaylene's father, Terry Harris, and had visited the family's home; news reports said they had met through a church. In the early hours, armed with a butcher knife, he entered the trailer while the father was away and five people were asleep inside. He assaulted Kaylene in the lower bunk of a bunk bed, and when she woke and called to her friend for help he stabbed her 16 times and cut her throat repeatedly. He then cut the throat of her friend, Krystal Surles, in the top bunk, wiped a doorknob and took two window screens he feared held his fingerprints. The appeals court dates the attack to early on December 30, 1999; prison records and most news reports give December 31, New Year's Eve. The court gives Surles's age as 11, while Associated Press reports said 10.

Surles, whose windpipe had been cut, pretended to be dead until the attacker left, then walked to a neighbor's house and wrote a note asking for help. From her description a composite sketch was made, and Sells was identified and arrested two days later; the Wikipedia article gives the arrest date as January 2, 2000. According to the Fifth Circuit, he confessed immediately in a videotaped statement, then accompanied police to the trailer and walked them through a recorded re-enactment. Forensic tests found his blood and clothing fibers on Kaylene and her blood and fibers on him.

At trial, Sells pleaded guilty to the attempted murder of Surles and presented no evidence on guilt in the murder count. Surles testified, and the jury convicted him of capital murder on September 18, 2000, after deliberating less than two hours. At the punishment phase the jury answered the special issues in favor of death, and the Texas prison system received him on death row on November 8, 2000. The Texas Court of Criminal Appeals affirmed the conviction and sentence in 2003, and the U.S. Supreme Court declined review. Three state habeas applications failed, as did a federal petition; in July 2013 the Fifth Circuit refused a certificate of appealability and additional funding to investigate mitigating evidence.

Sells's claims about other killings were broad and largely uncorroborated. Court records cited by the Associated Press show he claimed as many as 70 killings,. The AP reported in January 2014 that he had been linked to more than a dozen slayings, that investigators said some of his admissions had not checked out, and that he had been investigated for killings in Texas, Missouri, Illinois, Oklahoma, Kentucky, Tennessee, West Virginia, Arizona and Nevada. He confessed in 2005 to the 1987 killing of Suzanne Korcz, 27, a hairdresser from Amherst, New York, but was not tried there because he was already on death row. He was indicted in Missouri in 2003 for the death of 13-year-old Stephanie Mahaney but never tried, and he confessed to the 1987 killings of the Dardeen family in Ina, Illinois. ABC News reported that Illinois investigators said they would have arrested him in that case had he not already been condemned. None of these cases produced a conviction.

A Val Verde County district judge, Enrique Fernandez, set the execution date. In the final week, Sells's lawyers challenged Texas's refusal to identify the supplier of its newly obtained pentobarbital; a federal district court stay was lifted by the Fifth Circuit, and the Supreme Court denied a stay about an hour before the scheduled time. Sells made no final statement and was pronounced dead at 6:27 p.m. on April 3, 2014, 13 minutes after the drug was administered. He was 49. Terry Harris watched the execution.

name: Velma Barfield

victims.suspected: 5 to 7

victimProfile: People close to her in Robeson County, North Carolina: her mother, two elderly people she cared for as a private nurse, and the man she was dating
captureMethod: An autopsy found arsenic in Stuart Taylor's body and her sister alerted Lumberton police; questioned by officers in March 1978, she gave statements admitting she had poisoned Taylor and others
sentence: Death, imposed in Bladen County Superior Court in December 1978 for the first-degree murder by poisoning of Stuart Taylor
fateDetail: Executed by lethal injection at Central Prison, Raleigh, North Carolina; pronounced dead at 2:15 a.m. on November 2, 1984
summary: Executed. Velma Barfield was convicted in 1978 of poisoning her boyfriend Stuart Taylor with arsenic in Robeson County, North Carolina, and admitted poisoning three others, including her mother. In 1984 she became the first woman executed in the US since 1976.
narrative: Margie Velma Barfield was a North Carolina woman convicted in December 1978 of the first-degree murder of Stuart Taylor, a St. Pauls farmer she had been dating, who died of acute arsenic poisoning on February 3, 1978. She also admitted poisoning three other people between 1974 and 1977, including her own mother, but was never tried for those deaths. Sentenced to death in Bladen County Superior Court, she was executed by lethal injection at Central Prison in Raleigh on November 2, 1984, the first woman put to death in the United States since executions resumed in 1976 and the first since 1962.

Barfield was born in 1932; sources disagree on the exact date and birthplace, with the Wikipedia article giving October 29 in Eastover, North Carolina, and NCpedia giving October 23 on a farm in South Carolina. She married Thomas Burke as a teenager and lived for many years in Parkton, in Robeson County. Burke died in 1969 of smoke inhalation in a house fire. In August 1970 she married Jennings Barfield, a widower, who died in March 1971. NCpedia records that she served time in 1975 for writing bad checks, and court records describe a pattern of forged checks that she said she used to support a dependence on Valium and other prescription drugs.

According to United Press International, her mother, Lillie Bullard, 74, died in December 1974, and two elderly Lumberton residents who had hired Barfield as a private nurse, Dollie Edwards, 85, and John Henry Lee, 80, died in 1977. Each death was initially put down to natural causes. Taylor fell ill in early 1978, and when he was brought back to the hospital on February 3 he died in the emergency room about an hour after arrival. The autopsy found arsenic in his blood and liver, and the pathologist concluded that he had died from acute arsenic poisoning, according to the North Carolina Supreme Court's opinion.

NCpedia says Lumberton police were alerted by a call from Barfield's sister. The state Supreme Court opinion records that she was questioned at the sheriff's department on March 10, 1978, and gave four statements to officers on March 13, in one of which she said she had given poison to people before and they had died. She told investigators she had bought an arsenic-based ant poison and had put it in Taylor's drink; at trial she said she had forged checks on his account, feared he would report her, and meant only to make him too ill to examine his bank statements. On March 18, 1978, the bodies of her mother, Edwards and Lee were exhumed, and Jennings Barfield's body followed on May 31. The federal appeals court later noted that autopsies on the exhumed bodies showed arsenic poisoning. Barfield admitted poisoning her mother, Edwards and Lee, but consistently denied any role in the deaths of either husband.

The case was moved from Robeson County because of pretrial publicity, first to Scotland County and then, over defense objection, to Bladen County. She pleaded not guilty and not guilty by reason of insanity. The prosecution introduced evidence of the four other arsenic deaths to show intent. On December 2, 1978, the jury convicted her of first-degree murder and found three aggravating circumstances: that the killing was for pecuniary gain, was committed to hinder law enforcement, and was especially heinous, atrocious or cruel. It found no mitigating circumstances, and a death sentence was imposed.

The North Carolina Supreme Court affirmed the conviction and sentence on November 6, 1979. A state post-conviction motion was denied in November 1980, and federal habeas relief was refused by the Eastern District of North Carolina in May 1982 and by the Fourth Circuit in October 1983. During her years on death row Barfield described a religious conversion and drew support from evangelists including Billy Graham. Governor Jim Hunt denied clemency on September 27, 1984, saying her victims had been literally tortured to death, UPI reported. A final claim that drug withdrawal had left her unable to assist at trial was rejected by a Fourth Circuit panel on November 1, 1984, and she chose not to take it to the US Supreme Court.

Barfield was pronounced dead at 2:15 a.m. on November 2, 1984, aged 52. According to UPI, she told warden Nathan Rice she was sorry for the pain caused to all the families. She donated tissue for transplant, and her corneas, some skin and bone tissue were recovered. She was buried near Parkton beside her first husband. Taylor's daughter, Alice Storms, publicly supported the governor's decision. Barfield's memoir, Woman on Death Row, appeared in 1985, and Jerry Bledsoe's book Death Sentence followed in 1998.

name: Walter Ellis

victims.suspected: 9 (Milwaukee police said in 2009 that his DNA matched evidence from nine women killed 1986 to 2007; a former homicide detective later cited at least five more unsolved cases in which he was a suspect)

victimProfile: Women aged 16 to 41 on Milwaukee's north side, most of them described by police as sex workers
captureMethod: A Milwaukee police cold case review found one DNA profile across seven unsolved homicides; a sample later obtained from Ellis, whose DNA was missing from the state database, matched semen from six victims and blood on a pepper spray can at the seventh scene.
sentence: Seven consecutive life sentences without parole (February 24, 2011)
fateDetail: Died at a Sioux Falls, South Dakota hospital on December 1, 2013, while serving his Wisconsin sentence in a South Dakota state prison under an interstate compact
summary: Convicted of seven murders; died in prison in 2013. Walter Ellis strangled women on Milwaukee's north side between 1986 and 2007, was identified through a 2009 DNA review of unsolved homicides, and pleaded no contest in 2011.
narrative: Walter Ellis, known in Milwaukee as the North Side Strangler, was convicted of killing seven women in Milwaukee, Wisconsin, between 1986 and 2007. He was identified in 2009 after a police cold case review found that one DNA profile linked a series of unsolved homicides. In February 2011 he pleaded no contest to five counts of first-degree intentional homicide and two counts of first-degree murder, and Milwaukee County Circuit Judge Dennis Cimpl sentenced him to seven consecutive life sentences without parole. Ellis died on December 1, 2013, at age 53, while serving his sentence in South Dakota.

The seven charged homicides spanned 21 years. According to Associated Press reporting carried by CBS News, the victims were Deborah Harris and Tanya Miller, killed in October 1986; Florence McCormick, found dead in April 1995; Sheila Farrior, killed in 1995; Joyce Mims, killed in June 1997; and Ouithreaun Stokes, killed in April 2007. The seventh, Irene Smith, was killed in November 1992, according to the Wikipedia article on the case. All seven were strangled, by hand or with a rope or clothing, and one was also stabbed. Police said most were sex workers, which some families disputed.

In May 2009 the Milwaukee Police Department's cold case unit announced that DNA testing had linked seven unsolved deaths to a single unidentified man whose profile was in no database. CBS News reported that the unit sifted through thousands of cases and tested the DNA of more than 100 people. Police Chief Edward Flynn said investigators focused on Ellis after his name surfaced in several of the killings. Ellis was arrested on September 5, 2009, after police obtained his DNA; according to Wikipedia, officers seized a toothbrush from his apartment when he failed to appear for a court-ordered DNA collection, and he was taken into custody at a motel in Franklin, a Milwaukee suburb.

The Associated Press reported that his DNA matched semen from six victims and blood on a pepper spray can at the seventh scene. On September 10, 2009, District Attorney John Chisholm brought the charges to seven counts, and bond was set at one million dollars. Police said Ellis's DNA had in fact been matched to evidence from nine women, aged 16 to 41, though only seven deaths were charged.

The investigation exposed a failure in Wisconsin's DNA database. The Department of Corrections said it had taken a sample from Ellis in prison in 2001, but the state Justice Department said its crime laboratory never received it; authorities later said Ellis had persuaded a fellow inmate to submit a sample in his place. Chief Flynn said an earlier profile might have prevented at least one death, and the case prompted a full review of the state database.

Ellis first pleaded not guilty. On February 18, 2011, during a motion hearing, he unexpectedly entered no contest pleas, which carry a mandatory life sentence but do not admit guilt. Judge Cimpl, who could have allowed parole eligibility, declined and imposed seven consecutive life terms on February 24, 2011. The Wisconsin Supreme Court declined to hear his appeal in 2013, according to the Associated Press.

The DNA findings also unraveled two other convictions. FOX6 Milwaukee reported that Chaunte Ott and William Avery had each been convicted of a murder later linked to Ellis and were subsequently freed. According to Wikipedia, Ott served 14 years for the 1995 death of 16-year-old Jessica Payne before his 2009 release, and Avery was exonerated after Ellis's DNA was matched in 2010 to the 1998 killing of Maryetta Griffin. Ellis was never charged in either death.

Ellis was moved to South Dakota in June 2011 under an interstate compact and died in a Sioux Falls hospital on December 1, 2013, of what officials called natural causes; he never explained the killings. Born in Milwaukee on June 24, 1960, he left school after the eighth grade and, according to Wikipedia, built a record of robbery, theft, drug and assault offenses and served as a police informant in the 1990s.

name: Waneta Hoyt
victimProfile: Her own five biological children, aged between 48 days and 28 months, whose deaths were recorded at the time as sudden infant death syndrome
captureMethod: A prosecutor in Syracuse identified the family from a 1972 medical paper, and after a state police investigation she was questioned at the Owego barracks and confessed, a statement she later recanted
sentence: 75 years to life (five consecutive terms of 15 years to life), imposed September 11, 1995
fateDetail: Bedford Hills Correctional Facility, New York; pancreatic cancer, August 1998, aged 52, while her appeal was pending
summary: Died in prison. Waneta Hoyt of Tioga County, New York, was convicted in 1995 of murdering her five children between 1965 and 1971, deaths long attributed to SIDS. She recanted her confession, was sentenced to 75 years to life and died in 1998.
narrative: Waneta Hoyt was a woman from Tioga County, New York, who was convicted in April 1995 of murdering her five biological children, who died between 1965 and 1971. For more than two decades their deaths were attributed to sudden infant death syndrome (SIDS), and two of the children became case studies in an influential medical paper. After confessing to police in March 1994 and then recanting, Hoyt was found guilty by a jury in Owego and sentenced in September 1995 to 75 years to life. She died of pancreatic cancer at Bedford Hills Correctional Facility in August 1998, aged 52, while her appeal was pending.

Hoyt was born Waneta Nixon in Richford, New York, in 1946 and married Tim Hoyt in 1964, according to the Wikipedia article. Between 1965 and 1971 she gave birth to Eric, James, Julie, Molly and Noah. Each died suddenly, at ages ranging from 48 days to 28 months, according to the forensic psychologist Charles Patrick Ewing, who later evaluated her for the defense. The Wikipedia article gives the deaths as January 1965 (Eric), September 1968 (James, aged about two years and four months, and Julie, aged about seven weeks), June 1970 (Molly) and July 1971 (Noah). Each was recorded at the time as a natural death. The couple later adopted a son, who was a teenager living with them when Hoyt was arrested.

Molly and Noah had been studied before their deaths by Dr. Alfred Steinschneider, a research pediatrician at the Upstate Medical Center in Syracuse. His 1972 article in the journal Pediatrics, which identified the children only by their initials, used their histories of prolonged apnea to argue that SIDS could be linked to apnea and could run in families. Ewing writes that the article was quickly challenged in letters to the journal, including one from the medical examiner Vincent DiMaio, who wrote that the deaths were most probably homicides. The paper nonetheless stayed in the medical literature for about twenty years, according to Discover magazine, and Ewing writes that it helped spur the wide use of home apnea monitors.

In 1986 Dr. Linda Norton, a Dallas forensic pathologist consulting on a case in Syracuse, told prosecutor William Fitzpatrick that she believed the mother in the paper had smothered her children, according to the Los Angeles Times. In 1992, by then Onondaga County district attorney, Fitzpatrick traced the family through hospital records. Because the children had died in Tioga County, he referred the case to District Attorney Robert Simpson, who directed the New York State Police to investigate. Pathologists consulted by investigators, including Dr. Michael Baden, concluded that the deaths were not consistent with natural disease, though none had been classified as homicide at the time.

On March 23, 1994, a local officer she knew approached Hoyt near the post office and introduced her to a state police investigator, who said she was gathering information about SIDS. Hoyt was taken to the state police barracks in Owego, given Miranda warnings and questioned for several hours. By late afternoon she had signed a statement saying she had caused the deaths of all five children, and she told police she could not stand their crying, according to the Los Angeles Times. She was arrested that day and charged with ten counts of second-degree murder, according to the Gale reference Great American Trials. Soon afterward she recanted, saying the police had tricked and pressured her into agreeing with their account.

Her trial ran from March 30 to April 21, 1995, before Judge Vincent Sgueglia, with public defenders Robert Miller and Raymond Urbanski representing her. The admissibility and reliability of the confession were central issues. Ewing testified that she had dependent and avoidant personality disorders and that her statement was not made knowingly or voluntarily. Steinschneider testified for the defense and, under cross-examination, conceded that for all he knew the children could have been suffocated. Hoyt testified and denied killing her children. The jury convicted her on five counts of murder; the Wikipedia article describes all five as second-degree murder, while the Deseret News reported one count of first-degree and four of second-degree murder. On September 11, 1995, she received consecutive terms of 15 years to life for each child, 75 years to life in total.

Hoyt's lawyers sought her release while her appeal was pending, but New York did not permit medical parole for prisoners convicted of murder, the Deseret News reported. She died in August 1998. The Wikipedia article states that because she died before her appeal was decided, she was formally exonerated under New York law. The case is frequently cited in discussions of how a single published study shaped thinking about SIDS for two decades.
