name: Wayne Nance
victimProfile: Mostly women and teenage girls, several of them runaways or acquaintances, plus a married couple in Ravalli County to whom he had delivered furniture
fateDetail: Shot by Doug Wells during a home invasion at the Wells home in Missoula, Montana; died September 4, 1986, aged 30
summary: Killed. Wayne Nance, a Missoula furniture delivery driver, was shot dead in 1986 by a man he attacked at home. Investigators suspect him of at least six killings in western Montana from 1974 to 1985; he was never charged.
narrative: Wayne Nance was a Missoula, Montana, furniture delivery driver whom law enforcement suspects of at least six killings in Missoula and Ravalli counties between 1974 and 1985. He was never charged, tried or convicted of any homicide. In the early hours of September 4, 1986, he broke into the Missoula home of Doug Wells and his wife and attacked them; Wells freed himself, took a rifle and shot Nance, who died aged 30. Every attribution below therefore rests on investigators' conclusions after his death, not on a court finding.

Nance was born on October 18, 1955, in Clinton, Montana, according to the Wikipedia article, which says teachers and classmates remembered him as academically gifted but eccentric, and that friends recalled him boasting about Satanism. The earliest killing linked to him is that of Donna Pounds, 39, who was shot in the basement of her home in April 1974. She was the mother of some of Nance's school friends. Popular Science reported in 2009 that retired Missoula County investigator Larry Weatherman had briefly suspected the then high-school student, but a grand jury found insufficient evidence to charge him; the Associated Press reported in 2021 that prosecutors were unable to obtain an indictment. The Wikipedia article says a later search of Nance's home turned up evidence linking him to the case.

The 1985 deaths of Mike and Teresa Shook in Ravalli County are among the cases most firmly tied to him. According to AP reporting, the couple were bound and killed in their home in December 1985 and the house was set on fire; their three children were rescued. Two items stolen from the house were later found at Nance's residence, and the Wikipedia article adds that he had delivered a couch to the couple a few days earlier and that a neighbor saw a pickup matching his.

Investigators also connected Nance to the remains of young women found in the woods east and south of Missoula. A teenager's skeleton found beside Deer Creek Road on December 24, 1984, and nicknamed Debbie Deer Creek, was identified through DNA in April 2006 as Marcella (Marci) Bachmann, 16, a runaway from Vancouver, Washington. The Oregonian reported that she had lived with Nance for several months under the name Robin and had been shot three times in the head. Popular Science described how strands of dyed hair and a photograph of the woman bar patrons knew as Robin tied her to him. The Missoula County Sheriff's Office describes Bachmann as a known Nance victim, according to CNN reporting.

Two other cases remain suspicions rather than established links. Devonna Nelson, 15, went missing in 1978; her remains were found near Missoula in 1980 and identified in 1985. The Wikipedia article says Nance had visited Seattle around the time she vanished but has not been definitively linked to her death. A woman found shot twice in the skull near Crystal Creek in September 1985, long known as Christy Crystal Creek, was identified in May 2021 through forensic genetic genealogy by Othram and the sheriff's cold case team as Janet Lee Lucas, 23, of Spokane, last seen in Sandpoint, Idaho, in summer 1983. Othram and the sheriff's office said Nance is suspected but the connection was still under review; Detective Captain Dave Conway called it a cold case homicide investigation.

The attack that ended Nance's life involved people he knew through work. AP reporting from 1986, summarized in 2021, said Nance entered the Wells home, knocked Doug Wells unconscious and had him tied up, then beat and stabbed him and went upstairs to his wife. Wells freed himself, loaded a rifle and shot Nance. Both spouses survived. The Wikipedia article says police then found photographs of the wife in Nance's possession, some taken along her jogging route.

Totals vary by source. The AP described Nance in 2021 as suspected in at least six killings, the figure also cited by the Billings Gazette, while the Oregonian in 2006 wrote that police had linked him to at least five deaths. Police reports quoted by CNN say the true number will never be known. Because he died before any charge was filed, none of these killings has been tested in court. His case is the subject of John Coston's book To Kill and Kill Again.

timeline.text: Wayne Nathan Nance born in Clinton, Montana.

A girl's skeleton, later identified as Nelson, is found near Interstate 90 outside Missoula.

A hunter finds the remains of a woman shot twice in the skull near Crystal Creek south of Missoula.

name: Wayne Williams
victimProfile: Two adult Black men, aged 21 and 27 or 28, recovered from the Chattahoochee River in 1981; authorities later attributed the deaths of 22 further Black children and young adults in Atlanta to him without trial
captureMethod: A police stakeout on the Jackson Parkway Bridge stopped his car after officers heard a splash in the Chattahoochee River on May 22, 1981; he was arrested a month later after Nathaniel Cater's body was found downstream
sentence: Two consecutive life terms for the murders of Jimmy Ray Payne and Nathaniel Cater (February 27, 1982)
fateDetail: Telfair State Prison, Georgia (as of 2019); denied parole in November 2019, next eligible November 2027 according to Wikipedia
summary: Serving life. Wayne Williams was convicted in 1982 of murdering two adult men in Atlanta. Police then closed 22 other Atlanta child murders cases as attributed to him without trial; he maintains his innocence, and the city reopened an evidence review in 2019.
narrative: Wayne Bertram Williams is an Atlanta man who was convicted in February 1982 of murdering two adult men, Jimmy Ray Payne and Nathaniel Cater, whose bodies were recovered from the Chattahoochee River in 1981. He was sentenced to two consecutive life terms and remains in Georgia state custody. After the verdict, Atlanta authorities closed most of the city's missing and murdered children cases of 1979 to 1981 and attributed them to him, although he was never charged in any of those deaths. Williams has maintained his innocence throughout, and in 2019 the City of Atlanta announced a renewed review of the evidence.

The killings that became known as the Atlanta child murders began, by most accounts, in the summer of 1979. According to an Atlanta Journal-Constitution chronology, the bodies of Edward Hope Smith, 14, and Alfred Evans, 13, were found on Niskey Lake Road on August 7, 1979, the first of a series of young Black victims killed over roughly 22 months. Parents formed the Committee to Stop Children's Murders in April 1980, Atlanta police set up a special task force in July 1980 that later grew to dozens of officers, and the FBI was ordered into the case in November 1980. Contemporary reports put the number of deaths under task force investigation at 28.

According to the Supreme Court of Georgia's 1983 opinion, a police surveillance team stationed at the Jackson Parkway Bridge over the Chattahoochee heard a loud splash at about 3 a.m. on May 22, 1981, and then saw a white Chevrolet station wagon crossing the bridge. Officers stopped the car and found Williams, then 22, driving. Two days later, on May 24, Cater's body was found in the river downstream. A friend testified that he had seen Cater with Williams outside the Rialto Theatre on the evening of May 21. Payne, 21, had been last seen at home on April 21, 1981, and his body was recovered from the river on April 27. Williams was arrested on June 21, 1981, and a Fulton County grand jury indicted him on July 17, 1981, on two counts of murder.

The trial in Fulton County Superior Court, before Judge Clarence Cooper, opened in January 1982. The prosecution relied heavily on fiber and hair comparisons: state experts testified that fibers recovered from both victims were consistent with carpets, a bedspread and a rug from Williams's home and car, and that animal hairs were consistent with his German Shepherd. To help show identity and method, the state was also permitted to introduce evidence of ten other alleged homicides from the series. On February 27, 1982, after about 11 hours of deliberation, the jury convicted Williams of both murders and he was immediately sentenced to two consecutive life terms. The court records give Cater's age as 28; United Press International reported it as 27.

Within days the task force began closing its files. UPI reported on March 2, 1982, that investigators had attributed 23 slayings to Williams and left seven cases open. The Journal-Constitution chronology states that the task force announced on March 1, 1982, that it would close 21 other cases and later closed one more, for a total of 22 linked to Williams. The Wikipedia article likewise says police attributed 22 further deaths to him, 18 of them minors. None of these attributions was tested in court.

The Supreme Court of Georgia affirmed the convictions on December 5, 1983, rejecting challenges to the fiber evidence and to defense access to crime laboratory material. In July 1998, the Georgia Attorney General's office announced that Butts County Superior Court Judge Hal Craig had denied Williams's habeas corpus petition in a 60-page order. Williams and his lawyers have argued over the years that the fiber evidence was unreliable and, according to the Wikipedia article, that authorities suppressed evidence pointing to Ku Klux Klan involvement; those bids for a new trial have been unsuccessful. DeKalb County police reopened several of the cases in May 2005, and later DNA and hair testing produced results that each side has cited.

On March 21, 2019, Mayor Keisha Lance Bottoms announced that the Atlanta Police Department, the Fulton County District Attorney's Office and the Georgia Bureau of Investigation would re-examine stored evidence with modern techniques, while cautioning that there might be nothing left to test. At that time Williams, then 60, was held at Telfair State Prison in southeast Georgia. According to the Wikipedia article, he was denied parole in November 2019 and is next eligible for consideration in November 2027. No public results from the renewed testing had been reported in the sources reviewed for this profile.

Jury convicts Williams of both murders; he is sentenced to two consecutive life terms.

Supreme Court of Georgia affirms the convictions.
Georgia Attorney General announces that a Butts County judge has denied Williams's habeas corpus petition.
DeKalb County police chief reopens several of the cases.
Mayor Keisha Lance Bottoms announces that stored evidence will be re-examined with modern testing.

name: West Mesa Bone Collector

victims.suspected: 11 women and an unborn child recovered; police say up to 8 more missing women may be linked

victimProfile: Women and teenage girls aged 15 to 32 who disappeared from Albuquerque between 2003 and 2005; police say ten of the eleven had ties to drugs or sex work
summary: Unidentified. The remains of 11 women and an unborn child were found buried on Albuquerque's West Mesa in February 2009; the women had disappeared between 2003 and 2005. No one has been charged, and the case remains open with the Albuquerque Police Department.
narrative: The West Mesa Bone Collector is the unidentified person believed responsible for the deaths of eleven women and teenage girls whose remains were found buried on the West Mesa, an undeveloped area on the west side of Albuquerque, New Mexico, in 2009. According to the Albuquerque Police Department's case page, the victims were last seen between 2003 and 2005; one, Michelle Valdez, was pregnant, and the remains of her unborn child were found with her. No one has been arrested or charged, police have named no official suspect, and the investigation remains open.

The discovery began on February 2, 2009, when, as the APD case page records, a woman walking her dog found a human bone on a trail near 118th Street SW and reported it to police. Wikipedia notes that grading for a housing development had exposed bones in an arroyo bank. The Associated Press reported that the excavation ran around the clock and that identifying the remains through DNA and dental records took nearly a year. According to the APD page, Syllannia Edwards was identified on November 13, 2009, Virginia Cloven and Evelyn Salazar on November 17, 2009, and Jamie Barela on January 26, 2010, completing the identification of all eleven.

The eleven identified victims were Jamie Barela, 15; Monica Candelaria, 22; Victoria Chavez, 26; Virginia Cloven, 24; Syllannia Edwards, 15; Cinnamon Elks, 32; Doreen Marquez, 24; Julie Nieto, 24; Veronica Romero, 28; Evelyn Salazar, 27; and Michelle Valdez, 22. The APD page states that ten of the women had ties to drugs and prostitution and that Barela, Salazar's cousin, had no known involvement. Edwards had been reported missing in 2003 from Lawton, Oklahoma. According to the Associated Press, many of the women knew one another and some were mothers.

The AP and Wikipedia both record that Detective Ida Lopez had noticed women with drug and prostitution arrests disappearing from Albuquerque's streets in the mid-2000s and compiled a list of the missing before the graves were found; every woman found on the mesa was on her list. Other women on the list remain unaccounted for: KUNM reported in 2019 that six were still missing and that police believed the same person was responsible; the AP in 2022 and KOB in 2025 put the number at eight. Searches of the mesa in 2018 and 2021 found no further victims.

The APD runs the investigation through its 118th Street Task Force and, with the FBI and the victims' families, offers a reward of up to $100,000 for information leading to an arrest and conviction. In August 2010 police searched properties in Joplin, Missouri, belonging to a photographer and seized thousands of photographs; Wikipedia records that police later said he had been cleared. In December 2010 police released photographs of unidentified women found during the investigation; several were identified as alive. KUNM reported in February 2019 that Lt. Scott Norris, head of APD's violent crimes section, called it "an active case," with three detectives assigned and more than 1,000 tips a year.

Two men have been widely discussed in connection with the case, though neither was ever charged in it. KSFR, drawing on Albuquerque Journal reporting, named them in 2022 as Lorenzo Montoya, who was shot and killed in December 2006 by the boyfriend of a 19-year-old woman he had strangled at his trailer, and Joseph Blea, who is serving a 90-year sentence imposed in 2015 for sexual assaults unrelated to West Mesa. The AP reported in February 2022 that Liz Thomson, a retired APD homicide sergeant rehired as a contract cold-case investigator, said the number of suspects was "more than the two [people] that are commonly out there," and that detectives were auditing nearly 1,200 tips and had interviewed about 200 women. The Paper (abq.news) reported in 2021 that police had never publicly linked either man to the killings.

The city dedicated a one-acre Women's Memorial Park at the site on June 27, 2020. In February 2025, KOB reported that APD had received nearly 1,500 tips since 2009 and that Lopez, now a cold-case investigator, said detectives had "persons of interest that we're looking into" but no single lead suspect. As of 2026 the case remains unsolved.

Syllannia Edwards, 15, reported missing from Lawton, Oklahoma in 2003, is identified from a sketch and dental records.
Virginia Cloven and Evelyn Salazar are identified through DNA.
Jamie Barela, 15, is identified, completing the identification of all eleven victims.
Police search properties in Joplin, Missouri, belonging to a photographer and seize thousands of photos; he is later cleared.
Police release photographs of unidentified women found during the investigation; several are later identified as alive.
Bones found near the burial site are determined to be ancient and unrelated.
APD Lt. Scott Norris calls it an active case with three detectives assigned and more than 1,000 tips a year.
The city opens the Women's Memorial Park at the burial site.
At the 13th anniversary, APD says nearly 1,200 tips are being audited and that the suspect pool is larger than the two men commonly named publicly; reward of up to $100,000 reiterated.
APD says it has received nearly 1,500 tips since 2009 and still has persons of interest; eight women linked to the case remain missing.

name: Westley Allan Dodd
victimProfile: Young boys aged 4 to 11, two of them brothers riding bicycles in a Vancouver park and one taken from a Portland school playground
captureMethod: After a failed attempt to abduct a 6-year-old boy from a movie theater in Camas, Washington, he was chased by the boy's mother's boyfriend, who held him for police when his car broke down
sentence: Death, imposed by a Clark County jury on July 14, 1990, for the aggravated first-degree murders of Cole Neer, Billy Neer and Lee Iseli; plus a 50-year determinate sentence for attempted first-degree murder
fateDetail: Hanged at the Washington State Penitentiary, Walla Walla, at 12:05 a.m. on January 5, 1993, after waiving his appeals; pronounced dead at 12:09 a.m.
summary: Executed. Westley Allan Dodd pleaded guilty to murdering three boys in the Vancouver, Washington area in 1989. A jury sentenced him to death in 1990; he waived his appeals and was hanged at Walla Walla on January 5, 1993.
narrative: Westley Allan Dodd was an American serial killer who murdered three young boys in and around Vancouver, Washington, in the autumn of 1989. Arrested in November 1989 after a failed abduction at a movie theater in Camas, he confessed to all three killings, pleaded guilty in June 1990 and was sentenced to death by a Clark County jury on July 14, 1990. He refused to appeal, chose hanging over lethal injection, and was hanged at the Washington State Penitentiary in Walla Walla on January 5, 1993, at the age of 31.

Dodd was born on July 3, 1961, in Toppenish, Washington, and grew up mostly in Eastern Washington, attending schools in Richland. The Seattle Times, in a profile published two days before his execution, traced a long record of offenses against children that began in his teens and continued through a Navy enlistment that ended in discharge. In 1983 he pleaded guilty in Idaho to an offense against a minor and served a reduced jail term, and in 1987 he was charged in Seattle with attempted kidnapping after trying to lure a young boy into a building; he was convicted of a lesser gross misdemeanor and served 118 days. UPI reported at the time of his arrest that he had completed a sexual deviancy treatment program in Washington.

On September 4, 1989, the bodies of two brothers, Cole Neer, 11, and William, known as Billy, 10, were found in David Douglas Park in Vancouver, where they had been riding their bicycles. Both had been stabbed. On October 29, 1989, four-year-old Lee Iseli was taken from a school playground in Portland, Oregon, around midday. He was killed the next morning in Vancouver, and his body was found near Vancouver Lake; the Washington Supreme Court opinion gives the date of discovery as November 1, while UPI reported it as October 31. A two-state police task force that included the FBI worked the killings, and a $10,000 reward was offered, but UPI reported that Dodd had not been among the roughly 50 people investigators were examining.

The case was solved on November 13, 1989. Dodd tried to take a six-year-old boy from the restroom of the New Liberty Theatre in Camas. The boy broke free, theater staff raised the alarm, and William Graves of Washougal, the boyfriend of the boy's mother, followed Dodd's car. When the car broke down nearby, Graves held Dodd until police arrived. According to the Washington Supreme Court, detectives interviewed him from late that night into the early hours of November 14; he first denied any knowledge of the murders, then admitted the attempted abduction and the three killings, and repeated the account in a taped interview. A search of his Vancouver home turned up a diary and other evidence, according to the Wikipedia article.

Prosecutors charged Dodd with three counts of aggravated first-degree murder, attempted first-degree murder and first-degree kidnapping. He initially pleaded not guilty, but changed his pleas to guilty in June 1990 after adverse rulings on evidence. At the penalty phase in Clark County Superior Court he testified and asked for death, according to the Wikipedia article, and on July 14, 1990, the jury returned death sentences for the murders of the Neer brothers and Lee Iseli. He also received a 50-year sentence for the attempted murder. Washington law at the time allowed a condemned prisoner to choose between lethal injection and hanging, and Dodd chose hanging.

Dodd declined to appeal. After a June 1991 hearing, the trial court found him competent and his waiver knowing and voluntary. On October 8, 1992, the Washington Supreme Court held in State v. Dodd that a defendant may waive general appeal but not the mandatory statutory review of a death sentence; conducting that review, it found the sentence supported by the evidence and not disproportionate, and affirmed. Civil liberties groups, including the American Civil Liberties Union, argued that hanging was cruel, but their challenges did not stop the execution. On November 30, 1992, Judge Robert Harris reaffirmed Dodd's competence and signed a death warrant setting the date for January 5, 1993.

Dodd was hanged shortly after midnight on January 5, 1993, and pronounced dead at 12:09 a.m. Clair Neer, the father of Cole and Billy, and Jewell Cornell, Lee Iseli's mother, were among the witnesses. The Seattle Times reported that it was the first execution in Washington since 1963 and the first legal hanging anywhere in the United States since 1965. According to the Wikipedia article, his case was later cited in the debate that led Washington to authorize civil commitment of people found to be sexually violent predators.

name: William Bonin

victims.suspected: 22 to 36; police initially linked him to about 40 killings

victimProfile: Boys and young men aged 12 to 19, most of them hitchhikers picked up along Southern California freeways
captureMethod: Arrested on June 11, 1980, after Los Angeles police surveillance officers, acting on a tip from an acquaintance, followed his van and found him assaulting a teenage hitchhiker.
sentence: Death, 10 counts (Los Angeles County, March 12, 1982); death, 4 counts (Orange County, August 26, 1983)
fateDetail: Lethal injection at San Quentin State Prison on February 23, 1996; the first lethal injection carried out in California
summary: Executed in 1996. William Bonin, the Freeway Killer, was convicted by juries in Los Angeles and Orange counties of murdering 14 boys and young men along Southern California freeways in 1979 and 1980; he confessed to 21.
narrative: William George Bonin, known as the Freeway Killer, was convicted of murdering 14 boys and young men in Southern California between August 1979 and June 1980. A Los Angeles County jury convicted him of 10 murders in January 1982 and an Orange County jury of four more in August 1983; he was sentenced to death in both cases. According to the California Department of Corrections and Rehabilitation (CDCR), he was executed by lethal injection at San Quentin State Prison on February 23, 1996, the first California inmate put to death by that method. He had confessed to 21 killings to a television reporter, and investigators initially linked him to as many as 40 deaths.

The Ninth Circuit Court of Appeals summarised the pattern in its 1995 opinion: Bonin picked up boys aged roughly 12 to 19, usually hitchhikers, sexually assaulted them inside his van, killed them, generally by strangulation, and left the bodies beside freeways. The victims of which he was convicted were Markus Grabs, Donald Hyden, David Murillo, Charles Miranda, James Macabe, Ronald Gatlin, Harry Turner, Steven Wood, Darin Kendrick and Steven Wells in Los Angeles County, and Dennis Frank Fox, Glenn Barker, Russell Rugh and Lawrence Sharp in Orange County. CDCR dates the first of these killings, of Grabs, to August 5, 1979, and the last, of Wells, to June 2, 1980.

Bonin did not always act alone. Vernon Butts, suspected in several of the killings, died by suicide in jail in January 1981 before trial. Gregory Miley and James Munro, both about 19 at the time, pleaded guilty to their roles in individual murders and testified against Bonin; the California Supreme Court's 1988 opinion recounts Miley's testimony about the killing of Charles Miranda and Munro's about the killing of Steven Wells. A fourth man, William Pugh, pleaded guilty to voluntary manslaughter and also testified.

According to the Wikipedia account, information Pugh gave to a counsellor pointed Los Angeles police to Bonin, a paroled sex offender. Officers placed him under surveillance and, on June 11, 1980, followed his van to a service station near the Hollywood Freeway, where they found him assaulting a teenage hitchhiker who survived. He was arrested at the scene. He later spoke with KNXT reporter David Lopez, who testified at both trials that Bonin admitted the killings; the California Supreme Court noted Lopez described admissions to 14 killings beyond the six at issue in Orange County.

The Los Angeles County trial began in November 1981. The Ninth Circuit noted that Bonin had been charged with 14 murders there; two counts were dismissed before trial and the jury acquitted him of two more. On January 6, 1982, the jury convicted him of 10 murders and 10 robberies, and Judge William Keene imposed death sentences on March 12, 1982. The Orange County trial opened in Santa Ana on June 14, 1983. United Press International reported that on August 2, 1983, after three days of deliberation, the jury found him guilty of the murders of Fox, Barker, Rugh and Sharp; CDCR records four further death sentences on August 26, 1983.

The California Supreme Court affirmed the Orange County judgment on August 29, 1988 (People v. Bonin, 46 Cal.3d 659), vacating three duplicate multiple-murder special-circumstance findings but leaving the death sentences intact, and affirmed the Los Angeles judgment on January 9, 1989. In federal court Bonin argued that his trial lawyer, William Charvet, had been compromised by a literary-rights deal and had failed to present evidence of childhood abuse and brain damage. On June 28, 1995, the Ninth Circuit rejected those claims (Bonin v. Calderon, 59 F.3d 815). Governor Pete Wilson denied clemency days before the execution. CDCR records that Bonin was pronounced dead at 12:13 a.m. on February 23, 1996.

Bonin was born on January 8, 1947, in Willimantic, Connecticut, and served in the U.S. Air Force in Vietnam before an honourable discharge in 1968. CDCR lists kidnapping and sex-offence charges from November 1968, which led to commitment to Atascadero State Hospital and then state prison, and a 1975 conviction for sexually assaulting a 14-year-old boy, for which he received one to 15 years. He was paroled in October 1978.

name: Zodiac Killer

victims.suspected: 5 confirmed killed and 2 survivors; 37 claimed in a 1974 letter

victimProfile: Young couples parked at night in remote spots and a San Francisco cab driver, aged 16 to 29
summary: Unidentified. The Zodiac Killer attacked seven people in Northern California between December 1968 and October 1969, killing five, and taunted police and newspapers with letters and ciphers. The case remains open with the SFPD, Vallejo police and the FBI.
narrative: The Zodiac Killer is the unidentified person responsible for a series of attacks in the San Francisco Bay Area between December 1968 and October 1969. Five people were killed and two survived in four attacks in Benicia, Vallejo, Napa County and San Francisco. The attacker wrote to Bay Area newspapers under the name Zodiac, enclosed coded messages, and in a January 1974 letter to the San Francisco Chronicle claimed 37 victims. No one has ever been charged. The FBI's San Francisco field office said in December 2020 that the case remains an ongoing investigation, and the Wikipedia article records that the City of Vallejo and the Napa and Solano county sheriffs also list it as open.

The first confirmed attack came on December 20, 1968, when David Faraday, 17, and Betty Lou Jensen, 16, were shot with a .22-caliber pistol beside Lake Herman Road near Benicia. Shortly after midnight on July 5, 1969, Darlene Ferrin, 22, and Michael Mageau, 19, were shot in a parked car at Blue Rock Springs Park in Vallejo; Ferrin died and Mageau survived. According to the Wikipedia article, a man then telephoned Vallejo police to report the shooting and claim the Lake Herman Road murders.

On August 1, 1969, three letters arrived at the Vallejo Times-Herald, the San Francisco Chronicle and the San Francisco Examiner, each carrying a third of a 408-character cipher. A Salinas couple, Donald and Bettye Harden, solved it within days; it contained no name. On September 27, 1969, a hooded man stabbed Bryan Hartnell, 20, and Cecelia Shepard, 22, at Lake Berryessa in Napa County. Hartnell survived and Shepard died two days later. On October 11, 1969, cab driver Paul Stine, 29, was shot in Presidio Heights, San Francisco, the last killing conclusively linked to the series. A letter to the Chronicle afterward enclosed a piece of Stine's shirt, and a 340-character cipher followed on November 8, 1969.

Inspectors Bill Armstrong and Dave Toschi led the San Francisco investigation, while Vallejo police and the Napa and Solano county sheriffs handled the other attacks. Letters claiming to be from Zodiac continued into 1974, including the Chronicle letter of January 29, 1974 that ends "Me - 37, SFPD - 0," as transcribed on Wikisource. Police never confirmed any killings beyond the five.

The only person publicly named by police was Arthur Leigh Allen, a former schoolteacher from Vallejo. A Vallejo police captain named him as that department's suspect, according to a CNN interview with San Francisco inspector Kelly Carroll in October 2002. Vallejo police interviewed Allen in 1971 and served a search warrant on his home in February 1991, according to the Wikipedia article on Allen. He denied involvement, was never charged, and died on August 26, 1992. In October 2002, ABC News reported that SFPD crime lab supervisor Cydne Holt had recovered a partial DNA profile from a stamp on the envelope of the November 8, 1969 card, and that Allen's DNA did not match. Carroll told CNN the result "effectively clears him." The partial profile was too limited to identify anyone.

The San Francisco Police Department marked the case inactive in April 2004 and reactivated it in March 2007. In 2018, Vallejo police attempted investigative genetic genealogy on letter envelopes without definitive results, according to the Wikipedia article. On December 5, 2020, the 340 cipher was solved by David Oranchak of the United States, Sam Blake of Australia and Jarl Van Eycke of Belgium. The FBI confirmed the solution and said, as reported by KTVU and Global News, that the case "remains an ongoing investigation for the FBI San Francisco division and our local law enforcement partners." The decoded message, which begins "I hope you are having lots of fun in trying to catch me," does not name the writer. Two shorter ciphers from 1970 remain unsolved.

Because the Zodiac has never been identified, nothing is known of the person's background. Other cases have been linked to the series, including the 1966 murder of Cheri Jo Bates in Riverside and the 1970 abduction of Kathleen Johns near Patterson, but none has been confirmed by police. Several groups have announced identifications over the decades; none has been accepted by any investigating agency.
